In this study, an in-situ TiO(C) nanoparticles reinforced CoCrFeMnNi high entropy nanocomposite was fabricated through powder metallurgy routes. In this work, CoCrFeMnNi high entropy nanocomposite reinforced with in-situ nanoparticles was fabricated by powder metallurgy route. In this study, the CoCrFeMnNi high entropy nanocomposite was fabricated by powder metallurgy. Elemental powders of Co, Cr, Fe, Mn and Ni with equiatomic ratio were used as raw materials, FeTi alloy powder and stearic acid (C 18H 36O 2) were added to provide the sources of Ti, O and C. Powders with a nominal composition of CoCrFeMnNi, 4 at.% of Ti and 0.5 wt% of C 18H 36O 2were firstly mixed on a planetary ball mill (QM-3P4, Nanda Instrument Plant, China) at 200 rpm for 6 h to homogenize elemental powders, and then were milled at 400 rpm for a long duration of 66 h to achieve mechanical alloying. Subsequently, the milled powders were consolidated via die-pressing at 723 K and followed by hot extrusion (extrusion ratio of 9:1) at 1273 K. All the fabrication processes were performed under an Argon gas protection atmosphere to prevent oxidation.

Powders with a nominal composition of CoCrFeMnNi, 4 at.% of Ti and 0.5 wt% of C 18H 36O 2were firstly mixed on a planetary ball mill (QM-3P4, Nanda Instrument Plant, China) at 200 rpm for 6 h to homogenize elemental powders, and then were milled at 400 rpm for a long duration of 66 h to achieve mechanical alloying. Subsequently, the milled powders were consolidated via die-pressing at 723 K and followed by hot extrusion (extrusion ratio of 9:1) at 1273 K. All the fabrication processes were performed under an Argon gas protection atmosphere to prevent oxidation.

Following rolling, the samples were heat-treated at 1165 °C for 10 min to achieve a recrystallized FCC-type grain microstructure (abbreviated as HT alloy). Afterwards, the samples underwent further multi-pass rolling to achieve an 80 % reduction in thickness (from 5 mm to 1 mm), abbreviated as the CR alloy. The cold-rolled samples were then annealed in the FCC+L1 2two-phase region ( Fig. 1) at 760 and 800 °C for two hours and were designated as CR760 and CR800 alloys, respectively. All heat treatments were followed by quenching in water. The phase composition of the alloys was analyzed using a Bruker D8 DISCOVER A25 X-ray diffractometer (XRD). Tensile specimens with a dog-bone shape, featuring an 8 mm gauge length and a 2 × 1 mm² cross-sectional area, were prepared using EDM along the rolling direction of the material. The real-time strain of the tensile specimens was recorded using a Zwick Roell 1-15 HP laser extensometer with a tensile strain rate of 1 × 10 −3s−1. At least three samples were tested to ensure data reproducibility. Additionally, loading-unloading-reloading (LUR) cyclic tests were conducted on the tensile specimens to evaluate long-range residual stress and short-range effective stress during deformation. This approach enabled the characterization of hysteresis curves reflecting the alloy Bauschinger effect. The unloading strain increment was set at 2 %. The tensile specimens were initially loaded at a rate of 1 × 10 −3s−1to a specific strain, followed by unloading to 20 N at a rate of 2000 N/min, and then reloaded to initiate the next cycle. After electropolishing, a gold film was coated on the gauge section of the specimen surface using a vacuum sputter coater. The specimens were then placed in a vapour deposition apparatus and heated to 280 °C for approximately two hours. Tensile loading and unloading were conducted using a Kammrath & Weiss micro-test system equipped with a 5 kN load cell at a strain rate of 5 × 10 −4s−1. Upon reaching a defined strain, unloading was performed using the same strain rate, and the alloy deformation after unloading was recorded. Backscattered electron images at various deformation stages were captured after unloading with a resolution of 2048 × 2048 pixels (8 × 8 μm² field of view).

Different from the random distribution of elements in CM-HEA, the Mn segregation in LPBF-HEA was considered in our simulations.

The molecular dynamics (MD) simulations are employed to investigate the behavior of GBs in FeCoNiCrCu HEA and NiCu dilute alloy with precipitates and cracks. Two systems were established, one is FeCoCrNiCu HEA, and the other is NiCu dilute alloy, in the HEA model, the elements are mixed in equal proportion. Energy minimization was performed for all simulations using the standard conjugate gradient algorithm to ensure stable configurations of the GB, crack and precipitate. Following the minimization step, a relaxation process is performed with fully periodic boundary conditions in all directions. The system is subjected to an equilibrium step at 300 K and constant pressure of 0 bar in all directions for 500 ps, utilizing the NPT ensemble. The shear velocity is appropriately chosen to achieve a shear strain rate of 1 × 10 8s −1.

5Mn 30Co 10Cr 10C 0.5metastable interstitial high-entropy alloy (iHEA), developed by Li et al. [ 11] through precise modulation of its elemental composition. In this study, high-purity Fe, Mn, Co, Cr, and C (≥99.8 wt%) were utilized as raw materials. Initially, these materials were melted in a vacuum arc furnace to produce an ingot with a nominal composition of Fe 49. 5Mn 30Co 10Cr 10C 0.5(at.%), forming a metastable interstitial high-entropy alloy (iHEA). The ingot was hot-rolled at 900 °C with a thickness reduction of 50 %. Following this, it was homogenized at 1200 °C for 2 h in an argon-protected tube furnace. The alloy was then cold-rolled at room temperature with a 60 % thickness reduction. 5Mn 30Co 10Cr 10C 0.5iHEA specimens were annealed in the temperature range of 850 °C-1050 °C (with 100 °C intervals) for 3 min, producing the iHEAs with various grain sizes.

In this study, the ingots with a nominal composition of a chemically complex alloy consisting of Ni 45Co 21Fe 15Cr 10Al 4·5Ti 4.5(at. %) were arc-melted under a high-purity argon atmosphere with the elements Co, Cr, Ni, Al and Ti (>99.99% pure). The ingots were re-melted a minimum of five times. All button ingots were finally cast into a copper mold with a dimension of 10 × 10 × 100 mm 3. After homogenizing at 1323 K for 2 h and subsequent water quenching, the resultant ingots were cold-rolled in steps at 293 K along the longitudinal direction to a total thickness reduction of ∼85%. Ultimately, the as-rolled sheets were subjected to water quenching after being aged at 850 °C for 1 h and 550 °C for 36 h.

The (WTaNb) 50Hf 50high-entropy alloy was prepared by vacuum arc melting device with materials purity of 99.9 % in inert atmosphere. In order to ensure the uniformity of alloy composition, each ingot with a maximum of 200 g was subjected to 8-10 melting cycles. Calculation of phase diagrams (CALPHAD) approach was conducted by Pandat software with its thermodynamic phase diagram database. The as-cast alloy (referred to as AC alloy) ingots then underwent aging heat treatment at 1000 K for 4 h, followed by furnace cooling (referred to as Aged alloy).

A 50 mm × 35 mm × 7 mm rectangular ingot was subjected to a homogenization treatment at 1200 °C for 12 h. In this study, CrCoNi MEA was prepared via arc melting of pure Cr, Co and Ni metals (>99.9 wt%) in a copper crucible cooled by water under a low-pressure argon atmosphere. To ensure homogeneity of the elementary composition, the ingot was re-melted for five times. The as-cast ingot has dimensions of ϕ 40 mm × 20 mm. Then, the as-cast ingot was annealed at 800 °C for 24 h, and then cooled in air. The compressive tests were performed by a thermo-mechanical simulator (Gleeble-3180) using cylindrical specimens (Φ 8 mm × 12 mm). Samples were hot compressed at temperatures in the range of 700-1000 ℃ with strain rates of 0.001 s −1to 1 s −1. It is noted that specimens were heated up to the deformation temperature at a heating speed of 15 ℃/min and kept for 15 min before compression, in order to eliminate the thermal gradient of samples. After compression, the specimens were water quenched immediately to freeze the deformed microstructure.

Ingots of CoCrFeMnNi HEA were prepared by arc melting of elements with 99.9% purity in a Ti-gettered argon atmosphere. The ingots were arc-melted and flipped at least 5 times to ensure chemical homogeneity, and then drop casting into Cu molds with a size of 100 mm × 20 mm × 10 mm. The samples were sealed in a quartz tube and homogenized at 1473 K for 24 h followed water quenched and rolled. Room temperatures rolling were conducted on a rolling mill with 60 mm diameter rollers. For asymmetric rolling (ASR), the velocities top and bottom rollers were set as 4 m/s and 6 m/s (speed ratios of 1.5), respectively. The thickness of samples was finally reduced to 0.8 mm thick after 15 passes with a total rolling reduction of 92%. The subsequent annealing was conducted in both processed materials at 1073 K for 60 min to obtain fully recrystallized microstructure [ 8, 18, 20, 22, 31].

2Ni 39. 2Al 19. 6Ti 2was fabricated by arc-melting a mixture of constituent elements with a purity exceeding 99.99 ​wt% in a Ti-gettered and high-purity argon atmosphere. Following fabrication, the ingot was annealed at 1150 ​°C for 2 ​h and subsequently quenched in water to eliminate microsegregation. For these tests, cylindrical specimens with a height of 9 ​mm and a diameter of 6 ​mm were machined from the interior of a homogenized ingot, then the thermocouples were welded to the center of the specimen surfaces to monitor and control the temperature during testing. Unidirectional isothermal compression was performed using the Gleeble-3500 thermomechanical simulator. To minimize friction and prevent adhesion, tantalum foils were placed between the specimen and the indenter. The samples were initially heated to the predetermined temperature (950 ​°C, 1000 ​°C, 1050 ​°C, 1100 ​°C, respectively) with the heating rate of 10 ​K/min, then were isothermally held for 5 ​min to equalize the temperature. The compression processes were carried out at different strain rates of 1 s −1, 0.1 s −1, 0.01 s −1, 0.001 s −1respectively in transverse direction to a 50 ​% height reduction. The deformed samples were cooled down by water quenching to reserve the deformation microstructure.

The as-cast ingot with a nominal composition of CoCrFeMnNi is produced using a high-frequency vacuum induction melting furnace (SZRL-1700/10) with high-purity Co, Cr, Fe, Mn, and Ni elements with purities exceeding 99. Before the melting process, the furnace chamber is evacuated to a pressure of 10 −2Pa. Then the melting process is carried out under a protective argon atmosphere of 0. The forging process is conducted with the free forging method using a forging press machine (C86Y-125, 100 kN). In detail, the forging process is carried out in two steps. As illustrated in Fig. 1, the material is heated from room temperature (RT) to 1473K over 6 h and free forged with a 25% deformation rate, as shown in Fig. 1(b). Then the billet is forged to a dimension of ∅50mm×Lmmand cooled to RT. After the forging process, the rod is heated to 1273K for 16 h to achieve homogenization. Before EBSD analysis, the samples undergo a rigorous preparation process. Initially, mechanical polishing is employed using SiC papers up to 5000 grit to achieve a high surface finish. Subsequently, the samples are subjected to electropolishing at a temperature of 293K using a 10% etchant solution, which is a mixture of CH 3OH and HClO 4. The electropolishing procedure lasts approximately 20 s, effectively removing any surface imperfections and contaminants.

Master alloys with a nominal composition of Al0·1CrFeCoNi (Al2·4Cr24·4Fe24·4Co24·4Ni24.4, at.%) were prepared by arc-melting a mixture of pure constituent metals with a purity above 99.95% (wt.%) under a Ti-gettered high-purity argon atmosphere. The master ingots were flipped and remelted at least four times and then drop-cast into a water-cooled Cu mold to yield flats with a length of ~85 mm, a width of ~10 mm, and a thickness of ~2 mm. Cold-rolling along the longitudinal direction was performed stepwise (~0.02 mm per step) at a rolling speed of ~3.3 mm/s to reduce the thickness from ~2 mm to ~0.5 mm. The cold-rolled sheets were annealed for 1 h at 673, 873, 1,073, and 1273 K in air to investigate the effect of annealing temperature on the microstructure and deformation behavior.

Cold-rolling along the longitudinal direction was performed stepwise (~0.02 mm per step) at a rolling speed of ~3.3 mm/s to reduce the thickness from ~2 mm to ~0.5 mm. The cold-rolled sheets were annealed for 1 h at 673, 873, 1,073, and 1273 K in air to investigate the effect of annealing temperature on the microstructure and deformation behavior.

In a metastable Fe50Mn30Co10Cr10 high entropy alloy (HEA), a dual-heterogeneous structure, encompassing both grain size and dislocation heterogeneity, has been constructed to obtain excellent cryogenic mechanical performance by varying the annealing temperature (630 and 740 °C) following severe deformation. Thee ingots of HEA alloy, with a chemical composition of Fe 50Mn 30Co 10Cr 10(at. %), were melted and cast into 20 kg round billets. These billets were heated to 1200 °C for 90 min in an argon atmosphere for homogenization, and then hot rolled at 900 °C to 20 mm plates. Firstly, the plates were cold rolled asymmetrically with a reduction ratio of 75 % to 5 mm and a speed ratio of 1.3 through multiple rolling passes. Secondly, the cold-rolled plates were annealed at 630 °C and 740 °C for 10 min, followed by water quenching, which marked the HS-630 and HS-740 samples, respectively.

The FeNiCoCrMn HEA was produced by the magnetic levitation melting technique using pure metals with a purity greater than 99.9 wt%, to ensure the anticipated elemental homogeneity [13,35]. The as-cast rectangle ingots were hot-rolled to 4 mm, solution-treated at 1050 °C and 1200 °C for 1 h, and then water-quenched to room temperature (25 °C). Next, the bulk alloy was subjected to 60 % cold rolling after the removal of the surface oxide layer. To obtain a recrystallized structure with a suitable grain size, the sheets were annealed at 900 °C for 10 min and then water-cooled. The fabrication process of the non-equiatomic Fe 40Mn 40Cr 10Co 10ingot involves several steps. Initially, a mixture of pure metals with a purity exceeding 99.8 wt% was melted in a magnetic levitation melting furnace under the protection of a high-purity argon atmosphere. The molten metal was then solidified in a carbon steel mold. After solidification, the raw ingot was subjected to a solid solution treatment at 1100 °C for 2 h to homogenize the alloy composition. Following this, the ingot was hot-forged at 1000 °C, producing a rectangular ingot with a thickness of 25 mm. To further shape the material, the rectangular ingot was then hot-rolled at 900 °C, reducing its thickness to 4 mm, and subsequently air-cooled to room temperature. The sheets were then cold-rolled to a final thickness of 2 mm. To eliminate residual stress and achieve fully recrystallized equiaxed grains, the cold-rolled sheets underwent annealing at 900 °C for 30 min, followed by air cooling.

In this investigation, FeCrCoNi high entropy alloys doped with 0.5 at%, 1 at%, 2 at% C and 0.48 at% N, respectively, were prepared by arc melting followed by homogenization for 1 hr at 1100 °C. All ingots were remelted for 6 times with flipping between each melting for chemical homogeneity. 0.5 at% nitrogen doped FCCN ingot (abbreviated as FCCN05N) were made by remelting pure FCCN ingot prepared above under an atmosphere of N 2(purity: 99.999%) and Ar (purity: 99.995%) mixture with equal partial pressure while the total pressure was 0.8 bar in an arc-melter. All samples were homogenized in muffle furnace at 1100 ℃ for 1 hr before further tests and characterizations.

The CoCrFeMnNiC 0.5alloy (at.%, purity> 99.9 wt%) was prepared by arc melting of the elements Co, Cr, Fe, Mn, Ni in high-purity and low-pressure argon atmosphere inside a water-cooled copper crucible. Carbon was added in the form of Cr 3C 2block to avoid being blown away. To ensure the chemical homogeneity, the ingot was flipped over and re-melted for five times, and cooled naturally to room temperature. Homogenization annealing was carried out for 24 h at 1073 K, and then cooled by air. The compressive tests were performed on cylindrical specimens (ϕ8mm × 12 mm) using the thermo-mechanical simulator (Gleeble-3180) and the furnace chamber was evacuated to 10 −3torr before each test. Specimens were heated up to the deformation temperature with a fixed heating speed of 15 °C/min, and homogenized for 15 min before deformation to eliminate the thermal gradient of samples. After deformation, the specimens were water quenched immediately to preserve the deformation microstructure.

The solvent debinding process was operated by immersing the green body in N-Hexane, followed by thermal debinding and sintering in an Ar atmosphere, following the designed thermal schedule in Fig. 1c. After solvent debinding, the specimen was placed in a tube furnace (AJ-SKT3, AJEON) and heated to 250 °C at a rate of 1 °C/min, holding for 1 h, and then further heated to 450 °C at a rate of 1 °C/min, holding for 2 h to completely remove the binder. The sintering process involved heating to 1000 °C at a rate of 5 °C/min, then to 1275 °C at a rate of 2 °C/min at temporary air atmosphere, followed by a 3 h hold, optimizing the process based on a previous study [ 20]. During the sintering process, imperfect control of the Ar atmosphere induced oxygen dissolution around the pores of the specimen, leading to the formation of oxides with alloying elements. Despite the inert gas environment, residual oxygen within the sintering chamber or trapped in the pores can still diffuse into the alloy, reacting with Cr and Mn as the temperature increases and forming Cr 2O 3and MnO due to the high oxygen affinity of these elements [ 53].

An extrudable, pellet-shaped feedstock was prepared by mixing with gas-atomized CoCrFeMnNi HEA powders (MK Co.) with wax-based polymeric binders. The wax-based binders were composed of paraffin wax (PW, 40-50 wt%), ethylene-vinyl acetate (EVA, 20-40 wt%), polyethylene (LDPE, 15-30 wt%), and stearic acid (SA, 3-15 wt%). The optimized powder solid loading was determined to be 61 vol%, using a torque rheometer (HAAKE PolyLab QC, Thermo Scientific), based on the condition that the solid loading of the feedstock should be 2 to 5 vol% less than the critical value [ 31]. The MEX process was carried out using a 3D printer (D-MEX, Reprotech Co.), depositing layer by layer according to the sliced geometries ( Fig. 1a). The feedstock was fed into the hopper, where it was melted at a temperature of 100 °C. The melted feedstock was extruded from the nozzle, and the printer head moved to deposit the material according to the designed geometries, layer by layer. The printing strategy involved depositing two outline layers per printed layer and infilling patterns with zigzag rectilinear lines at a 45° angle, alternating the infill direction between the N thand N+1st layers. The green body manufactured through the MEX process underwent a debinding process to remove the binders, followed by a sintering process to directly form the final microstructure and eliminate internal pores. The solvent debinding process was operated by immersing the green body in N-Hexane, followed by thermal debinding and sintering in an Ar atmosphere, following the designed thermal schedule in Fig. 1c. After solvent debinding, the specimen was placed in a tube furnace (AJ-SKT3, AJEON) and heated to 250 °C at a rate of 1 °C/min, holding for 1 h, and then further heated to 450 °C at a rate of 1 °C/min, holding for 2 h to completely remove the binder. The sintering process involved heating to 1000 °C at a rate of 5 °C/min, then to 1275 °C at a rate of 2 °C/min at temporary air atmosphere, followed by a 3 h hold, optimizing the process based on a previous study [ 20]. The specimen with low porosity of ∼4% (P4) was heated to 1000 °C at a rate of 5 °C/min, then to 1275 °C at a rate of 2 °C/min, followed by the 3 h hold in Ar atmosphere, while the specimen with high porosity of ∼25% (P25) was heated to 1275 °C at a rate of 5 °C/min with same holding condition during sintering [ 32].

This cast material was initially homogenized briefly at high temperatures to eliminate any elemental segregation and to bring it to single-phase FCCbefore cold-rolling. In the first processing route, this strained material was first subjected to a solutionizing step of high temperature and long duration of 1 h to cause full recrystallization and growth of FCCgrains. The subsequent annealing step determined the nature, size, and distribution of the precipitate formation. In the second route of directly annealing the cold-worked material, the pre-strained grains sometimes simultaneously underwent partial recrystallization along with precipitation. The solutionized alloy, 50% cold-roll + 1150 °C/1 h, (CRSA) was single-phase FCCwith grains of ~ 150 µm. Subsequent annealing at 550 °C/150 h (CRSA-550) formed nanoscale L1 2precipitates. The as-cast ingots were then homogenized at 1200 °C for 3 hours, followed by water quenching. Subsequently, the homogenized samples were cold-rolled to achieve a thickness reduction of approximately 70%. Then, solid solution treatment at 1100 °C for 6 minutes and water quenching was carried out to obtain completely recrystallized microstructure. Subsequently, we carried out heat treatments with different aging time at 700 °C, and finally selected the 3h aging time process with excellent hardness and cryogenic tensile properties as the research object of this work. At the same time, the sample aging at 900 °C for 3h (expected to be some difference in grain and precipitate behavior) was introduced as the control group. Finally, two aging parameters,700 °C for 3 hours and 900 °C for 3 hours, were selected for comparative study, referred to as MEA-AT-700 and MEA-AT-900, respectively. The sample subjected to solid solution treatment only is referred to as MEA-SS.

Four equiatomic CoCrFeMnNi HEA ingots were cast using vacuum induction melting (MC100V, Indutherm, Germany) under an argon atmosphere with elements of 99.99% purity. The ingots were homogenized at 1100 ℃ under the argon atmosphere for 6 h followed by water quenching. The homogenized ingots of a 7-mm thickness were hot-rolled at 800, 825, 850, and 900 ℃ down to a thickness of 1.5 mm by a 78.6% thickness reduction ratio, followed by air quenching. After every two back-and-forth rolling passes, the rolled plate was reheated in a furnace for 5 min to retain the hot rolling temperature and to avoid redundant grain growth [31].

The studied Fe 49Mn 30Co 10Cr 10C alloy was produced by melting commercially pure metals and carbon (C) with a purity of 99.9 wt%, in a high-purity Ar atmosphere. The ingot was remelted seven times to guarantee compositional homogeneity. After casting, the alloy was homogenized at 1200 °C for 2 h, hot-rolled into plates at a final rolling temperature exceeding 950 °C, and then water-quenched. To introduce high-density ATBs, we applied the thermomechanical treatment combining nanostructuring with thermal annealing [ 31]. First, high-pressure torsion (HPT) processing was used to refine the grain size. Disks (16 mm in diameter and 2 mm in thickness), taken from the hot-rolled samples, were processed under an applied pressure of 6 GPa, at a rotation speed of 1 rpm, and for a total of 0.5 turn. Subsequently, the HPT-processed samples were annealed at 750 °C for 3 min.

In this study, the CoCrFeNi HEA samples were fabricated by powder metallurgy route. Co, Cr, Fe and Ni powders (purity >99.5 wt%, mean particle size <75 μm) were firstly mixed using a planetary ball mill (QM-3SP4, Nanda Instrument Plant, China) at 200 rpm for 6 h for powder homogenization, and then were milled at 300 rpm for 60 h for mechanical alloying. The mechanically-alloyed powders were compacted by hot pressing at 723 K and then were hot-extruded at 1273 K. The ball milling, hot pressing and hot extrusion were performed under an Argon protection atmosphere. For the pre-twinning treatment, the as-extruded sample was immersed in liquid nitrogen for 10 min and then was forged immediately with a 10% thickness reduction and finally annealed at 1073 K for 15 min to produce pre-twins. For comparison, a non-twinned counterpart was fabricated by annealing the as-extruded sample at 1423 K for 2 h.

2HEAs were prepared by vacuum arc-melting a mixture of pure metals (purity larger than 99.9 wt%) under a high-purity argon atmosphere and re-melted at least five times to ensure the chemical homogeneity. The master ingots were then drop-cast into a water-cooled copper mold with a dimension of 8×10×100mm3. The as-cast slabs were homogenized for 2 h at 1200 °C, water cooled, and then cold rolled with a thickness reduction of 80% to 1.6 mm. A two-step heat treatment was conducted as follows: the cold-rolled sheets were annealed at 1050 °C for 10 min to achieve a fully recrystallized microstructure (denoted as A0), and subsequently aged for 1 h and 5 h at 700 °C followed by water quenching (denoted as A1and A5, respectively).

The ingot was homogenized at 1,100 °C for 6 h in an argon atmosphere, followed by water quenching. To reduce the surface roughness and remove oxides, the homogenized ingot was mechanically milled before cold-rolling. The alloy was cold-rolled from an initial thickness of 7 mm down to 1.5 mm. The cold-rolled plate was annealed at 800 °C for 1 h in an argon atmosphere, and then water quenched. Tensile specimens were deformed at 77 K to true strains of 20% and 35% and then annealed at 500 °C, 550 °C, 600 °C, and 650 °C for 1 h in an argon atmosphere, followed by water quenching.

The single-phase FCC high-entropy alloy CoCrFeMnNi was fabricated using SLM technology, with a schematic diagram of the SLM process shown in Fig. 1(a). The HEA powders were fabricated using gas atomization, whose morphology feature is shown in Fig. 1(b). Before printing, the substrate is first preheated to 473 K to reduce the temperature gradient that may occur during the SLM process. A laser power of 275 W, scanning speed of 950 mm/s, layer thickness of 40 μm, and hatching space of 80 μm were employed as the optimal printing parameters to manufacture cuboid-type samples with dimensions of 70 mm × 40 mm × 18 mm. Specimens for compression tests were prepared by an electrical discharge machine (EDM) along the BD, SD, and TD ( Fig. 1 (e)). The mechanically ground specimens are then electrochemically polished in an electrolyte (90 % acetic acid & 10 % perchloric acid) with a voltage of 30 V and a polishing time of 30 s. After mechanical grinding, the samples are double-sprayed. The electrolyte is a mixture of 95 % ethanol and 5 % perchloric acid with a voltage of 20 V and a temperature of −28 °C.

The alloys were prepared through cold crucible induction melting using high-purity elements. Ingots with masses between 300 and 2500 g have been first cast. Subsequently, a portion of each ingot was remelted under a nitriding atmosphere with controlled pressure and time to promote nitrogen absorption in the liquid alloy. For each of optimised matrixes (M18, M21 and M25 alloys), one unique nitrogen containing alloy was produced with nitrogen content targeted to the values optimised for each (0.6, 0.5 and 0.4 wt% N respectively). In the present article, the new N-doped alloys are referred to by the name of their matrix followed by the N content. The complete chemical composition of all studied alloys can be found in Table 1. For Scanning Electron Microscope (SEM) observations and Energy-Dispersive X-ray spectroscopy (EDX) analyses, all the samples were ground with SiC papers down to 1200 grade. Final preparation was made by electropolishing (6 % HCl in ethanol, at 10-12 ∘C, at 25 V during 30 s). X-ray diffraction (XRD) measurements were made on bulk, just polished samples with a Bragg-Brentano diffractometer (X’Pert Pro MRD, PANalytical, Netherlands) using a Cu K αradiation with a step size of 0.08 ∘and a counting time of a few seconds per step. Transmission Electron Microscope (TEM) samples were prepared from discs of around 100 μm in thickness and 3 mm of diameter, twin-jet electropolished with a Struers TENUPOL-5. The electrolyte is composed of 10 % perchloric acid and 90 % ethanol cooled to − 4 ∘C while the voltage is set between 17 and 20 V. Observations were made on Philips CM200 microscope operating at 200 kV. Vickers hardness tests were performed on polished samples at a load of 10 kg (980 N). Each given value is the average value from at least ten measurements. Tensile tests were performed on threaded-head cylindrical specimens with a gauge length of 22 mm and a 4 mm diameter on an Instron 8861 testing system, with an initial strain rate of 10 −3s−1at room temperature. For each experimental point, two tests were performed. Conventional yield strength value (YS) was calculated as the stress corresponding to a plastic deformation of 0. 2 %. Strain-hardening rate (SHR) was calculated as the first derivative of true stress over true strain: SHR= dσt∕ dϵt. Ultimate tensile strength (UTS) and true ultimate tensile strength (true UTS) correspond to the maximum stress before necking of, respectively, the conventional stress-strain curve and true stress-strain curve. Fig. 5a to d show the microstructure of the M18, M25, M21N0.39 and M18N0.56 alloys in their reference state, e.gafter annealing. Fig. 5a to d show the microstructure of the M18, M25, M21N0.39 and M18N0.56 alloys in their reference state, e.gafter annealing. The results of mechanical characterization of studied alloys are presented in Fig. 7and Table 2. Fig. 7a and b show representative room temperature tensile tests curves for N-free alloys (Y3, M18, M21 and M25) and their N-doped counterparts, respectively. For N-free alloys, no effect of chemical composition on their mechanical characteristics is observed. A hardness of around 110 HV is measured for all 4 alloys (Y3, M18, M21 and M25 alloy). This trend is confirmed by tensile characteristics of the tested matrixes (Y3, M18, M21 and M25): a yield strength (YS) of approximately 200 MPa, an ultimate tensile strength (UTS) of 500 MPa, and an elongation at break exceeding 50 % are measured. The presence of N ( Fig. 7b) results, as expected, in a gradual enhancement of both the YS and UTS of the alloys without compromising their elongation at break. For instance, the M18N0.56 alloy exhibits a yield strength of 450 MPa and an UTS approaching 900 MPa, while a high elongation at break of approximately 58 % is maintained. These values are respectively 125 % and 80 % higher than those measured in the N-free M18 alloy (see Table 2). Consequently, the addition of N proves to be highly advantageous for the tensile behavior of the alloys even at such relatively high concentration. The evolution of tensile properties with nitrogen content is further illustrated in Fig. 7c. Consistent with the hardness evolution, the yield strength increases linearly with N concentration (430 MPa/wt% N) irrespective of the matrix’s chemical composition. This aligns with bibliographic data reported for Cantor alloy [33], a Co 10Cr 10Fe 50Mn 30(at%) HEA [67], and certain stainless steels [20,22,23]. Ultimate strength also exhibits a linear correlation with nitrogen concentration, albeit with a steeper slope (730 MPa/wt% N), while uniform elongation remains constant. This behavior, observed in the Y3 alloy [35], is still noticeable even with the change in composition. The difference between YS and UTS slopes is attributed to the increased work-hardening in the presence of nitrogen. However, one has to note that such an effect is not universally observed in nitrogen-doped alloys. Notably, alloys such as Fe-Cr 17Mn 10Ni 5[20]and Fe-Cr 18Mn 10Ni 16[68]do not exhibit a discernible increase in work-hardening. Similarly, in concentrated alloys, Co 10Cr 10Fe 50Mn 30(at%) manifests no notable rise in work-hardening: both yield strength and maximum strength increase by approximately 420 MPa/wt% N [67]. The addition of nitrogen may change deformation mechanisms depending on the matrix or nitrogen concentration. This will be further discussed in the following section. Fig. 7d illustrates the variation in elongation at break as a function of nitrogen concentration in all studied alloys. Without distinguishing the chemical composition of the matrix, the uniform elongation remains nearly constant despite the substantial improvement in mechanical resistance (UTS) thanks to the enhanced work-hardening in the alloy. This observation is consistent with Considère’s criterion, stating that an increase in strain hardening postpones necking, the latter initiating when the strain-hardening rate matches the stress. Consequently, an increase in strain hardening postpones necking, thereby delaying material’s failure. The fracture surfaces post-tensile tests are not shown but it is pointed out that, irrespective of the nitrogen concentration or the chemical composition of the matrix, they exhibit typical characteristics of ductile fracture: presence of numerous dimples, often formed around defects such as MnS inclusions. Fig. 8illustrates the variation in strain-hardening rate, SHR, ( dσtrue∕ dϵtrue) throughout the tensile tests. Previous study [35]showed that in the case of nitrogen-free alloys ( Fig. 8a), the curves consistently display a gradual decline in work-hardening during deformation, while nitrogen-rich alloys present a strain-hardening plateau at approximately 2500 MPa, and its magnitude increases with increasing nitrogen concentration ( Fig. 8b). Changes of matrix did not result in any modification of this effect. Consequently, alloys with nitrogen exhibit a substantial increase in strain-hardening rates - up to 70 % - compared to nitrogen-free alloys, explaining their pronounced increase in UTS in the presence of nitrogen. It is commonly admitted that the addition of nitrogen leads to a marked change in the dislocation structure: slip becomes planar, resulting in the accumulation of dislocations at grain boundaries ( pile ups) [69-72]and thus participating in the increase of the SHR as higher stresses are required to overcome it [21,73]. The reason why dislocation slip becomes planar is not clear but could be interpreted as a decrease of the SFE as partial dislocations cannot cross-slip. However this phenomenon is also observed in alloys where nitrogen is supposed to increase the SFE, that’s why it is often claimed that it is due to the formation of a short range order (SRO) [74,75]. Yet, it is still to be experimentally demonstrated that nitrogen promotes an SRO phenomenon [76]. The improvement of SHR in presence of nitrogen could also be caused by the activation of twinning-induced plasticity (TWIP effect). The formation of twins creates obstacles for dislocations, thereby increasing strain-hardening. However, when deformation increases, the nucleation of new twins becomes increasingly difficult due to the reduction in domain size induced by existing twins. Consequently, there is a decline in strain-hardening as the material approaches rupture. To confirm the twinning hypothesis in nitrogen-concentrated alloys, microstructures after rupture were analysed using transmission electron microscopy (TEM) ( Fig. 9). The specimen was prepared in the transverse direction of the tensile specimen, in a region close to the fracture. Thus, the corresponding deformation is estimated to be a uniform elongation of around 40 %. Fig. 9presents the microstructure of nitrogen-free M25 and M18 alloys deformed to fracture. Overall, a well-defined arrangement of dislocations in the form of cells is evident ( Fig. 9a-c), indicating that deformation is primarily achieved through dislocation gliding. The impact of compositional changes on these critical temperatures was evaluated through Thermo-Calc calculations and several optimised alloys, meeting the selected criteria, were obtained. Prioritizing some criteria resulted in the selection of three alloys, each containing 20 wt% Cr and accepting 0.4-0.6 wt% N in solid solution. In comparison with Co-free alloys referenced in the available literature, these new alloys exhibit a high solubility of nitrogen, potentially providing a significant solid solution hardening. The selected alloys have been elaborated with success; especially, the satisfactory mastering of introduction of controlled amounts of nitrogen in the liquid alloys is to be noted. Fig. 7a and b show representative room temperature tensile tests curves for N-free alloys (Y3, M18, M21 and M25) and their N-doped counterparts, respectively. For N-free alloys, no effect of chemical composition on their mechanical characteristics is observed. A hardness of around 110 HV is measured for all 4 alloys (Y3, M18, M21 and M25 alloy). This trend is confirmed by tensile characteristics of the tested matrixes (Y3, M18, M21 and M25): a yield strength (YS) of approximately 200 MPa, an ultimate tensile strength (UTS) of 500 MPa, and an elongation at break exceeding 50 % are measured. The presence of N ( Fig. 7b) results, as expected, in a gradual enhancement of both the YS and UTS of the alloys without compromising their elongation at break. For instance, the M18N0.56 alloy exhibits a yield strength of 450 MPa and an UTS approaching 900 MPa, while a high elongation at break of approximately 58 % is maintained. These values are respectively 125 % and 80 % higher than those measured in the N-free M18 alloy (see Table 2). Consequently, the addition of N proves to be highly advantageous for the tensile behavior of the alloys even at such relatively high concentration. The evolution of tensile properties with nitrogen content is further illustrated in Fig. 7c. Consistent with the hardness evolution, the yield strength increases linearly with N concentration (430 MPa/wt% N) irrespective of the matrix’s chemical composition. This aligns with bibliographic data reported for Cantor alloy [33], a Co 10Cr 10Fe 50Mn 30(at%) HEA [67], and certain stainless steels [20,22,23]. Ultimate strength also exhibits a linear correlation with nitrogen concentration, albeit with a steeper slope (730 MPa/wt% N), while uniform elongation remains constant. This behavior, observed in the Y3 alloy [35], is still noticeable even with the change in composition. The difference between YS and UTS slopes is attributed to the increased work-hardening in the presence of nitrogen. However, one has to note that such an effect is not universally observed in nitrogen-doped alloys. Notably, alloys such as Fe-Cr 17Mn 10Ni 5[20]and Fe-Cr 18Mn 10Ni 16[68]do not exhibit a discernible increase in work-hardening. Similarly, in concentrated alloys, Co 10Cr 10Fe 50Mn 30(at%) manifests no notable rise in work-hardening: both yield strength and maximum strength increase by approximately 420 MPa/wt% N [67]. The addition of nitrogen may change deformation mechanisms depending on the matrix or nitrogen concentration. This will be further discussed in the following section. Fig. 7d illustrates the variation in elongation at break as a function of nitrogen concentration in all studied alloys. Without distinguishing the chemical composition of the matrix, the uniform elongation remains nearly constant despite the substantial improvement in mechanical resistance (UTS) thanks to the enhanced work-hardening in the alloy. This observation is consistent with Considère’s criterion, stating that an increase in strain hardening postpones necking, the latter initiating when the strain-hardening rate matches the stress. Consequently, an increase in strain hardening postpones necking, thereby delaying material’s failure. The fracture surfaces post-tensile tests are not shown but it is pointed out that, irrespective of the nitrogen concentration or the chemical composition of the matrix, they exhibit typical characteristics of ductile fracture: presence of numerous dimples, often formed around defects such as MnS inclusions. Fig. 8illustrates the variation in strain-hardening rate, SHR, ( dσtrue∕ dϵtrue) throughout the tensile tests. Previous study [35]showed that in the case of nitrogen-free alloys ( Fig. 8a), the curves consistently display a gradual decline in work-hardening during deformation, while nitrogen-rich alloys present a strain-hardening plateau at approximately 2500 MPa, and its magnitude increases with increasing nitrogen concentration ( Fig. 8b). Changes of matrix did not result in any modification of this effect. Consequently, alloys with nitrogen exhibit a substantial increase in strain-hardening rates - up to 70 % - compared to nitrogen-free alloys, explaining their pronounced increase in UTS in the presence of nitrogen. It is commonly admitted that the addition of nitrogen leads to a marked change in the dislocation structure: slip becomes planar, resulting in the accumulation of dislocations at grain boundaries ( pile ups) [69-72]and thus participating in the increase of the SHR as higher stresses are required to overcome it [21,73]. The reason why dislocation slip becomes planar is not clear but could be interpreted as a decrease of the SFE as partial dislocations cannot cross-slip. However this phenomenon is also observed in alloys where nitrogen is supposed to increase the SFE, that’s why it is often claimed that it is due to the formation of a short range order (SRO) [74,75]. Yet, it is still to be experimentally demonstrated that nitrogen promotes an SRO phenomenon [76]. The improvement of SHR in presence of nitrogen could also be caused by the activation of twinning-induced plasticity (TWIP effect). The formation of twins creates obstacles for dislocations, thereby increasing strain-hardening. However, when deformation increases, the nucleation of new twins becomes increasingly difficult due to the reduction in domain size induced by existing twins. Consequently, there is a decline in strain-hardening as the material approaches rupture. To confirm the twinning hypothesis in nitrogen-concentrated alloys, microstructures after rupture were analysed using transmission electron microscopy (TEM) ( Fig. 9). The specimen was prepared in the transverse direction of the tensile specimen, in a region close to the fracture. Thus, the corresponding deformation is estimated to be a uniform elongation of around 40 %. Fig. 9presents the microstructure of nitrogen-free M25 and M18 alloys deformed to fracture. Overall, a well-defined arrangement of dislocations in the form of cells is evident ( Fig. 9a-c), indicating that deformation is primarily achieved through dislocation gliding. This type of microstructure results from the clustering and fragmentation of grains into multiple cells, with local orientations varying from one cell to another [77]. While both alloy presents mainly similar deformed microstructure, occasional twins, approximately 20 nm thick, are observed in some grains in the M18 alloy ( Fig. 9d). Their thickness is comparable to that observed at the initiation of twinning in an alloy deformed at low temperature, typically ranging from 12 to 15 nm for the initial twins, which tend to grow and become more abundant as deformation progresses [12]. In the M18 alloy, the occurrence of twinning is sporadic, appearing in a few grains, likely those with favorable orientations. The relatively small thickness of these twins suggests that twinning activation occurs towards the very end of the tensile test, as observed in the Cantor alloy deformed at room temperature [12]and, therefore, does not significantly alter the mechanical behavior of this alloy compared to other nitrogen-free alloys. However, the presence of deformation twins in well-oriented grains of alloy M18 suggests that the twinning stress of this alloy was freshly surpassed at the end of the tensile test. The maximum true stress reached in the M18 alloy is around 710 MPa ( Table 2), which can be compared to the twinning stress observed on the Cantor alloy at room temperature (720 MPa) [12]. It can therefore be hypothesized that the critical twinning stress is similar to that of the Cantor alloy, and, as with this alloy, is only reached just before fracture, explaining why no twinning is observed at room temperature. The fact that no deformation twins were observed in the M25 alloy which reached a similar true stress at the end of its deformation might be explained by a slight difference in the critical twinning stress value. According to Zaddach et al., an increase in Cr or a decrease in Ni in a CoCrFeMnNi matrix may lead to a reduction in stacking fault energy (SFE) [78]. In addition, assuming that the critical stress for activating twinning is considered to be proportional to the SFE [79-81], then the M25 alloy presents a slightly higher critical twinning stress than the M18 alloy and, therefore, is not reached during deformation. This hypothesis needs however to be further investigated. Nevertheless, even with the observation of deformation twins in the M18 alloy, dislocation glide remains the predominant deformation mechanism in nitrogen-free alloys, elucidating the consistent decrease in the strain-hardening rate during tensile test. The post-deformation microstructures of nitrogen-containing alloys (M25N0.36 and M18N0. 56) ( Fig. 10) exhibit clear distinctions from those of nitrogen-free alloys. They predominantly feature intersecting mechanical twins ( Fig. 10a and b), with an approximate thickness of about 100 nm. While the influence of nitrogen on the SFE is a subject of debate, the presence of mechanical twins in the deformed nitrogen samples may indicate that nitrogen reduces the SFE in such alloys. Nitrogen influence on the SFE is believed to vary based on both the amount of nitrogen introduced in the matrix and the alloy composition [37,82]. For instance, the addition of nitrogen decreases the SFE in Fe-Cr 21Mn 9Ni 6steel [83]as well as in Cr-Ni steels [84]. Conversely, in Fe-Mn-Si alloys, nitrogen increases the SFE [85]. Furthermore, Gavriljuk et al.demonstrated that the effect of nitrogen can depend on its concentration [86]. For example, in Fe-Cr 18Mn 10Ni 16, the SFE initially increases and then decreases with rising nitrogen levels, while the opposite trend is observed in Fe-Cr 15Mn 17, where the SFE decreases initially and then increases at higher nitrogen concentrations. In concentrated alloys, the effect of nitrogen on SFE is unclear and must certainly be related to alloy composition as well. The addition of nitrogen to a CoCrNi alloy does not alter the deformation mechanisms, since twins are observed after deformation at room temperature in both the nitrogen-free alloy and the nitrogen-containing alloy [34]. On the other hand, the addition of nitrogen in the alloy Co 10Cr 10Fe 50Mn 30(at%) leads, like carbon, to a change from a TRIP mechanism to a TWIP mechanism [61]. Nitrogen would then increase the SFE in this alloy. In our case, it seems that adding nitrogen in CrFeMnNi concentrated alloys might decrease the SFE, however actual measurement of the SFE should be performed to fully validate this hypothesis. For instance, the M18N0.56 alloy exhibits a yield strength of 450 MPa and an UTS approaching 900 MPa, while a high elongation at break of approximately 58 % is maintained. These values are respectively 125 % and 80 % higher than those measured in the N-free M18 alloy (see Table 2). Consequently, the addition of N proves to be highly advantageous for the tensile behavior of the alloys even at such relatively high concentration. The evolution of tensile properties with nitrogen content is further illustrated in Fig. 7c. Consistent with the hardness evolution, the yield strength increases linearly with N concentration (430 MPa/wt% N) irrespective of the matrix’s chemical composition. This aligns with bibliographic data reported for Cantor alloy [33], a Co 10Cr 10Fe 50Mn 30(at%) HEA [67], and certain stainless steels [20,22,23]. Ultimate strength also exhibits a linear correlation with nitrogen concentration, albeit with a steeper slope (730 MPa/wt% N), while uniform elongation remains constant. Without distinguishing the chemical composition of the matrix, the uniform elongation remains nearly constant despite the substantial improvement in mechanical resistance (UTS) thanks to the enhanced work-hardening in the alloy. Previous study [35]showed that in the case of nitrogen-free alloys ( Fig. 8a), the curves consistently display a gradual decline in work-hardening during deformation, while nitrogen-rich alloys present a strain-hardening plateau at approximately 2500 MPa, and its magnitude increases with increasing nitrogen concentration ( Fig. 8b). Changes of matrix did not result in any modification of this effect. Consequently, alloys with nitrogen exhibit a substantial increase in strain-hardening rates - up to 70 % - compared to nitrogen-free alloys, explaining their pronounced increase in UTS in the presence of nitrogen. It is commonly admitted that the addition of nitrogen leads to a marked change in the dislocation structure: slip becomes planar, resulting in the accumulation of dislocations at grain boundaries ( pile ups) [69-72]and thus participating in the increase of the SHR as higher stresses are required to overcome it [21,73]. The reason why dislocation slip becomes planar is not clear but could be interpreted as a decrease of the SFE as partial dislocations cannot cross-slip. However this phenomenon is also observed in alloys where nitrogen is supposed to increase the SFE, that’s why it is often claimed that it is due to the formation of a short range order (SRO) [74,75]. Yet, it is still to be experimentally demonstrated that nitrogen promotes an SRO phenomenon [76]. The improvement of SHR in presence of nitrogen could also be caused by the activation of twinning-induced plasticity (TWIP effect). The formation of twins creates obstacles for dislocations, thereby increasing strain-hardening. However, when deformation increases, the nucleation of new twins becomes increasingly difficult due to the reduction in domain size induced by existing twins. Consequently, there is a decline in strain-hardening as the material approaches rupture. To confirm the twinning hypothesis in nitrogen-concentrated alloys, microstructures after rupture were analysed using transmission electron microscopy (TEM) ( Fig. 9). The specimen was prepared in the transverse direction of the tensile specimen, in a region close to the fracture. Thus, the corresponding deformation is estimated to be a uniform elongation of around 40 %. Fig. 9presents the microstructure of nitrogen-free M25 and M18 alloys deformed to fracture. Overall, a well-defined arrangement of dislocations in the form of cells is evident ( Fig. 9a-c), indicating that deformation is primarily achieved through dislocation gliding. This type of microstructure results from the clustering and fragmentation of grains into multiple cells, with local orientations varying from one cell to another [77]. While both alloy presents mainly similar deformed microstructure, occasional twins, approximately 20 nm thick, are observed in some grains in the M18 alloy ( Fig. 9d). Their thickness is comparable to that observed at the initiation of twinning in an alloy deformed at low temperature, typically ranging from 12 to 15 nm for the initial twins, which tend to grow and become more abundant as deformation progresses [12]. The maximum true stress reached in the M18 alloy is around 710 MPa ( Table 2), which can be compared to the twinning stress observed on the Cantor alloy at room temperature (720 MPa) [12]. It can therefore be hypothesized that the critical twinning stress is similar to that of the Cantor alloy, and, as with this alloy, is only reached just before fracture, explaining why no twinning is observed at room temperature. The fact that no deformation twins were observed in the M25 alloy which reached a similar true stress at the end of its deformation might be explained by a slight difference in the critical twinning stress value. This hypothesis needs however to be further investigated. Nitrogen influence on the SFE is believed to vary based on both the amount of nitrogen introduced in the matrix and the alloy composition [37,82]. For instance, the addition of nitrogen decreases the SFE in Fe-Cr 21Mn 9Ni 6steel [83]as well as in Cr-Ni steels [84]. Conversely, in Fe-Mn-Si alloys, nitrogen increases the SFE [85]. For example, in Fe-Cr 18Mn 10Ni 16, the SFE initially increases and then decreases with rising nitrogen levels, while the opposite trend is observed in Fe-Cr 15Mn 17, where the SFE decreases initially and then increases at higher nitrogen concentrations. For instance, the M18N0.56 alloy exhibits a yield strength of 450 MPa and an UTS approaching 900 MPa, while a high elongation at break of approximately 58 % is maintained. Consequently, the addition of N proves to be highly advantageous for the tensile behavior of the alloys even at such relatively high concentration. The evolution of tensile properties with nitrogen content is further illustrated in Fig. 7c. Consistent with the hardness evolution, the yield strength increases linearly with N concentration (430 MPa/wt% N) irrespective of the matrix’s chemical composition. This aligns with bibliographic data reported for Cantor alloy [33], a Co 10Cr 10Fe 50Mn 30(at%) HEA [67], and certain stainless steels [20,22,23]. Without distinguishing the chemical composition of the matrix, the uniform elongation remains nearly constant despite the substantial improvement in mechanical resistance (UTS) thanks to the enhanced work-hardening in the alloy. This observation is consistent with Considère’s criterion, stating that an increase in strain hardening postpones necking, the latter initiating when the strain-hardening rate matches the stress. Consequently, an increase in strain hardening postpones necking, thereby delaying material’s failure. Previous study [35]showed that in the case of nitrogen-free alloys ( Fig. 8a), the curves consistently display a gradual decline in work-hardening during deformation, while nitrogen-rich alloys present a strain-hardening plateau at approximately 2500 MPa, and its magnitude increases with increasing nitrogen concentration ( Fig. 8b). Changes of matrix did not result in any modification of this effect. Consequently, alloys with nitrogen exhibit a substantial increase in strain-hardening rates - up to 70 % - compared to nitrogen-free alloys, explaining their pronounced increase in UTS in the presence of nitrogen. It is commonly admitted that the addition of nitrogen leads to a marked change in the dislocation structure: slip becomes planar, resulting in the accumulation of dislocations at grain boundaries ( pile ups) [69-72]and thus participating in the increase of the SHR as higher stresses are required to overcome it [21,73]. The reason why dislocation slip becomes planar is not clear but could be interpreted as a decrease of the SFE as partial dislocations cannot cross-slip. However this phenomenon is also observed in alloys where nitrogen is supposed to increase the SFE, that’s why it is often claimed that it is due to the formation of a short range order (SRO) [74,75]. Yet, it is still to be experimentally demonstrated that nitrogen promotes an SRO phenomenon [76]. The improvement of SHR in presence of nitrogen could also be caused by the activation of twinning-induced plasticity (TWIP effect). The formation of twins creates obstacles for dislocations, thereby increasing strain-hardening. However, when deformation increases, the nucleation of new twins becomes increasingly difficult due to the reduction in domain size induced by existing twins. Consequently, there is a decline in strain-hardening as the material approaches rupture. To confirm the twinning hypothesis in nitrogen-concentrated alloys, microstructures after rupture were analysed using transmission electron microscopy (TEM) ( Fig. 9). The specimen was prepared in the transverse direction of the tensile specimen, in a region close to the fracture. This type of microstructure results from the clustering and fragmentation of grains into multiple cells, with local orientations varying from one cell to another [77]. Nitrogen influence on the SFE is believed to vary based on both the amount of nitrogen introduced in the matrix and the alloy composition [37,82]. For instance, the addition of nitrogen decreases the SFE in Fe-Cr 21Mn 9Ni 6steel [83]as well as in Cr-Ni steels [84]. Conversely, in Fe-Mn-Si alloys, nitrogen increases the SFE [85]. For example, in Fe-Cr 18Mn 10Ni 16, the SFE initially increases and then decreases with rising nitrogen levels, while the opposite trend is observed in Fe-Cr 15Mn 17, where the SFE decreases initially and then increases at higher nitrogen concentrations. Fig. 7a and b show representative room temperature tensile tests curves for N-free alloys (Y3, M18, M21 and M25) and their N-doped counterparts, respectively. For instance, the M18N0.56 alloy exhibits a yield strength of 450 MPa and an UTS approaching 900 MPa, while a high elongation at break of approximately 58 % is maintained. These values are respectively 125 % and 80 % higher than those measured in the N-free M18 alloy (see Table 2). Consequently, the addition of N proves to be highly advantageous for the tensile behavior of the alloys even at such relatively high concentration. The evolution of tensile properties with nitrogen content is further illustrated in Fig. 7c. Consistent with the hardness evolution, the yield strength increases linearly with N concentration (430 MPa/wt% N) irrespective of the matrix’s chemical composition. This aligns with bibliographic data reported for Cantor alloy [33], a Co 10Cr 10Fe 50Mn 30(at%) HEA [67], and certain stainless steels [20,22,23]. Ultimate strength also exhibits a linear correlation with nitrogen concentration, albeit with a steeper slope (730 MPa/wt% N), while uniform elongation remains constant. The addition of nitrogen may change deformation mechanisms depending on the matrix or nitrogen concentration. This will be further discussed in the following section. Fig. 7d illustrates the variation in elongation at break as a function of nitrogen concentration in all studied alloys. Without distinguishing the chemical composition of the matrix, the uniform elongation remains nearly constant despite the substantial improvement in mechanical resistance (UTS) thanks to the enhanced work-hardening in the alloy. This observation is consistent with Considère’s criterion, stating that an increase in strain hardening postpones necking, the latter initiating when the strain-hardening rate matches the stress. Consequently, an increase in strain hardening postpones necking, thereby delaying material’s failure. The fracture surfaces post-tensile tests are not shown but it is pointed out that, irrespective of the nitrogen concentration or the chemical composition of the matrix, they exhibit typical characteristics of ductile fracture: presence of numerous dimples, often formed around defects such as MnS inclusions. Fig. 8illustrates the variation in strain-hardening rate, SHR, ( dσtrue∕ dϵtrue) throughout the tensile tests. Previous study [35]showed that in the case of nitrogen-free alloys ( Fig. 8a), the curves consistently display a gradual decline in work-hardening during deformation, while nitrogen-rich alloys present a strain-hardening plateau at approximately 2500 MPa, and its magnitude increases with increasing nitrogen concentration ( Fig. 8b). Changes of matrix did not result in any modification of this effect. Consequently, alloys with nitrogen exhibit a substantial increase in strain-hardening rates - up to 70 % - compared to nitrogen-free alloys, explaining their pronounced increase in UTS in the presence of nitrogen. It is commonly admitted that the addition of nitrogen leads to a marked change in the dislocation structure: slip becomes planar, resulting in the accumulation of dislocations at grain boundaries ( pile ups) [69-72]and thus participating in the increase of the SHR as higher stresses are required to overcome it [21,73]. The reason why dislocation slip becomes planar is not clear but could be interpreted as a decrease of the SFE as partial dislocations cannot cross-slip. However this phenomenon is also observed in alloys where nitrogen is supposed to increase the SFE, that’s why it is often claimed that it is due to the formation of a short range order (SRO) [74,75]. Yet, it is still to be experimentally demonstrated that nitrogen promotes an SRO phenomenon [76]. The improvement of SHR in presence of nitrogen could also be caused by the activation of twinning-induced plasticity (TWIP effect). The formation of twins creates obstacles for dislocations, thereby increasing strain-hardening. However, when deformation increases, the nucleation of new twins becomes increasingly difficult due to the reduction in domain size induced by existing twins. Consequently, there is a decline in strain-hardening as the material approaches rupture. To confirm the twinning hypothesis in nitrogen-concentrated alloys, microstructures after rupture were analysed using transmission electron microscopy (TEM) ( Fig. 9). The specimen was prepared in the transverse direction of the tensile specimen, in a region close to the fracture. Thus, the corresponding deformation is estimated to be a uniform elongation of around 40 %. Fig. 9presents the microstructure of nitrogen-free M25 and M18 alloys deformed to fracture. Overall, a well-defined arrangement of dislocations in the form of cells is evident ( Fig. 9a-c), indicating that deformation is primarily achieved through dislocation gliding. This type of microstructure results from the clustering and fragmentation of grains into multiple cells, with local orientations varying from one cell to another [77]. While both alloy presents mainly similar deformed microstructure, occasional twins, approximately 20 nm thick, are observed in some grains in the M18 alloy ( Fig. 9d). Their thickness is comparable to that observed at the initiation of twinning in an alloy deformed at low temperature, typically ranging from 12 to 15 nm for the initial twins, which tend to grow and become more abundant as deformation progresses [12]. The maximum true stress reached in the M18 alloy is around 710 MPa ( Table 2), which can be compared to the twinning stress observed on the Cantor alloy at room temperature (720 MPa) [12]. It can therefore be hypothesized that the critical twinning stress is similar to that of the Cantor alloy, and, as with this alloy, is only reached just before fracture, explaining why no twinning is observed at room temperature. The fact that no deformation twins were observed in the M25 alloy which reached a similar true stress at the end of its deformation might be explained by a slight difference in the critical twinning stress value. This hypothesis needs however to be further investigated. They predominantly feature intersecting mechanical twins ( Fig. 10a and b), with an approximate thickness of about 100 nm. Nitrogen influence on the SFE is believed to vary based on both the amount of nitrogen introduced in the matrix and the alloy composition [37,82]. For instance, the addition of nitrogen decreases the SFE in Fe-Cr 21Mn 9Ni 6steel [83]as well as in Cr-Ni steels [84]. Conversely, in Fe-Mn-Si alloys, nitrogen increases the SFE [85]. Furthermore, Gavriljuk et al.demonstrated that the effect of nitrogen can depend on its concentration [86]. For example, in Fe-Cr 18Mn 10Ni 16, the SFE initially increases and then decreases with rising nitrogen levels, while the opposite trend is observed in Fe-Cr 15Mn 17, where the SFE decreases initially and then increases at higher nitrogen concentrations. Without distinguishing the chemical composition of the matrix, the uniform elongation remains nearly constant despite the substantial improvement in mechanical resistance (UTS) thanks to the enhanced work-hardening in the alloy. Consequently, an increase in strain hardening postpones necking, thereby delaying material’s failure. Previous study [35]showed that in the case of nitrogen-free alloys ( Fig. 8a), the curves consistently display a gradual decline in work-hardening during deformation, while nitrogen-rich alloys present a strain-hardening plateau at approximately 2500 MPa, and its magnitude increases with increasing nitrogen concentration ( Fig. 8b). It is commonly admitted that the addition of nitrogen leads to a marked change in the dislocation structure: slip becomes planar, resulting in the accumulation of dislocations at grain boundaries ( pile ups) [69-72]and thus participating in the increase of the SHR as higher stresses are required to overcome it [21,73]. The reason why dislocation slip becomes planar is not clear but could be interpreted as a decrease of the SFE as partial dislocations cannot cross-slip. However this phenomenon is also observed in alloys where nitrogen is supposed to increase the SFE, that’s why it is often claimed that it is due to the formation of a short range order (SRO) [74,75]. Yet, it is still to be experimentally demonstrated that nitrogen promotes an SRO phenomenon [76]. The improvement of SHR in presence of nitrogen could also be caused by the activation of twinning-induced plasticity (TWIP effect). The formation of twins creates obstacles for dislocations, thereby increasing strain-hardening. However, when deformation increases, the nucleation of new twins becomes increasingly difficult due to the reduction in domain size induced by existing twins. Consequently, there is a decline in strain-hardening as the material approaches rupture. To confirm the twinning hypothesis in nitrogen-concentrated alloys, microstructures after rupture were analysed using transmission electron microscopy (TEM) ( Fig. 9). The specimen was prepared in the transverse direction of the tensile specimen, in a region close to the fracture. Thus, the corresponding deformation is estimated to be a uniform elongation of around 40 %. Fig. 9presents the microstructure of nitrogen-free M25 and M18 alloys deformed to fracture. Overall, a well-defined arrangement of dislocations in the form of cells is evident ( Fig. 9a-c), indicating that deformation is primarily achieved through dislocation gliding. This type of microstructure results from the clustering and fragmentation of grains into multiple cells, with local orientations varying from one cell to another [77]. While both alloy presents mainly similar deformed microstructure, occasional twins, approximately 20 nm thick, are observed in some grains in the M18 alloy ( Fig. 9d). Their thickness is comparable to that observed at the initiation of twinning in an alloy deformed at low temperature, typically ranging from 12 to 15 nm for the initial twins, which tend to grow and become more abundant as deformation progresses [12]. The maximum true stress reached in the M18 alloy is around 710 MPa ( Table 2), which can be compared to the twinning stress observed on the Cantor alloy at room temperature (720 MPa) [12]. The alloys were prepared through cold crucible induction melting using high-purity elements. Ingots with masses between 300 and 2500 g have been first cast. Subsequently, a portion of each ingot was remelted under a nitriding atmosphere with controlled pressure and time to promote nitrogen absorption in the liquid alloy. For each of optimised matrixes (M18, M21 and M25 alloys), one unique nitrogen containing alloy was produced with nitrogen content targeted to the values optimised for each (0.6, 0.5 and 0.4 wt% N respectively). In the present article, the new N-doped alloys are referred to by the name of their matrix followed by the N content. The complete chemical composition of all studied alloys can be found in Table 1. For Scanning Electron Microscope (SEM) observations and Energy-Dispersive X-ray spectroscopy (EDX) analyses, all the samples were ground with SiC papers down to 1200 grade. Final preparation was made by electropolishing (6 % HCl in ethanol, at 10-12 ∘C, at 25 V during 30 s). X-ray diffraction (XRD) measurements were made on bulk, just polished samples with a Bragg-Brentano diffractometer (X’Pert Pro MRD, PANalytical, Netherlands) using a Cu K αradiation with a step size of 0.08 ∘and a counting time of a few seconds per step. Transmission Electron Microscope (TEM) samples were prepared from discs of around 100 μm in thickness and 3 mm of diameter, twin-jet electropolished with a Struers TENUPOL-5. The electrolyte is composed of 10 % perchloric acid and 90 % ethanol cooled to − 4 ∘C while the voltage is set between 17 and 20 V. Observations were made on Philips CM200 microscope operating at 200 kV. Vickers hardness tests were performed on polished samples at a load of 10 kg (980 N). Each given value is the average value from at least ten measurements. Tensile tests were performed on threaded-head cylindrical specimens with a gauge length of 22 mm and a 4 mm diameter on an Instron 8861 testing system, with an initial strain rate of 10 −3s−1at room temperature. For each experimental point, two tests were performed. Conventional yield strength value (YS) was calculated as the stress corresponding to a plastic deformation of 0. 2 %. Strain-hardening rate (SHR) was calculated as the first derivative of true stress over true strain: SHR= dσt∕ dϵt. Ultimate tensile strength (UTS) and true ultimate tensile strength (true UTS) correspond to the maximum stress before necking of, respectively, the conventional stress-strain curve and true stress-strain curve.
