The results of mechanical characterization of studied alloys are presented in Fig. 7and Table 2. Fig. 7a and b show representative room temperature tensile tests curves for N-free alloys (Y3, M18, M21 and M25) and their N-doped counterparts, respectively. For N-free alloys, no effect of chemical composition on their mechanical characteristics is observed. A hardness of around 110 HV is measured for all 4 alloys (Y3, M18, M21 and M25 alloy). This trend is confirmed by tensile characteristics of the tested matrixes (Y3, M18, M21 and M25): a yield strength (YS) of approximately 200 MPa, an ultimate tensile strength (UTS) of 500 MPa, and an elongation at break exceeding 50 % are measured. The presence of N ( Fig. 7b) results, as expected, in a gradual enhancement of both the YS and UTS of the alloys without compromising their elongation at break. For instance, the M18N0.56 alloy exhibits a yield strength of 450 MPa and an UTS approaching 900 MPa, while a high elongation at break of approximately 58 % is maintained. These values are respectively 125 % and 80 % higher than those measured in the N-free M18 alloy (see Table 2). Consequently, the addition of N proves to be highly advantageous for the tensile behavior of the alloys even at such relatively high concentration. The evolution of tensile properties with nitrogen content is further illustrated in Fig. 7c. Consistent with the hardness evolution, the yield strength increases linearly with N concentration (430 MPa/wt% N) irrespective of the matrix’s chemical composition. This aligns with bibliographic data reported for Cantor alloy [33], a Co 10Cr 10Fe 50Mn 30(at%) HEA [67], and certain stainless steels [20,22,23]. Ultimate strength also exhibits a linear correlation with nitrogen concentration, albeit with a steeper slope (730 MPa/wt% N), while uniform elongation remains constant. This behavior, observed in the Y3 alloy [35], is still noticeable even with the change in composition. The difference between YS and UTS slopes is attributed to the increased work-hardening in the presence of nitrogen. However, one has to note that such an effect is not universally observed in nitrogen-doped alloys. Notably, alloys such as Fe-Cr 17Mn 10Ni 5[20]and Fe-Cr 18Mn 10Ni 16[68]do not exhibit a discernible increase in work-hardening. Similarly, in concentrated alloys, Co 10Cr 10Fe 50Mn 30(at%) manifests no notable rise in work-hardening: both yield strength and maximum strength increase by approximately 420 MPa/wt% N [67]. The addition of nitrogen may change deformation mechanisms depending on the matrix or nitrogen concentration. This will be further discussed in the following section. Fig. 7d illustrates the variation in elongation at break as a function of nitrogen concentration in all studied alloys. Without distinguishing the chemical composition of the matrix, the uniform elongation remains nearly constant despite the substantial improvement in mechanical resistance (UTS) thanks to the enhanced work-hardening in the alloy. This observation is consistent with Considère’s criterion, stating that an increase in strain hardening postpones necking, the latter initiating when the strain-hardening rate matches the stress. Consequently, an increase in strain hardening postpones necking, thereby delaying material’s failure. The fracture surfaces post-tensile tests are not shown but it is pointed out that, irrespective of the nitrogen concentration or the chemical composition of the matrix, they exhibit typical characteristics of ductile fracture: presence of numerous dimples, often formed around defects such as MnS inclusions. Fig. 8illustrates the variation in strain-hardening rate, SHR, ( dσtrue∕ dϵtrue) throughout the tensile tests. Previous study [35]showed that in the case of nitrogen-free alloys ( Fig. 8a), the curves consistently display a gradual decline in work-hardening during deformation, while nitrogen-rich alloys present a strain-hardening plateau at approximately 2500 MPa, and its magnitude increases with increasing nitrogen concentration ( Fig. 8b). Changes of matrix did not result in any modification of this effect. Consequently, alloys with nitrogen exhibit a substantial increase in strain-hardening rates - up to 70 % - compared to nitrogen-free alloys, explaining their pronounced increase in UTS in the presence of nitrogen. It is commonly admitted that the addition of nitrogen leads to a marked change in the dislocation structure: slip becomes planar, resulting in the accumulation of dislocations at grain boundaries ( pile ups) [69-72]and thus participating in the increase of the SHR as higher stresses are required to overcome it [21,73]. The reason why dislocation slip becomes planar is not clear but could be interpreted as a decrease of the SFE as partial dislocations cannot cross-slip. However this phenomenon is also observed in alloys where nitrogen is supposed to increase the SFE, that’s why it is often claimed that it is due to the formation of a short range order (SRO) [74,75]. Yet, it is still to be experimentally demonstrated that nitrogen promotes an SRO phenomenon [76]. The improvement of SHR in presence of nitrogen could also be caused by the activation of twinning-induced plasticity (TWIP effect). The formation of twins creates obstacles for dislocations, thereby increasing strain-hardening. However, when deformation increases, the nucleation of new twins becomes increasingly difficult due to the reduction in domain size induced by existing twins. Consequently, there is a decline in strain-hardening as the material approaches rupture. To confirm the twinning hypothesis in nitrogen-concentrated alloys, microstructures after rupture were analysed using transmission electron microscopy (TEM) ( Fig. 9). The specimen was prepared in the transverse direction of the tensile specimen, in a region close to the fracture. Thus, the corresponding deformation is estimated to be a uniform elongation of around 40 %. Fig. 9presents the microstructure of nitrogen-free M25 and M18 alloys deformed to fracture. Overall, a well-defined arrangement of dislocations in the form of cells is evident ( Fig. 9a-c), indicating that deformation is primarily achieved through dislocation gliding. This type of microstructure results from the clustering and fragmentation of grains into multiple cells, with local orientations varying from one cell to another [77]. While both alloy presents mainly similar deformed microstructure, occasional twins, approximately 20 nm thick, are observed in some grains in the M18 alloy ( Fig. 9d). Their thickness is comparable to that observed at the initiation of twinning in an alloy deformed at low temperature, typically ranging from 12 to 15 nm for the initial twins, which tend to grow and become more abundant as deformation progresses [12]. In the M18 alloy, the occurrence of twinning is sporadic, appearing in a few grains, likely those with favorable orientations. The relatively small thickness of these twins suggests that twinning activation occurs towards the very end of the tensile test, as observed in the Cantor alloy deformed at room temperature [12]and, therefore, does not significantly alter the mechanical behavior of this alloy compared to other nitrogen-free alloys. However, the presence of deformation twins in well-oriented grains of alloy M18 suggests that the twinning stress of this alloy was freshly surpassed at the end of the tensile test. The maximum true stress reached in the M18 alloy is around 710 MPa ( Table 2), which can be compared to the twinning stress observed on the Cantor alloy at room temperature (720 MPa) [12]. It can therefore be hypothesized that the critical twinning stress is similar to that of the Cantor alloy, and, as with this alloy, is only reached just before fracture, explaining why no twinning is observed at room temperature. The fact that no deformation twins were observed in the M25 alloy which reached a similar true stress at the end of its deformation might be explained by a slight difference in the critical twinning stress value. According to Zaddach et al., an increase in Cr or a decrease in Ni in a CoCrFeMnNi matrix may lead to a reduction in stacking fault energy (SFE) [78]. In addition, assuming that the critical stress for activating twinning is considered to be proportional to the SFE [79-81], then the M25 alloy presents a slightly higher critical twinning stress than the M18 alloy and, therefore, is not reached during deformation. This hypothesis needs however to be further investigated. Nevertheless, even with the observation of deformation twins in the M18 alloy, dislocation glide remains the predominant deformation mechanism in nitrogen-free alloys, elucidating the consistent decrease in the strain-hardening rate during tensile test. The post-deformation microstructures of nitrogen-containing alloys (M25N0.36 and M18N0. 56) ( Fig. 10) exhibit clear distinctions from those of nitrogen-free alloys. They predominantly feature intersecting mechanical twins ( Fig. 10a and b), with an approximate thickness of about 100 nm. While the influence of nitrogen on the SFE is a subject of debate, the presence of mechanical twins in the deformed nitrogen samples may indicate that nitrogen reduces the SFE in such alloys. Nitrogen influence on the SFE is believed to vary based on both the amount of nitrogen introduced in the matrix and the alloy composition [37,82]. For instance, the addition of nitrogen decreases the SFE in Fe-Cr 21Mn 9Ni 6steel [83]as well as in Cr-Ni steels [84]. Conversely, in Fe-Mn-Si alloys, nitrogen increases the SFE [85]. Furthermore, Gavriljuk et al.demonstrated that the effect of nitrogen can depend on its concentration [86]. For example, in Fe-Cr 18Mn 10Ni 16, the SFE initially increases and then decreases with rising nitrogen levels, while the opposite trend is observed in Fe-Cr 15Mn 17, where the SFE decreases initially and then increases at higher nitrogen concentrations. In concentrated alloys, the effect of nitrogen on SFE is unclear and must certainly be related to alloy composition as well. The addition of nitrogen to a CoCrNi alloy does not alter the deformation mechanisms, since twins are observed after deformation at room temperature in both the nitrogen-free alloy and the nitrogen-containing alloy [34]. On the other hand, the addition of nitrogen in the alloy Co 10Cr 10Fe 50Mn 30(at%) leads, like carbon, to a change from a TRIP mechanism to a TWIP mechanism [61]. Nitrogen would then increase the SFE in this alloy. In our case, it seems that adding nitrogen in CrFeMnNi concentrated alloys might decrease the SFE, however actual measurement of the SFE should be performed to fully validate this hypothesis. Additionally, some grains display twins that seem curved ( Fig. 10c and d). It is essential to note that these TEM observations are made post-fracture, representing an advanced state of deformation. Different mechanisms may thus emerge during deformation and coexist in the final microstructure. One possible assumption is that twinning occurs relatively early in the deformation process (around 6 % true strain, the beginning of the SHR plateau in Fig. 8b), initially activating a single twin plane and then, as deformation advances, involving the activation of different intersecting planes. Conversely, after reaching a certain degree of deformation, twinning might cease, and dislocation glide could once again become the dominant deformation mechanism as commonly observed in nitrogen steels [37]. This transition may result in the curvature of the twins concurrent with the grain’s rotation and could also explain the reduction in the strain-hardening rate toward the end of the tensile loading. Similar observations have been reported for a Fe-Cr 15Mn 17N 0.45alloy: numerous twins are visible when the alloy is deformed to 30 %; however, these twins deform or disappear after reaching 60 % deformation [37]. Analyzing the critical stress of twinning in nitrogen alloys is more complicated than in nitrogen free alloys. The strain-hardening plateau, assumed to be indicative of the twinning phenomenon, appears at approximately 6 % true strain for all nitrogen-containing alloys ( Fig. 8b). At such deformation level, the improvement of mechanical resistance by nitrogen addition implies that the corresponding true stress changes with nitrogen concentration. For instance, in the alloy containing 0.21 wt% nitrogen, this corresponds to a true stress of around 450 MPa, notably lower than that observed in the nitrogen-free M25 alloy, which exceeds 720 MPa. On the other hand, the true stress for the alloy containing 0.39 wt% nitrogen is approximately 550 MPa. Consequently, with an increasing nitrogen concentration, the critical stress appears to rise. This observation is in partial agreement with results on deformation mechanisms of a AISI 316 L steel doped with nitrogen [69]. It was demonstrated that increasing nitrogen content in such alloy, shifted the transition between gliding and twinning mode to higher stress and lower strain values. While in our alloys, there is no change of the strain values required for twinning, it might be hypothesized that there is also a need for a sufficient density of dislocations and stacking faults to trigger this phenomena. Further investigations still need to be done, especially on the initiation of the twinning mode in nitrogen-rich alloys. To do so, detailed TEM observations after various strain levels and especially in the early stages of the plastic deformation would be required. In this work, a numerical approach was applied to design new alloys on the basis of thermodynamic calculations. A single-phase austenitic structure with a high Cr content (18-20 wt%) both with substantial nitrogen solubility was searched for. To quantify and to optimise the stability of such a structure, two critical temperatures were identified and monitored: (i) the temperature of precipitation of the σphase, TSigma, which needed to be minimized; (ii) the extent of the solid solution range, which had to span over a hundred degrees. In comparison with Co-free alloys referenced in the available literature, these new alloys exhibit a high solubility of nitrogen, potentially providing a significant solid solution hardening. The selected alloys have been elaborated with success; especially, the satisfactory mastering of introduction of controlled amounts of nitrogen in the liquid alloys is to be noted. It is commonly admitted that the addition of nitrogen leads to a marked change in the dislocation structure: slip becomes planar, resulting in the accumulation of dislocations at grain boundaries ( pile ups) [69-72]and thus participating in the increase of the SHR as higher stresses are required to overcome it [21,73]. The formation of twins creates obstacles for dislocations, thereby increasing strain-hardening. However, when deformation increases, the nucleation of new twins becomes increasingly difficult due to the reduction in domain size induced by existing twins. Consequently, there is a decline in strain-hardening as the material approaches rupture. For Scanning Electron Microscope (SEM) observations and Energy-Dispersive X-ray spectroscopy (EDX) analyses, all the samples were ground with SiC papers down to 1200 grade. Final preparation was made by electropolishing (6 % HCl in ethanol, at 10-12 ∘C, at 25 V during 30 s). Fig. 7a and b show representative room temperature tensile tests curves for N-free alloys (Y3, M18, M21 and M25) and their N-doped counterparts, respectively. This trend is confirmed by tensile characteristics of the tested matrixes (Y3, M18, M21 and M25): a yield strength (YS) of approximately 200 MPa, an ultimate tensile strength (UTS) of 500 MPa, and an elongation at break exceeding 50 % are measured. The presence of N ( Fig. 7b) results, as expected, in a gradual enhancement of both the YS and UTS of the alloys without compromising their elongation at break. For instance, the M18N0.56 alloy exhibits a yield strength of 450 MPa and an UTS approaching 900 MPa, while a high elongation at break of approximately 58 % is maintained. These values are respectively 125 % and 80 % higher than those measured in the N-free M18 alloy (see Table 2). Consequently, the addition of N proves to be highly advantageous for the tensile behavior of the alloys even at such relatively high concentration. The evolution of tensile properties with nitrogen content is further illustrated in Fig. 7c. Consistent with the hardness evolution, the yield strength increases linearly with N concentration (430 MPa/wt% N) irrespective of the matrix’s chemical composition. This aligns with bibliographic data reported for Cantor alloy [33], a Co 10Cr 10Fe 50Mn 30(at%) HEA [67], and certain stainless steels [20,22,23]. Ultimate strength also exhibits a linear correlation with nitrogen concentration, albeit with a steeper slope (730 MPa/wt% N), while uniform elongation remains constant. The difference between YS and UTS slopes is attributed to the increased work-hardening in the presence of nitrogen. However, one has to note that such an effect is not universally observed in nitrogen-doped alloys. The addition of nitrogen may change deformation mechanisms depending on the matrix or nitrogen concentration. This will be further discussed in the following section. Fig. 7d illustrates the variation in elongation at break as a function of nitrogen concentration in all studied alloys. Without distinguishing the chemical composition of the matrix, the uniform elongation remains nearly constant despite the substantial improvement in mechanical resistance (UTS) thanks to the enhanced work-hardening in the alloy. This observation is consistent with Considère’s criterion, stating that an increase in strain hardening postpones necking, the latter initiating when the strain-hardening rate matches the stress. Consequently, an increase in strain hardening postpones necking, thereby delaying material’s failure. The fracture surfaces post-tensile tests are not shown but it is pointed out that, irrespective of the nitrogen concentration or the chemical composition of the matrix, they exhibit typical characteristics of ductile fracture: presence of numerous dimples, often formed around defects such as MnS inclusions. Fig. 8illustrates the variation in strain-hardening rate, SHR, ( dσtrue∕ dϵtrue) throughout the tensile tests. Previous study [35]showed that in the case of nitrogen-free alloys ( Fig. 8a), the curves consistently display a gradual decline in work-hardening during deformation, while nitrogen-rich alloys present a strain-hardening plateau at approximately 2500 MPa, and its magnitude increases with increasing nitrogen concentration ( Fig. 8b). Changes of matrix did not result in any modification of this effect. Consequently, alloys with nitrogen exhibit a substantial increase in strain-hardening rates - up to 70 % - compared to nitrogen-free alloys, explaining their pronounced increase in UTS in the presence of nitrogen. It is commonly admitted that the addition of nitrogen leads to a marked change in the dislocation structure: slip becomes planar, resulting in the accumulation of dislocations at grain boundaries ( pile ups) [69-72]and thus participating in the increase of the SHR as higher stresses are required to overcome it [21,73]. The reason why dislocation slip becomes planar is not clear but could be interpreted as a decrease of the SFE as partial dislocations cannot cross-slip. However this phenomenon is also observed in alloys where nitrogen is supposed to increase the SFE, that’s why it is often claimed that it is due to the formation of a short range order (SRO) [74,75]. Yet, it is still to be experimentally demonstrated that nitrogen promotes an SRO phenomenon [76]. The improvement of SHR in presence of nitrogen could also be caused by the activation of twinning-induced plasticity (TWIP effect). The formation of twins creates obstacles for dislocations, thereby increasing strain-hardening. However, when deformation increases, the nucleation of new twins becomes increasingly difficult due to the reduction in domain size induced by existing twins. Consequently, there is a decline in strain-hardening as the material approaches rupture. To confirm the twinning hypothesis in nitrogen-concentrated alloys, microstructures after rupture were analysed using transmission electron microscopy (TEM) ( Fig. 9). The specimen was prepared in the transverse direction of the tensile specimen, in a region close to the fracture. Thus, the corresponding deformation is estimated to be a uniform elongation of around 40 %. Fig. 9presents the microstructure of nitrogen-free M25 and M18 alloys deformed to fracture. Overall, a well-defined arrangement of dislocations in the form of cells is evident ( Fig. 9a-c), indicating that deformation is primarily achieved through dislocation gliding. This type of microstructure results from the clustering and fragmentation of grains into multiple cells, with local orientations varying from one cell to another [77]. While both alloy presents mainly similar deformed microstructure, occasional twins, approximately 20 nm thick, are observed in some grains in the M18 alloy ( Fig. 9d). Their thickness is comparable to that observed at the initiation of twinning in an alloy deformed at low temperature, typically ranging from 12 to 15 nm for the initial twins, which tend to grow and become more abundant as deformation progresses [12]. In the M18 alloy, the occurrence of twinning is sporadic, appearing in a few grains, likely those with favorable orientations. The relatively small thickness of these twins suggests that twinning activation occurs towards the very end of the tensile test, as observed in the Cantor alloy deformed at room temperature [12]and, therefore, does not significantly alter the mechanical behavior of this alloy compared to other nitrogen-free alloys. However, the presence of deformation twins in well-oriented grains of alloy M18 suggests that the twinning stress of this alloy was freshly surpassed at the end of the tensile test. The maximum true stress reached in the M18 alloy is around 710 MPa ( Table 2), which can be compared to the twinning stress observed on the Cantor alloy at room temperature (720 MPa) [12]. It can therefore be hypothesized that the critical twinning stress is similar to that of the Cantor alloy, and, as with this alloy, is only reached just before fracture, explaining why no twinning is observed at room temperature. The fact that no deformation twins were observed in the M25 alloy which reached a similar true stress at the end of its deformation might be explained by a slight difference in the critical twinning stress value. In addition, assuming that the critical stress for activating twinning is considered to be proportional to the SFE [79-81], then the M25 alloy presents a slightly higher critical twinning stress than the M18 alloy and, therefore, is not reached during deformation. This hypothesis needs however to be further investigated. Nevertheless, even with the observation of deformation twins in the M18 alloy, dislocation glide remains the predominant deformation mechanism in nitrogen-free alloys, elucidating the consistent decrease in the strain-hardening rate during tensile test. They predominantly feature intersecting mechanical twins ( Fig. 10a and b), with an approximate thickness of about 100 nm. While the influence of nitrogen on the SFE is a subject of debate, the presence of mechanical twins in the deformed nitrogen samples may indicate that nitrogen reduces the SFE in such alloys. Nitrogen influence on the SFE is believed to vary based on both the amount of nitrogen introduced in the matrix and the alloy composition [37,82]. For instance, the addition of nitrogen decreases the SFE in Fe-Cr 21Mn 9Ni 6steel [83]as well as in Cr-Ni steels [84]. Conversely, in Fe-Mn-Si alloys, nitrogen increases the SFE [85]. Furthermore, Gavriljuk et al.demonstrated that the effect of nitrogen can depend on its concentration [86]. For example, in Fe-Cr 18Mn 10Ni 16, the SFE initially increases and then decreases with rising nitrogen levels, while the opposite trend is observed in Fe-Cr 15Mn 17, where the SFE decreases initially and then increases at higher nitrogen concentrations. In concentrated alloys, the effect of nitrogen on SFE is unclear and must certainly be related to alloy composition as well. Without distinguishing the chemical composition of the matrix, the uniform elongation remains nearly constant despite the substantial improvement in mechanical resistance (UTS) thanks to the enhanced work-hardening in the alloy. This observation is consistent with Considère’s criterion, stating that an increase in strain hardening postpones necking, the latter initiating when the strain-hardening rate matches the stress. Consequently, an increase in strain hardening postpones necking, thereby delaying material’s failure. Previous study [35]showed that in the case of nitrogen-free alloys ( Fig. 8a), the curves consistently display a gradual decline in work-hardening during deformation, while nitrogen-rich alloys present a strain-hardening plateau at approximately 2500 MPa, and its magnitude increases with increasing nitrogen concentration ( Fig. 8b). It is commonly admitted that the addition of nitrogen leads to a marked change in the dislocation structure: slip becomes planar, resulting in the accumulation of dislocations at grain boundaries ( pile ups) [69-72]and thus participating in the increase of the SHR as higher stresses are required to overcome it [21,73]. The reason why dislocation slip becomes planar is not clear but could be interpreted as a decrease of the SFE as partial dislocations cannot cross-slip. However this phenomenon is also observed in alloys where nitrogen is supposed to increase the SFE, that’s why it is often claimed that it is due to the formation of a short range order (SRO) [74,75]. Yet, it is still to be experimentally demonstrated that nitrogen promotes an SRO phenomenon [76]. The improvement of SHR in presence of nitrogen could also be caused by the activation of twinning-induced plasticity (TWIP effect). The formation of twins creates obstacles for dislocations, thereby increasing strain-hardening. However, when deformation increases, the nucleation of new twins becomes increasingly difficult due to the reduction in domain size induced by existing twins. Consequently, there is a decline in strain-hardening as the material approaches rupture. The specimen was prepared in the transverse direction of the tensile specimen, in a region close to the fracture. This type of microstructure results from the clustering and fragmentation of grains into multiple cells, with local orientations varying from one cell to another [77]. Previous study [35]showed that in the case of nitrogen-free alloys ( Fig. 8a), the curves consistently display a gradual decline in work-hardening during deformation, while nitrogen-rich alloys present a strain-hardening plateau at approximately 2500 MPa, and its magnitude increases with increasing nitrogen concentration ( Fig. 8b). It is commonly admitted that the addition of nitrogen leads to a marked change in the dislocation structure: slip becomes planar, resulting in the accumulation of dislocations at grain boundaries ( pile ups) [69-72]and thus participating in the increase of the SHR as higher stresses are required to overcome it [21,73]. The reason why dislocation slip becomes planar is not clear but could be interpreted as a decrease of the SFE as partial dislocations cannot cross-slip. However this phenomenon is also observed in alloys where nitrogen is supposed to increase the SFE, that’s why it is often claimed that it is due to the formation of a short range order (SRO) [74,75]. Yet, it is still to be experimentally demonstrated that nitrogen promotes an SRO phenomenon [76]. The improvement of SHR in presence of nitrogen could also be caused by the activation of twinning-induced plasticity (TWIP effect). The formation of twins creates obstacles for dislocations, thereby increasing strain-hardening. However, when deformation increases, the nucleation of new twins becomes increasingly difficult due to the reduction in domain size induced by existing twins. Consequently, there is a decline in strain-hardening as the material approaches rupture. To confirm the twinning hypothesis in nitrogen-concentrated alloys, microstructures after rupture were analysed using transmission electron microscopy (TEM) ( Fig. 9). The specimen was prepared in the transverse direction of the tensile specimen, in a region close to the fracture. In this work, a numerical approach was applied to design new alloys on the basis of thermodynamic calculations. A single-phase austenitic structure with a high Cr content (18-20 wt%) both with substantial nitrogen solubility was searched for. However, the presence of deformation twins in well-oriented grains of alloy M18 suggests that the twinning stress of this alloy was freshly surpassed at the end of the tensile test. The maximum true stress reached in the M18 alloy is around 710 MPa ( Table 2), which can be compared to the twinning stress observed on the Cantor alloy at room temperature (720 MPa) [12]. It can therefore be hypothesized that the critical twinning stress is similar to that of the Cantor alloy, and, as with this alloy, is only reached just before fracture, explaining why no twinning is observed at room temperature. The fact that no deformation twins were observed in the M25 alloy which reached a similar true stress at the end of its deformation might be explained by a slight difference in the critical twinning stress value. According to Zaddach et al., an increase in Cr or a decrease in Ni in a CoCrFeMnNi matrix may lead to a reduction in stacking fault energy (SFE) [78]. In addition, assuming that the critical stress for activating twinning is considered to be proportional to the SFE [79-81], then the M25 alloy presents a slightly higher critical twinning stress than the M18 alloy and, therefore, is not reached during deformation. This hypothesis needs however to be further investigated. Nevertheless, even with the observation of deformation twins in the M18 alloy, dislocation glide remains the predominant deformation mechanism in nitrogen-free alloys, elucidating the consistent decrease in the strain-hardening rate during tensile test. The post-deformation microstructures of nitrogen-containing alloys (M25N0.36 and M18N0. 56) ( Fig. 10) exhibit clear distinctions from those of nitrogen-free alloys. They predominantly feature intersecting mechanical twins ( Fig. 10a and b), with an approximate thickness of about 100 nm. While the influence of nitrogen on the SFE is a subject of debate, the presence of mechanical twins in the deformed nitrogen samples may indicate that nitrogen reduces the SFE in such alloys. Nitrogen influence on the SFE is believed to vary based on both the amount of nitrogen introduced in the matrix and the alloy composition [37,82]. For instance, the addition of nitrogen decreases the SFE in Fe-Cr 21Mn 9Ni 6steel [83]as well as in Cr-Ni steels [84]. Conversely, in Fe-Mn-Si alloys, nitrogen increases the SFE [85]. Furthermore, Gavriljuk et al.demonstrated that the effect of nitrogen can depend on its concentration [86]. For example, in Fe-Cr 18Mn 10Ni 16, the SFE initially increases and then decreases with rising nitrogen levels, while the opposite trend is observed in Fe-Cr 15Mn 17, where the SFE decreases initially and then increases at higher nitrogen concentrations. In concentrated alloys, the effect of nitrogen on SFE is unclear and must certainly be related to alloy composition as well. The addition of nitrogen to a CoCrNi alloy does not alter the deformation mechanisms, since twins are observed after deformation at room temperature in both the nitrogen-free alloy and the nitrogen-containing alloy [34]. On the other hand, the addition of nitrogen in the alloy Co 10Cr 10Fe 50Mn 30(at%) leads, like carbon, to a change from a TRIP mechanism to a TWIP mechanism [61]. Nitrogen would then increase the SFE in this alloy. In our case, it seems that adding nitrogen in CrFeMnNi concentrated alloys might decrease the SFE, however actual measurement of the SFE should be performed to fully validate this hypothesis. Additionally, some grains display twins that seem curved ( Fig. 10c and d). It is essential to note that these TEM observations are made post-fracture, representing an advanced state of deformation. Different mechanisms may thus emerge during deformation and coexist in the final microstructure. One possible assumption is that twinning occurs relatively early in the deformation process (around 6 % true strain, the beginning of the SHR plateau in Fig. 8b), initially activating a single twin plane and then, as deformation advances, involving the activation of different intersecting planes. Conversely, after reaching a certain degree of deformation, twinning might cease, and dislocation glide could once again become the dominant deformation mechanism as commonly observed in nitrogen steels [37]. This transition may result in the curvature of the twins concurrent with the grain’s rotation and could also explain the reduction in the strain-hardening rate toward the end of the tensile loading. Similar observations have been reported for a Fe-Cr 15Mn 17N 0.45alloy: numerous twins are visible when the alloy is deformed to 30 %; however, these twins deform or disappear after reaching 60 % deformation [37]. Analyzing the critical stress of twinning in nitrogen alloys is more complicated than in nitrogen free alloys. The strain-hardening plateau, assumed to be indicative of the twinning phenomenon, appears at approximately 6 % true strain for all nitrogen-containing alloys ( Fig. 8b). At such deformation level, the improvement of mechanical resistance by nitrogen addition implies that the corresponding true stress changes with nitrogen concentration. For instance, in the alloy containing 0.21 wt% nitrogen, this corresponds to a true stress of around 450 MPa, notably lower than that observed in the nitrogen-free M25 alloy, which exceeds 720 MPa. On the other hand, the true stress for the alloy containing 0.39 wt% nitrogen is approximately 550 MPa. Consequently, with an increasing nitrogen concentration, the critical stress appears to rise. This observation is in partial agreement with results on deformation mechanisms of a AISI 316 L steel doped with nitrogen [69]. It was demonstrated that increasing nitrogen content in such alloy, shifted the transition between gliding and twinning mode to higher stress and lower strain values. While in our alloys, there is no change of the strain values required for twinning, it might be hypothesized that there is also a need for a sufficient density of dislocations and stacking faults to trigger this phenomena. Further investigations still need to be done, especially on the initiation of the twinning mode in nitrogen-rich alloys. To do so, detailed TEM observations after various strain levels and especially in the early stages of the plastic deformation would be required. In this work, a numerical approach was applied to design new alloys on the basis of thermodynamic calculations. A single-phase austenitic structure with a high Cr content (18-20 wt%) both with substantial nitrogen solubility was searched for. To quantify and to optimise the stability of such a structure, two critical temperatures were identified and monitored: (i) the temperature of precipitation of the σphase, TSigma, which needed to be minimized; (ii) the extent of the solid solution range, which had to span over a hundred degrees. The impact of compositional changes on these critical temperatures was evaluated through Thermo-Calc calculations and several optimised alloys, meeting the selected criteria, were obtained. Prioritizing some criteria resulted in the selection of three alloys, each containing 20 wt% Cr and accepting 0.4-0.6 wt% N in solid solution. In comparison with Co-free alloys referenced in the available literature, these new alloys exhibit a high solubility of nitrogen, potentially providing a significant solid solution hardening. The selected alloys have been elaborated with success; especially, the satisfactory mastering of introduction of controlled amounts of nitrogen in the liquid alloys is to be noted. The principal results of experimental characterization of the alloys are summarized below. •The stability of austenitic structure at high temperature has been confirmed for all alloys. An annealing treatment (1100 ∘C/90 min) of previously hot forged materials led to the formation of recrystallized microstructure with a grain size of about 50 μm, regardless of the matrix’s chemical composition or nitrogen concentration. In all studied alloys, nitrogen was fully dissolved in solid solution, thus confirming the expected high solubility of the interstitial element in the optimised matrixes. •No effect of chemical composition on mechanical properties (hardness and room temperature tensile properties) was observed in all optimised alloys when nitrogen is absent. •In N-doped alloys, it was verified that the linear behavior of the lattice parameter expansion and mechanical strength values (hardness, yield strength, ultimate tensile strength) with nitrogen concentration is valid up to, at least, 0.56 wt%. Moreover it is also independent of the matrix’s composition. It is important to note that in all N-doped alloys, elongation at fracture remains high and independent of nitrogen concentration. •Nanotwins can be observed in deformed nitrogen-rich alloys whereas none (or very scarcely) are found in deformed nitrogen-free alloys. Nitrogen appears to promote mechanical twinning, explaining the observed improvement in strain hardening. The stability of austenitic structure at high temperature has been confirmed for all alloys. In all studied alloys, nitrogen was fully dissolved in solid solution, thus confirming the expected high solubility of the interstitial element in the optimised matrixes. 1CoCrFeNi HEA castings with a purity of 99.9% were prepared by vacuum induction levitation melting method. In the first cycle of grain-selective growth (GSG), the As-cast alloy was cold-rolled by 40% and annealed at 900 °C for 10 min (represented as near complete recrystallization (NCR) alloy). During the second cycle of GSG, the NCR alloy was cold-rolled by 40% and annealed at 900 °C for 10 min (referred to as GSG alloy). As a point of comparison, the As-cast alloy was cold-rolled by 40% and annealed at 700 °C for 5 and 10 min to obtain the partially recrystallized and finer grain-sized alloy (referred to as PR and FG, respectively).

The HEA annealed at 1123 K for 30 min was selected for further study.

An equiatomic ratio CrMnFeCoNi HEA ingot was selected in this study, fabricated by raw Cr, Mn, Fe, Co, and Ni element with the purity of 99.9%, respectively. The well-proportioned raw materials were melted by vacuum-arc melting technique in an argon atmosphere. The ingot was flipped and re-melted at least five times to obtain a homogeneous composition. The cast sample was then homogenized at 1473 K for 12 h in a vacuum atmosphere and water quenched. Subsequently, the homogenized sample was cold-rolled with 50% reduction at room temperature, annealed at 1073 K for 0.5 h, and water quenched subsequently. Finally, the surface of the specimen was ground to 2000# with sandpaper and then treated with UNSM equipment. The UNSM treatment was acted on both sides of the plate specimens with a thickness of 2.5 mm.

NbMoZrTi LRHEAs samples were prepared by vacuum arc melting. To protect the metal material from oxidation during the melting process, the chamber must first be vacuumed to a vacuum level of 1 × 10 −4Pa. Due to the presence of refractory metal elements, the alloy ingots are re-melted at least eight times to ensure a homogeneous composition. Alloy ingots with nominal composition of equiatomic CoCrFeMnNi was prepared using vacuum arc melting. The alloy ingot 100 mm long × 80 mm wide × 15 mm high was cast into a quadrangle-shaped cold copper crucible. To homogenize the chemical composition, the ingot was re-melted five times and then annealed at 1373 K for 6 h in a high-purity argon atmosphere. The grains are elongated along the solidification direction. The microstructures after hot deformation under different processing conditions were observed by EBSD, and their IPF and grain boundary (GB) maps are shown in Fig. 8(a)-(f). The formation of a necklace-like structure composed of fine recrystallized grains along the initial grain boundaries and the absence of a subgrain structure within initial grains can be observed in the GB map at 1098 K-10 −3s −1( Fig. 8(a)), suggesting that discontinuous dynamic recrystallization (DDRX) is active. At 1173 K-10 −3s −1, however, in addition to the recrystallized grains that developed along the initial grain boundaries, domains composed of fine recrystallized grains were found within the initial grains where the substructure composed of low-angle boundaries developed. In addition, there is substantial evidence for the gradual transformation from low-angle grain boundaries to high-angle grain boundaries. These observations are indications of the occurrence of continuous dynamic recrystallization (CDRX). Further enhanced CDRX could also be observed at 1323 K-10 −3s −1, suggesting that the contribution of CDRX becomes pronounced as temperature increases.

The CoCrFeNiMn alloy was produced in a vacuum induction furnace using pure elements with a purity greater than 99.9 wt%. The size of the casting ingot was φ100 × 60 mm 3, and it was homogenized under an argon atmosphere at 1100 °C for 24 h and then annealed. Dog-bone-shaped samples, with a gauge section of 2 mm × 1mm × 0.4 mm, were cut from the as-forged sample with their long axes parallel to the radial direction and annealed at 1000 °C for 1 h.

An equiatomic high-entropy alloy with a nominal composition of Co 20Cr 20Fe 20Mn 20Ni 20C 0.8(at. %) was synthesized from high-purity metals (>99.5 wt. %) using a vacuum induction furnace for melting and casting. The resulting ingot was hot-rolled at 900 °C, achieving a thickness reduction of 50 % (from 10 mm to 5 mm), and then homogenized at 1200 °C for 2 h in a high-purity argon flow, followed by water quenching. The homogenized sheet underwent cold rolling, resulting in an overall thickness reduction of 60 %. It was then annealed at 1000 °C in an argon atmosphere for 10 min and water quenched to facilitate the formation of equiaxed grains (labeled original iHEA). For subsequent treatments, the equiaxed grain samples were subjected to SMAT, producing what we refer to as SMAT iHEA. The iHEA plates with dimensions of 35 × 25 × 2 mm 3were subjected to mechanical attrition in a chamber containing 3 mm hard balls at a frequency of 20 kHz for 30 min on both sides, maintaining a working distance of 15 mm. The SMAT samples were then annealed at 700 °C for 30 min, followed by water-quenching, with the resultant samples labeled as SMAT-annealed iHEA.

Enrichment of Co and Cr reduces the alloy's SFE, the objective is to ensure the induction of the FCC-HCP phase transformation during deformation, thus enhancing material work hardening and ductility. 6FeNi) 100-xCu xHEAs with a nominal composition was fabricated through vacuum melting using a mixture of constituent metal elements (purity >99.95 wt%), under an argon atmosphere containing Zr-gettered material. The melting process was repeated 6 times to ensure the uniformity of the chemical composition. Subsequently, electric discharge machining (EDM) was utilized to machine the button ingot to an 8 mm thickness, then homogenized at 1200 °C for 2 h and subsequent air cooling. The homogenized samples were subsequently subjected to multiple-pass hot rolling at 1000 °C, reducing their thickness to 1.6 mm (a reduction of 80 %). Prior to each rolling pass, the samples were preheated for 5 min and finally air-cooled. Following hot rolling, the samples were heat treated at 700 °C for 1 h and subsequently quenched in water, labeled as Cux (x = 0,2).

An equiatomic CoCrFeMnNi high-entropy alloy, which crystallizes in the face-centered cubic (fcc) crystal structure, was produced by arc melting and drop casting. The drop-cast ingots were homogenized, cold rolled and recrystallized to obtain single-phase microstructures with three different grain sizes in the range 4-160μm. Rectangular ingots (127 × 25.4 × 12.7 mm 3) of the equiatomic CoCrFeMnNi alloy weighing ∼475 g were produced by arc melting and drop casting under pure Ar atmosphere. Since Mn rapidly oxidizes in air, the Mn stock was cleaned in an aqueous solution of nitric acid immediately before it was added to the other materials in the arc melter. Nevertheless, we found that there was weight loss during arc melting and an additional gram of Mn had to be added per ingot to compensate for its evaporation. After the raw materials were loaded in the arc melter, the chamber was first evacuated to ∼7 × 10 −4Pa and then backfilled with Ar gas to a pressure of ∼8. Before the high-entropy alloy was melted, a small piece of Zr was melted to getter any residual oxygen that might be present in the chamber. The arc-melted buttons were flipped and remelted five times to promote homogeneity and thorough mixing of the elements before they were dropped into the rectangular Cu mold. The drop-cast ingots were cleaned in an aqueous solution of hydrochloric acid and hydrogen peroxide, encapsulated in evacuated quartz ampules and solution-annealed for 48 h at 1473 K. The ingots were subsequently cold rolled along the longitudinal ingot direction to sheets having a final thickness of ∼1.7 mm. The rolled sheets were annealed for 1 h at 1073, 1273 or 1423 K to obtain fully recrystallized microstructures with three different grain sizes. Flat dog-bone-shaped tensile specimens with a gauge length of 12.7 mm were machined from the recrystallized sheets by electric discharge machining with their longitudinal axes perpendicular to the rolling direction of the sheet.

2 HEA were fabricated through a precision process within a vacuum induction magnetic levitation furnace. For the subsequent rolling process, the as-cast ingots were subjected to a homogenization treatment at 1050 °C for a duration of 5 h within an argon atmosphere and following a water quenching. The homogenized alloys underwent a cryogenic rolling (CR) operation at a temperature of 77K, with a substantial reduction ratio of 80 %. Following the cold rolling, a sequence of recrystallization annealing was conducted at temperature of 1000 °C within argon atmosphere for 0.5 h and then followed by a water quenching (RA-1000).

In this study, gas atomized prealloyed powder of a baseline Al-Cr-Fe-Ni high-entropy alloy was mixed with Fe and Ni elemental fine powder particles, to produce a powder blend with a modified composition. It was aimed to improve the alloy processability via designing the solidification path by reducing the Al content. The synthesized novel alloy composition was processed by laser powder bed fusion and crack-free material with a metastable, near single-phase face-centered cubic microstructure was obtained. Process parameters for minimum porosity were identified and net-shape tensile specimens were produced. 9Cr 0. 9Fe 2. 1Ni 2. 1. The novel alloy composition was obtained by blending prealloyed baseline AlCrFe 2Ni 2powder with elemental Fe and Ni particles. The eventual reduction of the Al content changed the primary solidification phase from BCC B2 to FCC, thus successfully preventing hot cracking during LPBF even when processing without baseplate preheating. The response surface methodology (RSM) [41]approach was utilized to identify the optimum process window and select the LPBF process parameters for minimum porosity. The obtained parameters were used to build net-shape tensile specimens that were tested after heat treatment. Microstructural characterization of the material before and after heat treatment as well as the observation of the fracture surface of the tested specimens revealed the relationship between the microstructure and the obtained mechanical properties. Finally, a comparison of the mechanical properties between the Al 0. 9Cr 0. 9Fe 2. 1Ni 2. 1HEA and a standard high strength and corrosion-resistant alloy was performed by testing an EN 1.4517 super duplex steel as reference. AlCrFe 2Ni 2prealloyed powder, produced with gas atomization by Oerlikon Metco was used as the initial nominal composition. The final HEA composition was synthesized through the blending of the prealloyed powder with elemental fine (<23 µm) Fe and Ni particles. The powder blend was subsequently used for LPBF parameter development as well as tensile specimen builds. The LPBF builds were completed in a TRUMPF TruPrint 1000 printer, equipped with a 200 W Nd: YAG fiber laser with a beam spot size of 55 µm and a wavelength of 1064 nm. The main goal of the LPBF parameter development builds was to produce crack-free coupons for material property testing and to minimize the obtained material porosity. First, a build was completed for parameter screening purposes with the application of a wide energy density range. The energy density was calculated according to Ev=P/vhtwhere Evin (J/mm 3); volume energy density, Pin (W); laser power, vin (mm/s); scanning speed, hin (mm); hatch space and t in (mm); layer thickness. Within the tested energy density range an effective design space was identified and investigated with a subsequent parameter optimization build. The parameter optimization build was analyzed according to RSM. The Al 0. 9Cr 0. 9Fe 2. 1Ni 2.1tensile specimens were built with parameters selected based on the response surfaces and had a cylindrical geometry compatible with ASTM E8/E8M [44]. The tensile specimens were tested as-built and after heat treatment, without any post-processing of their surface. Heat treatment of the tensile specimens was performed at 950 °C for 6 h in a Carbolite Gero CWF 11/13 furnace under Ar atmosphere. In our previous work, reporting on HEA with similar composition, namely AlCrFe2Ni2, it was shown that dual phase microstructures with excellent mechanical properties were obtained with the prescribed heat treatment [23]. Therefore, it was also applied in the present study. The temperature was reached with a heating rate of 1. After the end of the treatment, furnace cooling was applied with a cooling rate of 0. 5 °C/s. 1Ni 2.1specimens were observed under SEM and failure analysis was carried out. The coupons of the parameter development builds were cut from the baseplate with WEDM. Their porosity percentage was measured by image analysis of longitudinal section (along the build direction) optical micrographs using the ImageJ software [45]. The optical micrographs were taken with a Zeiss Smartzoom optical microscope. Preparation of the specimens for metallurgical characterization involved mechanical grinding of the longitudinal sections followed by polishing using a diamond suspension and subsequently a colloidal silica suspension with a particle size of 0.04 µm. The morphology of the powder blend particles can be seen in the SEM micrographs of Fig. 4a. Most of them were spherical, but agglomeration and satellites due to the presence of finer particles were also observed. The cubic LPBF coupons on the baseplate after the completion of the screening and optimization builds can be seen in Fig. 5a and 5b, respectively. All coupons were built successfully. No visible cracks were found on the outer surface of the coupons, however, the top surface of the coupons built with higher energy density (>100 J/mm 3) showed signs of oxidation as a result of higher energy input. The analysis of the longitudinal section micrographs of the screening build and the measured porosity percentages showed that the applied energy density range can be partitioned into four distinct zones (I to IV), as seen in Fig. 6a. The limits between each zone were marked qualitatively. A local regression curve was also fitted for the data points that showed porosity less than 1 % to illustrate the effect of energy density. The representative longitudinal section micrographs from each zone can be seen in Fig. 6b. Coupons built within zone I showed the highest porosity percentages, due to insufficient melting of the powder bed. Zone II coupons showed significantly reduced porosity percentages compared to zone I, however, irregularly shaped defects were seen, indicating lack-of-fusion. Micrographs from coupons within zone III showed limited circular gas pores as well as the lowest porosity percentages. Zone IV coupons were built with the highest energy density range applied in the current study. They showed pores that were highly circular and relatively larger in diameter compared to the ones seen in zone III coupons, evidencing that overmelting caused gas porosity. For the optimization build, an effective design space within zone II and III was defined. The obtained porosity response surfaces can be seen in the contour graphs of Fig. 7b, c and d. Overall, a wide process parameter range that leads to porosity below 0.2 % was observed. The response surface for laser power and scanning speed, seen in Fig. 7b, showed that higher laser power could be combined with higher scanning speed to obtain low porosity material. Specifically, with maximum laser power (175 W), scanning speed up to 1,200 mm/s could be used to produce material with porosity lower than 0. 1 %. Similarly, for the interaction between laser power and hatch space, seen in Fig. 7c, it was seen that porosity less than 0.1 % was achieved with hatch space up to 90 µm when laser power is higher than approximately 160 W. Accordingly, the interaction between hatch space and scanning speed, seen in Fig. 7d, showed that with the use of greater hatch space, lower scanning speed should be applied to avoid pore formation. The longitudinal section micrographs of the LPBF processed Al 0. 9Cr 0. 9Fe 2. 1Ni 2.1alloy in the as-built state revealed a columnar-cellular microstructure, as seen in Fig. 9a. Elongated cells grew along the build direction due to the vertical heat flux, but also in other directions because of the scanning pattern rotation and the remelting that occurred during the fusion of the powder layers. At higher magnification, submicron-sized cellular-dendritic structures were observed, as seen in Fig. 9b. The chemical composition of the as-built material measured by EDS can be seen in Table 10. It was observed that the chemical composition was equivalent to that of the powder blend, given in Table 6, considering the uncertainty of the ICP-OES measurement. The EBSD phase map, seen in Fig. 10a, displayed a near single-phase FCC microstructure (97 % FCC - 3 % BCC). Local powder inhomogeneity caused by powder blending led to the formation of BCC phase islands due to the processing of the AlCrFe2Ni2 prealloyed powder [23]. The primary FCC grains grew through multiple layers, as seen In the inverse pole figure (IPF) map of Fig. 10b, and resulted in a near< 001 > fiber texture, according to the pole figures of Fig. 10c. This texture is quite frequently observed for FCC and BCC metals after additive manufacturing [46]. However, the observed texture was weak, also because elemental fine particles with higher melting temperatures could potentially serve as nucleation sites for new grains. In this study, a Co-free HEA powder with Al-lean composition, Al 0. 9Cr 0. 9Fe 2. 1Ni 2.1, was prepared by blending the baseline prealloyed powder of a crack-prone AlCrFe 2Ni 2alloy with fine Fe and Ni elemental particles. The HEA powder blend was processed successfully with LPBF and crack-free material was obtained. The porosity of the as-built material was minimized with the use of a DOE methodology and the optimum process parameters were identified according to RSM. Microstructural characterization showed that the as-built material had a metastable, near single-phase FCC microstructure. Subsequent heat treatment enabled the formation of Al- and Ni-rich BCC B2 precipitates dispersed homogeneously in the parent FCC matrix. To investigate the mechanical properties of the novel material, tensile specimens were produced with LPBF and tested without machining of their surface, in the as-built as well as heat-treated condition, i.e. 950 °C for 6 h. After tensile testing, fracture characterization was carried out. As a reference material, EN 1.4517 super duplex steel specimens extracted from a conventionally casted and solution heat-treated block, were tested and the obtained mechanical properties were compared with those of the presented HEA. The concluding findings of this work can be summarized as follows:

i) Blending of prealloyed powder with elemental fine particles can be utilized to obtain novel HEA compositions in homogenous powder blends, suitable for LPBF processing.

ii) DOE methodology and RSM can be used effectively to provide a range of LPBF process parameters suitable for low porosity material within a selected design space.

iii) The synthesized Al 0. 9Cr 0. 9Fe 2. 1Ni 2.1alloy showed good LPBF processability without cracks. Cracking elimination was driven by the as-built FCC microstructure, imposed by the reduction of the Al content in the powder blend. Additionally, a wide range of process parameters was found capable of providing minimum porosity material (<0.1 %).

iv) The microstructure of the as-built Al 0. 9Cr 0. 9Fe 2. 1Ni 2.1alloy consisted practically of FCC grains, while heat treatment at 950 °C for 6 h led to the formation of a refined dual-phase FCC A1 + BCC B2 microstructure. The formation of the refined microstructure through secondary phase precipitation after heat treatment of a metastable microstructure is an advantage of the LPBF processing route.

v) Tensile testing of the Al 0. 9Cr 0. 9Fe 2. 1Ni 2.1specimens showed that the novel alloy was capable of outperforming the reference material in mechanical strength in both the as-built and heat-treated conditions while showing lower, yet acceptable elongation. The fracture surface characterization revealed a ductile failure mode with dimple formation. Since the specimens were tested without post-processing of the surface, further improvement of the mechanical properties can be expected with machined specimens.

vi) Owing to the presence of fine BCC B2 precipitates, the heat-treated Al 0. 9Cr 0. 9Fe 2. 1Ni 2.1specimens exhibited significant strain hardening. According to the applied Hollomon’s model, the work hardening exponent of the novel alloy was approximately 58 % higher compared to that of the reference super duplex steel. In this study, a Co-free HEA powder with Al-lean composition, Al 0. 9Cr 0. 9Fe 2. 1Ni 2.1, was prepared by blending the baseline prealloyed powder of a crack-prone AlCrFe 2Ni 2alloy with fine Fe and Ni elemental particles. The HEA powder blend was processed successfully with LPBF and crack-free material was obtained. The porosity of the as-built material was minimized with the use of a DOE methodology and the optimum process parameters were identified according to RSM. Microstructural characterization showed that the as-built material had a metastable, near single-phase FCC microstructure. Subsequent heat treatment enabled the formation of Al- and Ni-rich BCC B2 precipitates dispersed homogeneously in the parent FCC matrix. To investigate the mechanical properties of the novel material, tensile specimens were produced with LPBF and tested without machining of their surface, in the as-built as well as heat-treated condition, i.e. 950 °C for 6 h. After tensile testing, fracture characterization was carried out. As a reference material, EN 1.4517 super duplex steel specimens extracted from a conventionally casted and solution heat-treated block, were tested and the obtained mechanical properties were compared with those of the presented HEA. The concluding findings of this work can be summarized as follows:

i) Blending of prealloyed powder with elemental fine particles can be utilized to obtain novel HEA compositions in homogenous powder blends, suitable for LPBF processing.

ii) DOE methodology and RSM can be used effectively to provide a range of LPBF process parameters suitable for low porosity material within a selected design space.

iii) The synthesized Al 0. 9Cr 0. 9Fe 2. 1Ni 2.1alloy showed good LPBF processability without cracks. Cracking elimination was driven by the as-built FCC microstructure, imposed by the reduction of the Al content in the powder blend. Additionally, a wide range of process parameters was found capable of providing minimum porosity material (<0.1 %).

iv) The microstructure of the as-built Al 0. 9Cr 0. 9Fe 2. 1Ni 2.1alloy consisted practically of FCC grains, while heat treatment at 950 °C for 6 h led to the formation of a refined dual-phase FCC A1 + BCC B2 microstructure. The formation of the refined microstructure through secondary phase precipitation after heat treatment of a metastable microstructure is an advantage of the LPBF processing route.

v) Tensile testing of the Al 0. 9Cr 0. 9Fe 2. 1Ni 2.1specimens showed that the novel alloy was capable of outperforming the reference material in mechanical strength in both the as-built and heat-treated conditions while showing lower, yet acceptable elongation. The fracture surface characterization revealed a ductile failure mode with dimple formation. Since the specimens were tested without post-processing of the surface, further improvement of the mechanical properties can be expected with machined specimens.

vi) Owing to the presence of fine BCC B2 precipitates, the heat-treated Al 0. 9Cr 0. 9Fe 2. 1Ni 2.1specimens exhibited significant strain hardening. According to the applied Hollomon’s model, the work hardening exponent of the novel alloy was approximately 58 % higher compared to that of the reference super duplex steel. In this study, a Co-free HEA powder with Al-lean composition, Al 0. 9Cr 0. 9Fe 2. 1Ni 2.1, was prepared by blending the baseline prealloyed powder of a crack-prone AlCrFe 2Ni 2alloy with fine Fe and Ni elemental particles. The HEA powder blend was processed successfully with LPBF and crack-free material was obtained. The porosity of the as-built material was minimized with the use of a DOE methodology and the optimum process parameters were identified according to RSM. Microstructural characterization showed that the as-built material had a metastable, near single-phase FCC microstructure. Subsequent heat treatment enabled the formation of Al- and Ni-rich BCC B2 precipitates dispersed homogeneously in the parent FCC matrix. To investigate the mechanical properties of the novel material, tensile specimens were produced with LPBF and tested without machining of their surface, in the as-built as well as heat-treated condition, i.e. 950 °C for 6 h. After tensile testing, fracture characterization was carried out. As a reference material, EN 1.4517 super duplex steel specimens extracted from a conventionally casted and solution heat-treated block, were tested and the obtained mechanical properties were compared with those of the presented HEA. The concluding findings of this work can be summarized as follows:

i) Blending of prealloyed powder with elemental fine particles can be utilized to obtain novel HEA compositions in homogenous powder blends, suitable for LPBF processing.

ii) DOE methodology and RSM can be used effectively to provide a range of LPBF process parameters suitable for low porosity material within a selected design space.

iii) The synthesized Al 0. 9Cr 0. 9Fe 2. 1Ni 2.1alloy showed good LPBF processability without cracks. Cracking elimination was driven by the as-built FCC microstructure, imposed by the reduction of the Al content in the powder blend. Additionally, a wide range of process parameters was found capable of providing minimum porosity material (<0.1 %).

iv) The microstructure of the as-built Al 0. 9Cr 0. 9Fe 2. 1Ni 2.1alloy consisted practically of FCC grains, while heat treatment at 950 °C for 6 h led to the formation of a refined dual-phase FCC A1 + BCC B2 microstructure. The formation of the refined microstructure through secondary phase precipitation after heat treatment of a metastable microstructure is an advantage of the LPBF processing route.

v) Tensile testing of the Al 0. 9Cr 0. 9Fe 2. 1Ni 2.1specimens showed that the novel alloy was capable of outperforming the reference material in mechanical strength in both the as-built and heat-treated conditions while showing lower, yet acceptable elongation. The fracture surface characterization revealed a ductile failure mode with dimple formation. Since the specimens were tested without post-processing of the surface, further improvement of the mechanical properties can be expected with machined specimens.

vi) Owing to the presence of fine BCC B2 precipitates, the heat-treated Al 0. 9Cr 0. 9Fe 2. 1Ni 2.1specimens exhibited significant strain hardening. According to the applied Hollomon’s model, the work hardening exponent of the novel alloy was approximately 58 % higher compared to that of the reference super duplex steel. In this study, a Co-free HEA powder with Al-lean composition, Al 0. 9Cr 0. 9Fe 2. 1Ni 2.1, was prepared by blending the baseline prealloyed powder of a crack-prone AlCrFe 2Ni 2alloy with fine Fe and Ni elemental particles. The HEA powder blend was processed successfully with LPBF and crack-free material was obtained. The porosity of the as-built material was minimized with the use of a DOE methodology and the optimum process parameters were identified according to RSM. Microstructural characterization showed that the as-built material had a metastable, near single-phase FCC microstructure. Subsequent heat treatment enabled the formation of Al- and Ni-rich BCC B2 precipitates dispersed homogeneously in the parent FCC matrix. To investigate the mechanical properties of the novel material, tensile specimens were produced with LPBF and tested without machining of their surface, in the as-built as well as heat-treated condition, i.e. 950 °C for 6 h. After tensile testing, fracture characterization was carried out. As a reference material, EN 1.4517 super duplex steel specimens extracted from a conventionally casted and solution heat-treated block, were tested and the obtained mechanical properties were compared with those of the presented HEA. The concluding findings of this work can be summarized as follows:

i) Blending of prealloyed powder with elemental fine particles can be utilized to obtain novel HEA compositions in homogenous powder blends, suitable for LPBF processing.

ii) DOE methodology and RSM can be used effectively to provide a range of LPBF process parameters suitable for low porosity material within a selected design space.

iii) The synthesized Al 0. 9Cr 0. 9Fe 2. 1Ni 2.1alloy showed good LPBF processability without cracks. Cracking elimination was driven by the as-built FCC microstructure, imposed by the reduction of the Al content in the powder blend. Additionally, a wide range of process parameters was found capable of providing minimum porosity material (<0.1 %).

iv) The microstructure of the as-built Al 0. 9Cr 0. 9Fe 2. 1Ni 2.1alloy consisted practically of FCC grains, while heat treatment at 950 °C for 6 h led to the formation of a refined dual-phase FCC A1 + BCC B2 microstructure. The formation of the refined microstructure through secondary phase precipitation after heat treatment of a metastable microstructure is an advantage of the LPBF processing route.

v) Tensile testing of the Al 0. 9Cr 0. 9Fe 2. 1Ni 2.1specimens showed that the novel alloy was capable of outperforming the reference material in mechanical strength in both the as-built and heat-treated conditions while showing lower, yet acceptable elongation. The fracture surface characterization revealed a ductile failure mode with dimple formation. Since the specimens were tested without post-processing of the surface, further improvement of the mechanical properties can be expected with machined specimens.

vi) Owing to the presence of fine BCC B2 precipitates, the heat-treated Al 0. 9Cr 0. 9Fe 2. 1Ni 2.1specimens exhibited significant strain hardening. According to the applied Hollomon’s model, the work hardening exponent of the novel alloy was approximately 58 % higher compared to that of the reference super duplex steel. In this study, a Co-free HEA powder with Al-lean composition, Al 0. 9Cr 0. 9Fe 2. 1Ni 2.1, was prepared by blending the baseline prealloyed powder of a crack-prone AlCrFe 2Ni 2alloy with fine Fe and Ni elemental particles. The HEA powder blend was processed successfully with LPBF and crack-free material was obtained. The porosity of the as-built material was minimized with the use of a DOE methodology and the optimum process parameters were identified according to RSM. Microstructural characterization showed that the as-built material had a metastable, near single-phase FCC microstructure. Subsequent heat treatment enabled the formation of Al- and Ni-rich BCC B2 precipitates dispersed homogeneously in the parent FCC matrix. To investigate the mechanical properties of the novel material, tensile specimens were produced with LPBF and tested without machining of their surface, in the as-built as well as heat-treated condition, i.e. 950 °C for 6 h. After tensile testing, fracture characterization was carried out. As a reference material, EN 1.4517 super duplex steel specimens extracted from a conventionally casted and solution heat-treated block, were tested and the obtained mechanical properties were compared with those of the presented HEA. The concluding findings of this work can be summarized as follows:

i) Blending of prealloyed powder with elemental fine particles can be utilized to obtain novel HEA compositions in homogenous powder blends, suitable for LPBF processing.

ii) DOE methodology and RSM can be used effectively to provide a range of LPBF process parameters suitable for low porosity material within a selected design space.

iii) The synthesized Al 0. 9Cr 0. 9Fe 2. 1Ni 2.1alloy showed good LPBF processability without cracks. Cracking elimination was driven by the as-built FCC microstructure, imposed by the reduction of the Al content in the powder blend. Additionally, a wide range of process parameters was found capable of providing minimum porosity material (<0.1 %).

iv) The microstructure of the as-built Al 0. 9Cr 0. 9Fe 2. 1Ni 2.1alloy consisted practically of FCC grains, while heat treatment at 950 °C for 6 h led to the formation of a refined dual-phase FCC A1 + BCC B2 microstructure. The formation of the refined microstructure through secondary phase precipitation after heat treatment of a metastable microstructure is an advantage of the LPBF processing route.

v) Tensile testing of the Al 0. 9Cr 0. 9Fe 2. 1Ni 2.1specimens showed that the novel alloy was capable of outperforming the reference material in mechanical strength in both the as-built and heat-treated conditions while showing lower, yet acceptable elongation. The fracture surface characterization revealed a ductile failure mode with dimple formation. Since the specimens were tested without post-processing of the surface, further improvement of the mechanical properties can be expected with machined specimens.

vi) Owing to the presence of fine BCC B2 precipitates, the heat-treated Al 0. 9Cr 0. 9Fe 2. 1Ni 2.1specimens exhibited significant strain hardening. According to the applied Hollomon’s model, the work hardening exponent of the novel alloy was approximately 58 % higher compared to that of the reference super duplex steel. In this study, a Co-free HEA powder with Al-lean composition, Al 0. 9Cr 0. 9Fe 2. 1Ni 2.1, was prepared by blending the baseline prealloyed powder of a crack-prone AlCrFe 2Ni 2alloy with fine Fe and Ni elemental particles. The HEA powder blend was processed successfully with LPBF and crack-free material was obtained. The porosity of the as-built material was minimized with the use of a DOE methodology and the optimum process parameters were identified according to RSM. Microstructural characterization showed that the as-built material had a metastable, near single-phase FCC microstructure. Subsequent heat treatment enabled the formation of Al- and Ni-rich BCC B2 precipitates dispersed homogeneously in the parent FCC matrix. To investigate the mechanical properties of the novel material, tensile specimens were produced with LPBF and tested without machining of their surface, in the as-built as well as heat-treated condition, i.e. 950 °C for 6 h. After tensile testing, fracture characterization was carried out. As a reference material, EN 1.4517 super duplex steel specimens extracted from a conventionally casted and solution heat-treated block, were tested and the obtained mechanical properties were compared with those of the presented HEA. The concluding findings of this work can be summarized as follows:

i) Blending of prealloyed powder with elemental fine particles can be utilized to obtain novel HEA compositions in homogenous powder blends, suitable for LPBF processing.

ii) DOE methodology and RSM can be used effectively to provide a range of LPBF process parameters suitable for low porosity material within a selected design space.

iii) The synthesized Al 0. 9Cr 0. 9Fe 2. 1Ni 2.1alloy showed good LPBF processability without cracks. Cracking elimination was driven by the as-built FCC microstructure, imposed by the reduction of the Al content in the powder blend. Additionally, a wide range of process parameters was found capable of providing minimum porosity material (<0.1 %).

iv) The microstructure of the as-built Al 0. 9Cr 0. 9Fe 2. 1Ni 2.1alloy consisted practically of FCC grains, while heat treatment at 950 °C for 6 h led to the formation of a refined dual-phase FCC A1 + BCC B2 microstructure. The formation of the refined microstructure through secondary phase precipitation after heat treatment of a metastable microstructure is an advantage of the LPBF processing route.

v) Tensile testing of the Al 0. 9Cr 0. 9Fe 2. 1Ni 2.1specimens showed that the novel alloy was capable of outperforming the reference material in mechanical strength in both the as-built and heat-treated conditions while showing lower, yet acceptable elongation. The fracture surface characterization revealed a ductile failure mode with dimple formation. Since the specimens were tested without post-processing of the surface, further improvement of the mechanical properties can be expected with machined specimens.

vi) Owing to the presence of fine BCC B2 precipitates, the heat-treated Al 0. 9Cr 0. 9Fe 2. 1Ni 2.1specimens exhibited significant strain hardening. According to the applied Hollomon’s model, the work hardening exponent of the novel alloy was approximately 58 % higher compared to that of the reference super duplex steel. In this study, a Co-free HEA powder with Al-lean composition, Al 0. 9Cr 0. 9Fe 2. 1Ni 2.1, was prepared by blending the baseline prealloyed powder of a crack-prone AlCrFe 2Ni 2alloy with fine Fe and Ni elemental particles. The HEA powder blend was processed successfully with LPBF and crack-free material was obtained. The porosity of the as-built material was minimized with the use of a DOE methodology and the optimum process parameters were identified according to RSM. Microstructural characterization showed that the as-built material had a metastable, near single-phase FCC microstructure. Subsequent heat treatment enabled the formation of Al- and Ni-rich BCC B2 precipitates dispersed homogeneously in the parent FCC matrix. To investigate the mechanical properties of the novel material, tensile specimens were produced with LPBF and tested without machining of their surface, in the as-built as well as heat-treated condition, i.e. 950 °C for 6 h. After tensile testing, fracture characterization was carried out. As a reference material, EN 1.4517 super duplex steel specimens extracted from a conventionally casted and solution heat-treated block, were tested and the obtained mechanical properties were compared with those of the presented HEA. The concluding findings of this work can be summarized as follows:

i) Blending of prealloyed powder with elemental fine particles can be utilized to obtain novel HEA compositions in homogenous powder blends, suitable for LPBF processing.

ii) DOE methodology and RSM can be used effectively to provide a range of LPBF process parameters suitable for low porosity material within a selected design space.

iii) The synthesized Al 0. 9Cr 0. 9Fe 2. 1Ni 2.1alloy showed good LPBF processability without cracks. Cracking elimination was driven by the as-built FCC microstructure, imposed by the reduction of the Al content in the powder blend. Additionally, a wide range of process parameters was found capable of providing minimum porosity material (<0.1 %).

iv) The microstructure of the as-built Al 0. 9Cr 0. 9Fe 2. 1Ni 2.1alloy consisted practically of FCC grains, while heat treatment at 950 °C for 6 h led to the formation of a refined dual-phase FCC A1 + BCC B2 microstructure. The formation of the refined microstructure through secondary phase precipitation after heat treatment of a metastable microstructure is an advantage of the LPBF processing route.

v) Tensile testing of the Al 0. 9Cr 0. 9Fe 2. 1Ni 2.1specimens showed that the novel alloy was capable of outperforming the reference material in mechanical strength in both the as-built and heat-treated conditions while showing lower, yet acceptable elongation. The fracture surface characterization revealed a ductile failure mode with dimple formation. Since the specimens were tested without post-processing of the surface, further improvement of the mechanical properties can be expected with machined specimens.

vi) Owing to the presence of fine BCC B2 precipitates, the heat-treated Al 0. 9Cr 0. 9Fe 2. 1Ni 2.1specimens exhibited significant strain hardening. Quantification of the BCC B2 precipitate size with image analysis showed that the majority of them had an equivalent circle diameter (ECD) of 1 µm or lower, as seen in Fig. 12a. The aspect ratio distribution, seen in Fig. 12b, indicated that most of the BCC B2 precipitates were elongated or disk-shaped.
