The current study showed that the dual-phase microstructure was obtained only after heat treatment, starting from a near single-phase FCC microstructure of the as-built material. This is different from the observation in conventional casting processes where the Al-depleted (0.5 <x < 0. 8) HEA alloys Al x(Co)CrFeNi, show both FCC and BCC phases in their microstructure after solidification [48,49]. While AM processing of the AlCrFe 2Ni 2alloy occurs through solidification of primary BCC B2, here the addition of Fe and Ni particles led to an Al 0. 9Cr 0. 9Fe 2. 1Ni 2.1composition which solidified with a near single-phase FCC microstructure. Accordingly, crack-free specimens were obtained without baseplate preheating. Subsequent heat treatment of the as-built material at 950 °C for 6 h led to the precipitation of BCC B2 and hence to a refined dual-phase FCC A1 + BCC B2 microstructure. Since heat treatment at high temperature stabilized a dual-phase microstructure, it is suggested that the as-built, near single-phase microstructure was metastable and was formed due to the high cooling rates of the LPBF process. Overall, the enriched presence of the FCC phase compared to BCC B2 after heat treatment was expected due to the reduced Al content in the obtained alloy composition after the blending of Fe and Ni particles with the AlCrFe2Ni2 prealloyed powder. Similar to Al-depleted alloys found in the Al-Co-Cr-Fe-Ni system, here Al acted as a BCC B2 phase stabilizing element in the studied Co-free system. The absence of the BCC A2 phase, frequently observed along with the BCC B2 phase in the Al-(Co)-Cr-Fe-Ni system [8,18,23,49], could be related to the reduction of the Cr content in the final alloy composition obtained after the addition of Fe and Ni particles to the powder blend. Cr was seen to be segregated along with Fe mainly in the FCC phase, although small amounts of the BCC phase could be still present but challenging to detect with EDS mapping. Since Cr has been reported to be a BCC A2 stabilizing element, increasing the Cr content in the alloy composition could potentially promote the formation of the BCC A2 along with the BCC B2 phase [15,50]. In this study, a Co-free HEA powder with Al-lean composition, Al 0. 9Cr 0. 9Fe 2. 1Ni 2.1, was prepared by blending the baseline prealloyed powder of a crack-prone AlCrFe 2Ni 2alloy with fine Fe and Ni elemental particles. The HEA powder blend was processed successfully with LPBF and crack-free material was obtained. The porosity of the as-built material was minimized with the use of a DOE methodology and the optimum process parameters were identified according to RSM. Microstructural characterization showed that the as-built material had a metastable, near single-phase FCC microstructure. Subsequent heat treatment enabled the formation of Al- and Ni-rich BCC B2 precipitates dispersed homogeneously in the parent FCC matrix. To investigate the mechanical properties of the novel material, tensile specimens were produced with LPBF and tested without machining of their surface, in the as-built as well as heat-treated condition, i.e. 950 °C for 6 h. After tensile testing, fracture characterization was carried out. As a reference material, EN 1.4517 super duplex steel specimens extracted from a conventionally casted and solution heat-treated block, were tested and the obtained mechanical properties were compared with those of the presented HEA. The concluding findings of this work can be summarized as follows:

i) Blending of prealloyed powder with elemental fine particles can be utilized to obtain novel HEA compositions in homogenous powder blends, suitable for LPBF processing.

ii) DOE methodology and RSM can be used effectively to provide a range of LPBF process parameters suitable for low porosity material within a selected design space.

iii) The synthesized Al 0. 9Cr 0. 9Fe 2. 1Ni 2.1alloy showed good LPBF processability without cracks. Cracking elimination was driven by the as-built FCC microstructure, imposed by the reduction of the Al content in the powder blend. Additionally, a wide range of process parameters was found capable of providing minimum porosity material (<0.1 %).

iv) The microstructure of the as-built Al 0. 9Cr 0. 9Fe 2. 1Ni 2.1alloy consisted practically of FCC grains, while heat treatment at 950 °C for 6 h led to the formation of a refined dual-phase FCC A1 + BCC B2 microstructure. The formation of the refined microstructure through secondary phase precipitation after heat treatment of a metastable microstructure is an advantage of the LPBF processing route.

v) Tensile testing of the Al 0. 9Cr 0. 9Fe 2. 1Ni 2.1specimens showed that the novel alloy was capable of outperforming the reference material in mechanical strength in both the as-built and heat-treated conditions while showing lower, yet acceptable elongation. The fracture surface characterization revealed a ductile failure mode with dimple formation. Since the specimens were tested without post-processing of the surface, further improvement of the mechanical properties can be expected with machined specimens.

vi) Owing to the presence of fine BCC B2 precipitates, the heat-treated Al 0. 9Cr 0. 9Fe 2. 1Ni 2.1specimens exhibited significant strain hardening. According to the applied Hollomon’s model, the work hardening exponent of the novel alloy was approximately 58 % higher compared to that of the reference super duplex steel. The longitudinal section micrographs of the LPBF processed Al 0. 9Cr 0. 9Fe 2. 1Ni 2.1alloy in the as-built state revealed a columnar-cellular microstructure, as seen in Fig. 9a. Elongated cells grew along the build direction due to the vertical heat flux, but also in other directions because of the scanning pattern rotation and the remelting that occurred during the fusion of the powder layers. At higher magnification, submicron-sized cellular-dendritic structures were observed, as seen in Fig. 9b. The chemical composition of the as-built material measured by EDS can be seen in Table 10. It was observed that the chemical composition was equivalent to that of the powder blend, given in Table 6, considering the uncertainty of the ICP-OES measurement. The EBSD phase map, seen in Fig. 10a, displayed a near single-phase FCC microstructure (97 % FCC - 3 % BCC). Local powder inhomogeneity caused by powder blending led to the formation of BCC phase islands due to the processing of the AlCrFe2Ni2 prealloyed powder [23]. The primary FCC grains grew through multiple layers, as seen In the inverse pole figure (IPF) map of Fig. 10b, and resulted in a near< 001 > fiber texture, according to the pole figures of Fig. 10c. This texture is quite frequently observed for FCC and BCC metals after additive manufacturing [46]. However, the observed texture was weak, also because elemental fine particles with higher melting temperatures could potentially serve as nucleation sites for new grains. After heat treatment at 950 °C for 6 h, the microstructure of the tensile specimens was observed in SEM. The back-scattered electron micrographs revealed a fine dual-phase microstructure. The parent FCC grains displayed elongated darker precipitates, as seen in Fig. 11a and b at higher magnification. Overall, it was seen that a combination of globular, disk-shaped, elongated and irregular-shaped precipitates were present and homogeneously dispersed in the FCC matrix. At grain boundaries, the precipitates appeared to be larger. The EDS map analysis displayed in Fig. 11c showed that they are rich in Al and Ni and therefore identified as BCC B2 phases, analogous to those observed in Al-depleted Al-Co-Cr-Fe-Ni systems [4,47]. On the other side, the parent FCC grains were A1, rich in Fe and Cr, as seen in Fig. 11c. The EBSD analysis confirmed that the precipitates are well indexed using the BCC B2 crystal structure data, as seen in the phase map presented in Fig. 11b. The fine precipitates were characterized by image analysis of SEM micrographs taken at high magnification. The overall fraction of the precipitates was measured by the ImageJ software, which showed a 75 %−25 % FCC-BCC B2 microstructure. Quantification of the BCC B2 precipitate size with image analysis showed that the majority of them had an equivalent circle diameter (ECD) of 1 µm or lower, as seen in Fig. 12a. The aspect ratio distribution, seen in Fig. 12b, indicated that most of the BCC B2 precipitates were elongated or disk-shaped. The detailed precipitate size distribution statistics are given in Table 11. An average ECD of 450 nm was measured, along with a 2.42 aspect ratio for the BCC B2 precipitates. The current study showed that the dual-phase microstructure was obtained only after heat treatment, starting from a near single-phase FCC microstructure of the as-built material. This is different from the observation in conventional casting processes where the Al-depleted (0.5 <x < 0. 8) HEA alloys Al x(Co)CrFeNi, show both FCC and BCC phases in their microstructure after solidification [48,49]. While AM processing of the AlCrFe 2Ni 2alloy occurs through solidification of primary BCC B2, here the addition of Fe and Ni particles led to an Al 0. 9Cr 0. 9Fe 2. 1Ni 2.1composition which solidified with a near single-phase FCC microstructure. Accordingly, crack-free specimens were obtained without baseplate preheating. Subsequent heat treatment of the as-built material at 950 °C for 6 h led to the precipitation of BCC B2 and hence to a refined dual-phase FCC A1 + BCC B2 microstructure. Since heat treatment at high temperature stabilized a dual-phase microstructure, it is suggested that the as-built, near single-phase microstructure was metastable and was formed due to the high cooling rates of the LPBF process. Overall, the enriched presence of the FCC phase compared to BCC B2 after heat treatment was expected due to the reduced Al content in the obtained alloy composition after the blending of Fe and Ni particles with the AlCrFe2Ni2 prealloyed powder. Similar to Al-depleted alloys found in the Al-Co-Cr-Fe-Ni system, here Al acted as a BCC B2 phase stabilizing element in the studied Co-free system. The absence of the BCC A2 phase, frequently observed along with the BCC B2 phase in the Al-(Co)-Cr-Fe-Ni system [8,18,23,49], could be related to the reduction of the Cr content in the final alloy composition obtained after the addition of Fe and Ni particles to the powder blend. Cr was seen to be segregated along with Fe mainly in the FCC phase, although small amounts of the BCC phase could be still present but challenging to detect with EDS mapping. Since Cr has been reported to be a BCC A2 stabilizing element, increasing the Cr content in the alloy composition could potentially promote the formation of the BCC A2 along with the BCC B2 phase [15,50]. Tensile and microhardness tests were performed on the as-built and heat-treated tensile specimens as well as the super duplex reference material. The obtained engineering stress-strain curves are displayed in Fig. 13. The stress-strain curves of the specimens that showed the highest tensile strength were selected, while the average values of the obtained mechanical properties are given in Table 12. The Al 0. 9Cr 0. 9Fe 2. 1Ni 2.1specimens showed a lower value of Young’s modulus compared to the reference super duplex steel. Specifically, the as-built Al 0. 9Cr 0. 9Fe 2. 1Ni 2.1specimens showed a 28 % decrease in Youngs’s modulus compared to the heat-treated specimens and a 52 % decrease compared to the reference material. However, the average obtained value of the heat-treated Al 0. 9Cr 0. 9Fe 2. 1Ni 2.1alloy was 161 GPa and therefore comparable to other AM-processed alloys, such as 316L and Inconel 718 [51]. In terms of yield stress and hardness, it was found that the as-built Al 0. 9Cr 0. 9Fe 2. 1Ni 2.1specimens exhibited 16 % higher hardness, and 25 % higher yield strength compared to the heat-treated specimens. This may be attributed to a stress-relief effect since the as-built material could have residual stresses originating from the rapid heating-cooling regime of the LPBF process. The yield strength of the heat-treated Al 0. 9Cr 0. 9Fe 2. 1Ni 2.1alloy was 9 % lower than that of the super duplex steel and the hardness was approximately the same. In the plastic strain region, a Portevin-Le Chatelier (PLC) effect was revealed for the obtained stress-strain curves. The periodical occurrence of serration at room or medium temperature tensile testing has been linked with high strain rates [52]. Furthermore, the mechanism of dynamic strain aging (DSA) through dislocation pinning by solute Al atoms has been hypothesized to explain serrations found in Al-containing HEA systems, such as Al 0. 3CoCreFeNi [53]and Al 0. 5CoCreFeNi [54]. Overall, it was seen that both the as-built and the heat-treated Al 0. 9Cr 0. 9Fe 2. 1Ni 2.1specimens outperformed the reference super duplex steel specimens in tensile strength and displayed average elongation of 15 % and 20 %, respectively. Specifically, an increase in tensile strength of approximately 27 % was observed for both the as-built and heat-treated Al 0. 9Cr 0. 9Fe 2. 1Ni 2.1specimens compared to the reference material. However, the super duplex specimens showed higher elongation at fracture compared to Al 0. 9Cr 0. 9Fe 2. 1Ni 2.1specimens. Yet it must be considered that the Al 0. 9Cr 0. 9Fe 2. 1Ni 2.1specimens were tested without post-processing of their surface and earlier failure could be caused due to stress concentration promoted by higher surface roughness. It is therefore expected that testing of machined specimens would further increase the obtained elongation values. Besides the fact that the Al 0. 9Cr 0. 9Fe 2. 1Ni 2.1specimens showed superior tensile strength compared to the reference material, improved elongation and notable strain hardening were observed for the heat-treated specimens. To quantify the strain hardening and compare the tested specimen mechanical responses, the true stress-strain curves were calculated and modeled using Hollomon’s equations [55], expressed in Eq.3and Eq.4: (3)σ=Κεn(4)lnσ=lnΚ+nlnεwhere σis the true stress, εis the true strain, Kis the work hardening coefficient and nis the work hardening exponent. With the use of Eq.4, the Kand nvalues can be obtained after the application of a linear regression model to the measured tensile stress-strain data. The true stress-strain curves of the tested specimens can be Fig. 14a. The double logarithmic diagnostic graphs of Fig. 14b-d display the fitted models along with the experimentally obtained curves. The Kand nvalues, as well as the coefficient of determination R2of the applied models, are given in Table 13. From the diagnostic graphs, it was seen that the fitted curves were consistent with the respective true stress-strain curves of the tested specimens, however, a small deviation could be seen for the as-built Al 0. 9Cr 0. 9Fe 2. 1Ni 2.1and the super duplex curves at low plastic strain. The latter fact is an indication that these specimens went through a two-stage hardening mechanism, thus, two models with different nvalues could be considered to optimize the fitting [56,57]. However, the applied models showed high R2values ( R2>0.95) and consequently, they were accepted. From the calculated nvalues, it was seen that among all specimens the rate of hardening was highest for the heat-treated Al 0. 9Cr 0. 9Fe 2. 1Ni 2.1specimens. Specifically, the work hardening exponent of the heat-treated specimen was 42 % higher than that of the as-built specimen and 58 % higher than that of the super duplex steel. Thus, it was evident that heat treatment increased the strain hardening capacity of the Al 0. 9Cr 0. 9Fe 2. 1Ni 2.1alloy. Since the heat-treated specimens incorporated a dual-phase microstructure, it is expected that strain hardening occurred due to the presence of fine Al-, Ni-rich BCC B2 precipitates that impeded the dislocation motion, a mechanism which has also been described for similar Co-containing systems [47,58]as well as Al-alloyed stainless steels [59]. The fractography investigations of Al 0. 9Cr 0. 9Fe 2. 1Ni 2.1tensile specimens can be seen in Fig. 15. The fracture surfaces formed a cup-cone shape. A crack propagation area was combined with shear lip formation, as seen in Fig. 15a and b. The shear lips area was more uniform and larger for the as-built specimens, while for the heat-treated specimens it was discontinuous. For both Al 0. 9Cr 0. 9Fe 2. 1Ni 2.1fracture surfaces, the shear lips were not surrounding the crack propagation area completely, denoting a moderately ductile fracture. Higher magnification micrographs, such as the one seen in Fig. 15c, showed that both Al 0. 9Cr 0. 9Fe 2. 1Ni 2.1fracture surfaces embodied defects that were generated during LPBF processing, such were lack-of-fusion and pores of approximately 10-20 µm in diameter. These voids could have acted as stress concentration and microcrack initiation sites as seen in Fig. 15d. Apart from the defects, the crack propagation area was covered with microscale dimples as seen in Fig. 15e. The dimple formation was a result of plastic deformation which verified the ductile nature of the failure. It was concluded that when the specimens reached the plastic deformation stage, coalescence of generated voids and microcracks reduced the critical area and ultimately led to failure. In this study, a Co-free HEA powder with Al-lean composition, Al 0. 9Cr 0. 9Fe 2. 1Ni 2.1, was prepared by blending the baseline prealloyed powder of a crack-prone AlCrFe 2Ni 2alloy with fine Fe and Ni elemental particles. The HEA powder blend was processed successfully with LPBF and crack-free material was obtained. The porosity of the as-built material was minimized with the use of a DOE methodology and the optimum process parameters were identified according to RSM. Microstructural characterization showed that the as-built material had a metastable, near single-phase FCC microstructure. Subsequent heat treatment enabled the formation of Al- and Ni-rich BCC B2 precipitates dispersed homogeneously in the parent FCC matrix. To investigate the mechanical properties of the novel material, tensile specimens were produced with LPBF and tested without machining of their surface, in the as-built as well as heat-treated condition, i.e. 950 °C for 6 h. After tensile testing, fracture characterization was carried out. As a reference material, EN 1.4517 super duplex steel specimens extracted from a conventionally casted and solution heat-treated block, were tested and the obtained mechanical properties were compared with those of the presented HEA. The concluding findings of this work can be summarized as follows:

i) Blending of prealloyed powder with elemental fine particles can be utilized to obtain novel HEA compositions in homogenous powder blends, suitable for LPBF processing.

ii) DOE methodology and RSM can be used effectively to provide a range of LPBF process parameters suitable for low porosity material within a selected design space.

iii) The synthesized Al 0. 9Cr 0. 9Fe 2. 1Ni 2.1alloy showed good LPBF processability without cracks. Cracking elimination was driven by the as-built FCC microstructure, imposed by the reduction of the Al content in the powder blend. Additionally, a wide range of process parameters was found capable of providing minimum porosity material (<0.1 %).

iv) The microstructure of the as-built Al 0. 9Cr 0. 9Fe 2. 1Ni 2.1alloy consisted practically of FCC grains, while heat treatment at 950 °C for 6 h led to the formation of a refined dual-phase FCC A1 + BCC B2 microstructure. The formation of the refined microstructure through secondary phase precipitation after heat treatment of a metastable microstructure is an advantage of the LPBF processing route.

v) Tensile testing of the Al 0. 9Cr 0. 9Fe 2. 1Ni 2.1specimens showed that the novel alloy was capable of outperforming the reference material in mechanical strength in both the as-built and heat-treated conditions while showing lower, yet acceptable elongation. The fracture surface characterization revealed a ductile failure mode with dimple formation. Since the specimens were tested without post-processing of the surface, further improvement of the mechanical properties can be expected with machined specimens.

vi) Owing to the presence of fine BCC B2 precipitates, the heat-treated Al 0. 9Cr 0. 9Fe 2. 1Ni 2.1specimens exhibited significant strain hardening. According to the applied Hollomon’s model, the work hardening exponent of the novel alloy was approximately 58 % higher compared to that of the reference super duplex steel. The HEA samples were produced using HVAM-3 non-consumable vacuum arc melting. The cast plate was homogenized at 1200 °C for 2 h using air furnace followed by water quenching. Cold rolling reduced the plate thickness from 5 mm to 1 mm, achieving a thickness reduction ratio of 80 %. Consequently, the heat treatments were carried out at 700 °C, 800 °C, and 900 °C for 1 h using air furnace followed by water quenching. Based on this trend, a high-temperature (850 °C), short-duration (5 min) annealing process followed by water quenching was proposed to optimize the size and volume fraction of both the sigma phase and the RX region.

The equiatomic NiCoCrFe HEA was synthesized with a vacuum magnetic levitation melting high-purity constituent elements (purity >99.9 wt%) in a high-purity argon atmosphere. The ingots were flipped and remelted at least three times to ensure thorough mixing and chemical uniformity. The cylindrical ingots with a dimension of Φ60 × 50 mm 3were cold-forged with a 50% reduction in height, and then cut into sheets with 1.6 mm thickness along the longitudinal section, followed by a cold-rolling with 50% reduction to 0.8 mm thickness. Subsequently, these sheets were annealed at 1,173 K for 1 h for full recrystallization, followed by water-quenching. Rectangular dog-bone tensile specimens were sectioned from the recrystallized sheets by electrical discharge machine (EDM) with the tensile axis oriented along the rolling direction. The gage dimensions (width, thickness, and length) of quasi-static and dynamic tensile specimens were 3.8 × 0.8 × 10.0 mm 3and 3.8 × 0.8 × 4.0 mm 3. In addition, the quasi-static tensile specimens with the gage dimensions of 3.8 × 0.8 × 4.0 mm 3were also prepared for comparison. All faces of the specimens were mechanically polished using 800-grit SiC paper.

Different to conventional bulk metallurgy, powder metallurgy (PM) by spark plasma sintering (SPS) gas-atomized powder is used in the present study to produce single FCC phase CrFeCoNiMo 0. The gas-atomized CrFeCoNiMo 0.2powders with an initial particle size distribution ranging from several microns to more than 100 µm were sintered in the FCT HP D 25/3 SPS device at 1000 °C with a heating rate of 100 °C/min. Constant pressure of 30 MPa was applied, and held for 10 min during sintering. PM CrFeCoNiMo 0.2high entropy alloys were produced by spark plasma sintering (SPS) with gas-atomized powders.

Fe x(CoCrMnNi) 100-xingots were fabricated by vacuum-arc melting using over 99.9 wt.% high purity Co, Cr, Mn, Ni, and Fe under argon atmosphere. The ingot was re-melted and flipped at least 5 times to ensure chemical composition homogeneity during the melting process. Sequentially, as-cast ingots were cold-rolled up to 90 % thickness reduction. Annealing at 1150 °C for 15 min and further water quenching was performed for coarse recrystallized grain size. Before the UNSM treatment, the surface of all alloys was mechanically polished by SiC paper. UNSM treatment was conducted on both front and backside surfaces of 1 mm thick alloys applying the 20 kHz frequency, 30 um strike amplitude and 30 m/min scanning speed with 10 N static load.

The samples of CrFeCoNi alloy were prepared by arc-melting a mixture of pure elements. The ingots were re-melted several times, to ensure the compositional homogeneity, before casting into Cu-molds. The ingots were homogenized at 1200 °C for 24 h under argon (Ar) flow and then quenched in the iced water. The cold-rolling was carried out to a ∼80% reduction in thickness. The cold-rolled samples were annealed at 800 °C for 1 h, to achieve complete recrystallization. The samples were quenched in the iced water again. After this processing, the samples had equiaxed grains with an average grain size of ∼5 μm. Finally, the samples were machined into the flat dog-bone shaped tensile specimens with 25 mm gage length, 4 mm width, and 3 mm thickness.

The HEA was fabricated by a compact vacuum induction melting equipment (model; MC100V, Indutherm, Walzbachtal-Wossingen, Germany) under an argon atmosphere using commercial pure elements (the purity of each raw material was 99.9% at least). Raw elements were alloyed in a ZrO 2-coated alumina crucible to make a master alloy of 150 g in weight. The master alloy was molten and poured into a rectangular graphite module (length; 100 mm, width; 35 mm, thickness; 8 mm). The ingot was homogenized at 1100 °C for 6 h, pickled in a 20% HCl, and then cold-rolled (75%) at room temperature with a thickness reduction of 75% to produce a 2-mm-thick sheet. The sheets were annealed at 1000 °C, 950 °C, 900 °C for 10 min. S1), the sheet was annealed for 1 h at that temperature.

The equiatomic ingots of CrMnFeCoNi were fabricated using raw materials with a purity of 99.9% by a vacuum induction melting technique in an argon atmosphere. Prior to melting, the raw materials were cleaned and dried with acetone to prevent the moist furnace charge from generating gas during the melting process. During melting, a high vacuum was maintained, and the melting temperature was raised to 1900 ℃ within 25 min. The ingot was flipped and re-melted at least 4 times to ensure composition homogeneity. In order to eliminate local segregation of elements, the ingot was kept at 1200 ℃ for 15 h and then rolled and forged into bars with a diameter of 60-65 mm after being kept at 1230 ℃. The bars were further cut into plates with a thickness of 3 mm by a wire saw for the ultrasonic shot peening process. Prior to the ultrasonic shot peening, all samples were mechanically polished with a grinding machine and ultrasonically cleaned in an ethanol bath. The USP process was carried out with the peening durations of 3 min, 6 min and 9 min for the samples.

The equimolar CoCrFeNi MEA samples were synthesized by arc melting Co, Cr, Fe and Ni with > 99.9 wt.% purity under an argon atmosphere in a vacuum induction furnace and then directionally solidified into [001] SC rods using the Bridgeman technique at a constant withdrawal rate of 3.5 mm/min. The as-cast samples were heated to 1200 °C for 24 h followed by air cooling to ambient temperature ( Xiao et al. The rod was cut into bulks with three specific orientations of 〈001〉, 〈011〉 and 〈111〉 as shown in Fig. 1(b), then mechanically ground by conventional metallographic routines and further polished by SiO 2suspension into a mirror. The alloy ingots with nominal compositions of NiCoCrFe, NiCoCrFeSi 0.3, and NiCoCrFeAl 0. 3Si 0.3(molar ratio, abbreviated as NiCoCrFe, Si 0.3, and Al 0. 3Si 0.3, respectively) were fabricated by arc-melting of high purity metals (purity greater than 99.95 %) in a high purity argon atmosphere. The alloy ingots were re-melted five to eight times, with magnetic agitation, to ensure chemical uniformity. Subsequently, they were rapidly drop-casted into a water-cooled copper mold measuring 100 × 10 × 2 mm 3. The resulting sheets were homogenized at 1100 ℃ for 5 h, cold rolled to 70 % thickness, and then subjected to recrystallization annealing at 900 ℃ for 1 h, followed by water quenching. Tensile samples in the shape of rectangular dog bones were prepared using electrical discharge machining (EDM), with a gauge length of 8 mm, width of 2 mm and thickness of 0.6 mm.

This alloy was melted by vacuum induction melting and cast into a 50 kg ingot. The thermomechanical process is shown in Fig. The ingot was first machined into blocks then heated to 1030 °C for 1 h to obtain the highest γ fraction for raising the workability during the rolling processes. The as-austenitized samples were hot-rolled for a 60 % reduction in thickness and then quenched into water. The hot-rolled sheets were then annealed at 1030 °C for 1 h and cold-rolled for 75 %. To obtain dual phase structure, the cold-rolled sheets were then annealed at 950 °C for 30 min, followed by water quenching to ambient temperature.

The dog-bone specimens were annealed at temperatures of 1200 °C for times of 45 min in evacuated quartz tube with 5 × 10 −3torr to acquire equiaxed microstructures.

The three investigated alloys were prepared by vacuum arc melting in a Ti-gettered argon atmosphere. The ingots were flipped over and remelted at least five times for chemical homogeneity and then rapidly dropped into a water-cooled copper mold with a dimension of 100 mm × 12 mm × 5 mm. Subsequently, the cast ingots were homogenized at 1200 °C for 2 h to reduce solute segregation and recrystallized using a phase-selective recrystallization method [ 11], which was achieved by 30 % cold rolling and annealing at 1200 °C for two cycles to completely recrystallize the FCC phase while recovering the B2 phase (Fig. Finally, the samples were subjected to aging at 700 °C for 2 h.

A non-equiatomic FeMnCrNiAl high-entropy alloy (HEA) has been processed by cold rolling and annealing to prepare samples with a fully-recrystallized structure, and composite structures of recovered and recrystallized structures. XRD patterns of the Fe 40Mn 15Cr 15Ni 25Al 5HEA in the homogenization (S0), 75% cold rolling (S1), recrystallization (S2), and partially recrystallization (S3) samples. To ensure chemical homogeneity, each ingot was flipped and re-melted 5 times and then drop cast into a rectangular plate with the dimension of 100 × 10 × 2 mm 3. Further grain refinement was achieved through cold rolling to a thickness reduction of 75% (the thickness changed from 2 to 0.5 mm), followed by a recrystallization process at 1000 °C for 5 min. For another sample, the rolled sheets were annealed at a temperature of 700 °C for 5 h. The cooling method for the above heat treatment was water quenching.

In this paper, CoCrCu1. 2FeNi high entropy alloy (HEA) was prepared by vacuum suspension melting. 2FeNi high entropy alloy (HEA) was prepared by vacuum suspension melting. The original ingot of CoCrCu 1. 2FeNi HEA was prepared by 5 five-times vacuum suspension melting. The cylinder sample of φ16 × 25 mm was cut from the ingot, and then the cold-deformation experiment with 50 % deformation was carried out via the hydraulic press of 2000 kN. The recrystallization annealing experiment was carried out on the sample after the experiment. The recrystallization annealing process was selected as follows: annealed at 650 ℃, 750 ℃, 850 ℃ and 950 ℃ for 30 min, 60 min, 90 min and 120 min, respectively, and then cooled with the furnace. In this experiment, the pure metal with molar ratio of Co, Cr, Cu, Fe, Ni = 1:1:1.2:1:1 (99.9 % purity) was used as the experimental raw material. After 50 % cold-deformation, recrystallization annealing experiments involving the annealing temperatures of 650-950 ℃ and the annealing times of 30-120 min were carried out on the cold-deformed HEA.

In this paper, Ti, Al and other raw materials with a purity exceeding 99.7 % were selected to prepare LRHEAs by vacuum induction melting furnace. Before melting, the raw materials are mechanically ground to remove surface impurities, followed by ultrasonic cleaning with anhydrous ethanol or acetone to remove the surface oxide film. During the metal melting process, the alloy ingot is repeatedly melted four times in the melting furnace to ensure the uniformity of the composition. The molten alloy is then poured into the ingot mold to form a dense ingot. The ingot was homogenized for 1 hour at 1000℃ in an environment filled with argon gas, and then water quenched to obtain a uniform alloy. The G160 alloy was processed through die forging and annealing to achieve a bimodal heterostructure. Radial forging was performed at room temperature with a 45 % deformation using a C41-2000 air hammer, which elongated the grains and introduced an uneven grain size distribution.

The Co 35Cr 20Fe 15Mn 15Ni 15HEA ingot was prepared by arc melting high-purity elements (with a purity greater than 99.9% in weight percentage) in an Ar gas atmosphere and repeatedly melted 5 times to ensure the uniformity of chemical composition. The ingot was homogenized at 1200 °C for 5 h and then rolled at room temperature for a reduction of 40%, followed by annealing at 900 °C for 20 min and then rolled at room temperature for 40% reduction, followed by annealing at 1000 °C for 30 min to obtain recrystallized microstructure, all by water quenching to room temperature. Then, the specimens were rolled with a reduction of 10% at room temperature (denoted by 10% RR), 10% (denoted by 10% CR), 20% (denoted by 20% CR) and 30% reduction (denoted by 30% CR) at cryogenic temperature (−196 °C), respectively. Then, heat treatment (HT) of the 20% CR sample was conducted at 600 °C for 1 h (denoted by 20% CR + HT).

In the preliminary work, after testing the dynamic impact performances of the specimens at 77/298 K, specimen B was selected for the subsequent heat treatment process [25]. The process parameters for specimen B were as follows: laser power is 300 W, laser scanning speed is 800 mm/s, layer thickness is 0.06 mm, and layer spacing is 0.1 mm. The printed specimens were prepared into the cylindrical specimens of φ6 * 7.2 mm and the hat-shaped specimens as shown in Fig. 1(d). Through the utilization of cold-rolling and short-duration annealing techniques, we successfully achieved a partially recrystallized microstructure in the MEA, primarily consisting of nearly single face-centered cubic (FCC) microstructure with NiAl-rich B2 nano-precipitates. Arc-melting was employed to produce Fe 62Ni 15Cr 13Si 7Al 3(at%) MEA ingots with high purity elements (>99.9 wt%), under the protection of a Ti-gettered argon atmosphere. The ingots were re-melted 5 times with electromagnetic stirring and then drop casted into water-cooled Cu molds measuring 30 mm × 10 mm × 10 mm. The as-cast ingots were cold rolled, reducing their thickness by ∼85%. The rolled sheets were annealed at 1073 K for 5 min and then quenched in water.

The ingots were re-melted 5 times with electromagnetic stirring and then drop casted into water-cooled Cu molds measuring 30 mm × 10 mm × 10 mm. The as-cast ingots were cold rolled, reducing their thickness by ∼85%. The rolled sheets were annealed at 1073 K for 5 min and then quenched in water.

The equimolar CrMnFeCoNi HEA is prepared by vacuum induction melting with high purity Fe, Mn, Cr, Co and Ni powders (99.9 wt%). After homogenization at 1200 °C, the as-cast alloy ingot (thickness 20 mm) undergoes hot rolling with approximately 50% reduction in thickness. Dynamic compression experiments are performed on the as-rolled CrMnFeCoNi HEA at low temperatures with an SHPB. Cylindrical samples with a diameter 4.0 mm and a length of 3.6 mm are prepared via electrical discharge machining. The samples are sanded with sandpaper and polished with silica solution sequentially, and then subjected to electro-polishing in a solution of 10% perchloric acid and 90% ethanol at 30 V and −20°C. Before TEM characterization, the sample is ground to a thickness of 100μmand then punched into disks with a 3-mm diameter. Then the disks are thinned down using an automatic twin-jet electro-polisher (Struers TenuPol-5) with a solution of 10% perchloric acid and 90% ethanol.

The equimolar CoCrFeNi HEA ingot used in this work was prepared by vacuum induction levitation melting from pure Co, Cr, Fe, and Ni metals with 99.9 wt.% purity constituent elements. The ingot was remelted four times to promote chemical homogeneity and then dropped into a rectangular cross-section copper mold with a length of 300 mm and an inner diameter of 25 mm. The ingot was cut to a rod of diameter 20 mm and length 200 mm, which was then homogenized at 1473 K for 24 h. The rod was first hot-rotary swaged to 8 mm in diameter along the longitudinal direction after preheating at 1173 K for 1 h, and then hot-drawn to 1 mm in steps at 1023 K. Subsequently, the HEA wires of diameter 1 mm was subjected to multi-pass cold-drawing at ambient temperature with an areal reduction of ∼10% followed by annealing at 1173 K for 1 h in each step, resulting in a final diameter of ∼70 μm with a length of more than 300 m. The CoCrFeNi microfibers were further treated by ECT. The electric current was applied parallel to the length direction of the treated microfiber using a precision direct current (DC) power supply for 480 s with various current densities of j= 100, 120, 140, 160, 180, 200 A/mm 2, and the corresponding specimens are labeled as ECT100, ECT120, ECT140, ECT160, ECT180 and ECT200, which reach a stable temperature of 623 K, 747 K, 850 K, 943 K, 1013 K, and 1075 K during the ECT, respectively, as measured by an FLIR A325sc infrared camera. For comparison, CHT was also performed on another batch of CoCrFeNi microfibers at 623 K, 747 K, 850 K, 943 K, 1013 K, and 1075 K for 480 s, with the samples labeled as CHT623, CHT747, CHT850, CHT943, CHT1013 and CHT1075, respectively.

The ingot of iHEA was cast in a vacuum induction furnace using pure metals and carbon (>99.8% pure). The sample was then successively hot-rolled, homogenized and water quenched to refine the grain size of iHEA material. The iHEA sample was then processed into a circular plate with a diameter of 42 mm and a thickness of 2 mm to satisfy the size requirement of SMAT. After the SMAT processing, the iHEA sample was cut into six small samples (10 mm × 10 mm × 2 mm). Subsequently, five of the small samples were subjected to thermal aging treatment in a muffle furnace at 400 °C for 10 h, 100 h, 500 h, 800 h and 1000 h, respectively.

Fe 45Mn 35Co 10Cr 10powders were prepared through vacuum melting atomization under an argon atmosphere. A 45# steel plate (275 mm × 275 mm) was used as the building substrate for the fabrication process. The MHEA samples, measuring 30 mm × 60 mm × 20 mm, were produced using an HR-SFPFH-FT1H06 machine (Huirui, China). This machine is equipped with an IPG Gaussian fiber laser capable of reaching a maximum output power of 2 kW and features an adjustable laser spot diameter of 1-2 μm. The L-DED equipment and the laser scan strategy are depicted in Fig. 1d and e, respectively. The employed deposition parameters in this work included a focused laser spot diameter of 1.5 mm, laser power ranging from 200 to 600 W, scan speed ranging from 4 to 10 mm/s, hatch spacing between 0.4 and 0.6 mm, and a powder feed rate of 2.8 g/min. A powder carrier and shielding gas of argon at a flow rate of 9 L/min were also used.

99 % Ni, Fe, Co, Cr, V, and Al was synthesized using a vacuum arc-melting furnace under a high-purity argon atmosphere. The resulting ingots underwent a minimum of five melting cycles and were subsequently air-cooled in a copper mold at 25 °C. To eliminate elemental segregation during solidification, the alloys were then homogenized at 1000 °C for 4 h. Following this, a 70 % thickness reduction cold rolling was performed, followed by static recrystallization at 800 °C for 30 min. All heat treatments were conducted in a controlled environment, with water quenching to room temperature.

%) HEA was produced using a vacuum arc remelting (VAR) furnace (AVA-1500, ACE Vacuum, South Korea) under a high-purity argon (Ar) atmosphere. Commercially pure Co chips (99.9 wt%), Cr chips (99.9 wt%), Ni chips (99.9 wt%), Fe sheets (99.9 wt%) and Mo bars (99.8 wt%) were melted in a water-cooled copper hearth with a tungsten electrode. The ingots were subsequently flipped and remelted five times under an Ar atmosphere to guarantee chemical homogeneity. After homogenization at 1230 °C for 2 h under an Ar atmosphere, the ingots were quickly gas-cooled in the furnace. Consequently, a 2-h heat treatment at 1230 °C, followed by rapid cooling, was conducted after casting to achieve a homogeneous microstructure of the single FCC phase.

The raw material was prepared by suspension melting of elemental ingredients (purity >99.9 wt.%) in high-purity argon atmosphere. To ensure uniformity, the ingot was re-melted at least five times. Then, the as-cast ingot was homogenized at 1200 °C for 24 h followed by air cooling. The as-homogenized material was rolled to 0.5 mm thick after 20 rolling passes with a thickness reduction of 90 %, using a customized machine with rolls fully immersed in liquid nitrogen, to obtain severely refined nanostructure with as high as possible stored energy. By trial and error, the annealing parameters for expected heterostructure, 550 °C for 1 hour followed by air cooling, were identified, by which the resulting microstructure of constituent zones conforms to the key design principles of strong-yet-tough material. As shown in Figs. 3a1-a2, a homogeneous NS experienced recovery but almost no recrystallization, which closely resembles the non-recrystallized zone in heterostructure ( Fig. 1c), was synthesized by annealing as-rolled sheets at 475 °C for 1 h Hardness examination confirms that it does have comparable hardness to the non-recrystallized zone in heterostructure ( Fig. 2f). A fully recrystallized FG structure, whose grain morphology (Figs. 3b1-b2), average grain size (2.1 μm, Fig. 3d) and hardness ( Fig. 2b) are consistent with those of the recrystallized matrix in the heterostructure, was produced by annealing at 600 °C for 1 h Since both the microstructure and hardness are in good agreement, the deformation responses of such homogeneous NS and FG samples can, respectively, represent the intrinsic properties of the non-recrystallized hard zone and recrystallized soft matrix, i.e., the properties of constituent zones when they are deformed independently. Moreover, a CG structure in average grain size of 8.5 μm was prepared as well ( Figs. 3c& e).

The current MEA was prepared by arc melting under an argon atmosphere using pure metals (purity >99.95 wt%) and casted into a 50 × 150 × 15 mm 3copper mold, followed by homogenization at 1200 °C for 5 h. After homogenization, the ingot was hot-rolled at 1100 °C to a sheet with a thickness of 10 mm. The hot-rolled sheet was further cold-rolled (CR) at 25 °C to ∼3 mm thick sheets (∼70 % thickness reduction). The first one involves solution treatment of the CR sample at 1150 °C for 10 min (referred to as CRS), followed by aging at 600 °C, 650 °C, and 700 °C for 96 h (referred to as CRSA−600, CRSA−650, and CRSA−700). The second heat treatment process is that the CR sheet was directly annealed at 600 °C, 650 °C, and 700 °C for 96 h (referred to as CRA−600, CRA−650, and CRA−700). All samples are cooled down to room temperature by water quenching (WQ).

In the current work, gradient microstructures are obtained on laser-powder bed fusion processed (LPBF) CoCrFeMnNi high entropy alloy using ultrasonic nanocrystal surface modification (UNSM). Gas atomized CoCrFeMnNi alloy powders with spherical morphology were prepared from vacuum induction melted ingots. The LPBF experiments were conducted on a commercially available Concept Laser Mlab (GE additive, USA) machine. Cuboidal samples with 6 × 6 × 30 mm 3(width x height x length) dimensions were produced using processing parameters given in Table 1. The wrought samples were prepared from vacuum induction melted CoCrFeMnNi ingots homogenized at 1000 °C for 24 h in an Ar atmosphere. Subsequently, the homogenized slab was hot-rolled at 1000 °C and then annealed at 900 °C for 60 min. To obtain gradient microstructures, the LPBF and wrought samples were UNSM treated. Before the UNSM treatment, the samples were sliced to 1 mm thickness (using wire-electric discharge machining), polished until 1200 grit silicon carbide paper, and then cleaned in ethanol to obtain a clean surface with uniform surface roughness. Later UNSM treatment was conducted on both sides of the sample, as shown in Fig. 1, using the process parameter given in Table 3.

The LPBF experiments were conducted on a commercially available Concept Laser Mlab (GE additive, USA) machine. Cuboidal samples with 6 × 6 × 30 mm 3(width x height x length) dimensions were produced using processing parameters given in Table 1. The wrought samples were prepared from vacuum induction melted CoCrFeMnNi ingots homogenized at 1000 °C for 24 h in an Ar atmosphere. Subsequently, the homogenized slab was hot-rolled at 1000 °C and then annealed at 900 °C for 60 min. To obtain gradient microstructures, the LPBF and wrought samples were UNSM treated. Before the UNSM treatment, the samples were sliced to 1 mm thickness (using wire-electric discharge machining), polished until 1200 grit silicon carbide paper, and then cleaned in ethanol to obtain a clean surface with uniform surface roughness. Later UNSM treatment was conducted on both sides of the sample, as shown in Fig. 1, using the process parameter given in Table 3.

The CoCrFeNi alloys were prepared by vacuum arc melting under a high purity argon atmosphere. Raw materials (purity ≥ 99.95 %) were placed in a water -cooled copper mold and melted for four times to enhance chemical homogeneity. The ingots (50 × 25 × 8 mm 3) were homogenized in vacuum at 1100 °C for 24 h and then cold-rolled to sheets with thickness of 1 mm (87.5 % reduction). The sheets were subsequently annealed in air at 600, 650, and 700 °C for 5 min to obtain three different HSMs (henceforth called HSM1, HSM2, and HSM3, respectively).

A magnetic suspension melting technology was used to fabricate both Ni 43. 4Co 25. 3Cr 25. 3Al 3Ti 3(referred to as V0) and Ni 42. 4Co 24. 3Cr 24. 3Al 3Ti 3V 3(referred to as V3) from an appropriate mixture of Ni, Co, Cr, Al, Ti, and V metal pieces (purity ≥99.7 wt%). Ingots with a diameter of 110 mm and a height of 90 mm were cast from both MEAs. A 10 mm thick piece was cut off via electrical discharge machining and homogenized at 1150 °C for 4 h followed by water-quenching. Subsequently, the piece was cold-rolled to a total thickness reduction of 80 %. To produce fine recrystallized grains and introduce L1 2-type nanoparticles, aging was performed at 900 °C for 24 h.

80 mm × 30 mm × 2 mm plates of both cold-rolled MEAs were welded using EBOCAM EK150C-EG150-60BL EBW equipment (Steigerwald Strahltechnik GMBH). EBW was performed at an accelerating voltage of 150 kV, a current of 7.5 mA, and a welding rate of 600 mm/min under a vacuum of 8 × 10 −3Pa. Therefore, both the cold-rolled V-free and V-doped MEA were aged at 900 °C for 24 h in order to introduce L1 2nanoparticles and improve the mechanical properties of the weld. These specimens are referred to as EBWed V0 and EBWed V3.

High-pressure torsion (HPT) was applied to a lamellar eutectic high-entropy alloy (EHEA) to study the effect of severe plastic deformation (SPD) on the composite structure and mechanical properties. An EHEA ingot with a nominal composition of AlCoCrFeNi 2.1(elements in atomic ratios) was prepared by vacuum arc melting of mixtures of the constituent elements (purity ≥99.95 %) and was remelted at least five times in a Ti-gettered high-purity argon atmosphere to ensure chemical homogeneity. The molten alloy was suction-cast into a 10 mm (width) × 100 mm (length) × 2 mm (thickness) water-cooled Cu mold. This was followed by homogenization annealing in a vacuum furnace (Xerion Xtube) at 1023 ± 5 K for 12 h. The disks were deformed using a quasi-constrained HPT system in anvils with a total groove depth of 0.5 mm at a nominal pressure of 6 GPa and a rotational speed of 0.6 rotations/min for 1/4, 1, and 5 rotations at room temperature.

In the present work, the CoCrFeMnNi HEA with heterogeneous structure is prepared by means of cold rolling and subsequent partial recrystallization annealing process. The cast ingot of the equiatomic CoCrFeMnNi HEA was produced by vacuum arc melting using the starting alloy elements with purities of more than ∼99.7 wt%. In order to ensure chemical homogeneity, the cast ingot used in this study was re-melted at least five times, and the corresponding homogeneity detection results can be viewed in the previous paper [ 23]. The final ingot had a diameter of ∼50 mm and a height of ∼265 mm. Subsequently, the cylindrical ingot was hot forged into a slab with the sizes of ∼30 mm × ∼50 mm × ∼340 mm within the temperature ranging from ∼1273 K to ∼1423 K. After annealing at ∼1273 K for ∼90 min, the slab was cold-rolled along its length direction (∼340 mm) from ∼30 mm thick plate to ∼1.2 mm thick sheet. Previous study has revealed the relationship between annealing process parameters, microstructure evolution and strength-ductility synergy [ 23]. According to the further modifying annealing temperature and holding time, a heterostructured CoCrFeMnNi HEA with relatively superior strength-ductility combination was obtained by annealing at ∼973 K for ∼5 min (denoted as 973-5), which was used as the experimental samples in this study.

The Al 0·1CoCrFeNi HEA used in present experiments was prepared by vacuum induction casting with 99.9% purity constituent elements. Hot isostatic pressure (HIP) treatment for the cast ingots were carried out at 1100 °C and 100 MPa for 6 h. After the HIP treatment, the ingots were cooled to 340 °C for 3 h, and then 190 °C for 1 h before releasing the pressure. Thereafter, cubic specimens (5 mm × 5 mm × 5 mm) are prepared by using wire cut electrical discharge machining for both quasi-static and dynamic compression tests. All specimens are mechanically polished before the mechanical tests to remove the surface irregularities.

Herein, heterogeneous and ultra-fine eutectic lamellar microstructure with directional growth along the deposition direction (DD) was obtained by adjusting the process parameters of AM to improve the strength and ductility of EHEAs. Laser melting deposition (LMD) is a unique AM technique combining laser (as an energy source) and powder (as feedstock) processing, which allows direct fabrication of high-density near-net-shape metallic parts from computer-aided design (CAD) files by coaxial powder-delivery layer-by-layer deposition [ 6, 27, 28, 44]. In this work, samples were fabricated by LMD. To obtain a fully lamellar eutectic structure during the LMD process, Al 19. 6EHEA sample with identical composition was also synthesized through vacuum arc melting under a high purity argon atmosphere. The master ingots were completely re-melted at least 5 times to ensure chemical composition homogeneity.

Based on the experimental preparation method [40], this paper simulates the experimental preparation process of FeNiCrCoCu HEA by the MD method and then establishes the related models. The specific methods are provided as follows: (1) The five atoms of the FeNiCrCoCu HEA are randomly distributed in equal proportions (i.e., 1:1:1:1:1) on the FCC crystal structure, and the lattice constant ais set to be 3. (2) At the melting stage, all atoms in the system are heated to 1500 K at a rate of 1 K/ps, and then are relaxed for a while at this temperature to reach the equilibrium state. (3) At the quenching stage, the temperature of the system is reduced at the same rate of 1 K/ps until 300 K and then the atoms are relaxed for a while at this temperature to reach the equilibrium state.

A ∼500 g ingot with a nominal composition of Fe 48. The ingot was homogenized at 1100 °C for 12 h under an argon atmosphere, followed by water-quenching. The influence of DCT on the residual stress, microstructural evolution, and mechanical properties of LMD-fabricated CoCrFeMnNi HEA was elucidated. All the HEA samples were fabricated using an additive manufacturing system. After deposition by the LMD process, all of the samples were cooled to room temperature in the operating chamber, and deep cryogenic treatment were immediately carried out to cool the LMD-built samples in the liquid nitrogen chamber. The samples were rapidly cooled from room temperature to liquid nitrogen temperature in boiling liquid nitrogen within approximately 10 min, at an average cooling rate of ~20 K/min. When the samples reached 77 K, they were soaked at this temperature for different durations. The samples subjected to DCT by soaking for 12 h, 24 h, 48 h and 120 h at liquid nitrogen temperature are hereafter labeled as DCT12h, DCT24h, DCT48h and DCT120h, respectively. Finally, the DCT-processed samples were re-heated back to room temperature via water bath heating within 5 min, at an average heating rate of ~40 K/min. In summary, DCT of bulk CoCrFeMnNi HEA samples prepared via LMD was examined.

In this study, a series of Al5Nb(25-x)Ti35Zr35Mox (x = 0, 5, 10, 15 at% (atomic fraction), defined as Mo0, Mo5 Mo10 and Mo15, respectively) novel refractory high entropy alloys (RHEAs) was prepared by vacuum arc furnace. The Al 5Nb (25-x)Ti 35Zr 35Mo x(x = 0, 5, 10, 15 at%, at% represents atomic fraction) alloys, hereafter referred to as Mo0, Mo5, Mo10, and Mo15 alloys, were produced through vacuum arc melting under a high-purity argon atmosphere using constituent metals (Al, Nb, Ti, Zr, Mo) with purities ≥ 99. To achieve uniform element distribution in the alloys, all ingots were turned over and remelted at least 5 times. To retain the high temperature deformation microstructure, the compressed samples were immediately water-quenched following compression testing.

To investigate the effect of defects on mechanical properties, a set of experiments with various volume energy densities ( VED= P/ vht[ 38], where Pis the laser power, vis the scanning speed, his the hatch spacing and tis the powder layer thickness) were conducted with the cross-hatching strategy. The as-cast CoNiCr 2(elements in atomic ratios) alloy (about 200 g in weight) was synthesized from pure metals (Co, Ni: 99. 995 %; Cr: 99.99 %) by vacuum arc-melting furnace under a high-purity argon atmosphere. The ingot was remelted five times to ensure a homogeneous composition. The initial and deformed specimens for TEM observations were firstly ground to about 50 µm and then twin-jet electro-polished by an RL-2 instrument in a solution of 8 vol% perchloric and 92 vol% alcohol with a constant voltage (50 V) at -293 to -303 K. The electropolishing specimens for SEM observations were acquired via the same instrument, solution, and voltage.

The CoCrFeNi alloy and CoCrFeNiRe 0.05alloy (molar fraction) were prepared by arc-melting a mixture of principal elements with high purity (using pure metal elements with purities of more than 99.9 at.%) in a Ti-gettered high-purity argon atmosphere. The process of melting and solidification was repeated at least five times to achieve high homogeneity, followed by drop casting into a copper mold with a dimension of 10 × 18 × 80 mm 3. The ingot was sealed in a quartz tube, followed by 1200 °C/4 h annealing. Subsequently, the CoCrFeNi alloy and CoCrFeNiRe 0.05alloy ingot were cold rolled with 80 % thickness reduction at room temperature (RT). The rolling plates were recrystallized at different temperatures (900 °C and 1100 °C) for 30 min, respectively. In this way, three kinds of specimens were obtained: CG specimen (the rolled CoCrFeNi alloy recrystallized at 1100 °C/30 min), FG specimen (the rolled CoCrFeNi alloy recrystallized at 900 °C/30 min), and FG-Re0.05 specimen (the rolled CoCrFeNiRe 0.05alloy recrystallized at 900 °C/30 min).

In this study, non-equiatomic V32Co33Ni33Cr1N1 MEA was prepared by vacuum arc melting, and its comprehensive mechanical properties were improved by nitrogen alloying and subsequent thermo-mechanical processing. Alloy ingots with a theoretical composition of V 32Co 33Ni 33Cr 1N 1(atomic ratio, at%) were produced by melting a mixture of pure metals and CrN (purity ≥99.95 wt. percent, wt%) ceramic powder in a vacuum arc furnace in a high purity argon atmosphere. The ingots were re-melted six times to ensure compositional homogeneity. Then, the ingots were homogenized at 1200 ℃ for 2 h to reduce component segregation. Subsequently, the homogenized ingots were cold-rolled with a total thickness reduction of 70 %. The samples annealed at 900 ℃ for 2 h and 1000 ℃ for 5 min were named N0-CR900, N0-CR1000, N1-CR900, and N1-CR1000, followed by water quenching (WQ), respectively.

The alloy is cast in a conventional electric arc melting furnace by mixing constituent elements of a purity greater than 99.9 % in a liquid-cooled hearth made of copper under an atmosphere of pure argon. A titanium ingot is used to absorb oxygen before melting, followed by repetitive melting of five times, and finally casting into a copper mold with dimensions of 90 mm◊10 mm◊5 mm. The cast samples are subjected to solid solution annealing (SA) at 1150 °C for 2 h to homogenize, and then water quenched to ambient temperature. The SA samples are cold rolled (one-stage cold rolling, CR) to a 50 % reduction, followed by another solid solution annealing. After that, the samples are cold rolled again to 1 mm (two-stage cold rolling, 2CR) and rapidly annealed at 1150 °C for 0.5 min, and finally aged at 800 °C for 2 h to promote precipitation (Figs. During the process, argon gas was introduced for purging, and a mechanical pump was employed to create a vacuum.

The FeCoCrNiCu HEA ingot with an equal atomic ratio was prepared from metals with >99.9 % purity by vacuum arc smelting under argon protection. To ensure chemical homogeneity, an ingot was remelted five times and then poured into the copper mold to prepare the HEA plate. The prepared plate was further rolled at 1150 °C to reduce the thickness by 50 %, and the rolled plate was cut into a plurality of blocks with a dimension of 5 mm × 5 mm × 4 mm by the slow wire cutting. Ulteriorly, the blocks were divided into three batches for annealing at different temperatures. Specifically, the first batch of blocks was annealed at 300 °C, which was recorded as Specimen B. The second batch of blocks was annealed at 700 °C and was recorded as Specimen C. The third batch of blocks was annealed at 1100 °C and was recorded as Specimen D. All the above blocks were annealed in a vacuum tube furnace at a temperature-rise rate of 8°/min for 4 h. Meanwhile, the as-cast specimen without rolling and annealing treatments was recorded as Specimen A, as a control experimental group.

The prepared plate was further rolled at 1150 °C to reduce the thickness by 50 %, and the rolled plate was cut into a plurality of blocks with a dimension of 5 mm × 5 mm × 4 mm by the slow wire cutting. Ulteriorly, the blocks were divided into three batches for annealing at different temperatures. Specifically, the first batch of blocks was annealed at 300 °C, which was recorded as Specimen B. The second batch of blocks was annealed at 700 °C and was recorded as Specimen C. The third batch of blocks was annealed at 1100 °C and was recorded as Specimen D. All the above blocks were annealed in a vacuum tube furnace at a temperature-rise rate of 8°/min for 4 h. Meanwhile, the as-cast specimen without rolling and annealing treatments was recorded as Specimen A, as a control experimental group.

The iHEA (Fe 49. 5Mn 30Co 10Cr 10C 0.5, at.%) with a nominal composition in atomic percent was synthesized in an environment of high-purity argon atmosphere. The process involved melting pure metals with a purity exceeding 99.8 wt% and subjecting them to multiple melting cycles, repeatedly melting four times to cast an ingot. The resulting ingot was then subjected to vacuum homogenization at 1473 K for 12 h, forged into a billet with a sectional area of 100 × 15 mm 2, and air-cooled. The forging billet was hot rolled at 1173 K to a thickness reduction of 67 % (thickness changed from 15 to 5 mm). Subsequently, the billet was homogenized in an argon atmosphere at 1473 K for 2 h, followed by water-quenching.

CoCrFeMnNi high entropy alloy (HEA) parts were fabricated by laser powder bed fusion (LPBF), and their dynamic compressive properties at different temperatures as well as the resulting microstructures were analyzed. Spherical gas-atomized CoCrFeNiMn powders with a mean particle size of 35 µm were used for LPBF-processing. Samples for dynamic impact testing (Ø5 × 5 mm 3) were manufactured in an in-house developed LPBF device (DiMetal-100H). Following processing parameters were employed to fabricate defect-free samples: laser power of 160 W, laser scanning speed of 800 mm/s, hatching space of 50 µm and layer thickness of 30 µm.

Based on these, we proposed an equiatomic five-element CoCrFeMnNi HEA containing 0.5 at% carbon with a partially recrystallized microstructure created by means of an appropriate heat treatment after cold rolling. The carbon alloyed equiatomic CoCrFeMnNi high-entropy alloy (c-HEA) ingots with dimensions of 25 × 60 × 65 mm 3were produced in vacuum induction melting furnace from carbon and corresponding metals with the purity better than 99.8% to the achieve chemical composition Co 19. The cast ingots were subsequently hot-rolled with 50% thickness reduction at 900 °C and were subjected to homogenization treatment at 1200 °C for 4 h in Ar atmosphere followed by water-quenching. When the annealing temperature is below 1000 °C and annealing time becomes shorter, none-recrystallized zones can be retained. Therefore, to obtain a partially recrystallized microstructure, the hot-rolled samples were cold-rolled with a thickness reduction of 60% and annealed at 900 °C for 3 min in Ar atmosphere followed by water-quenching in the present work. In order to keep the proper grain size and enhanced mechanical properties of c-HEA, the annealing heat treatment was conducted in a short time (5 min) and at low temperature (900 °C).

In this study, a novel high entropy shape memory alloy (HESMEA) was developed using in-situ alloying laser powder bed fusion (LPBF) by introducing a moderate amount of silicon (10 % atomic percent) to a metastable Fe50Mn30Co10Cr10 HEA matrix. Multi-remelting strategy was employed to improve the chemical homogeneity of the printed HESMA with enhanced diffusion occurring during the remelt scan. In this study, a novel high entropy shape memory alloy (HESMEA) was developed using in-situ alloying laser powder bed fusion (LPBF) by introducing a moderate amount of silicon (10 % atomic percent) to a metastable Fe 50Mn 30Co 10Cr 10HEA matrix. Multi-remelting strategy was employed to improve the chemical homogeneity of the printed HESMA with enhanced diffusion occurring during the remelt scan. In this study, we designed a new Fe 45Mn 27Co 9Cr 9Si 10HESMA (at%) using in-situ alloying LPBF, remelting strategy was employed to improve the compositional homogeneity. Spherical pre-alloyed HEA powders of Fe 50Mn 30Co 10Cr 10(at%) and pure silicon (Si) powders were used for the in-situ alloying during LPBF. The mixed powders were printed employing an EOSINT M280 LPBF machine equipped with a 400 W Yb-fiber laser. To optimize the processing parameters, square samples with dimensions of 8×8×8 mm³ were printed using different laser powers (150-300 W) and scanning speeds (600-1600 mm/s). To improve the uniformity of the Si element distribution, a multi-remelting strategy, as shown in Fig. 2, was employed based on the above optimized LPBF parameters. It is worth noting that the printing parameters used for remelting were the same as the initial printing parameters. To remove the residual stress introduced during wire cutting and grinding steps, the strip samples were subjected to a heat treatment at 600°C for 5 minutes before bending.

A novel refractory high-entropy alloy (RHEA) spherical powder WTaMoNbZr was synthesized successfully through four-steps: melting, hydrogenation, crushing and spheroidization. The alloy ingot with ~110 mm in diameter and ~120 mm in height was prepared by vacuum electron beam melting. And this increased the difficulty to pulverize it into fine powder. It was found that hydrogenated treatment can embrittle the ingot, and irregular powders with the particle size ranging from 1.56 µm to 59.5 µm were then easily obtained by using a disk crusher. Finally, highly spheroidized RHEA powders with spheroidization ratio of 95.3% were fabricated by plasma spheroidization. The alloy ingot with ~110 mm in diameter and ~120 mm in height was prepared by vacuum electron beam melting. And this increased the difficulty to pulverize it into fine powder. It was found that hydrogenated treatment can embrittle the ingot, and irregular powders with the particle size ranging from 1.56 µm to 59.5 µm were then easily obtained by using a disk crusher. Finally, highly spheroidized RHEA powders with spheroidization ratio of 95.3% were fabricated by plasma spheroidization. The WTaMoNbZr RHEA ingot was fabricated by VEBM equipped with a water-cooled copper crucible in high-purity argon atmosphere. Because of the large discrepancy in element melting points, the raw powders were melted step-by-step in the high-to-low sequence of Tm. After refining of high melting points elements, low melting points elements were added. The RHEA ingot was re-melted and flipped many times to obtain homogeneous chemical distribution. Considering the high toughness of the RHEA, hydrogenated treatment on ingot was conducted before mechanical crushing. After hydrogenation, WTaMoNbZr ingot swelled and splintered into small pieces. Then, the bite-size WTaMoNbZr specimens were disk-milled using a couple of tungsten carbide disks. After milling, the crushed irregular powders were fed into the upper part of plasma torch through water-cooled feeder. Then the injected powders were melted instantaneously after absorbing great amount of heat and spheroidized by plasma spheroidizing system (Tekna Nano-15) to produce the spherical-shape RHEA powders.

The fabricated CoCrFeMnNi alloy specimens were polished using 600, 800, and 1200 grit SiC sheets, followed by polishing in liquid diamond suspensions (3.0, 1.0, and 0.25 µm) and final polishing using 0.02 µm colloidal silica. The respective values were 7.94, 7.93, and 7.92 g/cm 3, which correlate well with the theoretical density of the Cantor alloy (7.96 g/cm 3). Tensile tests were conducted at ambient (298 K) and cryogenic (77 K) temperatures using an Instron universal testing machine (UTM) (Instron 1361) at a quasi-static strain rate of 10 −3s −1. The FeCoCrNi HEA ingot was melted and cast in a vacuum induction furnace using mixture of pure Fe, Co, Cr and Ni (≥99.9 wt%) in a high-purity argon atmosphere. The ingot was hot forged at 1200 °C and then hot rolled at 1050 °C, achieving a total thickness reduction of 50 %. Subsequently, the FeCoCrNi sheet underwent homogenization at 1200 °C for 2 h in an argon atmosphere, followed by water quenching to eliminate segregation. To achieve a uniform fine-grained structure, the homogenized material was then cold rolled to a total reduction of 50 % and annealed at 900 °C for 20 min, which was considered as base material (BM). Therefore, for the FeCoCrNi HEA, 5 %-reduction cold rolling followed by annealing at 900 °C for 4 h is the optimal GBCD optimization process; the samples in this state are therefore defined as GBE samples. Instead of the BM sample without GBE treatment, the sample that underwent a homogenization annealing followed by 50 %-reduction cold rolling and annealing at 950 °C for 3 h was chosen as the Non-GBE sample for a comparison.

To experimentally verify the thermodynamic modelling predictions, 50 g of HECA and Cu-30Fe alloy were fabricated using an HHV-3070 vacuum arc-melting furnace. Whereas the HECA was fabricated in the following two steps: (i) Two master alloys namely Cu 70Mn 8, and Fe 12Co 7. A vacuum level of ∼5 × 10 −5mbar was achieved in the casting chamber which was then backfilled with high-purity argon to 700 mbar prior to melting of both the alloys. After the final melts, HECA and Cu-30Fe were quenched in the red-hot condition. A rectangular piece of 26 × 14 × 4 mm 3was machined from the as-fabricated ingots using EDM and was cold rolled in a high-capacity roll mill till 70 % thickness reduction with 0.1 mm reduction per rolling pass.

In this study, CoCrFeNi was initially selected as the matrix alloy, and Al and Ti elements were introduced to enhance mechanical properties by promoting the formation of L1 2precipitates. To ensure compositional homogeneity, the ingots were re-melted six times, followed by a homogenization treatment at 1200 °C for 2 h to eliminate segregation. The homogenized button ingots were cold rolled to 8 mm thickness, followed by another homogenization at 1200 °C for 2 h and rapid water quenching. Subsequently, the homogenized samples were cold-rolled through multiple passes to a final thickness of 1.6 mm, achieving an 80 % reduction in thickness. The cold-rolled samples were annealed at 1150 °C for 3 min to ensure complete recrystallization (HA), followed by aging at 800 °C for 2 h (HA800).

In this experiment, spherical pure metal powders (Cr, Ni, Cu, purity ≥ 99.9 wt.%) with a diameter of 45-105 μm were used to configure CrNiCu x( x= 0.2, 0.6, 1, and 1.4) medium-entropy alloys according to the corresponding atomic ratios. The prepared metal powders were mixed using a planetary ball mill to prepare homogeneous alloy powders. After ball milling, the alloy powders were vacuum-dried and then sealed for storage. The prepared CrNiCu xalloy powders were used as the raw material to deposit CrNiCu xmedium-entropy alloys layer by layer on a 316 L substrate (size 100 mm ×100 mm ×10 mm) and successfully prepared a batch of CrNiCu xmedium-entropy alloys with a length of 40 mm, a width of about 3 mm, and a height of 20 mm. The processing parameters used during preparation included a laser wavelength of 915 nm, a spot diameter of 2 mm, a laser power of 1400 W, a scanning speed of 8 mm/s, a powder feed rate of 6 g/min, and a single-layer height of 0.8 mm.

The prepared CrNiCu xalloy powders were used as the raw material to deposit CrNiCu xmedium-entropy alloys layer by layer on a 316 L substrate (size 100 mm ×100 mm ×10 mm) and successfully prepared a batch of CrNiCu xmedium-entropy alloys with a length of 40 mm, a width of about 3 mm, and a height of 20 mm. The processing parameters used during preparation included a laser wavelength of 915 nm, a spot diameter of 2 mm, a laser power of 1400 W, a scanning speed of 8 mm/s, a powder feed rate of 6 g/min, and a single-layer height of 0.8 mm.

99 % Ni were proportionally weighed according to the atomic ratio of AlCoCrFeNi 2.1and remelted at least five times in Ti-gettered argon atmosphere to ensure compositional uniformity. Subsequently, the AlCoCrFeNi 2. 1EHEA ingot was cut into blocks with a cross section of 4 × 10 mm 2and a height of 3 mm. The sample surfaces were sequentially sanded down with 240#, 800#, and 2000# sandpaper to eliminate surface oxides. A quasi-static loading with a rate of 50 N/s to 14,000 N was performed on the AlCoCrFeNi 2. 1EHEA specimens, then, the ultrasonic vibration with a frequency of 20 KHz and amplitude of 20 μm was superimposed on the specimens for various time, e.g., 0 min (the original state), 10 min, 20 min, and 30 min, respectively. In addition, the specimens compressed at 14,000 N without ultrasonic vibration were subjected to comparative analysis. The ultrasonically processed EHEA samples were then wire-cut into dog-bone shaped tensile specimens with a gauge size of 3 × 1 × 1 mm 3.

High purity (>99.9% wt%) metal particles were melted by vacuum arc in argon environment. Before melting, evacuate to 3 × 10 −3Pa and then press in high purity argon to 0. During melting, additional pure titanium is first melted to absorb the residual oxygen in the furnace. The ingots were repeatedly melted at least 5 times in a water-cooled copper crucible to ensure homogeneity of chemical composition. The samples with the size of 10 mm × 9 mm × 6 mm were cut by wire cutting for microstructure observation and crystal structure analysis.

An HEA ingot with a nominal atomic composition of Cr 25. 0Mn 12. 5Fe 25. 0Ni 25. 0Cu 12.5was fabricated by vacuum induction melting (VIM) using high-purity (>99.9 at%) elements under an argon atmosphere. Microstructural characterization and analysis were performed using multiple techniques. The corresponding phase diagram was simulated using a thermodynamic software (JMATPRO®) to predict the possible phases in the designed alloy. For microscopic analysis, typical mechanical preparation using SiC papers of up to 4000-grit was carried out, followed by electropolishing using a mixed electrolyte of H 3PO 4+C 2H 5OH (ratio 1:1) at 1 V for 60 s. Based on the possibility of galvanic corrosion in multiphase microstructures, two different specimen preparation approaches, jet electropolishing and focused ion beam (FIB), were used for transmission electron microscopy (TEM). Punched disk specimens (diameter: 3 mm, thickness:<100 µm) were prepared through fine mechanical grinding using a 1-μm diamond suspension followed by piercing using a twin-jet electropolisher and a mixed electrolyte of HNO 3+CH 3OH (ratio 1:4) at an operating temperature of< −40 °C and an applied voltage of 25 V. A rectangular site with dimensions of 8 × 8 µm 2was selected and extracted using a dual-beam FIB (Helios NanoLab, FEI). The tensile and compressive properties were examined using uniaxial testing at room temperature. For the tensile experiments, dog-bone-type specimens with gauge dimensions of 9.0 × 3.4 × 1.0 mm 3were cut from the cast ingot. Cubic-type compression specimens with dimensions of 4 × 4 × 5 mm 3were carved out; all specimens for mechanical examination were prepared via wire-cut electrical discharge machining.

Builds are fabricated with laser powers of 1100, 1400, 1700, 2000, and 2300 W. The laser spot size, feeding rate and scanning rate are ∼3 mm, ∼12 g/min and ∼600 mm/min, respectively. Moreover, the hatch-overlap and layer thickness are 30 % and 0.5 mm, respectively. Finally, to minimize oxygen pick-up, argon is purged during LMD. After fabrication, the builds are directly soaked in a container filled with liquid nitrogen (77 K) for 12 h. Then, the samples were quenched in a water bath held at room temperature (293 K). Before performing microstructural and mechanical characterization, the as-built and DCT treated builds were annealed at 773 K for 8 h to alleviate the residual stresses.

Therefore, in this paper, CoCrFeMnNi HEA and the eutectic composition of EHEA strengthed of Laves phases were determined by thermodynamic calculations and fabricated by vacuum induction melting. 5HEA (denoted as the EHEA) were fabricated in a vacuum induction furnace (MC 100, Germany) using the high purity metal particles (≥99.5 wt%) of Cr, Fe, Mn, Ni, Co and Nb. Moreover, dog-bone-shaped samples, with gauge dimensions of 15 × 3 × 1.5 mm 3, were machined from the casting using the electric discharging machining. Perior to hydrogen adsorption experiment, dog-bone-shaped samples were polished with SiC sandpapers up to 1200-grit to remove oxides and contaminants on their surfaces. Hydrogen was imported into the sanmples by the electrochemical hydrogen pre-charging in an electrolytic solution (0. 3 % NH 4SCN+3 % NaCl) for 24 h at room temperature, and the current density was 10 mA/cm 2.

An equiatomic CoFeNiMnV high-entropy alloy with a face-centred cubic phase was cast and cold-rolled. Ingots of CoFeNiMnV HEAs were prepared by arc melting high purity Co, Fe, Ni, Mn, and V mixtures comprising pure metals (purity > 99.9 wt %) under an argon atmosphere. During the smelting process, the alloys were re-smelted at least four times to ensure their compositional homogeneity. The as-cast ingots were encapsulated in quartz ampules, homogenised for 4 h at 1000 °C, and then cold-rolled (CR) at room temperature with a thickness reduction of 60 % to produce a 1.3-mm-thick sheet. The CR sheets were individually annealed at 700, 800, 900, and 1000 °C for 1 h, denoted as 700A, 800A, 900A and 1000A samples, respectively, followed by air cooling.

Ingots were remelted completely more than eight times under electromagnetically stirring to make their chemical composition homogeneity. The rectangular specimens with dimensions of 10 mm × 20 mm × 30 mm were obtained using the in-situ drop casting the superheated melts into a water-cooled copper mold. After that, the specimens were homogenized at 1573 K for 12 h under the argon atmosphere. The TEM samples were prepared by twin-jet electro-polishing in a mixture solution of 10 vol% perchloric acid and 90 vol% alcohol.

Master alloy ingots were prepared by arc melting pure metals (>99.9 %) in a high-purity argon atmosphere. These master alloy ingots were re-melted and cast to obtain a cylindrical rod with a diameter (Φ) of 20 mm. The as-cast alloys were held at 1200 °C for 24 h, followed by water quenching to dissolve the precipitates, transform the alloy into a single-phase state, and eliminate compositional segregation. The solution-treated alloys were then swaged at room temperature with an average reduction of 75 % in the cross-sectional area. The stored energy introduced by cold deformation can act as the driving force for recrystallization and promote the precipitation process during subsequent aging. Finally, the as-swaged samples of Φ10 mm were aged at 600 °C for 1 h, followed by air cooling.

CoCrFeNiMn high-entropy alloy (HEA) sheets were processed by 223 K cryorolling, cold rolling, and subsequent annealing. Cryorolling (223 K) and cold rolling were used to process the sheets, respectively. The overall reduction ratio was 90% (0.2 mm). The samples for cryorolling were cooled down to 223 K in the cryogenic container for 30 min before rolling. To maintain the target temperature, the samples were cooled for 10 min before each pass and were put back in the cryogenic container immediately after each pass. The total cryorolling process only took several seconds (which is the exposure time of the sample to ambient conditions). About 5 % of the reduction for each pass was set to avoid adiabatic heating. The rolled sheets were then annealed at 873 K and 973 K for a dwell time of 30 min

Energy-dispersive spectroscopy (EDS) was used to determine the elemental composition of the samples. It can be seen in Fig. 11a that the primary mechanism in the cold-rolled HEA during the rolling period was dislocation slip deformation, followed by a small number of nano twins. While in Fig. 11d, the cryorolled HEA was dominated by the shear band and deformation twinning, with a quite high activity of twinning. Recrystallization occurred in cold-rolled HEA following annealing at 873 K, as shown in Fig. 11b. Coarse equiaxed grains appeared at this stage and the dislocation density decreased. Annealing twins were formed within the grains. After annealing at the same temperature, elongated microstructures and interlaced subgrain boundaries were observed in cryorolled HEA shown in Fig. 11e. These subgrain boundaries may account for the improved mechanical properties after cryorolling. Similar to grain boundaries, the interface energy generated by subgrain boundaries can effectively inhibit and accommodate dislocation movement. After annealing at a higher temperature (973 K), the grain size of the cryorolled HEA was finer than that of cold rolled HEA. Meanwhile, the retained subgrain boundaries and intersected twins provided more interfaces for strengthening, as shown in Fig. 11c and f.
