In this work, AlCoCrFeNi2.1 eutectic high-entropy alloy (EHEA) was prepared by laser metal deposition (LMD). In this study, AlCoCrFeNi 2.1sample was fabricated by LMD. The pre-alloyed spherical AlCoCrFeNi 2.1powder was produced by argon gas atomization. The powder was dried at 127 K for 8 h. The LMD experiments were performed with a laser power source of 1000 W, a laser scanning velocity of 500 mm/min, a powder feeding rate of 8∼12 g/min and a protective gas flow rate of 5∼8 L/min. The powder was delivered into the laser molten pool on a 304L steel substrate through a coaxial nozzle at an argon gas flow of 12 ∼ 20 L/min and a feeding powder rate of 7 ∼ 9 g/min. For comparison, the AlCoCrFeNi 2.1sample with an identical composition was also produced using copper mold casting. The fabrication process was performed with raw materials with purity ≥99.9 wt% under the protection of high purity argon gas.

An equi-atomic CoCrNi alloy was produced by vacuum induction melting using commercially pure elements (purity of 99.95 wt%). The cast ingot was homogenized at 1200 °C for 6 h and then hot swaged into a square bar with side lengths of 20 mm using a four-die rotary swaging machine. Subsequently, these bars were recrystallized for 1 h at 850 °C followed by air-cooling. Given the present microstructure observation shows that the CoCrNi MEA deformed in liquid nitrogen containing high density DTs, this deformed sample is named as heavily twinned CoCrNi MEA, and the illustration is inserted in Fig. 1(b). The present study utilizes mixed powders that have fabricated A 2/B 2RHEA with no defects, uniform microstructure, dispersed nanoscale ellipsoidal B 2domains, and smooth GBs by optimizing process parameters and leveraging the intrinsic thermal-cycling of additive manufacturing without expensive Ru element or post-treatments. This study employs laser in-situ alloying technology by optimizing process parameters and leveraging the intrinsic thermal cycling during deposition to fabricate defect-free, homogeneous RHEAs using elemental mixed powders. Following the stipulated proportional requirements (Al 2Zr 2Ti 7Nb 3Ta 3atomic ratio), the powders above were blended for 2 h via high-energy ball milling, and the rotational speed of the ball mill was calibrated at 300 r/min, with a weight ratio of balls to powders maintained at 8:1. The entire laser deposition process was conducted on an additive manufacturing system comprising a 10 KW fiber laser, a four-axis computer numerical control machine, an argon-protected chamber, and a coaxial powder feeding system. The parameters employed are as follows: laser power ranged from 3000 to 5000 W, laser beam diameter from 6 to 8 mm, powder delivery rate from 12 to 24 g/min, and scanning speed from 400 to 800 mm/min. The defect-free, low-cost, and homogeneous A 2/B 2RHEAs were successfully fabricated by laser in-situ alloying technology using elemental mixed powders in this study.

The powder metallurgy method is employed to prepare the unreinforced and particle-reinforced aluminum alloys. Firstly, the aluminum powder ( D= 40 μm) and SiC particle ( D= 7 μm) are mixed by ball milling. Then, the mixed powders are packed by a pure aluminum hollow casing and compacted and vacuumized. Subsequently, the ingots are extruded into plates with a thickness of 10 mm at 480 °C. The plates are rolled into 2 mm at 480 °C. The rolled plates are solid solution treated at 520 °C for 2 h followed by water quenching, and then artificial aging treatments are performed at 180 °C for 6 h.

5Mo 3C 1(at%) FeMEA was cast using the vacuum induction melting method. The ingot was homogenized at 1100°C for 6 h under an argon atmosphere, followed by water-quenching. The homogenized ingot was then cold-rolled at room temperature. The thickness reduction ratio was ∼86 % (from 7.0 to 1.0 mm). The cold-rolled sheet was annealed under two distinct conditions to control precipitation without altering the grain size: at 800°C for 3 h (A800) and at 900°C for 10 min (A900). All annealed samples were subjected to water quenching.

Ingots of the (FeNi) 67Cr 15Mn 10- xAl 4Ti 4Mo xalloys were prepared by arc-melting a stoichiometric mixture of metals with purities greater than 99.95% under an Ar atmosphere and allowing the ingots to cool naturally to room temperature. All ingots were re-melted and allowed to cool four times to ensure homogeneity. Considering the volatility of the Mn element, the other elements were melted evenly before adding Mn to the melt, and an additional 5 wt% Mn was added to compensate for the expected loss. The molten alloy was cast in a thin rectangular water-cooled copper mold with dimensions of 60 mm × 10 mm × 5 mm. The as-cast plates were solution treated at a temperature of 1423 K for 2 h and then cold-rolled to a thickness commensurate with a reduction of 67%. The alloys experienced 67% cold rolling without rolling-induced cracking. The cold-rolled plates were annealed for 2 min at a temperature of 1423 K and then aged at 1023 K for 5 h. All heat treatment processes were conducted under a standard air atmosphere and subsequently cooled by water quenching.

Eventually, each drop-cast ingot was homogenized at 1473 K for 24 h under an argon atmosphere, followed by water quenching. Unpolished tensile and fatigue samples with ∼700 μm in thickness were cut from the homogenized drop-cast ingots along the length direction by using electrical discharge machining (EDM). ∼300 μm materials were first removed from each surface of the gauge sections by carefully grinding in the water with 400-grit to 3000-grit SiC papers and then electropolishing with a mixed solution of HClO 4(perchloric acid):C 2H 6O (ethyl alcohol) = 1:9 (volume fraction) under a DC voltage of 20 V for ∼40 s at a temperature of −15 °C, to fully get rid of the damage zones caused by EDM and the residual stress caused by mechanical grinding. TEM samples were punched directly out from the fatigued samples near the fractures and then mechanically ground to ∼35 μm in thickness in the water by using 2000-grit and 3000-grit SiC papers and finally thinned by using a twin-jet electrolytic polisher (Lebo Science TJ100-SE) with a mixed solution of HClO 4:CH 8O 3(glycerine):CH 4O (methanol) = 1:2:7 (volume fraction) under an applied voltage of 26 V at a temperature of −20 °C.

To ensure low porosity, the processing parameters were optimized using an orthogonal scanning strategy as follows: laser power of 200 W, scanning speed of 500 mm/s, scanning spacing of 70 μm, and layer thickness of 30 μm, as shown in Fig. 1c and d. The dog bone-shaped tensile samples were cut by electrical discharge wire-cutting, as shown in Fig. 1e. Prior to tensile testing, all samples were meticulously sanded and polished using SiC paper to eliminate the influence of uneven surfaces and defects. Prior to microstructural observation, the samples were mechanically polished with 200-5000 mesh sandpaper and then mirror polished using 2.5 μm and 1 μm diamond polish. Subsequently, the polished surfaces were etched with diluted aqua regia (HCl: HNO 3: H 2O = 3:1:4) for 30 s.

99 % (Ti) and 99. The ingot was homogenized at 1373 K for 24 h in an Ar atmosphere before being water quenched. It was then hot forged at 1173 K into a plate with a cross-section of 85 × 30 mm. Subsequently, the plate was hot rolled at 1173 K to a thickness of 24 mm (20 % reduction). After removing the oxide surfaces using a milling machine, the alloy plate was cut into cuboids and cold-rolled to achieve an 80 % thickness reduction. The rolled sheets were sealed in quartz tubes filled with Ar, subjected to recrystallization at 1123 K for 60 min, and finally water-quenched by breaking the tubes to obtain the solution-treated (ST) samples.

08FeCoCrNiMn HEA was prepared by medium-frequency induction melting in a high-purify argon environment. After then, the molten alloy was sucked into a yttrium oxide tube (inner diameter: 6 mm, external diameter: 8 mm) and quenched into the 25 °C liquid metal (Ga-In-Sn) rapidly. The Φ 6 mm ingot was subjected to cold rolling (CR) using a laboratory-scale rolling mill to a final thickness of ∼0.7 mm, reducing 88. The further annealing treatments were done in this cold rolling alloy at 600 °C for 1 min (CR + A 1 min), 32 min (CR + A 32 min), 64 min (CR + A 64 min), 128 min (CR + A 128 min), and 360 min (CR + A 360 min), respectively.

%) MEA powder with a particle size of 15-53 μm was used to manufacture samples. The composition of the raw Ni 35Co 35Cr 25Ti 3Al 2powder is listed in Supplementary Table 1. Samples were built using a SLM280HL (SLM Solutions, Germany) machine equipped with a maximum power of 400 W fiber laser and a laser spot size of 80 µm. To minimize the thermal residual stress, the 316 L stainless steel substrate plate was pre-heated to 200 °C. The following parameters were applied: laser power of 320 W, layer thickness of 30 μm, hatch distance of 70 μm, and scanning speed of 1000 mm/s. The as-built samples were annealed for the duration of 12 h at 500 °C - 1000 °C, followed by water quenching. Alloy with a nominal chemical composition of Ni 35Co 35Cr 25Ti 3Al 2was also prepared in conventional vacuum arc melter under argon atmosphere. Repeated melting was carried out at least five times to ensure chemical homogeneity and then dropped into water-cooled copper molds with the dimensions of 50 × 10 × 5 mm 3. The cast ingot was cold rolled to ∼12 % total thickness reduction and thereafter isothermally annealed at 700 °C. We performed isothermal annealing at 700 °C for various durations (0, 12, 240, 480, 720, 1440 h) on the as-built alloy to gain further insights into the impact of annealing time on the microstructure. We first conducted a detailed microstructural investigation of the LPBF alloy after a short-duration heat treatment (annealing at 700 °C for 10 min). We also examined the microstructure of the as-built alloy after annealing at 600 °C for 12 h.

In the BN-HEA annealed at 1000 and 1100 °C, the BN precipitates are detected without the Cr 2B precipitates.

In this work, we demonstrate changing the scanning mode of laser powder bed fusion (LPBF) to create heterogeneous regions, thereby successfully preparing AlCoCrFeNi2.1 eutectic high entropy alloy (EHEA) with a layered heterostructure. A commercial LPBF machine (TECHGINE TS120) equipped with a self-developed control module for circular oscillation scanning was utilized to fabricate several samples in this study. The laser oscillation scanning strategy employs a galvanometer scanner to oscillate a high-frequency laser beam, creating different scanning trajectories. The laser beam follows a predetermined path, using its regular high-frequency motion to stir the molten pool. In linear scanning, the laser follows a standard straight-line trajectory, whereas in oscillating scanning, the laser head follows a predetermined slicing trajectory, oscillating longitudinally while advancing laterally. Layered HS materials were fabricated by alternating between linear scanning and oscillating scanning, as shown in Fig. 2c. The powder layer thickness was 0.03 mm, with the scanning method alternating every 5 layers, forming 0.15 mm thick regions for both linear and oscillating scanning. Additionally, a series of samples using only the linear scanning method and only the oscillating scanning method were prepared. All the LPBF samples were built on a 316L stainless steel substrate in a high-purity argon atmosphere (99.9 %) to ensure the oxygen content remained below 400 ppm during the forming process.

Pre-alloyed 18Ni300 steel and Cantor HEA powders with a particle size range of 15-53 µm were individually fabricated using the vacuum-induced gas atomization technique. The powders underwent vacuum drying in a vacuum oven for 8 hours before MM-LPBF processes. The dual-alloy samples of 18Ni300 steel and Cantor HEA were fabricated in a nitrogen atmosphere with an oxygen content of less than 200 ppm, using a 316 L stainless steel substrate. The MM-LPBF experiments were conducted employing a home-made MM-LPBF device, possessing a 500 W fiber laser power with a laser wavelength of 1064 nm. The tailored MM-LPBF AM process parameters were as follows: a laser power of 240 W and a scanning speed 800 mm/s for the Cantor HEA, and a laser power 230 W and a scanning speed 1000 mm/s for the 18Ni300 steel. For the Type 1 structural block, after completing the L-PBF printing with two hundred powder laying times for building a Cantor HEA bar with a cumulative layer thickness of 10 mm, the 18Ni300 steel powder bed was directly laid on the top surface of the Cantor HEA bar, to build a 18Ni300 steel bar with another cumulative layer thickness of 10 mm after another two hundred powder laying times using 18Ni300 steel powder for the L-PBF printing. For the Type 2 structural block with nearly equal layer-thicknesses of the laminate within it, after completing the printing with one hundred and fifty powder laying times for building a Cantor HEA bar with a cumulative layer thickness of 7.5 mm, successively alternating the use of 18Ni300 steel and Cantor HEA powders, with each powder material continuously laid and printed for 5 layers before being replaced by the other material, a dual-alloy laminate structure with an approximately 250 μm layer thickness alternating distribution was prepared through this alternating printing method of the MM-LPBF. While for the Type 3 structural block consisting of the dual-alloy or dual-phase laminate with alternating layer thicknesses of the two alloys with stepwise variations, its building procedure or MM-LPBF printing strategy was differentiated to that of the Type 2 block in that the powder-bed laying numbers for each material were gradually changed. Subsequently, post-treatment was performed on select as-printed Type 2 specimens, involving heat treatment (HT) at 950 °C for 2 hours, followed by furnace cooling (refer to the experimental details in the Supplementary Materials). Through the EBSD detection results ( Fig. 7), it is found that the layer thickness of the FCC phase region of the Cantor HEA is evidently larger than that of the BCC phase region of the 18Ni300 steel. Hence, when the 18Ni300 steel powder-bed is laid on the surface of the as-solidified Cantor HEA layer, the laser melts the two alloys together in one newly generated melt-pool to conduct the complex dynamic action inside the melt-pool, including the Marangoni effect, resulting in that the element atoms from the two alloy are mixed and redistributed. By comparing the microstructural characteristics of the AB-H specimen ( Fig. 13a and b) and the AB-H-HT specimen ( Fig. 13c and d) before the tension, it is found that after heat treatment, the grain morphology and size of the FCC phase region do not change much, but the BCC phase region range decreases significantly. When the dual-phase structure is heated to near the austenitizing temperature, austenite nucleates and grows after the martensite structure dissolves. Then, during the subsequent heat-holding process, the elements gradually tend to homogenize inside the FCC phase grain structure through thermal diffusion. During the subsequent cooling process, the grain morphology in the FCC phase region does not change significantly, but due to the diffusion behavior of the elements, the Cr, Mn, and Ni elements rich in the Cantor HEA further diffuse into the 18Ni300 steel region, resulting in a further decrease in martensitic transformation temperature point, thereby further reducing the proportion of the BCC phase during the cooling.

5RHEA was fabricated via arc-melting in a high-purity argon atmosphere containing titanium getter. Each alloy ingot was melted at least three times, followed by eight remelting cycles in a combined crucible to achieve compositional homogeneity. The molten alloy was subsequently dropped into a water-cooled copper mold with the dimensions of 36 × 12 × 6 mm 3. The as-cast plate was cold-rolled with 80% thickness reduction (final thickness was 1.2 mm). Subsequently, the sheets for irradiation were precisely cut into 4 × 4 × 1.2 mm 3samples using electrical discharge wire cutting. Then, the samples were sealed in quartz tubes filled with high-purity argon gas to prevent oxidation during heat treatment. These sealed samples were then annealed at 1,100°C for 1 h, followed by water quenching. And then the quartz tubes were broken in water to ensure a fast-cooling rate. Before irradiation, the sample surfaces were prepared by grinding with SiC sandpapers of 5,000 grits, followed by mechanical polishing with SiO 2suspension. At last, the samples were electrochemically polished using the mixed solution of 6%HClO 4+35%C 4H 10O+59%CH 3OH at room temperature with a voltage of 30 V, with the current between 1.

To shed light on the impact of severe deformation on the elemental segregation of high-entropy alloys (HEAs) as well as the related changes in mechanical properties, we systematically investigated the equiatomic CrMnFeCoNi HEA cold rolled and aging treated subsequently at 450 °C for varying time periods. The CrMnFeCoNi HEA ingot was cast in a vacuum induction furnace with high purity constituent metals. The cast alloy was processed through hot rolling with a thickness reduction of 50% and subsequent homogenization at 1200 °C in Ar atmosphere for 2 h. Then the homogenized alloy was cold rolled with a thickness reduction of 60%. The as-cold-rolled samples were then subjected to aging treatment at 450 °C for 18 to 96 h to induce the formation of nanoprecipitation. Besides, some of the as-cold-rolled samples were fully recrystallized by annealing treatment at 900 °C for 10 min in Ar atmosphere.

The alloys of the composition (CoCrFeNi) 100-x(SiC) x(x = 0, 0.05, 0.5, 1 and 3, at.%) were synthesized using vacuum non-consumable arc melting. The starting materials comprised SiC ceramic particles and powders of the matrix elements (Co, Cr, Fe, Ni), details of which are provided in Table S1. These powders were mixed and subjected to ball milling using stainless steel balls in a ball-milling machine operated at 122 rpm for 4 h. The milled powders were then uniaxially compressed into cylindrical billets. To ensure a homogeneous distribution of elements, the billets were melted and remelted four times, subsequently being cast into button-shaped ingots in a water-cooled copper mold under a high-purity argon atmosphere. Post-casting, the ingots were subjected to hot compression (at a strain of approximately 45 %) and annealed at 1000 °C for 2 h. Samples for further processing were cut into square sections measuring 36 × 12 × 7 mm 3from the mid-section of the ingots. These square samples underwent further cold rolling deformation (at a strain of approximately 70 %) followed by a short annealing treatment at 1000 °C for 5 min to yield the as-annealed samples, designated as SiC 0, SiC 0. 05, SiC 0. 5, SiC 1, and SiC 3. Additionally, the SiC 1samples were synchronously rolled at room temperature using a two-roll mill.

These powders were mixed and subjected to ball milling using stainless steel balls in a ball-milling machine operated at 122 rpm for 4 h. The milled powders were then uniaxially compressed into cylindrical billets. To ensure a homogeneous distribution of elements, the billets were melted and remelted four times, subsequently being cast into button-shaped ingots in a water-cooled copper mold under a high-purity argon atmosphere. Post-casting, the ingots were subjected to hot compression (at a strain of approximately 45 %) and annealed at 1000 °C for 2 h. Samples for further processing were cut into square sections measuring 36 × 12 × 7 mm 3from the mid-section of the ingots. These square samples underwent further cold rolling deformation (at a strain of approximately 70 %) followed by a short annealing treatment at 1000 °C for 5 min to yield the as-annealed samples, designated as SiC 0, SiC 0. 05, SiC 0. 5, SiC 1, and SiC 3. Additionally, the SiC 1samples were synchronously rolled at room temperature using a two-roll mill.

A series of AlMo 0. 5NbTiVSi xlightweight refractory high-entropy alloys were produced by DHL-500 II non-consumable vacuum arc melting of pure (≥ 99.9 wt%) elements (Beijing Dream Material Technology Co. , Ltd.) in a Ti-gettered argon atmosphere, where x is the molar ratio of Si content (x = 0, 0.1, 0.2, 0.3, 0.4, and 0.5, denoted Si0, Si0. 1, Si0. 2, Si0. 3, Si0.4, and Si0.5 alloy, respectively). Each ingot was remelted at least 5 times to ensure their chemical homogeneity. During the melting process, the current is gradually loaded to 300 A and maintained for 2 min to ensure sufficient melting of the raw materials.

Raw Al, Co, Cr, Fe, and Ni metals with a purity exceeding 99.9 wt percent ( wt.%) were used to produce Al 0. 1CoCrFeNi HEAs. The HEAs were fabricated by suction casting into a copper mold with a dimension of 100 × 20 ×3 mm 3under an argon atmosphere. In order to promote the chemical homogeneity, the ingots were flipped and remelted at least four times. The as-cast ingots were first homogenization-treated at 1100 °C for 5 h and then cold rolled (CR) to the thickness of ~1.5 mm (~50% reduction) and 0.9 mm (~70% reduction) along the longitudinal direction. The 70% reduction cold-rolled samples were isochronally annealed at temperatures in the range between 800 °C and 1000 °C for 1 h to tune the mechanical behavior. All the heat treatments were conducted in an air furnace, followed by water quenching to room temperature. The HEAs show a completely recrystallized microstructure after annealing at 800 °C. It is almost impossible to have a full recrystallization when annealing present heavily-deformed HEAs (not shown here) and Nb-dopped TWIP steels below 600 °C for 1h, partial recrystallization happened at 650 and 700 °C for 1 h, and the complete recrystallization microstructure is also formed at 800 °C in CoCrFeMnNi HEAs [ 13, 35]. Annealing at 900 °C and 1000 °C for 1 h, as expected, results in discernable grain growth.

A master alloy with a nominal composition of Ni 49Fe 20Al 17V 6Co 4Cr 4(at%) was prepared by arc melting using high-purity Ni, Fe, Al, V, Co, and Cr elements. Each ingot was remelted at least five times to ensure chemical homogeneity. The molten liquid was then dropped into water-cooled copper molds with dimensions of 70 × 10 × 10 mm 3. The as-cast plate was cold-rolled with a thickness reduction of ∼90 % and then subjected to 600, 650, 750, 800, and 900 ℃ for 2 hours. The as-cast, cold-rolled, and annealed Ni 49Fe 20Al 17V 6Co 4Cr 4EHEA at 600, 650, 750, 800, and 900 ℃ were denoted as AC, CR, CR-600, CR-650, CR-750, CR-800, and CR-900 EHEAs, respectively.

The content of Ni element in FCC phase is slightly higher than B2 phase. Fig. 6(a) depicts the XRD patterns of the Ni 49Fe 20Al 17V 6Co 4Cr 4EHEA in different states. All alloys still maintain the dual-phase structure with FCC/L1 2and BCC/B2 phases, which suggests that the alloys possess good thermal stability at high temperatures. Compared with the AC EHEA, the CR EHEA shows the high diffraction peak intensity corresponding to the (220) FCCplane at 75°, which indicates that the (220) FCCplane grows preferentially. When annealing treatment was performed on the CR EHEA, the diffraction peak intensity shows little change ( Fig. 6(b)), revealing that the texture is mainly caused by cold rolling. This preferred orientation is attributed to the formation of deformation texture along (220) FCCplane in the studied EHEA after thermal-mechanical processing, inducing a high diffraction peak intensity [33-36]. Fig. 7shows the SEM images of Ni 49Fe 20Al 17V 6Co 4Cr 4EHEA in different states (refer to Fig. S1in the Supplementary for the corresponding magnified image). Clearly, after cold rolling of the AC EHEA, the lamellar structure underwent obvious bending deformation, which was due to the plastic deformation and the fragmentation of the hard B2 phase. After thermal mechanical processing, the studied EHEAs still maintain eutectic structure. Compared with the CR EHEA ( Fig. 7(a)), the CR-600 and CR-650 EHEAs showed unobvious recrystallization behavior due to the low annealing temperature, as shown in Fig. 7(b) and (c). However, for the CR-750 EHEA, fine partially recrystallized grains primarily appeared, revealing the occurrence of recrystallization, as shown in Fig. 7(d). For the CR-800 and CR-900 EHEAs, higher levels of recrystallization and phase decomposition occur due to high annealing temperatures, as shown in Fig. 7(e) and (f), which is similar with that of the reported AlCoCrFeNi 2.

The ingots were repeatedly melted 5 times to ensure homogeneity and then cast into a 50 mm × 15 mm × 10 mm copper mold. All the samples were homogenized at 1200 °C for 2 h and then cold rolled with a ∼67 % thickness reduction. Subsequently, the cold-rolled sheets were annealed at 1165 °C for 1 min, followed by aging at 760 °C for 4 h.

All the samples were homogenized at 1200 °C for 2 h and then cold rolled with a ∼67 % thickness reduction. Subsequently, the cold-rolled sheets were annealed at 1165 °C for 1 min, followed by aging at 760 °C for 4 h.

In the current study, the CoCrFeMnNi HEAs processed by various annealing temperature (773∼1423 K) and time (2∼90 min) are compared in terms of microstructural characteristics and mechanical properties. The equiatomic CoCrFeMnNi HEA was vacuum arc-melted from the starting alloy elements with purities higher than 99.7 wt. %. The ingots used in the present research work were re-melted at least five times to ensure the chemical homogeneity. Subsequently, the cast ingots were hot forged into slabs with dimensions of 30 mm × 50 mm × 140 mm at 1373∼1423 K. After the hot-forged slabs were soaked at 1273 K for 1 h, the slabs were further cold-rolled from the thickness of ∼30 mm to ∼1 mm thick sheets. In order to establish the relationship between annealing process parameters, microstructural evolution and strength-ductility combination, the cold-rolled sheets were annealed at different temperatures ranging from 773 K to 1423 K and for various durations (2∼90 min).

25FeCoNiV HEA initial preparation via vacuum levitation melting. To facilitate the subsequent cold rolling and annealing, the ingot was sliced into 100 × 30 × 10 mm bulks using wire-cut electrical discharge machining (WEDM). These bulks were homogenized at 1373 K for 10 h in an argon-protected environment and furnace-cooled to eliminate defects resulting from the casting process. The blocks were initially cold rolled (CR) at room temperature using a multiroll mill, achieving a 50% reduction in thickness from 10 to 5 mm. This cold-rolled material was subsequently subjected to intermediate annealing at 1123 K for 1 h and used as the starting material for subsequent rolling [ 26]. The material was then cold-rolled to reduce the thickness from 5 to 1.5 mm, resulting in a specimen referred to as CR-70%. Subsequently, the rolled sheets were annealed at 973, 1073, 1173, 1273, and 1373 K for 1.5 h, followed by water quenching. Dog-bone-shaped specimens were prepared using WEDM. Mechanical polishing of up to 2000 mesh was performed on the specimens with no stringent surface quality requirements. For the EBSD samples, SiC sandpaper was used to polish a 3000-mesh finish, followed by diamond suspension polishing to obtain a mirror-like surface. Then, the samples were electrolytically polished (EP) for 50 s using a solution containing 10% perchloric acid and 90% anhydrous ethanol at 25 V and 248 K. For Transmission Electron Microscopy (TEM) specimens, a twin-jet electropolishing (TJE) at 20 V and 248 K was performed after mechanical polishing.

The received Fe 55Mn 20Cr 15Ni 10MEA was melted at least four times from the starting elements with a purity exceeding 99.9% in a magnetic levitation melting furnace. The ingots underwent homogenization at 1373 K for four hours under vacuum, followed by water quenching. Subsequently, a two-step rolling and heat treatment process was conducted. Initial room-temperature rolling (50% reduction) and annealing at 973 K for 10 min, followed by quenching, were carried out to obtain a refined grain structure. Subsequently, cryorolling was conducted with a reduction of 67%, followed by annealing at 923 K for 10 min and quenching. The samples thus obtained are denoted as T0. The samples annealed at 1023 K for 10 min after cryorolling were also prepared to achieve a coarse-grained (CG) structure for comparison. For cryorolling, the sheets were immersed in liquid nitrogen for 10 min before each pass and rolled immediately to minimize the increase in deformation temperature. The per-pass reduction was maintained below 0.1 mm, and final sheets with a thickness of 0.5 mm were obtained. Following the final annealing, dog-bone-shaped tensile specimens with gauge dimensions of 3 × 22 mm were sliced along the rolling direction and ground with SiC papers up to 2000 grit. The Shimadzu AGS-X 10 kN universal testing machine was employed for cryo-pre-straining at 77 K and subsequent tensile tests at 293 K. For the T0 samples, tensile experiments at 77 K with a crosshead movement speed of 0.75 mm/min were interrupted at plastic strains of 6, 12, 21, and 36% to obtain the cryo-pre-strained samples with different deformation amounts (denoted as T1, T2, T3, and T4, respectively), as illustrated in Fig.

We obtained the CoCrNi alloy composite with TiC fraction as high as 5 wt% by laser powder bed fusion (LPBF) of blended powder of Ti, C and CoCrNi medium entropy alloy (MEA). We have previously eliminated the agglomeration of nano TiC in the CoCrNi composite containing high fraction of TiC by the in-situ alloying of TiC with Ti and C elemental powders during the LPBF process. In this paper, we LPBF fabricated the agglomeration-free CoCrNi composite containing TiC as high as 5 wt% [ 6]. The blended powders of CoCrNi pre-alloyed spherical powder (average size of 35 μm), spherical Ti powder (average size of 15 μm) and nano-C powder (average size of 26 nm) with CoCrNi: Ti: C weight ratio of 95:4:1 was tumbling mixed for 2 h and further balling milled for 2 h with a ball to powder ratio of 2:1 at 450 rpm. Then the blended powders were processed by the BLT s200 machine to perform the LPBF process. The blended powders were laser melted twice with laser power of 180 w and scan speed of 1000 mm/s, with hatch space of 80 μm and powder layer thickness of 30 μm.

The as-cast Al3Ti7 alloy was homogenized at 1150 °C for 8 h to make the alloy composition uniform. The homogenized alloy ingot was cut into 5 mm thick plate for cold rolling, through multi-step rolling, the plate is rolled into 1 mm thick sheet. Then the rolled sheet was recrystallized at 1100 °C for 1.5 min to obtain fully recrystallized grains. Finally, the recrystallized sheet was aged at 700 °C for 1 h and water quenched (denoted as-aged Al3Ti7 MEA hereafter). In addition, the other rolled sheet is treated by another heat treatment procedure which is just aged at 700 °C for 1 h and water quenched, but without recrystallization treatment (denoted non-recrystallized Al3Ti7 MEA hereafter).

In this study, the Al 0. 3CoCrFeNi alloy ingots were prepared by vacuum arc melting furnace (HNCA-2) using a high purity (≥99. 9%) Al, Co, Cr, Fe, and Ni metals as raw materials in a high purity argon atmosphere. The actual chemical composition of the ingots was determined to be 3. 47Al-25. 23Co-22. 62Cr-23. 91Fe-25. 13Ni (wt. %). To reduce the effect of pollution elements on the ingots, the titanium sponge was first smelted to remove oxygen in the furnace chamber before the casting of alloy ingots. In order to ensure the uniform composition, the ingots were first repeatedly smelted for more than five times, then homogenized at 1150 °C for 48 h and water quenched, and finally processed under different histories to obtain various types of heterogeneous microstructures. The experimental details were presented as follows:

Procedure 1. As-homogenized samples with a thickness of 10 mm were cold-rolled to the final thickness of ∼1 mm (90% reduction), then annealed at 550 °C for 24 h and water quenched to generate a heterogeneous microstructure containing nano-scale γ′ precipitates (marked as S1). Procedure 2. The fully as-homogenized samples were used as the starting material for subsequent a multi-pass cold-rolled to the thickness of ∼3 mm (∼70% reduction), these cold-rolled samples were annealed at 1100 °C for 10 min in air-cooled (Stage I). The fully annealed samples were used as the starting material for subsequent cryo- and cold-rolled processing to achieve a final thickness of ∼1 mm. These cryo- and cold-rolled specimens were carried out at 800 °C for 1 h and air-cooled (Stage II), respectively (labeled as S2 and S3, respectively).

The equiatomic CoCrFeMnNi HEA was produced by vacuum arc melting using starting alloy elements with purities exceeding 99.7 wt. To ensure chemical homogeneity, the ingots used in this study were remelted at least five times (the corresponding tests of homogeneity can be referred to in our previous paper [ 30]). Subsequently, the cast ingots were hot forged into slabs measuring 30 mm × 50 mm × 140 mm at temperatures ranging from ∼1373 K to ∼1423 K. Following a soaking period of 1 h at ∼1273 K, the slabs underwent further cold rolling to achieve sheet thicknesses of ∼1 mm. The first type, designated as CHS-I, involves direct laser scanning of a ∼1 mm thick cold-rolled plate using a rectangular beam (beam size: 3 mm × 8 mm) with scanning speed set at ∼7 mm/s and output power at ∼960 W. For the second type, named CHS-II, an annealing process was performed at a low temperature (∼873 K for ∼5 min) prior to laser scanning. Subsequently, as same as the CHS-I sample, a rectangular laser beam was used for scanning with consistent parameters.

Fabrication was carried out using vacuum arc melting in a water-cooled copper crucible under a high-purity argon atmosphere to prevent oxidation and contamination. To ensure chemical homogeneity, each ingot was re-melted 6-8 times and flipped between melts. The homogenized ingots underwent multi-pass CR at room temperature, achieving a total thickness reduction of approximately 85 %. The reduction per pass was controlled between 10 % and 15 % to prevent cracking and ensure uniform internal deformation. The total cold rolling reduction was set at 85 %, which ensured sample continuity and surface quality while providing sufficient plastic strain and stored energy to drive subsequent recrystallization and secondary-phase precipitation. The thickness reduction per pass was controlled within 10 %-15 % to achieve uniform deformation and prevent strain localization or cracking, thereby balancing microstructural control effectiveness with processing safety. To examine the effect of thermal treatment on microstructure and mechanical properties, CR-processed plates were annealed at 650 °C, 700 °C, 800 °C, and 900 °C for 5 h, followed by rapid water quenching to retain the annealed microstructures.

To better understand the advantages of cryogenic deformation on microstructure refinement and deformation strengthening of FCC alloy, multi-pass heavy drawing was performed on Al0. 1CoCrFeNi HEA at 77 K and 298 K. 1CoCrFeNi HEA wires were drawn at room (298 K) and cryogenic temperatures (77 K) to a strain of 2. The ingots were homogenized at 1473 K for 6 h and then quenched in water. The homogenized ingot was hot forged into a rectangular slab at 1323 K with a forging compression ratio of ∼80 % to eliminate casting defects. The 5.5 mm rods were finally annealed at 1173 K for 1 h, followed by quenching in water before the drawing process. The 5.5 mm rods were drawn to 2.0 mm in diameter ( ε= 2.0) by a multi-pass (5.0, 4.5, 4.1, 3.7, 3.35, 3.05, 2.75, 2.5, 2.25 and 2.0 mm orderly) drawing process at room temperature (298 K) and cryogenic temperature (77 K). The bonded coatings of graphite and molybdenum disulfide (MoS2; MOLYKOTE® D-321 R produced by DuPont corporation) were used for both temperatures. The wires and diamond drawing dies were immersed in water or liquid nitrogen for 15 min before the drawing deformation.

To break through the inverse relationship between strength and ductility in engineering alloys, laminated heterostructural CoCrFeNi-based HEAs have been developed by LAM and subsequent hot rolling using an Al-bearing chemical boundary engineering strategy. The final microstructure of ultrafine martensite and nano-twin austenite rendered the steel with ultrahigh σ UTS~ 2 GPa yet excellent δ~ 20 %. The effect of the holding time of recrystallization on the microstructure and phase structure of each layer has been investigated. Besides, the underlying strain-hardening mechanism has been carefully studied by observation of the deformation mechanism in the soft and hard layers. Secondly, these as-weighed powders were dry-mixed for 1 h in a stainless steel jar using a ball mill at a rotation rate of 300 rpm. After LMD, the LHA samples were peeled off from the 304 substrates by a wire-cut machine. Then they were hot-rolled to approximately 50 % of the initial thickness at 800 °C. After rolling, the samples are recrystallized for 1.5 and 10 min at 1000 °C.

5Si 0.5(at%), was cast using a vacuum-induction melting (VIM) setup with high-purity (99.9%) elemental components. A series of sequential thermo-mechanical processes were carried out, including homogenization at 1150 °C for 6 h, cold rolling with 74% thickness reduction, annealing at 900 °C for 30 min, aging at 480 °C for 6 h, and reversion heat treatment at 640 °C for different durations of 420 s and 460 s. All heat treatments were conducted in an argon (Ar) atmosphere, followed by water quenching to room temperature. 5MEA exhibits a BCC microstructure with an average grain size of 7.6 µm after the annealing treatment. The electron back-scattered (EBSD) results depicted in Fig. 4a,b show that the austenite fraction in the selected samples increases from 9.7% to 35.4% as the reversion time is extended from 420 s to 460 s, respectively. Through a series of thermo-mechanical processes, the cast alloy underwent engineering to establish a dual-phase microstructure adorned with nano-precipitates. Short reversion times of 420 s and 460 s were selected to maintain the dominance of the martensite phase.

All heat treatments were conducted in an argon (Ar) atmosphere, followed by water quenching to room temperature. 5MEA exhibits a BCC microstructure with an average grain size of 7.6 µm after the annealing treatment. The electron back-scattered (EBSD) results depicted in Fig. 4a,b show that the austenite fraction in the selected samples increases from 9.7% to 35.4% as the reversion time is extended from 420 s to 460 s, respectively. Through a series of thermo-mechanical processes, the cast alloy underwent engineering to establish a dual-phase microstructure adorned with nano-precipitates. Short reversion times of 420 s and 460 s were selected to maintain the dominance of the martensite phase.

The equi-molar CoCrNi alloy and the Mo-doped CoCrNi alloy with a nominal composition (CoCrNi) 97Mo 3(at.%) were produced by arc melting pure Co, pure Cr, pure Ni and pure Mo (purity > 99.9 %) in an Ar atmosphere. All ingots were flipped and remelted five times to normalize the chemical composition and then dropped into a rectangular cross-section copper mold with a dimension of 5×10×100mm 3. The as-cast alloys were homogenized at 1200 ℃ for 2 h to eliminate macro-segregation and then cold rolling along the casting direction with a reduction of ∼80 %. The cold rolled sheets were annealed at 1200 ℃ for 2 min to reduce the residual stress and obtain equiaxed grain. Hydrogen charging was conducted in a 100 MPa hydrogen gas environment at 200 ℃ for a duration of 160 h.

Ingots of Al x(CuFeMn) 100-x( x= 0, 7.5, and 15 at%) alloys were fabricated by vacuum induction melting in high-purity argon inside a graphite mold. The homogenization annealing for the ingot was carried out at 800 °C for 6 h in an argon atmosphere, followed by cold rolling from 7 to 1 mm thickness. After that, annealing at 800 °C for 1 h was carried out with water quenching. For 15Al alloy, the alloy was annealed at two different temperatures, 800 °C (referred to as 15Al-A800) and 900 °C (referred to as 15Al-A900), for 1 h after cold rolling.

The homogenization was carried out in Ar protective atmosphere at 1050 °C for 2 h, followed by quenching into water. To reduce casting defects and refine the grain size, the original casting was cold-rolled to 70 % reduction rate (from 10 mm to 3 mm). Three variations of non-equiatomic low-density HEAs viz Al 30Ni 20Cu 15Fe 25Ti 10(Al 30Ni 20, henceforth), Al 25Ni 25Cu 20Fe 25Ti 05(Al 25Ni 25, henceforth) and Al 15Cu 20Fe 25Ni 30Ti 10(Al 15Ni 30, henceforth) and synthesized via vacuum arc-melting technique. The arc melting was performed using high-purity (99.9 %) metallic elements, namely Al, Cu, Fe, Ni, and Ti in an inert atmosphere, and each ingot was remelted at least five times for homogeneity on a water-cooled copper crucible. The thickness of button-shaped ingots was obtained in the 10 - 12 mm range, which was sectioned using a wire EDM. Subsequently, these three HEA samples were heat treated in a tube furnace (CARBOLITE, HTF 18/8) at 900 ℃ for 24 h in an argon environment. Before heat treatment, a vacuum pressure of 2. 6 Pa was created in the tube, while the samples were water quenched after 24 h. As-cast (AsC) and heat-treated (HT) samples were mounted and then polished using silicon carbide (SiC) papers (BUEHLER, AutoMet 250), progressively from 120 to 1200 grit. The final metallographic mirror-like finish was acquired using vibrometer polishing (BUEHLER, VibroMet 2) with colloidal silica suspension followed by ultrasonic cleaning.

The as-cast alloy (10 mm × 40 mm × 60 mm) was homogenized at 1100 °C for 1 h, water quenched, hot rolled at 1000 °C to 40% thickness reduction and annealed at 1100 °C for 30 min before water quenching. The slab was then cold rolled with a thickness reduction of 66%, annealed at 900 °C for 1 h, water quenched and then was used for different microstructural characterizations and mechanical tests.

Two MEA ingots with nominal composition of Ni 50Cr 25Co 25and (Ni 2CrCo) 96Nb 4(denoted as Nb4 MEA hereafter) were prepared by arc-melting mixtures of the constituent elements (purity > 99.95 wt%) in a Ti-gettered high-purity argon atmosphere. The alloy ingots were re-melted at least four times to ensure homogeneity, and drop-casted into a copper mold with a dimension of 10×10×50 mm3, then subsequently homogenized at 1473 K for 6 h and cold rolled (CR) along the longitudinal direction with a total thickness reduction of 80 %. Three kinds of heat treatments were conducted on the as-rolled Nb4 MEA to obtain different microstructures. The first one, denoted as P1 alloy, includes 1473 K/10 min annealing and 973 K/100 h isothermal aging. All the heat treatments were followed by water quenching.

5HEAs were prepared by vacuum arc melting. Each ingot was turned over and remelted five times to ensure chemical uniformity, and then it drops into a copper mold with a thickness of 10 mm. The as-cast sheet was homogenized at 1250 °C for 2 h, water-quenched. Then, the homogenized alloys were room-temperature rolled and cryo-rolled by step to 75% (referred to as RR and CR, respectively). Before each CR pass, the sample was immediately immersed in a liquid nitrogen bath for 10 min to ensure the extremely low temperature of the sample during the rolling process. The CR samples were annealed at 900 °C and 1000 °C for 60 min, respectively, followed by water quenching (referred to as CRA-900 and CRA-1000 sample).

Dense, crack-free FeCoNiCrTi0. 4 HEA bulk samples and tensile specimens were fabricated via optimized SLM parameters. Post-fabrication annealing was conducted at 600 °C, 800 °C, and 1000 °C for 4 h to systematically evaluate the temperature-dependent effects on microstructure, phase constitution, texture evolution, relative density, and mechanical properties of the HEA. 4HEA bulk samples and tensile specimens were fabricated via optimized SLM parameters. Post-fabrication annealing was conducted at 600 °C, 800 °C, and 1000 °C for 4 h to systematically evaluate the temperature-dependent effects on microstructure, phase constitution, texture evolution, relative density, and mechanical properties of the HEA. This study systematically investigated the microstructural evolution and mechanical properties of as-built (ASB) SLMed FeCoNiCrTi 0. 4HEA and SLMed FeCoNiCrT i0. 4HEA after annealing at 600 °C(T1), 800 °C(T2), and 1000 °C(T3). Before SLM processing, the powder was placed in a vacuum drying oven for 8 h to remove moisture. A stainless-steel substrate measuring 100 mm × 100 mm × 18.5 mm was prepared by grinding its surface with sandpaper, polishing, and ultrasonic cleaning prior to SLM fabrication. The substrate was preheated to 100 °C to minimize thermal stress. The experimental procedure for fabricating HEA via SLM, along with the scanning strategy schematic, is illustrated in Fig. 2(a) , while the tensile specimen dimensions are detailed in Fig. 2(b). Processing was conducted on a Bright Laser Technologies S200 machine (BLT S200, maximum power: 500 W, China) using argon gas as a shielding medium to maintain oxygen levels below 200 PPM, effectively minimizing oxidation risks. During the forming process, argon gas was circulated at an actual airflow rate of 1200 r/min to purify the atmosphere in the chamber. 4HEA square bulk and tensile specimens were annealed at different temperatures using a high-temperature annealing furnace (Tytan1000, USA). The vertical cross-section of the bulk was ground with 80-3000 grit sandpapers, polished with 0.05 μm colloidal SiO 2suspension using an automatic grinding-polishing machine (Mecatech 234, France), and etched with HCl:HNO 3(3:1 vol%). HEA powder morphology and annealed microstructures were characterized by field emission scanning electron microscope (MAIA3 LMH, Czech Republic), with EBSD measurements conducted on multiple cross-sections. Aberration-corrected transmission electron microscopy (ARM200F, Japan) was employed for microstructural analysis of morphology, crystallographic features, and interfaces. The SLM samples were separated from the 316 stainless steel substrate using CNC ultra-high pressure water jet cutting equipment (HEAD42037Z, China). The sample surfaces were then polished with 2000-grit sandpaper. The microhardness at different positions on the cross-section of specimens was measured using a micro multifunctional hardness tester (FALCON 5000, Netherlands) under a 500 g load for 10 s, with at least eight test positions to ensure scientific validity. The density of the samples was measured by the Archimedes drainage method. Tensile strength along the scanning direction under varying heat treatment temperatures was determined at room temperature using a universal testing machine (Instraon5969, USA), with five replicates per condition. Fractography was characterized via field-emission scanning electron microscopy (SEM) (Gemini SEM 500, Germany). The XRD patterns of FeCoNiCrTi 0. 4HEA subjected to annealing at different temperatures are shown in Fig. Compared with annealed HEA samples, the as-built (ASB) samples exhibit distinct U-shaped melt pool morphology ( Fig. 4(a)). Cellular substructures appear locally at the melt pool boundary region ( Fig. 4(a1)) and the overlapping heat-affected zone between adjacent melt pools ( Fig. 4(a2)), while elongated dendrites dominate the central region of melt pools. This observation arises because the microstructure primarily consists of dendritic morphology. During SLM processing, each newly formed layer undergoes secondary heating of the previously solidified cladding layer. As observed in Fig. 4(a3), the specimen's internal microstructure demonstrates stable composition with homogeneous distribution of five elements and absence of elemental segregation. EDS elemental measurements at interdendritic regions (Point P1) and dendrites (Point P2) show higher Fe and Cr concentrations in dendrites, while Ni and Ti levels are elevated in interdendritic zones. This preferential elemental distribution stems from Ti's stronger negative mixing enthalpy with Ni/Cr compared to other elemental pairs, which may induce limited segregation. The T1 HEA exhibits an elongated dendritic microstructure with vanished melt pool boundaries due to recrystallization or grain boundary migration in the SLM-formed structure during annealing. Melt pool boundaries, typically formed by rapid solidification-induced substructures such as cellular structures, are eliminated during annealing through substructure dissolution and grain boundary reorganization, rendering the original boundaries invisible. Fig. 4(c3) displays the EDS elemental mapping of the central region, showing trace precipitation of Co 2Ti and NiTi intermetallic compounds in localized regions of the T2 HEA. This behavior arises from the strong negative mixing entropy between Ti and Co/Cr/Ni, favoring intermetallic compound formation. A minor diffraction peak near 2θ = 44.04° in the alloy's XRD spectrum further supports this conclusion. The SLM process generates extreme thermal gradients and rapid cooling in HEA, producing high-density dislocations and substructures. During annealing, these defects promote recrystallization. However, precipitates or secondary phase particles may pin grain boundaries, leading to grain refinement [ 40, 41]. The EDS analysis indicates that the compounds are enriched in Co 2Ti, Cr 2Ti, and NiTi. This is attributed to the significantly enhanced atomic diffusion capacity and substantially increased grain boundary mobility at 1000 °C, which promotes further precipitation of compounds, consistent with subsequent EBSD characterization results. However, “island-like” large grains form around the fine-grained structure. This phenomenon arises because the annealing temperature approaches the critical point for rapid grain coarsening, where a few grains undergo abnormal growth due to orientation advantages or localized pinning failure. The influence of annealing temperature on grain size, morphology, and crystallographic orientation of FeCoNiCrTi 0. 4HEA was analyzed using EBSD. As shown in Fig. 5(a) , high-angle grain boundaries in the ASB sample predominantly appeared at melt pool boundaries in the longitudinal section (BD direction), with grains exhibiting a high proportion of low-angle grain boundaries. As the annealing temperature increased, the fraction of low-angle grain boundaries decreased from 17.9 % to 11. 1 %. Color variations within individual grains suggest the possible presence of dislocations. This occurs because SLM, as a rapid solidification process, typically produces fine grains, high residual stress, and non-equilibrium microstructures such as high fault density and residual stress [ 28, 29]. The primary purpose of annealing heat treatment is to eliminate residual stress. It promotes recrystallization and grain growth. Additionally, it may facilitate the precipitation of secondary phases or compounds [ 27]. The pole figs. (PF) ( Fig. 5(b)) and inverse pole figures (IPF) ( Fig. 5(c)) of different samples reveal a pronounced 〈001〉 texture orientation along the building direction (BD). This direction corresponds to the preferential growth orientation of the alloy and the maximum temperature gradient direction. The as-built ASB sample typically exhibits strong texture features, such as the <001> texture along BD, due to directional solidification of melt pools during SLM processing. The PF ( Fig. 5(b)) and inverse pole figures (IPF) ( Fig. 5(c)) of different samples reveal a pronounced <001> texture orientation along the building direction. This direction corresponds to the preferential growth orientation of the alloy and the maximum temperature gradient direction. The as-built ASB sample typically exhibits strong texture features, such as the <001> texture along BD, due to directional solidification of melt pools during SLM processing. Dense, crack-free FeCoNiCrTi0. 4 HEA bulk samples and tensile specimens were fabricated via optimized SLM parameters. Post-fabrication annealing was conducted at 600 °C, 800 °C, and 1000 °C for 4 h to systematically evaluate the temperature-dependent effects on microstructure, phase constitution, texture evolution, relative density, and mechanical properties of the HEA. 4HEA bulk samples and tensile specimens were fabricated via optimized SLM parameters. Post-fabrication annealing was conducted at 600 °C, 800 °C, and 1000 °C for 4 h to systematically evaluate the temperature-dependent effects on microstructure, phase constitution, texture evolution, relative density, and mechanical properties of the HEA. This study systematically investigated the microstructural evolution and mechanical properties of as-built (ASB) SLMed FeCoNiCrTi 0. 4HEA and SLMed FeCoNiCrT i0. 4HEA after annealing at 600 °C(T1), 800 °C(T2), and 1000 °C(T3). Before SLM processing, the powder was placed in a vacuum drying oven for 8 h to remove moisture. A stainless-steel substrate measuring 100 mm × 100 mm × 18.5 mm was prepared by grinding its surface with sandpaper, polishing, and ultrasonic cleaning prior to SLM fabrication. The substrate was preheated to 100 °C to minimize thermal stress. The experimental procedure for fabricating HEA via SLM, along with the scanning strategy schematic, is illustrated in Fig. 2(a) , while the tensile specimen dimensions are detailed in Fig. 2(b). Processing was conducted on a Bright Laser Technologies S200 machine (BLT S200, maximum power: 500 W, China) using argon gas as a shielding medium to maintain oxygen levels below 200 PPM, effectively minimizing oxidation risks. During the forming process, argon gas was circulated at an actual airflow rate of 1200 r/min to purify the atmosphere in the chamber. 4HEA square bulk and tensile specimens were annealed at different temperatures using a high-temperature annealing furnace (Tytan1000, USA). The vertical cross-section of the bulk was ground with 80-3000 grit sandpapers, polished with 0.05 μm colloidal SiO 2suspension using an automatic grinding-polishing machine (Mecatech 234, France), and etched with HCl:HNO 3(3:1 vol%). HEA powder morphology and annealed microstructures were characterized by field emission scanning electron microscope (MAIA3 LMH, Czech Republic), with EBSD measurements conducted on multiple cross-sections. Aberration-corrected transmission electron microscopy (ARM200F, Japan) was employed for microstructural analysis of morphology, crystallographic features, and interfaces. The SLM samples were separated from the 316 stainless steel substrate using CNC ultra-high pressure water jet cutting equipment (HEAD42037Z, China). The sample surfaces were then polished with 2000-grit sandpaper. The microhardness at different positions on the cross-section of specimens was measured using a micro multifunctional hardness tester (FALCON 5000, Netherlands) under a 500 g load for 10 s, with at least eight test positions to ensure scientific validity. The density of the samples was measured by the Archimedes drainage method. Tensile strength along the scanning direction under varying heat treatment temperatures was determined at room temperature using a universal testing machine (Instraon5969, USA), with five replicates per condition. Fractography was characterized via field-emission scanning electron microscopy (SEM) (Gemini SEM 500, Germany). Dense, crack-free FeCoNiCrTi0. 4 HEA bulk samples and tensile specimens were fabricated via optimized SLM parameters. Post-fabrication annealing was conducted at 600 °C, 800 °C, and 1000 °C for 4 h to systematically evaluate the temperature-dependent effects on microstructure, phase constitution, texture evolution, relative density, and mechanical properties of the HEA. 4HEA bulk samples and tensile specimens were fabricated via optimized SLM parameters. Post-fabrication annealing was conducted at 600 °C, 800 °C, and 1000 °C for 4 h to systematically evaluate the temperature-dependent effects on microstructure, phase constitution, texture evolution, relative density, and mechanical properties of the HEA. This study systematically investigated the microstructural evolution and mechanical properties of as-built (ASB) SLMed FeCoNiCrTi 0. 4HEA and SLMed FeCoNiCrT i0. 4HEA after annealing at 600 °C(T1), 800 °C(T2), and 1000 °C(T3). Before SLM processing, the powder was placed in a vacuum drying oven for 8 h to remove moisture. A stainless-steel substrate measuring 100 mm × 100 mm × 18.5 mm was prepared by grinding its surface with sandpaper, polishing, and ultrasonic cleaning prior to SLM fabrication. The substrate was preheated to 100 °C to minimize thermal stress. The experimental procedure for fabricating HEA via SLM, along with the scanning strategy schematic, is illustrated in Fig. 2(a) , while the tensile specimen dimensions are detailed in Fig. 2(b). Processing was conducted on a Bright Laser Technologies S200 machine (BLT S200, maximum power: 500 W, China) using argon gas as a shielding medium to maintain oxygen levels below 200 PPM, effectively minimizing oxidation risks. During the forming process, argon gas was circulated at an actual airflow rate of 1200 r/min to purify the atmosphere in the chamber. 4HEA square bulk and tensile specimens were annealed at different temperatures using a high-temperature annealing furnace (Tytan1000, USA). The vertical cross-section of the bulk was ground with 80-3000 grit sandpapers, polished with 0.05 μm colloidal SiO 2suspension using an automatic grinding-polishing machine (Mecatech 234, France), and etched with HCl:HNO 3(3:1 vol%). HEA powder morphology and annealed microstructures were characterized by field emission scanning electron microscope (MAIA3 LMH, Czech Republic), with EBSD measurements conducted on multiple cross-sections. Aberration-corrected transmission electron microscopy (ARM200F, Japan) was employed for microstructural analysis of morphology, crystallographic features, and interfaces. The SLM samples were separated from the 316 stainless steel substrate using CNC ultra-high pressure water jet cutting equipment (HEAD42037Z, China). The sample surfaces were then polished with 2000-grit sandpaper. The microhardness at different positions on the cross-section of specimens was measured using a micro multifunctional hardness tester (FALCON 5000, Netherlands) under a 500 g load for 10 s, with at least eight test positions to ensure scientific validity. The density of the samples was measured by the Archimedes drainage method. Tensile strength along the scanning direction under varying heat treatment temperatures was determined at room temperature using a universal testing machine (Instraon5969, USA), with five replicates per condition. Fractography was characterized via field-emission scanning electron microscopy (SEM) (Gemini SEM 500, Germany). Dense, crack-free FeCoNiCrTi0. 4 HEA bulk samples and tensile specimens were fabricated via optimized SLM parameters. Post-fabrication annealing was conducted at 600 °C, 800 °C, and 1000 °C for 4 h to systematically evaluate the temperature-dependent effects on microstructure, phase constitution, texture evolution, relative density, and mechanical properties of the HEA. 4HEA bulk samples and tensile specimens were fabricated via optimized SLM parameters. Post-fabrication annealing was conducted at 600 °C, 800 °C, and 1000 °C for 4 h to systematically evaluate the temperature-dependent effects on microstructure, phase constitution, texture evolution, relative density, and mechanical properties of the HEA. This study systematically investigated the microstructural evolution and mechanical properties of as-built (ASB) SLMed FeCoNiCrTi 0. 4HEA and SLMed FeCoNiCrT i0. 4HEA after annealing at 600 °C(T1), 800 °C(T2), and 1000 °C(T3). Before SLM processing, the powder was placed in a vacuum drying oven for 8 h to remove moisture. A stainless-steel substrate measuring 100 mm × 100 mm × 18.5 mm was prepared by grinding its surface with sandpaper, polishing, and ultrasonic cleaning prior to SLM fabrication. The substrate was preheated to 100 °C to minimize thermal stress. The experimental procedure for fabricating HEA via SLM, along with the scanning strategy schematic, is illustrated in Fig. 2(a) , while the tensile specimen dimensions are detailed in Fig. 2(b). Processing was conducted on a Bright Laser Technologies S200 machine (BLT S200, maximum power: 500 W, China) using argon gas as a shielding medium to maintain oxygen levels below 200 PPM, effectively minimizing oxidation risks. During the forming process, argon gas was circulated at an actual airflow rate of 1200 r/min to purify the atmosphere in the chamber. 4HEA square bulk and tensile specimens were annealed at different temperatures using a high-temperature annealing furnace (Tytan1000, USA). The vertical cross-section of the bulk was ground with 80-3000 grit sandpapers, polished with 0.05 μm colloidal SiO 2suspension using an automatic grinding-polishing machine (Mecatech 234, France), and etched with HCl:HNO 3(3:1 vol%). HEA powder morphology and annealed microstructures were characterized by field emission scanning electron microscope (MAIA3 LMH, Czech Republic), with EBSD measurements conducted on multiple cross-sections. Aberration-corrected transmission electron microscopy (ARM200F, Japan) was employed for microstructural analysis of morphology, crystallographic features, and interfaces. The SLM samples were separated from the 316 stainless steel substrate using CNC ultra-high pressure water jet cutting equipment (HEAD42037Z, China). The sample surfaces were then polished with 2000-grit sandpaper. The microhardness at different positions on the cross-section of specimens was measured using a micro multifunctional hardness tester (FALCON 5000, Netherlands) under a 500 g load for 10 s, with at least eight test positions to ensure scientific validity. The density of the samples was measured by the Archimedes drainage method. Tensile strength along the scanning direction under varying heat treatment temperatures was determined at room temperature using a universal testing machine (Instraon5969, USA), with five replicates per condition. Fractography was characterized via field-emission scanning electron microscopy (SEM) (Gemini SEM 500, Germany). Dense, crack-free FeCoNiCrTi0. 4 HEA bulk samples and tensile specimens were fabricated via optimized SLM parameters. Post-fabrication annealing was conducted at 600 °C, 800 °C, and 1000 °C for 4 h to systematically evaluate the temperature-dependent effects on microstructure, phase constitution, texture evolution, relative density, and mechanical properties of the HEA. 4HEA bulk samples and tensile specimens were fabricated via optimized SLM parameters. Post-fabrication annealing was conducted at 600 °C, 800 °C, and 1000 °C for 4 h to systematically evaluate the temperature-dependent effects on microstructure, phase constitution, texture evolution, relative density, and mechanical properties of the HEA. This study systematically investigated the microstructural evolution and mechanical properties of as-built (ASB) SLMed FeCoNiCrTi 0. 4HEA and SLMed FeCoNiCrT i0. 4HEA after annealing at 600 °C(T1), 800 °C(T2), and 1000 °C(T3). Before SLM processing, the powder was placed in a vacuum drying oven for 8 h to remove moisture. A stainless-steel substrate measuring 100 mm × 100 mm × 18.5 mm was prepared by grinding its surface with sandpaper, polishing, and ultrasonic cleaning prior to SLM fabrication. The substrate was preheated to 100 °C to minimize thermal stress. The experimental procedure for fabricating HEA via SLM, along with the scanning strategy schematic, is illustrated in Fig. 2(a) , while the tensile specimen dimensions are detailed in Fig. 2(b). Processing was conducted on a Bright Laser Technologies S200 machine (BLT S200, maximum power: 500 W, China) using argon gas as a shielding medium to maintain oxygen levels below 200 PPM, effectively minimizing oxidation risks. During the forming process, argon gas was circulated at an actual airflow rate of 1200 r/min to purify the atmosphere in the chamber. 4HEA square bulk and tensile specimens were annealed at different temperatures using a high-temperature annealing furnace (Tytan1000, USA). The vertical cross-section of the bulk was ground with 80-3000 grit sandpapers, polished with 0.05 μm colloidal SiO 2suspension using an automatic grinding-polishing machine (Mecatech 234, France), and etched with HCl:HNO 3(3:1 vol%). HEA powder morphology and annealed microstructures were characterized by field emission scanning electron microscope (MAIA3 LMH, Czech Republic), with EBSD measurements conducted on multiple cross-sections. Aberration-corrected transmission electron microscopy (ARM200F, Japan) was employed for microstructural analysis of morphology, crystallographic features, and interfaces. The SLM samples were separated from the 316 stainless steel substrate using CNC ultra-high pressure water jet cutting equipment (HEAD42037Z, China). The sample surfaces were then polished with 2000-grit sandpaper. The microhardness at different positions on the cross-section of specimens was measured using a micro multifunctional hardness tester (FALCON 5000, Netherlands) under a 500 g load for 10 s, with at least eight test positions to ensure scientific validity. The density of the samples was measured by the Archimedes drainage method. Tensile strength along the scanning direction under varying heat treatment temperatures was determined at room temperature using a universal testing machine (Instraon5969, USA), with five replicates per condition. Dense, crack-free FeCoNiCrTi0. 4 HEA bulk samples and tensile specimens were fabricated via optimized SLM parameters. Post-fabrication annealing was conducted at 600 °C, 800 °C, and 1000 °C for 4 h to systematically evaluate the temperature-dependent effects on microstructure, phase constitution, texture evolution, relative density, and mechanical properties of the HEA. 4HEA bulk samples and tensile specimens were fabricated via optimized SLM parameters. Post-fabrication annealing was conducted at 600 °C, 800 °C, and 1000 °C for 4 h to systematically evaluate the temperature-dependent effects on microstructure, phase constitution, texture evolution, relative density, and mechanical properties of the HEA. This study systematically investigated the microstructural evolution and mechanical properties of as-built (ASB) SLMed FeCoNiCrTi 0. 4HEA and SLMed FeCoNiCrT i0. 4HEA after annealing at 600 °C(T1), 800 °C(T2), and 1000 °C(T3). Before SLM processing, the powder was placed in a vacuum drying oven for 8 h to remove moisture. A stainless-steel substrate measuring 100 mm × 100 mm × 18.5 mm was prepared by grinding its surface with sandpaper, polishing, and ultrasonic cleaning prior to SLM fabrication. The substrate was preheated to 100 °C to minimize thermal stress. The experimental procedure for fabricating HEA via SLM, along with the scanning strategy schematic, is illustrated in Fig. 2(a) , while the tensile specimen dimensions are detailed in Fig. 2(b). Processing was conducted on a Bright Laser Technologies S200 machine (BLT S200, maximum power: 500 W, China) using argon gas as a shielding medium to maintain oxygen levels below 200 PPM, effectively minimizing oxidation risks. During the forming process, argon gas was circulated at an actual airflow rate of 1200 r/min to purify the atmosphere in the chamber. 4HEA square bulk and tensile specimens were annealed at different temperatures using a high-temperature annealing furnace (Tytan1000, USA). The vertical cross-section of the bulk was ground with 80-3000 grit sandpapers, polished with 0.05 μm colloidal SiO 2suspension using an automatic grinding-polishing machine (Mecatech 234, France), and etched with HCl:HNO 3(3:1 vol%). HEA powder morphology and annealed microstructures were characterized by field emission scanning electron microscope (MAIA3 LMH, Czech Republic), with EBSD measurements conducted on multiple cross-sections. Aberration-corrected transmission electron microscopy (ARM200F, Japan) was employed for microstructural analysis of morphology, crystallographic features, and interfaces. The SLM samples were separated from the 316 stainless steel substrate using CNC ultra-high pressure water jet cutting equipment (HEAD42037Z, China). The sample surfaces were then polished with 2000-grit sandpaper. Dense, crack-free FeCoNiCrTi0. 4 HEA bulk samples and tensile specimens were fabricated via optimized SLM parameters. Post-fabrication annealing was conducted at 600 °C, 800 °C, and 1000 °C for 4 h to systematically evaluate the temperature-dependent effects on microstructure, phase constitution, texture evolution, relative density, and mechanical properties of the HEA. 4HEA bulk samples and tensile specimens were fabricated via optimized SLM parameters. Post-fabrication annealing was conducted at 600 °C, 800 °C, and 1000 °C for 4 h to systematically evaluate the temperature-dependent effects on microstructure, phase constitution, texture evolution, relative density, and mechanical properties of the HEA. This study systematically investigated the microstructural evolution and mechanical properties of as-built (ASB) SLMed FeCoNiCrTi 0. 4HEA and SLMed FeCoNiCrT i0. 4HEA after annealing at 600 °C(T1), 800 °C(T2), and 1000 °C(T3). Before SLM processing, the powder was placed in a vacuum drying oven for 8 h to remove moisture. A stainless-steel substrate measuring 100 mm × 100 mm × 18.5 mm was prepared by grinding its surface with sandpaper, polishing, and ultrasonic cleaning prior to SLM fabrication. The substrate was preheated to 100 °C to minimize thermal stress. The experimental procedure for fabricating HEA via SLM, along with the scanning strategy schematic, is illustrated in Fig. 2(a) , while the tensile specimen dimensions are detailed in Fig. 2(b). Before SLM processing, the powder was placed in a vacuum drying oven for 8 h to remove moisture. A stainless-steel substrate measuring 100 mm × 100 mm × 18.5 mm was prepared by grinding its surface with sandpaper, polishing, and ultrasonic cleaning prior to SLM fabrication. Before SLM processing, the powder was placed in a vacuum drying oven for 8 h to remove moisture. A stainless-steel substrate measuring 100 mm × 100 mm × 18.5 mm was prepared by grinding its surface with sandpaper, polishing, and ultrasonic cleaning prior to SLM fabrication. Dense, crack-free FeCoNiCrTi0. 4 HEA bulk samples and tensile specimens were fabricated via optimized SLM parameters. Post-fabrication annealing was conducted at 600 °C, 800 °C, and 1000 °C for 4 h to systematically evaluate the temperature-dependent effects on microstructure, phase constitution, texture evolution, relative density, and mechanical properties of the HEA. 4HEA bulk samples and tensile specimens were fabricated via optimized SLM parameters. This study systematically investigated the microstructural evolution and mechanical properties of as-built (ASB) SLMed FeCoNiCrTi 0. 4HEA and SLMed FeCoNiCrT i0. 4HEA after annealing at 600 °C(T1), 800 °C(T2), and 1000 °C(T3). Before SLM processing, the powder was placed in a vacuum drying oven for 8 h to remove moisture. A stainless-steel substrate measuring 100 mm × 100 mm × 18.5 mm was prepared by grinding its surface with sandpaper, polishing, and ultrasonic cleaning prior to SLM fabrication. The substrate was preheated to 100 °C to minimize thermal stress. The experimental procedure for fabricating HEA via SLM, along with the scanning strategy schematic, is illustrated in Fig. 2(a) , while the tensile specimen dimensions are detailed in Fig. 2(b). Processing was conducted on a Bright Laser Technologies S200 machine (BLT S200, maximum power: 500 W, China) using argon gas as a shielding medium to maintain oxygen levels below 200 PPM, effectively minimizing oxidation risks. During the forming process, argon gas was circulated at an actual airflow rate of 1200 r/min to purify the atmosphere in the chamber. 4HEA square bulk and tensile specimens were annealed at different temperatures using a high-temperature annealing furnace (Tytan1000, USA). The vertical cross-section of the bulk was ground with 80-3000 grit sandpapers, polished with 0.05 μm colloidal SiO 2suspension using an automatic grinding-polishing machine (Mecatech 234, France), and etched with HCl:HNO 3(3:1 vol%). HEA powder morphology and annealed microstructures were characterized by field emission scanning electron microscope (MAIA3 LMH, Czech Republic), with EBSD measurements conducted on multiple cross-sections. Aberration-corrected transmission electron microscopy (ARM200F, Japan) was employed for microstructural analysis of morphology, crystallographic features, and interfaces. The SLM samples were separated from the 316 stainless steel substrate using CNC ultra-high pressure water jet cutting equipment (HEAD42037Z, China). The sample surfaces were then polished with 2000-grit sandpaper. The microhardness at different positions on the cross-section of specimens was measured using a micro multifunctional hardness tester (FALCON 5000, Netherlands) under a 500 g load for 10 s, with at least eight test positions to ensure scientific validity. The density of the samples was measured by the Archimedes drainage method. Tensile strength along the scanning direction under varying heat treatment temperatures was determined at room temperature using a universal testing machine (Instraon5969, USA), with five replicates per condition. Fractography was characterized via field-emission scanning electron microscopy (SEM) (Gemini SEM 500, Germany). Fig. 9shows the tensile fracture morphologies of FeCoNiCrTi 0. 4HEA after heat treatments at different temperatures. The fracture surface of the as-deposited ASB HEA exhibits a relatively flat and grayish appearance with no obvious necking, where the fracture location may correlate with interlayer printing defects such as pores and lack of fusion [ 46, 47]. This phenomenon occurs because although the FCC structure promotes multi-system slip, the titanium addition forms dendritic structures that create intersecting regions where micropores develop. Shallow and small dimples (1-3 μm in diameter) were locally observed, with microcrack initiation sites potentially containing unfused defects or gas pores at their bases. After 600 °C heat treatment, the fracture surface showed increased roughness and slight necking, suggesting improved plasticity. Meanwhile, obvious wrinkles and slip lines can be observed from the side of the fracture. Cleavage steps were interspersed among dimples, corresponding to residual stress concentration areas not fully eliminated. A limited number of voids formed by precipitated phase detachment were observed at dimple edges (arrow-indicated), leading to final fracture. Under heat treatment at 800 °C, intergranular fracture features appeared, with smooth surfaces formed along grain boundaries in some regions. At this point, it can also be observed that the wrinkle and slip lines have significantly decreased. This phenomenon may be attributed to interfacial weakening caused by the enrichment of precipitated phases (Cr₂Ti, Co₂Ti) at grain boundaries. Concurrently, the reduced sample density adversely affected its mechanical properties, leading to premature fracture. Experimental results indicated that phase interfaces may serve as critical failure sites. At this heat treatment temperature, the wrinkles and slip lines on the side of the fracture surface are significantly reduced. Large areas of cleavage facets covered the fracture surface, displaying smooth textures and visible river patterns, indicative of intergranular cleavage fracture. Before SLM processing, the powder was placed in a vacuum drying oven for 8 h to remove moisture. Before SLM processing, the powder was placed in a vacuum drying oven for 8 h to remove moisture. Before SLM processing, the powder was placed in a vacuum drying oven for 8 h to remove moisture. The EHEA ingot with a nominal composition of AlCoCrFeNi 2.1(at.%) was prepared by vacuum arc melting of a nominal mixture of the constituent elements (purity ≥99.95%) and was remelted at least five times in a Ti-gettered high-purity Ar atmosphere to ensure chemical homogeneity. The molten alloy was suction-cast into a 10 mm (width) × 100 mm (length) × 2 mm (thickness) water-cooled Cu mold. This was followed by stress relieving in a vacuum furnace (Xerion Xtube) at 1023 ± 5 K for 12 h with furnace cooling to reduce potential internal stresses coming from non-uniform cooling during suction casting. For the high-pressure torsion (HPT) process, disks with a diameter of 8 mm and an initial thickness of 2 mm were machined from the as-cast plates using electric discharge machining, followed by grinding with P280 (FEPA, The Federation of European Producers of Abrasives) abrasive papers to a reduction of the thickness to 1.9 mm. The disks were deformed by HPT at a nominal pressure of 6 GPa and a rotational speed of 0.6 rotations/min for 5 rotations at room temperature. The HPT-processed disks were annealed at 1173 K ± 5 K for 10 min in atmosphere followed by water quenching to get the EDPS alloy.

The CoCrNi MEA powder was processed using LPBF. The raw powder for AM was prepared by gas atomization with high purity Ar (≥99.99 %), and the particle size ranged from 13 to 53 μm. The as-printed sample was fabricated by the DiMetal-150 machine at room temperature, equipped with a 500 W Gaussian beam fiber laser, with a spot size ranging from 80 to 100 μm. During the LPBF processing, high purity Ar was used as a protective gas to maintain an oxygen content below 0. After the selection of preliminary process parameters, bulk samples (40∗40∗25 mm) with a relative density (99.5 %) were prepared by setting the laser power, scanning speed, laser hatch and layer thickness at 170 W, 900 mm/s, 0.08 mm and 0.03 mm, the energy density adopted in this experiment is 78. The scanning direction between adjacent layers was rotated by 90°. After LPBF processing, the as-printed samples and the substrate were separated by using electrical discharge machining. In addition, HIP was performed on the as-printed samples at 1150 °C and 150 MPa pressure for 3 h under an argon atmosphere [ 24].

Its spherical powders with uniform composition were successfully prepared by the new mechanical alloying - high temperature remelting spheroidization dual process (DP) method. In this work, we mainly focused on single phase face-centered cubic (FCC) type CrCoNi medium-entropy alloy (MEA), fabricated the homogeneous and heterogeneous grain structure through heavily deformation and subsequent annealing treatment, then investigated the Hall-petch relationship and heterogeneous strength of CrCoNi MEA. The equimolar CrCoNi MEA was produced via electromagnetic levitation melting in a high-purity argon atmosphere, remelted at least four times to ensure chemical homogeneity, then cast to ingots with a diameter of 100 mm and a height of 100 mm. The ingots were first homogenized at 1473 K for 12 h, then cut into samples with dimensions 20 mm(width) ×20 mm(thickness) ×100 mm(length) by electric spark wire machine, finally cold-rolled to 90% reduction in thickness using a laboratory scale rolling equipment with roll diameter 400 mm. The cold-rolled sheets were subsequently annealed at different temperature (range from 973 K to 1373 K) for different times, and immediately water quenched.
