Processing routes including a cold rolling with subsequent annealing were applied on the alloy samples prepared by gas atomization and spark plasma sintering (SPS). Sintering was performed by compacting the CoCrNi powder in a graphite die, followed by SPS. The as-SPSed alloy samples were then sliced to 10 mm thick strips and subsequently rolled by 50% and 70% reduction in thickness at room temperature. Afterwards, the as-rolled samples were annealed individually in an electric resistance furnace at a temperature from 600 °C to 900 °C, followed by water quenching. The CoCrNi alloy powder was fabricated by the gas atomization using high-pressure N 2. The sintering temperature, heating rate, pressure and holding time were 1130 °C, 100 °C/min, 40 MPa and 15 min, respectively.

CoCrFeMnNi HEAs were prepared by magnetic levitation melting technique. The cast ingot was firstly hot forged into rods with 30 mm in diameter, and was further cold rolled into sheets 1 mm in thickness. Then the UFG specimens were obtained by annealing at 998 K for 5 min (named as ORI). Tensile specimens with a gauge length of 10 mm, a width of 2 mm and a thickness of 1 mm were firstly prestrained on an Instron 5982 testing machine at a crosshead speed of 0.6 mm/min. The specimens were loaded up to an engineering strain of 10% at room temperature (named as PRT) and liquid nitrogen temperature (named as PLN), respectively, and then unloaded.

Nano-sized TiC particles (2 wt%) with a mean size of ~50 nm were mixed with the HEA powders to obtain the composite powders using a planetary ball mill device (Fritsch GmbH, Germany), and ball milling parameters can be found in our former work [16]. Samples were built using a commercial LPBF machine (LPBF solutions, 280 HL) equipped with a ytterbium fiber laser (YLR-500, Germany) at a spot size of 70 µm and a maximum power of 500 W. The effect of laser power on densification behaviour of HEA and HEC sample is investigated through the evaluation of relative density ( Fig. 2d and e). There are many gas pores, keyholes and cracks in the HEA sample, while the defects in the HEC sample are small gas pores, as observed in Fig. 3a and d. As Fig. 3f and Fig. 5show, the HEC sample also presents a cellular substructure with an average size of 528.4 ± 65.1 nm in the TD-ND plane. The CoCrFeMnNi HEA matrix composite reinforced with 2 wt% TiC nanoparticles was successfully fabricated via laser-based additive manufacturing.

(Co 40Fe 25V 20Ni 15) 100−xAl x(x = 0, 5 at%) alloy ingots were prepared via arc-melting in a Zr-gettered vacuum atmosphere. Each ingot was melted at least 5 times to ensure chemical homogeneity. The alloy sheets of respective compositions were vacuum sealed in quartz tubes and homogenized at 1423 K for 2 h, then water quenched. The homogenized sheets were cold-rolled to a 65% thickness reduction. The cold-rolled alloys were then annealed at 1123 K and 1323 K for 2 h and water quenched. To determine the Hall-Petch grain size effect in the alloys, the cold-rolled Co 40Fe 25V 20Ni 15alloys were also annealed at 1123 K, 1173 K, 1273 K, and 1373 K for 1 h, followed by water quenching. The Co 40Fe 25V 20Ni 15and (Co 40Fe 25V 20Ni 15) 95Al 5HEA samples are hereby denoted as Al0-1123 K, Al0-1323 K, Al5-1123 K, and Al5-1323 K, respectively. Fig. 4shows the XRD patterns of the Al0 and Al5 samples.

The base alloy is Fe 49. 6Mn 30. 0Co 10. 0Cr 10.4, hereafter denoted as N 0. The N-doped alloy showing the best strength and ductility combination is Fe 45. 9Mn 30. 4Co 10. 5Cr 10. 6N 2.6(at.%), hereafter denoted as N 2. 6. The ingots were hot-forged at 1200 °C and then hot-rolled with initial and final rolling temperatures of 1050 and 900 °C, respectively, reaching a total thickness reduction of 50%. Subsequently, the alloy sheets were homogenized at 1200 °C for 2 h in an Ar atmosphere, followed by water quenching to eliminate the element segregation, which was denoted as the homogenized (HOMO) state. To get refined microstructures, the homogenized alloys were further subjected to multi-pass cold rolling with a total reduction of 60%, and then annealed at 750 °C (below the recrystallization temperature) or 900 °C (above the recrystallization temperature) in a salt bath furnace for 3 min followed by water quenching. The resultant alloys were denoted as at the partially recrystallized (PC) and the fully recrystallized (FC) states, respectively. To quantify the influence of N on the formation of the α-martensite, microstructures of the FeMnCoCrN alloys with different N contents (0.8, 1.8 and 2.6 at.%) at the PC state (i.e. after 750 °C annealing for 180 s and the subsequent water quenching) are compared. In the N 0. 8-, N 1.8- and N 2. 6-PC materials, area fractions of the recrystallized grains are 85%, 80% and 20%, respectively ( Fig. S4). As the α-martensite laths show the similar average thickness and spacing in those materials, the corresponding bcc martensite fractions are estimated to be 4.5%, 6% and 24%, respectively. Microstructures of the cold-rolled as well as the short-time annealed N 2.6materials followed by quenching at different rates are also examined. As shown in Fig. 9a-f, both the air-cooled and the furnace-cooled materials are with a partially recrystallized microstructure and ε-martensite is not identified in either of them.

Here, we architected a duplex heterostructure with FCC/L12 and B2 phases in Ni49Fe28Al17V6 eutectic high-entropy alloy (EHEA) by thermal-mechanical process. The alloy ingot with the composition of Ni 49Fe 8Al 17V 6(at.%) was prepared by melting high-purity (99.95 wt%) alloy elements in argon atmosphere by arc melting. The ingot was melted at least five times to ensure its chemical uniformity, and subsequently the molten liquid was then drop-cast into a water-cooled copper mold with a size of 70 mm × 10 mm × 10 mm. The cast sheet was cold-rolled with a thickness reduction of ∼87 %, and then subjected to annealing at 750 °C for 1 h. The obtained sample was denoted as “CR-A750”.

The HEA samples were prepared using arc melting with a mixture of high-purity raw materials (purity>99.9 wt.%) under a Ti-getter argon atmosphere. The ingot was turned over and remelted eight times to reduce compositional inhomogeneity and then dropped into a rectangular-section copper mold with a dimension of 5 × 12 × 100 mm 3. The as-cast samples were first solution treated at 1200 °C for 2 h, and then furnace cooled to 800 °C at a cooling rate of ∼4 °C/min followed by air cooling to room temperature. Subsequently, these samples were cold rolled along the longitudinal direction with a thickness reduction of ∼65 %. The cold-rolled samples were recrystallized at 1200 °C for 2 min and then furnace cooled to 800 °C at a cooling rate of ∼4 °C/min followed by air cooling to room temperature. Finally, the recrystallized samples were aged at ∼800 °C for 24 h and then cooled to room temperature by air cooling. To investigate the effect of cooling rate during heat treatment on the morphology of L1 2particle and grain boundary, counterpart samples were prepared by using air cooling during the whole heat treatment processing.

The as-cast samples were first solution treated at 1200 °C for 2 h, and then furnace cooled to 800 °C at a cooling rate of ∼4 °C/min followed by air cooling to room temperature. Subsequently, these samples were cold rolled along the longitudinal direction with a thickness reduction of ∼65 %. The cold-rolled samples were recrystallized at 1200 °C for 2 min and then furnace cooled to 800 °C at a cooling rate of ∼4 °C/min followed by air cooling to room temperature. Finally, the recrystallized samples were aged at ∼800 °C for 24 h and then cooled to room temperature by air cooling. To investigate the effect of cooling rate during heat treatment on the morphology of L1 2particle and grain boundary, counterpart samples were prepared by using air cooling during the whole heat treatment processing.

The Nb 39Ta 25Ti 15Hf 15Zr 5Re 1(at.%) and Nb 40Ta 25Ti 15Hf 15Zr 5(referred to as 1Re and 0Re alloy, respectively) ingots with a size of Φ40 × 40 mm 3was prepared by a levitation melting furnace. Each ingot was remelted at least 8 times to ensure the homogeneous distribution of the elements. The plate with 29 mm thickness was obtained by wire electrical discharge machining and cold rolled at room temperature to reduce its thickness by 80%. Finally, the cold-rolled plates were processed via partial recrystallization annealing (Partial-Rx) and complete recrystallization annealing (Complete-Rx), respectively. The complete Rx was determined by analyzing the grain size formed under various annealing process, and the condition of 1050 °C at 2 hours, which resulted in the smallest grain size, were selected (Figure S1). For the partial Rx, the tensile properties of a series of annealed samples were tested at room temperature, and the condition of 850 °C for 2 hours, which offered the best combination of strength and plasticity, were chosen (Figure S2).

Ingots with a nominal composition of Ni 64Cr 25Co 5Al 3Ti 3(at. %) were arc-melted with the elements Co, Cr, Ni, Al and Ti (>99.9% pure) under high purity argon atmosphere. All button ingots are finally cast into a copper mold with a dimension of 10 × 10 × 100 mm 3. After homogenizing at 1323 K for 6 h followed by water quenching, the resultant ingots were then cold-rolled in steps at 293 K along the longitudinal direction to a total thickness reduction of ∼90% (reaching ∼1.0 mm). Finally, the as-rolled sheets were annealed at 800 K for 24 h, followed by water quenching, to introduce simultaneously the discontinuously precipitated L1 2-type ordered phase and heterogeneously grained structure, i.e., the dual heterogeneous structure.

The samples used for the present study were prepared by arc-melting a mixture of pure elements. The ingots were re-melted five times to ensure compositional homogeneity before being drop-cast into a copper mold. Subsequently, samples were homogenized at 1200 °C for 24 h, water-quenched, and then cold-rolled to a thickness reduction of approximately 75 %. In order to obtain samples with different grain sizes, the cold-rolled sheets were annealed at various temperatures ranging from 650 °C to 1250 °C for various time intervals.

Three alloys with nominal components of CoCrNi, (CoCrNi) 96Al 2Ti 2and (CoCrNi) 95Al 2Ti 2Ta 1(at%, named as AT00, AT22, and ATT221 in the context for convenience), were melted by vacuum induction furnace, using pure metal with a purity higher than 99.9%, as shown in Fig. 1(a). Then, the as-cast alloys were solution-treated at 1100 °C for 2 h, followed by hot-forged longitudinally into rods with a diameter of 40 mm ( Fig. 1(b)) at the same temperature. The rods were then annealed at 1100 °C for 2 h and aged at 850 °C for 10 h, which is considered as standard heat treatment technology for superalloys (named as standard heat treatment in the context). In order to study the microstructure by TEM, a 0.4 mm thin foil was cut from aged rods with EDM, and the thin foil was mechanically ground to a thickness of ~30 μm with SiC paper. The specimens were finally thinned out using an ion thinner equipment.

Thermomechanical processing via FSP enabled microstructural control in Fe 40Mn 20Co 20Cr 15Si 5TRIP HEA where the initial phase fraction could be controlled by accurate selection of FSP parameters [ 38]. Unlike conventional alloys where an improvement in strength is achieved at the expense of ductility, Fe 40Mn 20Co 20Cr 15Si 5showed a reversed strength-ductility behavior ( Fig. 22a-b) which was attributed to the microstructural flexibility achieved upon thermo-mechanical processing. % Cu was added at the expense of Fe (Fe 40-xMn 20Co 20Cr 15Si 5Cu x), a γ-dominant microstructure was obtained irrespective of the processing condition which substantiates that Cu addition improved the stability of γ phase [ 88]. 5Mn 20Co 20Cr 15Si 5Cu 1. When minor amount of Al (1.0 at.%) was added to the Fe 40Mn 20Co 20Cr 15Si 5HEA at the expense of Fe, the resulting alloy system showed an unexpected phase transformation response upon annealing ( Fig. 22c), where the final phase fraction upon annealing dramatically changed with annealing temperature and time. However, cold rolling (strain controlled) resulted in a ε-dominant microstructure with high dislocation accumulation. Above observations on microstructural evolution as a function of phase metastability driven alloy chemistry by addition of ε-phase stabilizers and subsequent thermomechanical processing with synergistic action of temperature, strain and strain rate gave rise to the concept of ‘composition-processing-phase stability’ governed microstructural flexibility in TRIP HEAs [ 235]. Generally, BCC alloys have two temperature-stress dependent regimes. However, at low stress/high temperature regime kink pair is effectively characterized by uniform motion of dislocations [ 252]. Deformation mechanism of an alloy is first assessed by activation volume calculation. From stress relaxation tests one could evaluate the activation volume from the value of stress variation during relaxation as per the following equation [ 253]: (18)Δσ(t)=−MkTVa∗ln(1+tc)where Va∗is activation volume, Tis temperature, kis Boltzmann constant and cis a time constant. Lilensten et al. [ 253] performed single and multi-relaxation tests on annealed equiatomic TiZrHfNbTa HEA to understand the deformation mechanism activated during deformation. Activation volume for the alloy was determined to be 25 b 3to 40 b 3which is strain independent. Moreover, similarity in the values of apparent and physical activation volume for the alloy indicated that the hardening process hardly modifies the deformation mechanism [ 253]. Monotonic loading and load relaxation compression tests performed in HfNbTaTiZr HEA by Couzinie et al. [ 254] revealed a monotonic reduction in activation volume from 50 b 3-30 b 3from initial stages of deformation towards failure. Such a reduction in activation volume is related to Peierls stresses experienced by screw dislocations having Burger's vector b= a/2 <111> in early stages of deformation and dislocation band formation in the later stages. Although there is lack of availability of extensive research on dislocation mechanisms in BCC based HEAs, this section is intended to provide a brief description on dislocation mediated plasticity in BCC HEAs. Study of TiZrNbHfTa BCC HEA showed that screw dislocation glide primarily controls the deformation [ 254]. In another study on NbMoTaW BCC HEA, nano-pillar compression tests revealed that deformation is mainly due to lattice resistance to dislocation motion [ 255]. Lilensten et al. [ 253] studied deformation mechanisms in a homogenized single-phase BCC HfNbTaTiZr HEA deformed to a plastic strain level of 0. 0265. Features related to dislocation glide were observed in the SEM micrographs of the deformed sample. TEM analysis revealed presence of two slip systems which were identified as screw dislocations with a/2<111> orientation parallel to {110} and {112} planes ( Fig. 29). The deformation is mainly characterized by the glide of screw dislocations. Measurement of activation volume suggested high Peierls stress in HfNbTaTiZr at room temperature. High yield stress reported for the alloy was associated with the interaction of dislocations with the solute atoms whereas high strain hardening in the material was attributed to higher dislocation density and formation of deformation bands [ 253]. Similar results were also reported by Dirras et al. [ 249] for HfNbTaTiZr HEA. Atomistic simulation performed by Rao et al. [ 256] for BCC multicomponent HEAs revealed the influence of short range order due to local concentration fluctuations which acted as short range obstacles for dislocation motion. Podolskiy et al. [ 257] studied compression behavior and flow stress sensitivity in Ti 30Zr 25Hf 15Nb 20Ta 10alloy in order to accomplish a complete overview of the mechanical behavior in the low temperature regime. The alloy exhibited excellent ductility of ~20% above 77 K irrespective of temperature, whereas yield strength improved with decrease in temperature. Thermally activated plasticity in the alloy at lower temperatures was attributed to the mechanism of kink pair formation along the dislocation line rather than the possibility of hindrance to dislocation due to local short-range clustering. Strain rate dependence on the plastic deformation of quinary HfNbTaTiZr single phase BCC HEA [ 258] revealed intense slip activity and macroscopic shear band formation at strain rate of 1 s -1, whereas at strain rate of 4.53 s −1deformation was localized and heterogeneous within the grains, including observation of intense lattice rotations. Senkov et al. [ 259] studied the cold rolling behavior of HfNbTaTiZr HEA with 65% thickness reduction. Although the flow stress followed the Taylor hardening law, large adiabatic shear band formation in the rolled samples led to failure of the specimen. Nevertheless, achievement of large reduction in thickness during cold rolling keeps the alloy among the limited number of BCC HEAs with tensile ductility. Adding heterogeneities to the BCC HEAs can be an effective way to enhance strain hardening along with the strength of the material. Precipitation is generally not exploited in BCC HEAs due to low ductility of the matrix; however, the precipitate precursors have been utilized. In a recent study [ 260], addition of small amount of oxygen (2 at %) in TiZrHfNb BCC HEA resulted in the formation of (O,Ti,Zr) complexes. Interaction of dislocations with these complexes resulted in dislocation pinning which enhanced the strength and work hardening of the alloy. Metastability based engineering approach has been widely used in FCC HEAs to promote plastic deformation via TRIP [ 35]. Huang et al. [ 261] utilized similar approach in BCC HEAs to explore the possibility of improving ductility. By varying Ta concentration from 1 to 0.4 (mole fraction) in a TaHfZrTi HEA, composition varies from single phase solid solution in equiatomic quaternary TaHfZrTi HEA to dual-phase BCC + HCP microstructure for a Ta concentration of x = 0. 4 ( Fig. 30(a)). With a decrease in Ta content from x = 1 to x = 0.4, uniform ductility improved from mere 4%-~27% ( Fig. 30(b)) upon the activation of BCC→HCP TRIP. Increase in work hardening rate with deformation in alloys with lower Ta content also substantiates the invocation of TRIP ( Fig. 30(c)). Similarly, Lilensten et al. [ 262] proposed an alloy design strategy to control the metastability in Ti containing BCC RHEAs based on the strategy implemented by Abdel-Hady and Morinaga [ 263] in β-Ti alloys by tuning the alloy composition in order to bring the alloy position close to Ms= RTline in B0‾−Md‾diagram, where Msis the martensitic transformation temperature, B0‾is the bond order and Md‾is the energy associated with the d-orbitals. Upon deformation, the microstructure of optimized composition of Ti-rich HEA Ti 35Zr 27. 5Hf 27. 5Nb 5Ta 5revealed the formation orthorhombic α׳׳ martensite phase. High hardening and ductility achieved in the alloy were attributed to interplay of two competing mechanisms, viz., dynamic Hall-Petch effect in which formation of new interfaces due to TRIP effect hinder the dislocation glide, and dynamic composite effect due to accumulation of necessary dislocation near the interfaces. Similar design strategy was employed by Eleti et al. [ 264] to activate TRIP by designing a Ti-rich BCC HEA with composition Ti 38Zr 25Hf 25Ta 10Sn 2which exhibited BCC (β) to HCP (α′) martensitic transformation. TEM analysis of the alloy after deformation revealed that the deformation in BCC phase was characterized by dislocation slip whereas transformed HCP phase further deformed by twinning or dislocation slip. Hence, fine tuning of alloying element concentration in a multicomponent RHEAs to engineer the metastability of the matrix phase enable excellent hardening and ductility in the alloy, thereby creating a balance in mechanical properties. Even though the compositional space available for high entropy alloys is wide, their matrix phase window is mostly restricted to FCC, BCC, or HCP based crystal structures. Mostly, HEAs adopt either FCC or BCC crystal structures, formation of HCP crystal structure is rather rare. BCC HEAs possess high strength but limited ductility whereas FCC HEAs show extensive plastic ductility at low strength. HCP HEAs are desirable as they are expected to have a combination of both high strength and reasonable ductility. Zhao et al. [ 265] discussed mechanical behavior of HCP based HEA GdHoLaTbY which showed a compressive fracture strength of 880 MPa and 21.8% plastic deformation till failure. Rogal et al. [ 266] studied single phase HfScTiZr HEA with a HCP crystal structure which exhibited a Widmanstatten structure. As-cast alloy exhibited compressive strength of 1802 MPa with indication of post deformation shear band formation and presence of high dislocation density. Zhang et al. [ 267] performed compressive deformation study on a CuYZrTiHf dual phase HEA consisting of HCP matrix and ordered BCC phase. Microstructure of the alloy consists of HCP dendrites with BCC interdendritic regions. CuYZrTiHf HEA showed compressive strength of 1340 MPa and plastic strain of 13. 2%. Easy dislocation glide in the HCP solid solution provided plasticity to the alloy when deformed. Cameron et al. [ 268] used high pressure synthesis to stabilize HCP phase in CrMnFeCoNi HEA, where decompression led to the formation of metastable FCC-HCP mixture. Mechanical response of the alloy was not reported. A detailed deformation study on pure HCP HEAs is still lacking. However, a detailed description of deformation mechanisms in dual phase (FCC + HCP) Fe 40Mn 20Cr 15Co 20Si 5HEA is available [ 37, 38]. HCP dominant microstructure obtained after FSP as well as AM showed excellent combination of strength and ductility. Frank et al. [ 242, 244] performed in-situ neutron diffraction study to understand the deformation mechanism in the alloy. Stress is partitioned between both FCC and HCP phases. Excellent ductility obtained for the alloy is attributed to non-basal <c+a> pyramidal slip and deformation twinning achieved in the alloy at larger strains. Detailed discussion on the deformation mechanism in Fe 40Mn 20Cr 15Co 20Si 5HEA was already provided in section 4. 1. 3. In order to qualify an HEA for structural applications, an evaluation of the mechanical performance of the material is critical.

[ 254] revealed a monotonic reduction in activation volume from 50 b 3-30 b 3from initial stages of deformation towards failure. BCC HEAs possess high strength but limited ductility whereas FCC HEAs show extensive plastic ductility at low strength. HCP HEAs are desirable as they are expected to have a combination of both high strength and reasonable ductility. Zhao et al. [ 265] discussed mechanical behavior of HCP based HEA GdHoLaTbY which showed a compressive fracture strength of 880 MPa and 21.8% plastic deformation till failure. Rogal et al. [ 266] studied single phase HfScTiZr HEA with a HCP crystal structure which exhibited a Widmanstatten structure. [ 267] performed compressive deformation study on a CuYZrTiHf dual phase HEA consisting of HCP matrix and ordered BCC phase. [ 268] used high pressure synthesis to stabilize HCP phase in CrMnFeCoNi HEA, where decompression led to the formation of metastable FCC-HCP mixture. [ 242, 244] performed in-situ neutron diffraction study to understand the deformation mechanism in the alloy. Stress is partitioned between both FCC and HCP phases. [ 254] revealed a monotonic reduction in activation volume from 50 b 3-30 b 3from initial stages of deformation towards failure. [ 253] studied deformation mechanisms in a homogenized single-phase BCC HfNbTaTiZr HEA deformed to a plastic strain level of 0. 0265. [ 256] for BCC multicomponent HEAs revealed the influence of short range order due to local concentration fluctuations which acted as short range obstacles for dislocation motion. Podolskiy et al. [ 257] studied compression behavior and flow stress sensitivity in Ti 30Zr 25Hf 15Nb 20Ta 10alloy in order to accomplish a complete overview of the mechanical behavior in the low temperature regime. [ 261] utilized similar approach in BCC HEAs to explore the possibility of improving ductility. Although the flow stress followed the Taylor hardening law, large adiabatic shear band formation in the rolled samples led to failure of the specimen. Nevertheless, achievement of large reduction in thickness during cold rolling keeps the alloy among the limited number of BCC HEAs with tensile ductility. Precipitation is generally not exploited in BCC HEAs due to low ductility of the matrix; however, the precipitate precursors have been utilized. In a recent study [ 260], addition of small amount of oxygen (2 at %) in TiZrHfNb BCC HEA resulted in the formation of (O,Ti,Zr) complexes. [ 261] utilized similar approach in BCC HEAs to explore the possibility of improving ductility. [ 262] proposed an alloy design strategy to control the metastability in Ti containing BCC RHEAs based on the strategy implemented by Abdel-Hady and Morinaga [ 263] in β-Ti alloys by tuning the alloy composition in order to bring the alloy position close to Ms= RTline in B0‾−Md‾diagram, where Msis the martensitic transformation temperature, B0‾is the bond order and Md‾is the energy associated with the d-orbitals. [ 264] to activate TRIP by designing a Ti-rich BCC HEA with composition Ti 38Zr 25Hf 25Ta 10Sn 2which exhibited BCC (β) to HCP (α′) martensitic transformation. Even though the compositional space available for high entropy alloys is wide, their matrix phase window is mostly restricted to FCC, BCC, or HCP based crystal structures. Mostly, HEAs adopt either FCC or BCC crystal structures, formation of HCP crystal structure is rather rare. BCC HEAs possess high strength but limited ductility whereas FCC HEAs show extensive plastic ductility at low strength. HCP HEAs are desirable as they are expected to have a combination of both high strength and reasonable ductility. Zhao et al. [ 265] discussed mechanical behavior of HCP based HEA GdHoLaTbY which showed a compressive fracture strength of 880 MPa and 21.8% plastic deformation till failure. Rogal et al. [ 266] studied single phase HfScTiZr HEA with a HCP crystal structure which exhibited a Widmanstatten structure. [ 267] performed compressive deformation study on a CuYZrTiHf dual phase HEA consisting of HCP matrix and ordered BCC phase. Microstructure of the alloy consists of HCP dendrites with BCC interdendritic regions. CuYZrTiHf HEA showed compressive strength of 1340 MPa and plastic strain of 13. 2%. Easy dislocation glide in the HCP solid solution provided plasticity to the alloy when deformed. Cameron et al. [ 268] used high pressure synthesis to stabilize HCP phase in CrMnFeCoNi HEA, where decompression led to the formation of metastable FCC-HCP mixture. Mechanical response of the alloy was not reported. A detailed deformation study on pure HCP HEAs is still lacking. However, a detailed description of deformation mechanisms in dual phase (FCC + HCP) Fe 40Mn 20Cr 15Co 20Si 5HEA is available [ 37, 38]. HCP dominant microstructure obtained after FSP as well as AM showed excellent combination of strength and ductility. Frank et al. [ 242, 244] performed in-situ neutron diffraction study to understand the deformation mechanism in the alloy. Stress is partitioned between both FCC and HCP phases. Excellent ductility obtained for the alloy is attributed to non-basal <c+a> pyramidal slip and deformation twinning achieved in the alloy at larger strains. Detailed discussion on the deformation mechanism in Fe 40Mn 20Cr 15Co 20Si 5HEA was already provided in section 4. 1. 3. 25Co 0. 25Ni 0. 25(Si 0. 3B 0. 7) 0. 25] 99. 7Cu 0.3(here after denoted as FeCoNi-Cu0.3) were synthesized using a torch-melting process. Subsequently, the resulting master alloy ingots were subjected to a fluxing treatment in a fluxing agent composed of B 2O 3and CaO with a mass ratio of 3:1 at 1473 K for 4 h under a vacuum pressure of ∼50 Pa. After the fluxing treatment, the ingots were cooled down to room temperature and then processed into cylindrical rods with a diameter of 1 mm using the J-quenching technique, the details of which are described elsewhere [ 20]. Compression specimens with an aspect ratio of 2 : 1 were cut from the produced rods for CTC and CEL treatment. For the CTC treatment, the upper temperature were set at 354 K, 393 K, 432 K, 472 K, and 511 K, respectively, while maintaining a constant lower temperature of 77 K, as illustrated in Fig. 1a. Each specimen underwent 15 cycles of CTC treatment, with each cycle lasting 2 min: 1 min at the upper temperature and 1 min of cooling in liquid nitrogen to induce internal structural changes. This process yielded five samples, designated as CTC354K, CTC393K, CTC432K, CTC472K, and CTC511K, the as cast sample named as AC. The CEL treatment, depicted in Fig. 1b, applied constant forces of 260 N, 1300 N, and 2000 N over 8 cycles, and real-time compression curves were provided for each.

Schematic diagram of the rolling and annealing process of L-DED Ti 3Zr 1. 5NbVAl 0. 25RHEA. The process parameters for L-DED in the production of dense Ti 3Zr 1. 5NbVAl 0.25alloy were as follows: laser power of 2000 W, laser scanning speed of 8 mm/s, overlap ratio of 40 % and zigzag pattern ( Fig. 1a). In order to guarantee the uniform powder deposition and substrate preheating, the initial first five layers were deposited with a laser power of 2500 W. The prefabricated alloy powder was transported by argon and deposited in a successive manner, in layers, onto the TC4 titanium alloy substrate. The cold rolling and annealing process of the alloy, shown in Fig. 2, involves cold rolling at room temperature with rollers along the direction of deposition until the thickness is reduced by 50 % (referred to as CR). Following this, the material is heat-treated at various temperatures, with additional details on the rolling process provided in the supplementary materials. The cold-rolled sheet is annealed at 600 °C for 1 h (the annealed sample is represented by CR-600). Similarly, samples of cold-rolled annealed at 700 °C, 800 °C and 900 °C for 1 h respectively are represented by CR-700, CR-800 and CR-900, respectively.

In this work, Fex(CoCrMnNi)100-x (x = 40, 60 and 80 at.%) medium-entropy ferrous alloys (MEFAs) were fabricated through laser powder bed fusion (LPBF) of mixed powders composed of FeCoCrNiMn and Fe powders, and the dynamic compressive properties and deformation mechanisms were studied with combination of experiment and molecular dynamics simulation. The gas-atomized and pre-alloyed Fe x(CoCrNiMn) 100-x( x= 40, 60 and 80 at.%) powders were prepared by mixing FeCoCrNiMn and pure Fe powders with designed ratios of 3:1, 1:1 and 1:3 (hereafter named Fe40, Fe60 and Fe80 respectively), as shown in Fig. 1a-c . The blending of the mixtures was conducted using a planetary ball mill (NanDa Instrument QM-3SP4) at speed of 300 RPM for duration of 5 h, as depicted in Fig. 2a . After the optimization of processing parameter (laser energy density, the number of layers, etc.), these powder mixtures were fabricated via laser powder bed fusion (LPBF) process on an DiMetal-100H (LaserAdd GmbH, Guangzhou, China) device with laser power of 200 W, scanning speed of 800 mm/s, hatch spacing of 70 μm, layer thickness of 30 μm and orthogonal scanning strategy, respectively ( Fig. 2b).

Aging treatment following cold rolling and recrystallization successfully induced L1 2and BCC precipitates in the alloys. The Ni 50Cr 20Co 15Al 10V 5(at. %) HEAs in this work were synthesized using an arc-melting furnace in a Ti-getter, high-purity Ar atmosphere. High-purity Ni, Cr, Co, Al, and V metals (>99.9 wt %) were melted to cast the alloys. To ensure compositional uniformity, the alloys underwent more than seven repeated melting cycles under electromagnetic stirring. The alloys were then cast into a water-cooled copper mold, producing ingots measuring 10 mm × 10 mm × 80 mm. Subsequently, homogenization treatment was carried out at 1200 °C for 24 h in an Ar atmosphere, followed by water quenching. The homogenized ingots underwent cold rolling, resulting in an 80 % reduction in thickness. Following cold rolling, the alloys were recrystallized at 1100 °C for 10 min and then water-quenched to room temperature.

With the characterization of microstructure and tensile properties, the feasibility of preparing Fe50Mn30Co10Cr10 high-entropy alloys (HEAs) via powder metallurgy was explored, and the effect of sintering temperature and deformation temperature on the microstructure and tensile properties of the alloy was investigated. Herein, we explored the feasibility of preparing the metastable Fe 50Mn 30Co 10Cr 10HEAs by PM, i.e., solidification of gas-atomized Fe 50Mn 30Co 10Cr 10pre-alloy powders via SPS, and systematically investigated the effect of sintering temperature and deformation temperature on the microstructure and tensile properties of the alloys. The commercial Fe 50Mn 30Co 10Cr 10(at%) pre-alloy powder prepared by GA was supplied by Beijing Yijin New Material Co. , China) for 30 min at a pressure of 45 MPa and a vacuum of 7 × 10 −3Pa. The sintering temperatures were 800 ℃, 900 ℃, 1000 ℃, and 1100 ℃, respectively. Hence, the as-sintered alloys obtained by SPS were named A8, A9, A10, and A11 alloys, respectively.

An L12-strengthened Co30Cr18Ni42Al5Ti5 medium-entropy alloy was fabricated via directed energy deposition (DED)-Arc technique, focusing on investigating the modulation mechanism of the process on L12 phase precipitation behavior. This work can provide guidance for the fabrication of L1 2-strengthened MEAs/HEAs with excellent mechanical properties by AM. In this work, high-purity Co, Cr, Ni, Al and Ti mono metal powders (>99.5 at.% pure) were mixed by a high-energy ball mill as raw materials for the PPA-AM process. Nominal composition of Co 30Cr 18Ni 42Al 5Ti 5MEA metal powder configured according to atomic percentage and then processed for homogeneous mixing with a high-energy ball mill (YXQM-12L, MITR Ltd, Hunan, China) for 8 h. Samples were built using a PPA-AM (DML-VO3AD, Duomu Company, Shanghai, China) machine equipped. The specimen fate for direct deposition is defined as As-printed MEA. The process of heat treatment of the deposited specimens was annealing treatment at 1273 K for 30 min, followed by rapid water cooling, followed by annealing at 1073 K for 2 h and water quenching. The heat treated specimens were defined as QTAA MEA. The CoCrNi MEA was also prepared by using the PPA-AM process for comparison. From the atom maps of Co, Cr, Ni, Al and Ti elements shown in Fig. 6(a), it is seen that the Ni, Al, and Ti atoms enrich in L1 2phase and Co and Cr atoms enrich in matrix. In this work, we demonstrate that DED-Arc process can be effectively modulate the precipitation behavior of L1 2phase in L1 2-strengthened CoCrNi MEAs. By effectively suppressing DP behavior, we successfully fabricated a Co 30Cr 18Ni 42Al 5Ti 5MEAs with an excellent combination of strong plasticity via DED-Arc process. The effect of heat treatment on the microstructure and properties of Co 30Cr 18Ni 42Al 5Ti 5MEAs was also investigated. The main conclusions are as follows: 1. Co 30Cr 18Ni 42Al 5Ti 5MEA with excellent mechanical properties was printed using a strategy developed for CP of L1 2phase by DED-Arc process. The mechanical properties of the directly printed alloys were superior to those of MEAs/HEAs prepared by many other AM processes, with YS of 736 MPa, UTS of 1090 MPa and UE of 28. 2. After heat treatment, the YS, UTS and UE of the QTAA MEA were 849 MPa, 1110 MPa and 16.8 %, respectively. Co 30Cr 18Ni 42Al 5Ti 5MEA with excellent mechanical properties was printed using a strategy developed for CP of L1 2phase by DED-Arc process. The mechanical properties of the directly printed alloys were superior to those of MEAs/HEAs prepared by many other AM processes, with YS of 736 MPa, UTS of 1090 MPa and UE of 28. After heat treatment, the YS, UTS and UE of the QTAA MEA were 849 MPa, 1110 MPa and 16.8 %, respectively. The deformation mechanism suggests that the network of nanometer-spaced SFs is activated after heat treatment, while the number of L-C locks increases. The high YS of As-printed and QTAA MEAs are due to a combination of strengthening mechanisms, with precipitation strengthening playing a primary role, contributing more than 70 % to the strength of both alloys. This work shows the DED-Arc printed Co 30Cr 18Ni 42Al 5Ti 5MEA with excellent mechanical properties, demonstrating the strong potential of this AM for engineering applications.

Material Name: (Mo, Cr)-rich M6C type carbides, Cr-rich μ phase
Processing Text: Microstructural investigation revealed that the cell boundaries of the as-built sample, which were decorated by Mo segregation, are replaced by µ phase and M6C type carbide precipitates during annealing while the grain structure and size remain unaffected, indicating that the post-LPBF annealing delivered the proper amount of heat input to alter only the cell structure. It can be thus elucidated that, during annealing at 900 °C, the original Cr-rich μ phase precipitates in the as-built sample completely transform into the Cr-rich M 6C type carbides first, and some of them transform again into the new Cr-lean μ phase by overcoming the energy barrier through further heat input. It is possible that the M 6C type carbides have acted as an intermediate phase on the way to forming the new Cr-lean μ phase during the 900 °C annealing, which is stable at higher temperatures than the carbide is: the carbides may have acted as nucleation sites or directly transformed into the μ phase by releasing C and Cr, to eventually form the microstructure of A900 that bears both the μ phase and M 6C type carbide.

The alloy ingots were synthesized in a vacuum induction levitation furnace using high-purity elemental metals (purity >99. 9 %). The melting and casting processes were conducted in an argon atmosphere, and five remelting flips were performed to ensure uniform chemical composition. Two CoCrFexNiMn high-entropy alloys (HEAs) with varying Fe contents (x = 0.2 and 4, referred to as Fe0.2 and Fe4, respectively) were designed and prepared to combine the advantages of metastability and heterostructure within a single-phase FCC matrix. The ingots with nominal molar compositions of CoCrFe xNiMn (referred to simply as Fex, x = 0.2, 4) were synthesized through vacuum-arc melting under an argon atmosphere. Each ingot was remelted at least five times to ensure thorough mixing of the alloying elements, followed by homogenization at 1100 °C for 6 h under argon protection in a vacuum furnace (GSL-1600X, Vacuum Tube Furnace). After achieving complete homogenization, the alloy samples underwent cold rolling, achieving an 80 % reduction in thickness, resulting in sheets with a final thickness of ∼1.2 mm. Subsequently, the cold-rolled samples were annealed at 600 °C for 1 h to induce recrystallization, followed by natural air cooling to ambient temperature. To clarify the strengthening contributions on strength of the annealed Fex alloys, various annealing treatments were performed on the cold rolled Fe0.2 alloy to achieve a comparable level of recrystallization to that observed in the annealed Fe4-T600-1H alloy sample. 2-T800-0.

Each ingot was remelted at least five times to ensure thorough mixing of the alloying elements, followed by homogenization at 1100 °C for 6 h under argon protection in a vacuum furnace (GSL-1600X, Vacuum Tube Furnace). After achieving complete homogenization, the alloy samples underwent cold rolling, achieving an 80 % reduction in thickness, resulting in sheets with a final thickness of ∼1.2 mm. Subsequently, the cold-rolled samples were annealed at 600 °C for 1 h to induce recrystallization, followed by natural air cooling to ambient temperature. To clarify the strengthening contributions on strength of the annealed Fex alloys, various annealing treatments were performed on the cold rolled Fe0.2 alloy to achieve a comparable level of recrystallization to that observed in the annealed Fe4-T600-1H alloy sample. 2-T800-0.

Four V xCr 1-xCoNi (x = 0, 0.4 0.7, and 1) alloys (180 g) were produced using a vacuum induction melting technique (model: MC100V, Indutherm, Walzbachtal-Wössingen, Germany). To manufacture ingots (length × width × thickness: 80 × 35 × 8 mm 3), high-purity elements of 99.95% were stacked in a zirconia crucible and then cast in a graphite mold. Prior to melting, the melting furnace chamber was evacuated to a pressure of 6 × 10 −2Pa and refilled with high-purity Ar gas until the pressure reached 6 × 10 4Pa. This cleaning process was repeated five times to prevent the mixing of the impurity gas. The cast ingots were homogenized at 1150 °C for 2 h in a tube furnace under an Ar atmosphere and then water-quenched, followed by cold-rolling to achieve a thickness reduction. The roll was operated at a speed of 3.0 rpm, and the desired reduction in thickness of 80% was achieved by decreasing the roll gap from 7 mm to 0.5 mm. The 1.5-mm-thick cold-rolled sheets were annealed in an Ar atmosphere and quenched with water. Hydrogen was electrochemically pre-charged in the electrolyte using a cathodic charging method. A mixture of 0. 5 M H 2SO 4was employed as the charging solution with 5 g/L thiourea as a recombination poison, and charging was conducted at a consistent current density of 50 mA cm −2for 24 h.

The as-cast Fe 40Co 20Cr 20Mn 10Ni 10metastable HEAs used in this study were prepared by vacuum induction levitation melting with 99.9% purity constituent elements. Plate samples were cold-rolled at room temperature from an initial thickness of ∼5 mm to a final thickness of ∼0.5 mm, and the thickness reduction for each pass is ∼0.05 mm. To obtain the HS samples, the cold-rolled samples were annealed at 650 °C for 15 min and 750 °C for 2 min followed by water cooling, which are defined as HS650 sample and HS750 sample, respectively. The heat-treated samples were ground on sandpaper and polished with a SiO 2suspension. The samples were prepared by electro-polishing with 60% CH 3OH+ 30% C 4H 9OH+ 10% HCLO 4solution at − 30 °C for electron backscatter diffraction (EBSD) analysis.

A new 3d transition metal high entropy alloy (3d TM HEA) CoFeNiTiV was prepared by vacuum arc-melting. In the present work, the CoFeNiTiV alloy was prepared by vacuum arc melting of the equimolar mixtures of elemental Co, Fe, Ni, Ti and V which were in bulk form with a purity of Co 99. Arc melting of the alloy was conducted on a water-cooled copper crucible under a titanium gettered argon atmosphere. To ensure homogeneously compositional distribution, the alloy ingot was flipped and re-melted four times with electromagnetic stirring and retained in liquid state for about 3 min during each melting event. The ingot pieces were melted by arc melting and then poured into a cylindrical copper mold with a diameter of 4 mm and a length of 60 mm. In the present work, CoFeNiTiV alloy together with the aforementioned CoFeNiTiCu and CoFeNiTiAl alloys were fabricated by vacuum arc melting in a high-purity argon atmosphere, and directly solidified in water-cooled copper molds.

These MEAs were prepared by vacuum arc melting and copper mold casting in an argon atmosphere. The MEAs were melted five times to ensure their homogeneity and then solidified in a 20 mm diameter water-cooled copper crucible. The ingots were homogenized at 1200 °C for 2 h and hot rolled to 3.6 mm. Then, MEAs were cold rolled to 1.8 mm and solid-solution heat treated at 1200 °C for 4 min followed by quenching in water. To promote nanoprecipitates, the solid-solution MEAs were aged at 650 °C for 10 h.

Alloy ingots with a nominal composition Ni 2·5CrFeAl 0·25Ti 0.25(denoted as A5T5 hereafter) were obtained by arc-melting the mixture of high-purity metals (>99.9 wt % in purity) under pure argon atmosphere in a water-cooled crucible and were re-melted at least five times to ensure the chemical homogeneity. These ingots were then drop-cast into a copper mold with a dimension of 8 × 10 × 100 mm 3. The as-cast slabs were cold-rolled 80% along the longitudinal direction. Next, these samples were annealed at 1323 K for 15 min, and then isothermally aged at 973 K for 10 h, followed by water quenching.

%) HEA ingots of size Φ52 × 156 mm were prepared using high purity (99.9 wt %) Co, Cr, Fe, Ni, and Al, followed by melting using a levitation-melting furnace. To avoid the impact of cooling rate and casing defects, the cylindrical specimens of sizeΦ6 × 9 mm were machined from the bottom of the cast ingots at the same height. The as-cast samples were compressed using a Gleeble-3500 thermal simulator at T= 1073 K, 1173 K, 1273 K, 1373 K and ε˙= 10 −3s −1, 10 −2s −1, 10 −1s −1, 1s −1, respectively. Before compression, the samples were heated at the rate of 25 K/s and held for 120s in order to minimize the temperature gradient. When the true strain was up to 0.7, all the samples were cooled via water-quench to freeze the microstructures, and the specimens for microstructural examinations were sectioned in the center parallel to the compressive direction.

The as-cast alloys were cold-rolled with a thickness reduction of ∼90 % and then annealed at 775 °C for 2 h. Here, based on the equilibrium phase diagram of Ni 49Fe 20Al 17Cr 8V 6EHEA, we have performed a series of annealing treatment within a range temperature of 750∼900 °C for 2 h on the cold-rolled samples to achieve a superior mechanical performance. Thus, to reveal the origin for simultaneous strengthening of strength and plasticity compared with the as-cast samples, the annealing temperature of 775 °C for 2 h was performed on the cold-rolled samples and systematic research was conducted in this work. To further enhance the mechanical performance of the as-cast Ni 49Fe 20Al 17Cr 8V 6EHEA, cold-rolling and annealing treatment were performed on the AC EHEA, architecting a heterogeneous structure in the CR-775 EHEA.

5Ni 2.5(at.%) were produced by a vacuum arc melting furnace with a water-cooled copper mold using pure metals (purity higher than 99.9 wt%). The ingots were re-melted at least five times to improve chemical homogeneity. The obtained button ingots were homogenized at 1200 °C for 5 h followed by water-quenching. Then, the samples were cold rolled to a thickness reduction ratio of 65%. Subsequently, the rolled sheets were annealed at different temperatures (from 600 °C to 900 °C) for 60 min, respectively, followed by water-quenching or liquid nitrogen quenching.

CoCrNi medium entropy alloy (MEA) and stainless steel 316L (SS316L) were manufactured by direct energy deposition of additive manufacturing (DED-AM). Liquid hydrogen green-energy has recently attracted much attention in solving the environmental pollution. In this work, we manufactured CoCrNi MEA and SS316L by the AM-DED process (DED CoCrNi MEA and DED SS316L). All specimens were manufactured using commercial DED equipment (INSSTEK MX-400) under an argon gas atmosphere, a laser source of fiber, a laser power of 380 ∼ 400 W, a scan speed of 14 mm/s, a spot size of 0.8 ∼ 1.2 mm, powders made by gas-atomizing (AMC-powders Co. , Ltd), a powder size of 50∼150μm, a powder feed rate of 4 ∼ 5 L/min, a layer thickness of 250 μm, a hatch spacing of 400 μm, and a building direction of the Z axis ( Fig. 1). We manufactured bulk sample with a rectangular shape, whose dimension is about 13 mm (x) × 13 mm (y) × 100 mm (z). The DED bulk samples were cut using electrical discharging machining (EDM) to prepare the cylindrical tensile specimen. Then, the EDM sample was polished for neutron diffraction experiment. The chemical composition of the powders was confirmed by an inductively coupled plasma-atomic emission spectrometer (ICP-AES). The chemical composition of DED samples was confirmed by energy dispersive X-ray spectroscopy (EDS). The microstructure was examined on the plane parallel to the building direction. The surface of the specimens was mechanically polished by using 6, 3, and 1 μmdiamond suspension. Then the mirror finished surface was electrically etched and/or polished using a nitric acid (35%) solution for optical microscope (OM), scanning electron microscope (SEM, CARL ZEISS MERLIN COMPACT) and electron backscatter diffraction (EBSD, OXFORD AZTEC HKL NORDLYS NANO) analyses. The conditions of the electrical etching for CoCrNi MEA were as follows: voltage 2V, exposure time 25s and operating temperature room temperature; for SS316L: 2V, 8s, and room temperature. The conditions of electrical polishing for CoCrNi MEA were as follows: 5V, 20s, and room temperature; for SS316L: 4V, 7s, and room temperature.

After homogenizing the molten alloys were poured into a water-cooled steel die with a dimension of about 150 mm × 120 mm × 20 mm. To facilitate the description, the NbC-free and NbC-bearing equiatomic FeCoCrNi HEAs are hereinafter denoted as H1 and H2 in this study. Firstly, the rectangular ingots of H1 and H2 were hot rolled at 1050 °C to a thickness of ∼12 mm (corresponding to a thickness reduction of 40%). Then the hot-rolled sheets were annealed at 1300 °C for 40 min and followed by water quenching to obtain the complete solid solution microstructure. The two specimens were subsequently cold rolled at room temperature along their long axis to a thickness of ∼5 mm (corresponding to a thickness reduction of 58%). Finally, the two cold-rolled specimens were annealed at 1000 °C for 2 min (H1) and 30 min (H2) respectively and followed by immediate water quenching. After being abraded with emery paper from 150 to 4000 grit, H1 and H2 specimens with and without hydrogen charging were tensioned at an engineering strain rate of 10 −4s −1in an Instron 5569 mechanical testing machine at room temperature. Hydrogen was pre-charged into the specimens using a cathodic electrochemical charging technique in a 0.1 mol/L H 2SO 4+ 2 g/L CH 4N 2S (thiourea) solution with a constant current density of 30 mA/cm 2for 72 h at room temperature.

The Gd xCoCrFeNiV 0.4(x = 0, 0.01, 0.03, 0.05 at%) alloys were prepared using a vacuum non-consumable arc melting furnace (MZ-1250). To ensure the homogeneity of the alloy ingots, each ingot was remelted at least five times. Subsequently, the ingots were homogenized at 1150 °C for 2 h. The alloys were then subjected to cold rolling with a reduction of 50 %. After cold rolling, the Gd0 and Gd1 samples were annealed at 650 °C, 750 °C, and 850 °C for 2 h.

In this study, a novel method for multi-material laser powder bed fusion (MM-LPBF) with staggered printing was developed. Using AlCuCoCrFeNi-HEA and MnCoCrFeNi-HEA powders as starting materials, three heterogeneous bi-metallic structures were fabricated. The MM-LPBF process utilizes gas-atomized and pre-alloyed MnCoCrFeNi and AlCuCoCrFeNi HEA (Labeled as Mn-HEA and AlCu-HEA, respectively) powders, with particle sizes ranging from 15 to 53 micrometers. Prior to the MM-LPBF process, all powders were vacuum-dried in a desiccator for 8 h. In contrast, the AlCu-HEA was processed using a laser power of 230 W and a scanning speed of 1000 mm/s. The process begins with the deposition of a 25 μm layer of alloy A powder, followed by laser selective melting of the alloy A region. The build platform is then lowered by 25 μm, and a layer of alloy B powder is deposited from a different powder feeder. After completing the alloy B region, the remaining unmelted alloy B powder is removed. The build platform is lowered by another 25 μm, and the process of alternating powder deposition and laser melting continues with alloy A.

The process begins with the deposition of a 25 μm layer of alloy A powder, followed by laser selective melting of the alloy A region. The build platform is then lowered by 25 μm, and a layer of alloy B powder is deposited from a different powder feeder. After completing the alloy B region, the remaining unmelted alloy B powder is removed. The build platform is lowered by another 25 μm, and the process of alternating powder deposition and laser melting continues with alloy A.

In this study, (Fe50Mn30Co10Cr10) 100−xSix (x = 0, 4, 8, 12 at%) high-entropy alloys were successfully prepared by laser melting deposition technology. The aim is to explore the effects of silicon on the microstructure evolution and mechanical properties of Fe 50Mn 30Co 10Cr 10high-entropy alloys. In order to investigate the effect of Si on the microstructure and properties of laser-deposited Fe 50Mn 30Co 10Cr 10alloy, the powders were mixed by ball milling at a speed of 340 r/min for 3 h, according to the atomic ratio of elements listed in Table 1. After mixing, the powder is dried at 50 °C for 2 h in a vacuum oven. Subsequently, the powders are used to prepare alloy samples with a size of 65 (length) × 20 (width) × 7 (height) mm by laser melting deposition (LMD) technology and argon protection. During the laser deposition process, the processing parameter is: laser power 1000w, scanning speed 300 mm/min, spot diameter 2 mm, and overlap rate 50 %. To ensure the uniformity of the deposition layer, the laser route of the Nth layer and the N + 1th layer are reversed by 180°.

In order to investigate the effect of Si on the microstructure and properties of laser-deposited Fe 50Mn 30Co 10Cr 10alloy, the powders were mixed by ball milling at a speed of 340 r/min for 3 h, according to the atomic ratio of elements listed in Table 1. After mixing, the powder is dried at 50 °C for 2 h in a vacuum oven. Subsequently, the powders are used to prepare alloy samples with a size of 65 (length) × 20 (width) × 7 (height) mm by laser melting deposition (LMD) technology and argon protection. During the laser deposition process, the processing parameter is: laser power 1000w, scanning speed 300 mm/min, spot diameter 2 mm, and overlap rate 50 %. To ensure the uniformity of the deposition layer, the laser route of the Nth layer and the N + 1th layer are reversed by 180°.

This work proposed a simple bionic-inspired strategy to in situ construct a root-like interfacial interlocked structure in the refractory high-entropy alloys (RHEA) particle-reinforced Ni matrix composites by activated sintering. MoNbTaW RHEA particles (15-53 μm) and pure Ni particles (15-53 μm) fabricated by plasma and gas atomization ( Fig. 1a) without any pre-treatment were chosen as the reinforcement and matrix to fabricate the RHEA/Ni composites. The mixed powders with different RHEA volume fraction ratios (0 vol%, 5 vol%, 10 vol%, and 15 vol%) were ball milled for 6 h at 350 rpm rotation speed under the Ar atmosphere protection ( Fig. 1b and c). The mixed powders after ball milling were synthesized at 1100 °C by spark plasma sintering (SPS), as shown in Fig. 1d.

Ni 2FeCrW x( x= 0, 0.1, 0.2, 0.3, 0.4, and 0.5 in molar ratio) MEAs ingots weighting 130 g were prepared by vacuum arc melting in a high purity argon atmosphere and cooled in a water-cooled Cu crucible. In the melting process, pure Ni and W were initially melted together to form an intermediate alloy with a lower melting point, then Fe, and Cr elements were added, and each ingot was remelted at least 10 times. Half of each component button ingot was annealed at 1473 K for 3 h followed by in-furnace cooling. The samples were heated to 1200 °C at a rate of 10 °C/min in a dynamic atmosphere of high-purity argon gas and held for 120 min to make them transformed completely. Then, they were cooled at a rate of 200 °C/min to obtain high-temperature microstructures.

The homogenized ingots underwent thermomechanical processing, which included a thickness reduction from approximately 8 mm to 1.6 mm. The cold-rolled samples were annealed at 1150 ℃ for 3 min to achieve complete recrystallization, followed by aging at 800 ℃ for 2 h to promote precipitation of the L1 2precipitate.

The raw materials were melted using arc melting with a high-purity argon atmosphere. Prior to the melting process, Al was placed at the bottom of the copper crucible, followed by a uniform mixture of Ti, V, Zr, and Nb on the top. To ensure the chemical homogeneity, each button ingot was flipped and re-melted at least eight times. Subsequently, the alloys were drop-cast into a water-cooled copper crucible, forming rectangular ingots measuring 15mm × 10mm × 40 mm in size. The obtained ingot was then cold-rolled at room temperature to achieve an 80 % reduction in thickness, with in a final thickness of around 2 mm. Finally, the cold-rolled plates were subjected to a recrystallization annealing at 900 °C for 30 min, followed by an immediately water quenching. The specimens were sealed in a vacuum quartz tube before the annealing treatment to avoid oxidation.

Pre-alloyed equimolar CrCoNi MEA powder with a particle size distribution of 15-53 μm was used in this study. Prior to SLM fabrication, CrCoNi MEA powder was sieved, dried at 80 °C in a vacuum chamber, and was transported to the SLM system immediately to avoid contamination and dampness. Cubic testing blocks and dog-bone-shape tensile specimens were subsequently built directly on stainless steel substrate employing a scanning strategy presented in Fig. 1(c). Ex-situuniaxial tensile tests were performed on pre-polished, dog-bone shaped, specimens using Instron-5982 testing system with a strain rate of 0.02/min at 77 K (liquid nitrogen), 195 K (liquid carbon dioxide), and 293 K (room temperature, RT). To further inspect microstructural response with high spatial and temporal resolution, in-situsynchrotron X-ray diffraction (SXRD) interrupted tensile tests were performed at beamline BL14B1, Shanghai Synchrotron Radiation Facility (SSRF) at RT. A brief evaluation of SLM parameters (laser power, scanning speed, hatching space, and VED) was conducted in this work to maintain simplicity and conciseness without losing control of product quality. In the orthogonal tests, laser power, scanning speed, and hatching space would lie in the range of 140 W-180 W, 1000 mm/s-1500 mm/s, and 50 μm-90 μm, respectively. Laser focus diameter and layer thickness were fixed at 60 μm and 30 μm, respectively. As VED went greater, the relative density reached a local optimum at 109. 1 J/mm 3. By applying a semi-empirical criterion, the parameter combination yielded the highest sample relative density: 180 W of laser power, 1100 mm/s of scanning speed, 50 μm of hatching space, and a corresponding VED of 109. 1 J/mm 3was chosen in the following primary manufacturing processes. Here we performed in-situSXRD interrupted tensile tests at RT to precisely determine the onset of twinning with a schematic shown in Fig. 9(a).

The CoCrFeNi (at%) HEA as a reference alloy was prepared by arc-melting. Ingots were re-melted five to eight times to ensure chemical homogeneity and then cast into a water-cooled copper mold with a dimension of 2 mm × 10 mm × 100 mm. The as-cast plates were homogenized at 1200 °C for 2 h, followed by cold-rolling to achieve a 70 % reduction ratio in thickness. Subsequently, the cold-rolled plates were annealed at 700 °C and 1000 °C for 10 min (labeled as alloy-700 and alloy-1000, respectively). All the thermo-mechanical procedures were performed in an argon atmosphere, with final quenching with water.

In this study, isotropically high strength AlCrCuFeNi high-entropy alloy (HEA) reinforced Al12Si composites were successfully fabricated by laser powder bed fusion (L-PBF) process. The mixing of Al12Si and HEA particles was performed in a powder mixer (Huozao SYH-5) with a 5 L volume mixing chamber. Blending is performed using 5 mm diameter zirconia balls (roughly 500 g), and powders (approximately 1500 g of Al12Si with 0 wt %, 1 wt %, 3 wt % and 5 wt % HEA powders, respectively). All samples were produced by EP-M250plus (Beijing E-plus-3D, China) with a 500W Yb fiber laser.

The hot deformation behavior of the as-cast ingot was investigated to guide the hot forging process. Annealing was further conducted on the as-forged samples to obtain more optimized mechanical properties. The as-forged HEA had yield strength (YS) of 792 MPa, ultimate tensile strength of 1055 MPa and a satisfactory fracture elongation (EL) of 22. 6%. The YS of the HEA annealed at 1050 °C increased from 393 MPa to 512 MPa and EL from 26.5% to 55.3% in comparison with the as-cast HEA. To ensure chemical homogeneity, each ingot was re-melted three times. The as-cast ingots had a diameter of 110 mm and a height of 110 mm. Subsequently, the ingots were homogenized at 1100 °C for 6 h. The cylindrical samples with a diameter of 8 mm and a height of 12 mm were cut for the hot compression tests. The hot compression tests were conducted using a Gleeble-3800 thermo-simulation machine at three different temperatures (900 °C, 1000 °C and 1100 °C) and three different strain rates (0.01 s −1, 0.1 s −1and 1 s −1). The temperature was controlled with the aid of the thermocouple fixed on the surface of the samples. Maximum temperature variation was controlled within 2 °C of the set temperature during the whole test. The chamber was first vacuumed and then the sample was heated to the testing temperature at a rate of 10 °C/s. Before the hot compression, the samples were soaked at the given temperature for 5 min to achieve stability with the environment. Based on the results of hot compression tests, the cylindrical ingots were hot forged at 1100 °C to sheets with a final thickness of 20 mm, followed by air cooling. Then, annealing treatment was conducted on the as-forged HEA to recrystallize at different temperatures (950 °C, 1050 °C and 1100 °C) for 30 min, where the as-annealed samples were hereafter denoted as A950, A1050 and A1100, respectively. However, the microstructure of the as-forged sample (as shown in Fig. 5a) is different from that of the 1100 °C hot compressed sample ( Fig. 4d). The matrix is not completely recrystallized after forging at 1100 °C and the recrystallized volume fraction is approximate 60%. Moreover, a large amount of precipitates is observed in the grain boundary of the as-forged sample (the inset of Fig. 5a). The EDS analysis ( Fig. 5e) shows that these precipitates are mainly Cr-rich carbides. These observations indicate that the actual forging parameters may deviate from the optimum hot working window obtained from hot compression tests. As shown in the inset of Fig. 5a, the recrystallized grains of the as-forged sample are obviously elongated, indicating that the finish forging temperature may be far less than 1100 °C. Combined with the microstructures of the samples compressed below 1100 °C ( Fig. 4b and c), it can be suggested that the incomplete recrystallization of the as-forged sample is mainly attributed to the temperature drop during forging. Additionally, the precipitation of carbides may be due to the relatively slower cooling rate (air cooling, large thickness). Again, the microstructure is closely related with the ingot size. Annealing treatment at 950 °C, 1050 °C and 1100 °C for 30 min was further performed to recrystallize and dissolve the precipitates of the as-forged samples. Back scattering electron observations in Fig. 5b-d indicate that the microstructures of the as-annealed samples consist of recrystallized grains and residual precipitates. It can be found that the YS and UTS of the C-free HEA are dramatically improved from 213 MPa to 471 MPa-393 MPa and 634 MPa, respectively. In particular, the YS is almost doubled by C doping. The hot forging further enhances the strength and the as-forged sample exhibits a high YS of 792 MPa and a high UTS of 1055 MPa. These values are much higher than those of the as-cast sample (393 MPa and 634 MPa). Meanwhile, the as-forged sample also exhibits a satisfactory EL of 22. 6%. After annealing at 950 °C, the ductility is enhanced from 22.6% to 33.9%, at the expense of YS which reduces from 792 MPa to 559 MPa, but the UTS changes little (from 1055 MPa to 1004 MPa). Compared with the A950, the ductility of the A1050 and A1100 increases significantly from 33.9% to 55.3% and 69.4%, respectively, while the YS only slightly drops from 559 MPa to 512 MPa and 476 MPa, respectively. Consequently, an excellent combination of YS (>470 MPa), UTS (>940 MPa) and ductility (>55%) is obtained in these two samples, which can be comparable to fine grain C-containing HEAs [ 15, 20, 30]. To ensure chemical homogeneity, each ingot was re-melted three times. The as-cast ingots had a diameter of 110 mm and a height of 110 mm. Subsequently, the ingots were homogenized at 1100 °C for 6 h. The cylindrical samples with a diameter of 8 mm and a height of 12 mm were cut for the hot compression tests. The temperature was controlled with the aid of the thermocouple fixed on the surface of the samples. Maximum temperature variation was controlled within 2 °C of the set temperature during the whole test. The chamber was first vacuumed and then the sample was heated to the testing temperature at a rate of 10 °C/s. Before the hot compression, the samples were soaked at the given temperature for 5 min to achieve stability with the environment. A CoFeMnNi medium-entropy alloy (MEA) was prepared by mechanical alloying (MA) and spark plasma sintering (SPS). Co, Fe, Mn, Ni elemental powders (ZhongNuo Advanced Material (Beijing) Technology Co. , Ltd. , China) having a purity >99.9% and a particle size of <45 μm were mixed at an equiatomic ratio and subsequently milled in a high-energy planetary ball mill. Stainless steel balls and vials were used for ball milling at a ball-to-powder weight ratio of 13:1. The vial was filled with high purity argon to protect the powder from excess oxidation during the milling process. At milling times of 5, 10, 20, and 30 h, samples of the ball-milled powders were taken out for analysis, and the rest was removed after 40 h. The powder milled for 40 h was loaded into a graphite die and subsequently heated by a spark plasma sintering machine (SPS-825, Sumitomo Coal Mining Co. Ltd. , Japan) with a heating rate of 100 °C min −1and kept at 800-1050 °C for 10 min under a pressure of 50 MPa. After high-temperature sintering, the consolidated specimen was cooled to 500 °C with a cooling rate of about 300 °C min −1and then slowly cooled down to room temperature.

CrCoNi-Al 2O 3composites were prepared using Cr, Co, Ni powders (Beijing Xingrongyuan Technology Co. Firstly, Al 2O 3nano powders with content of 2.5-7.5 wt% and Cr, Co and Ni powders with equal atomic ratio were successively added into stainless steel vials in a sealed operation glove box protected by high-purity argon (≥99. The hard Al 2O 3particles can be embedded into the metal matrix through the ball milling process, so that they can be homogenously distributed in the matrix. Stainless steel balls were used for ball milling with a ball to powder weight ratio of 10:1, and 2.5 wt% of absolute ethanol as a process control agent (PCA) was added to prevent cold welding on the vial walls and stainless steel balls, and finally the sealed stainless steel vials were installed on a QM-QX2 omnidirectional planetary ball mill. The powders of CrCoNi, CrCoNi-2.5 wt%Al 2O 3, CrCoNi-5.0 wt%Al 2O 3and CrCoNi-7.5 wt%Al 2O 3were prepared by ball milling at 300 rpm for 35 h under ambient temperature. The prepared powders were loaded into the graphite mold with graphite paper and inner diameter of 30 mm. After cold pressing with a pressure of 15-20 MPa, hot pressing sintering was conducted using a fully automated SPS instrument (LABOX-330, Japan) under vacuum condition. In the sintering process, the temperature from room temperature to 570 °C was measured by a thermocouple, and that above 570 °C was measured by an infrared sensor.

In this study, the energy density was varied from 65 to 80 J mm −3to explore the optimal processing conditions while fixing the hatch spacing and layer thickness to 80 and 25 µm, respectively. The corresponding laser power and scanning speed were controlled in the ranges of 78-80 W and 600-500 mm s −1, respectively. For the Ed700 specimen with the lowest defect density among the specimens, a post-heat treatment was conducted to modify the mechanical properties. The heat treatment was conducted at 1000 °C for 10 min in an Ar atmosphere, followed by water quenching. The specimens for the metallographic observation were mechanically polished using a SiC abrasive paper, a diamond suspension of 1 µm, and a colloidal silica for 0.5 h. The large defects such as voids and cracks were observed using optical microscopy (OM, Imager D1m, ZEISS, Germany), and their fractions were quantified using the ImageJ analysis program. At least five images were analyzed for each datum point. Scanning electron microscopy (SEM, Quanta FEG 250, FEI, United States) and electron backscatter diffraction (EBSD, S-4300SE, Hitachi, Japan) were used to investigate the micro-sized inner defects and microstructures. The planar defects were observed by distinguishing contrast differences using SEM-BSE mode with operation conditions of 15 kV voltage, 0.15 nA current density, and 8 mm working distance. The characterization of the nano-scale cell structures and inclusions was conducted using transmission electron microscopy (TEM, JEM-2100F, JEOL, Japan). For the TEM analysis of the initial microstructures, the specimens were ground to 70 µm, and then punched into 3 mm diameter disks. These thin foils were electro-polished using a twin-jet polisher (TenuPol-5, Struers, Denmark) using a 95 % acetic acid + 5 % perchloric acid solution. Needle-shaped specimens were prepared using a focused ion beam (FIB, NX5000, Hitachi, Japan) for atom probe tomography (APT, LEAP4000X HR, CAMECA, France) to investigate the atomic-scale compositions and morphologies of the nanostructures. For the mechanical testing, dog-bone-shaped specimens (gauge length of 1.5 mm, gauge width of 1 mm, and thickness of 1 mm) were extracted from the L-PBF-processed specimens according to the processing parameters and tensile directions. The uniaxial testing was conducted at a strain rate of 10 −3s −1at room temperature. The tensile strain was measured using a digital image correlation (DIC, ARAMIS v6. 1, GOM Optical Tech. , Germany) technique. The tensile deformation behavior was investigated using SEM and TEM (Titan 80-30, FEI, United States). The TEM specimens were prepared using an FIB lift-out for analysis along a specific zone axis <110> to reveal the dislocation structures in the {111} planes during deformation.
