The studied alloy was prepared by vacuum induction melting and gravity casting, followed by three-step hot forging at a temperature of 1250 °С. Heat treatment at 1330 °C for 10 min resulted in a homogenized equiaxed grain structure with a face-centered cubic crystal structure. Before melting, the vacuum chamber of the induction furnace was evacuated to a pressure of 4. The ingots were subjected to solution annealing at a temperature of 1330 °С for 6 h under a protective dynamic argon atmosphere to homogenise their microstructure and chemistry before hot forging and further heat treatments. The hot forging experiments were conducted at a temperature of 1250 °C in three steps, where 30 %, 60 %, and 40 % of the machine energy was used to press the samples in each step. The forged samples were subjected to heat treatment at a temperature of 1330 °С for 10 min, followed by air cooling to remove internal stresses and achieve a uniformly distributed equiaxed grain structure. Hydrogen was introduced into the alloy by cathodic charging in a solution of 3.6 ml H 2SO 4, 1330 ml H 2O, and 0.011 g As 2O 3at a constant current density of 0.6 mA/mm 2using the platinum electrode. Charging was performed at a temperature of 70 °C for 72 h. The chemical composition of the studied HEA measured by EDS ( Table 1) is in good agreement with the nominal composition of (CoCrFeNi) 92Al 8(at%). The structure of the as-cast ingot consisting of large columnar grains ( Fig. 1a) transformed during applied hot forging to fine grain structure with the average grain size of (22 ± 2) µm, as is shown in Fig. 1b. Heat treatment of the forged samples at a temperature of 1330 °С for 10 min led to the increase of grain size to the average (340 ± 20) µm ( Fig. 1c). Fig. 3complements Fig. 1c by providing grain orientation and boundary data in the HT condition using EBSD analysis. Applied heat treatment resulted in the formation of a homogenized equiaxed grain structure with random orientations, as shown in the EBSD inverse pole figure (IPF) in Fig. 3a. During the applied heat treatment, Σ3 twins were predominantly formed within the FCC (A1) grains, while a smaller fraction of Σ9 twin boundaries (∼3.4 %) was also identified, as highlighted in yellow and red, respectively, in Fig. 3b. As shown in Fig. 5, a numerical simulation was conducted to determine the strain value in the area of EBSD analysis. The initial equiaxed grains ( Figs. 1c and 3) underwent severe deformation and rotation due to the acting stress, as shown in Fig. 6a. Next to the active slip systems, numerous fine twins were detected in the grains during tensile deformation. Fig. 6b shows the misorientation profile along line 1 in band contrast figure ( Fig. 6a), which confirms the dominant formation of fine Σ3 twins. Fig. 6c shows EBSD-IPF map of the grains close to < 111 > direction parallel with load direction. Fig. 6d shows a KAM map of the same region, which indicates different dislocation densities along grain boundaries and inside the grains. Dislocations are accumulated at HAGB, TB, and slip bands (SB). Fig. 6e shows the Schmid factor (SF) map of the deformed microstructure. Fig. 7displays the fracture surface of tensile samples before and after hydrogen charging for 72 h at 70 °C. During plastic deformation, clear necking indicates a ductile behaviour in the hydrogen-uncharged samples ( Fig. 7a). After hydrogen charging, this necking effect is reduced ( Fig. 7d). Fig. 7b and e show typical fracture morphology of the hydrogen-uncharged and hydrogen-charged samples. In both conditions, dimples and voids are visible on the fracture surface. The homogenized, hydrogen-uncharged samples display primarily ductile features characterized by numerous dimples. These dimples likely result from the nucleation and coalescence of microvoids during deformation. A similar behaviour was observed in CoCrFeMnNi high entropy alloy with FCC structure during RT tensile tests by Li et al. [29]. They demonstrated that hydrogen-uncharged samples exhibit a ductile fracture surface after tensile tests, characterized by a central zone covered with numerous dimples, a mark of ductile behaviour. It was also observed that a pronounced necking accompanied by distinct slip-band patterns [29]. The fracture surface of hydrogen-charged sample reveals a higher density of voids and surface-connected cracks than that of the hydrogen-uncharged one, indicating a shift in the dominant fracture mechanism ( Fig. 7b, c, e, and f). The fracture surface of the hydrogen-charged sample is severely influenced by hydrogen, causing the ductile central region to lose its ductile characteristics and become brittle near the sample surface ( Fig. 7d and f). This transition from ductile to brittle behaviour as hydrogen concentration increases aligns well with findings from other studies in CrMnFeCoNi [60]and Al 0. 25CoCrFeNi HEAs [61]. Several studies showed that hydrogen-charged samples exhibit a multi-mode failure process, characterized by a central ductile zone and a brittle zone near the

surface. A dimpled fracture pattern predominates in the ductile area, whereas the brittle region exhibits a quasi-cleavage or intergranular failure mode, depending on the duration of hydrogen charging [29,43,60]. Several mechanisms have been proposed to explain hydrogen embrittlement of FCC structure: hydrogen-enhanced localized plasticity, hydrogen-enhanced decohesion (HEDE), and adsorption-induced dislocation emission [62-64]. The HEDE mechanism, in particular, posits that predominantly in regions with high local hydrogen concentration, hydrogen atoms weaken bonds of metallic atoms, reducing the stress required for their decohesion [64]. The fracture features observed in the hydrogen-charged samples, particularly the combination of intergranular cracks and localized cleavage-like areas, are indicative of the hydrogen-enhanced decohesion (HEDE) mechanism, in which high hydrogen concentration at grain and twin boundaries reduces cohesive strength. As a result of the high hydrogen concentration, numerous slip bands can be observed in this region as well. Decreasing the hydrogen concentration in the alloy volume affects the fracture character. The transition from brittle to ductile morphology across the sample cross-section is consistent with hydrogen-enhanced localized plasticity (HELP), which can cause intense dislocation activity and subsequent microvoid coalescence near hydrogen-trapped regions. The observed fracture behavior therefore reflects the combined action of HEDE and HELP, both of which are strongly influenced by the grain boundary network and presence of annealing twins. To further substantiate this transition, BSE imaging ( Fig. 8) was conducted near the fracture surfaces, showing the longitudinal section of tensile samples in hydrogen-charged and hydrogen-uncharged states. These images highlight crack propagation paths, suggesting hydrogen-assisted weakening along grain boundaries. This morphological evidence aligns with the mechanical data showing reduced ductility in hydrogen-exposed samples. While the surface of hydrogen-uncharged samples is dominantly influenced by slipping processes during tensile tests ( Fig. 8a), the surface of the hydrogen-charged samples shows large cracks formed and propagated along the boundaries ( Fig. 8b). In comparison with the central region, the surface region is less prone to plastic deformation. The calculation of the penetration length of microcracks formed on the surface of the hydrogen-charged sample during the tensile testing process showed that the majority of the surface cracks measure approximately 30 μm in length, while about 10 % of the cracks are approximately 110 μm in length. The microcracks propagate along grain boundaries and occasionally along twin boundaries under suitable conditions. High hydrogen accumulation at the surface results in HE, which may induce crack initiation and propagation under stress. In addition to hydrogen concentration, crack lengths are affected by the applied tensile strain rate, as well as the size, orientation, and deformation characteristics of the grains at the local strain zone. In the necking region, cracks exceeding 150 μm in length. These surface cracks are distinctly identifiable on the cross sections of the fracture surfaces, as illustrated in Figs. 7 and 8. Fig. 8c shows a detail of the surface crack formed due to hydrogen charging with Σ3 twins and slip bands. Fig. 8d shows an EBSD-IPF map with some surface grains that did not undergo rotation in orientation near the <111> direction parallel to the load direction, as observed in the central region. Surface cracks are connected with active slip bands and twin formation, which are affected by hydrogen. The Σ3 twin boundaries typically demonstrate excellent resistance to HE because of their high cohesion strength and low hydrogen diffusivity [26]. As recently reported by Chen T. et al. [65], coherent Σ3 TBs may serve as low-energy pathways for hydrogen diffusion, acting as “hydrogen channels” that promote intergranular cracking under stress. Based on EBSD analysis ( Figs. 6 and 8), Σ3 TBs seem to align with several near-surface crack paths. In hydrogen-charged Al 0. 35CrCrFeNi HEA with FCC structure, the interaction of Σ3 boundaries with SBs must be considered under tension, which can lead to microcrack initiation and growth along Σ3 twin boundaries that promote the hydrogen diffusion. As shown in Fig. 8b, evidence of crack propagation along twin interfaces, combined with SBs interaction, local grain rotation, and dislocation accumulation near TBs, supports their role as potential hydrogen-assisted fracture routes. However, significant crack propagation occurs along grain boundaries. The average KAM distribution ( Fig. 8e) of dislocations in the under-surface region is lower in comparison with the central region. It means that dislocation density changes across the sample section. In the surface region, it is typical that dislocations are concentrated mainly near GB and cracks, but some signs can be observed along slip bands as well. As indicated by the values of SF in Fig. 8f, the higher the rotation of the FCC structure towards the <111> plane parallel to the load direction, the lower the capacity to activate its slip systems. Once the hydrogen concentration reaches a critical level, the reduction in cohesive strength leads to the initiation of cracks and their propagation preferentially along grain boundaries. Dong-Hyun Lee et al. [66]observed in their research a high density of dislocation slip bands around cracks and grain boundaries in hydrogen-charged CoCrFeNi alloy after tensile tests, indicating that the accumulation of dislocations contributes to significant local stress. Additionally, moving dislocations can transport hydrogen, enriching grain boundaries where dislocation slip bands intersect. Even under ex-situ hydrogen charging, dislocation slip continues to transfer hydrogen to the grain boundaries during deformation. Although the hydrogen-charged

samples exhibit localized intergranular cracking near the surface, the overall tensile curves ( Fig. 4a) show that plastic deformation remains extensive, with failure occurring after significant strain. This suggests that the effects of hydrogen embrittlement are mostly limited to the surface regions, while the rest of the material remains ductile and maintains good mechanical performance. Such behaviour supports the conclusion that the Al 0. 35CoCrFeNi HEA exhibits moderate resistance to hydrogen embrittlement at applied charging conditions. It is worth mentioning that electrochemical hydrogen charging at a temperature of 70 °C for 72 h did not significantly affect the mechanical properties of the alloy in terms of the deformation process, as uncharged samples exhibit nearly identical shapes in their tensile response. While this study investigates hydrogen effects under a single charging condition, the trends observed are consistent with prior HEA studies. It is well known that hydrogen embrittlement is sensitive to charging time, temperature, and hydrogen concentration. The fracture mode transitions and mechanical behaviour reported here should therefore be interpreted within this specific exposure regime. The hot forging experiments were conducted at a temperature of 1250 °C in three steps, where 30 %, 60 %, and 40 % of the machine energy was used to press the samples in each step. The forged samples were subjected to heat treatment at a temperature of 1330 °С for 10 min, followed by air cooling to remove internal stresses and achieve a uniformly distributed equiaxed grain structure. Applied heat treatment resulted in the formation of a homogenized equiaxed grain structure with random orientations, as shown in the EBSD inverse pole figure (IPF) in Fig. 3a. During the applied heat treatment, Σ3 twins were predominantly formed within the FCC (A1) grains, while a smaller fraction of Σ9 twin boundaries (∼3.4 %) was also identified, as highlighted in yellow and red, respectively, in Fig. 3b. As shown in Fig. 5, a numerical simulation was conducted to determine the strain value in the area of EBSD analysis. The initial equiaxed grains ( Figs. 1c and 3) underwent severe deformation and rotation due to the acting stress, as shown in Fig. 6a. Next to the active slip systems, numerous fine twins were detected in the grains during tensile deformation. Fig. 6b shows the misorientation profile along line 1 in band contrast figure ( Fig. 6a), which confirms the dominant formation of fine Σ3 twins. Fig. 6c shows EBSD-IPF map of the grains close to < 111 > direction parallel with load direction. Fig. 6d shows a KAM map of the same region, which indicates different dislocation densities along grain boundaries and inside the grains. Fig. 7displays the fracture surface of tensile samples before and after hydrogen charging for 72 h at 70 °C. During plastic deformation, clear necking indicates a ductile behaviour in the hydrogen-uncharged samples ( Fig. 7a). After hydrogen charging, this necking effect is reduced ( Fig. 7d). Fig. 7b and e show typical fracture morphology of the hydrogen-uncharged and hydrogen-charged samples. In both conditions, dimples and voids are visible on the fracture surface. The homogenized, hydrogen-uncharged samples display primarily ductile features characterized by numerous dimples. These dimples likely result from the nucleation and coalescence of microvoids during deformation. They demonstrated that hydrogen-uncharged samples exhibit a ductile fracture surface after tensile tests, characterized by a central zone covered with numerous dimples, a mark of ductile behaviour. It was also observed that a pronounced necking accompanied by distinct slip-band patterns [29]. The fracture surface of hydrogen-charged sample reveals a higher density of voids and surface-connected cracks than that of the hydrogen-uncharged one, indicating a shift in the dominant fracture mechanism ( Fig. 7b, c, e, and f). The fracture surface of the hydrogen-charged sample is severely influenced by hydrogen, causing the ductile central region to lose its ductile characteristics and become brittle near the sample surface ( Fig. 7d and f). surface. A dimpled fracture pattern predominates in the ductile area, whereas the brittle region exhibits a quasi-cleavage or intergranular failure mode, depending on the duration of hydrogen charging [29,43,60]. Several mechanisms have been proposed to explain hydrogen embrittlement of FCC structure: hydrogen-enhanced localized plasticity, hydrogen-enhanced decohesion (HEDE), and adsorption-induced dislocation emission [62-64]. The HEDE mechanism, in particular, posits that predominantly in regions with high local hydrogen concentration, hydrogen atoms weaken bonds of metallic atoms, reducing the stress required for their decohesion [64]. The fracture features observed in the hydrogen-charged samples, particularly the combination of intergranular cracks and localized cleavage-like areas, are indicative of the hydrogen-enhanced decohesion (HEDE) mechanism, in which high hydrogen concentration at grain and twin boundaries reduces cohesive strength. As a result of the high hydrogen concentration, numerous slip bands can be observed in this region as well. Decreasing the hydrogen concentration in the alloy volume affects the fracture character. The transition from brittle to ductile morphology across the sample cross-section is consistent with hydrogen-enhanced localized plasticity (HELP), which can cause intense dislocation activity and subsequent microvoid coalescence near hydrogen-trapped regions. The observed fracture behavior therefore reflects the combined action of HEDE and HELP, both of which are strongly influenced by the grain boundary network and presence of annealing twins. This morphological evidence aligns with the mechanical data showing reduced ductility in hydrogen-exposed samples. While the surface of hydrogen-uncharged samples is dominantly influenced by slipping processes during tensile tests ( Fig. 8a), the surface of the hydrogen-charged samples shows large cracks formed and propagated along the boundaries ( Fig. 8b). In the necking region, cracks exceeding 150 μm in length. These surface cracks are distinctly identifiable on the cross sections of the fracture surfaces, as illustrated in Figs. 7 and 8. Fig. 8c shows a detail of the surface crack formed due to hydrogen charging with Σ3 twins and slip bands. Fig. 8d shows an EBSD-IPF map with some surface grains that did not undergo rotation in orientation near the <111> direction parallel to the load direction, as observed in the central region. Surface cracks are connected with active slip bands and twin formation, which are affected by hydrogen. [65], coherent Σ3 TBs may serve as low-energy pathways for hydrogen diffusion, acting as “hydrogen channels” that promote intergranular cracking under stress. As shown in Fig. 8b, evidence of crack propagation along twin interfaces, combined with SBs interaction, local grain rotation, and dislocation accumulation near TBs, supports their role as potential hydrogen-assisted fracture routes. However, significant crack propagation occurs along grain boundaries. The average KAM distribution ( Fig. 8e) of dislocations in the under-surface region is lower in comparison with the central region. It means that dislocation density changes across the sample section. In the surface region, it is typical that dislocations are concentrated mainly near GB and cracks, but some signs can be observed along slip bands as well. Dong-Hyun Lee et al. [66]observed in their research a high density of dislocation slip bands around cracks and grain boundaries in hydrogen-charged CoCrFeNi alloy after tensile tests, indicating that the accumulation of dislocations contributes to significant local stress. Additionally, moving dislocations can transport hydrogen, enriching grain boundaries where dislocation slip bands intersect. samples exhibit localized intergranular cracking near the surface, the overall tensile curves ( Fig. 4a) show that plastic deformation remains extensive, with failure occurring after significant strain. The hot forging experiments were conducted at a temperature of 1250 °C in three steps, where 30 %, 60 %, and 40 % of the machine energy was used to press the samples in each step. The forged samples were subjected to heat treatment at a temperature of 1330 °С for 10 min, followed by air cooling to remove internal stresses and achieve a uniformly distributed equiaxed grain structure. Applied heat treatment resulted in the formation of a homogenized equiaxed grain structure with random orientations, as shown in the EBSD inverse pole figure (IPF) in Fig. 3a. During the applied heat treatment, Σ3 twins were predominantly formed within the FCC (A1) grains, while a smaller fraction of Σ9 twin boundaries (∼3.4 %) was also identified, as highlighted in yellow and red, respectively, in Fig. 3b. As shown in Fig. 5, a numerical simulation was conducted to determine the strain value in the area of EBSD analysis. The initial equiaxed grains ( Figs. 1c and 3) underwent severe deformation and rotation due to the acting stress, as shown in Fig. 6a. Next to the active slip systems, numerous fine twins were detected in the grains during tensile deformation. Fig. 6b shows the misorientation profile along line 1 in band contrast figure ( Fig. 6a), which confirms the dominant formation of fine Σ3 twins. Fig. 6c shows EBSD-IPF map of the grains close to < 111 > direction parallel with load direction. Fig. 6d shows a KAM map of the same region, which indicates different dislocation densities along grain boundaries and inside the grains. Fig. 7displays the fracture surface of tensile samples before and after hydrogen charging for 72 h at 70 °C. During plastic deformation, clear necking indicates a ductile behaviour in the hydrogen-uncharged samples ( Fig. 7a). After hydrogen charging, this necking effect is reduced ( Fig. 7d). Fig. 7b and e show typical fracture morphology of the hydrogen-uncharged and hydrogen-charged samples. In both conditions, dimples and voids are visible on the fracture surface. The homogenized, hydrogen-uncharged samples display primarily ductile features characterized by numerous dimples. These dimples likely result from the nucleation and coalescence of microvoids during deformation. They demonstrated that hydrogen-uncharged samples exhibit a ductile fracture surface after tensile tests, characterized by a central zone covered with numerous dimples, a mark of ductile behaviour. It was also observed that a pronounced necking accompanied by distinct slip-band patterns [29]. The fracture surface of hydrogen-charged sample reveals a higher density of voids and surface-connected cracks than that of the hydrogen-uncharged one, indicating a shift in the dominant fracture mechanism ( Fig. 7b, c, e, and f). The fracture surface of the hydrogen-charged sample is severely influenced by hydrogen, causing the ductile central region to lose its ductile characteristics and become brittle near the sample surface ( Fig. 7d and f). surface. A dimpled fracture pattern predominates in the ductile area, whereas the brittle region exhibits a quasi-cleavage or intergranular failure mode, depending on the duration of hydrogen charging [29,43,60]. Several mechanisms have been proposed to explain hydrogen embrittlement of FCC structure: hydrogen-enhanced localized plasticity, hydrogen-enhanced decohesion (HEDE), and adsorption-induced dislocation emission [62-64]. The HEDE mechanism, in particular, posits that predominantly in regions with high local hydrogen concentration, hydrogen atoms weaken bonds of metallic atoms, reducing the stress required for their decohesion [64]. The fracture features observed in the hydrogen-charged samples, particularly the combination of intergranular cracks and localized cleavage-like areas, are indicative of the hydrogen-enhanced decohesion (HEDE) mechanism, in which high hydrogen concentration at grain and twin boundaries reduces cohesive strength. As a result of the high hydrogen concentration, numerous slip bands can be observed in this region as well. Decreasing the hydrogen concentration in the alloy volume affects the fracture character. The transition from brittle to ductile morphology across the sample cross-section is consistent with hydrogen-enhanced localized plasticity (HELP), which can cause intense dislocation activity and subsequent microvoid coalescence near hydrogen-trapped regions. The observed fracture behavior therefore reflects the combined action of HEDE and HELP, both of which are strongly influenced by the grain boundary network and presence of annealing twins. This morphological evidence aligns with the mechanical data showing reduced ductility in hydrogen-exposed samples. While the surface of hydrogen-uncharged samples is dominantly influenced by slipping processes during tensile tests ( Fig. 8a), the surface of the hydrogen-charged samples shows large cracks formed and propagated along the boundaries ( Fig. 8b). In the necking region, cracks exceeding 150 μm in length. These surface cracks are distinctly identifiable on the cross sections of the fracture surfaces, as illustrated in Figs. 7 and 8. Fig. 8c shows a detail of the surface crack formed due to hydrogen charging with Σ3 twins and slip bands. Fig. 8d shows an EBSD-IPF map with some surface grains that did not undergo rotation in orientation near the <111> direction parallel to the load direction, as observed in the central region. Surface cracks are connected with active slip bands and twin formation, which are affected by hydrogen. [65], coherent Σ3 TBs may serve as low-energy pathways for hydrogen diffusion, acting as “hydrogen channels” that promote intergranular cracking under stress. As shown in Fig. 8b, evidence of crack propagation along twin interfaces, combined with SBs interaction, local grain rotation, and dislocation accumulation near TBs, supports their role as potential hydrogen-assisted fracture routes. However, significant crack propagation occurs along grain boundaries. The average KAM distribution ( Fig. 8e) of dislocations in the under-surface region is lower in comparison with the central region. It means that dislocation density changes across the sample section. In the surface region, it is typical that dislocations are concentrated mainly near GB and cracks, but some signs can be observed along slip bands as well. Dong-Hyun Lee et al. [66]observed in their research a high density of dislocation slip bands around cracks and grain boundaries in hydrogen-charged CoCrFeNi alloy after tensile tests, indicating that the accumulation of dislocations contributes to significant local stress. Additionally, moving dislocations can transport hydrogen, enriching grain boundaries where dislocation slip bands intersect. samples exhibit localized intergranular cracking near the surface, the overall tensile curves ( Fig. 4a) show that plastic deformation remains extensive, with failure occurring after significant strain. 7CoCrFeNi2.4 alloy with a low cracking susceptibility index was designed by Thermo-Calc calculation and fabricated by laser powder bed fusion. 7CoCrFeNi 2.4alloy with a low cracking susceptibility index was designed by Thermo-Calc calculation and fabricated by laser powder bed fusion. The layers were rotated by 67° to minimize the accumulation of samples' defects in the same direction [ 17]. After several rounds of experimental exploration, the scanning strategy of interpolating chessboard and stripe was selected for printing. The samples were built with the hatch spacing of 70 μm and a layer thickness of 50 μm through the chessboard/stripe scanning strategies. According to the calculated results, aging treatments were carried out at 635, 700, 800, and 910 °C. After aging at 800 °C for 30 min, the obtained sample not only maintains a high yield strength (1157 MPa), but also increases elongation slightly from 16.7% to 17. After 30 min, elongation increases slightly to 27.3%, but the yield strength decreases significantly. As a result of 120 min aging treatment at 910 °C, the elongation increases significantly from 24.8% to 36.2% which was selected as the optimal aging treatment parameter for elongation enhancement.

The nominally equiatomic NbMoTaW alloy was produced by arc melting commercially pure (purity> 99. The arc melting process was conducted in a water-cooled Cu crucible placed in a vacuum chamber back-filled with Ar gas to introduce an inert atmosphere. The buttons were remelted ten times to achieve a homogeneous composition. During the final remelting process, the melting current was gradually reduced from full power to 60 % at a 30-second interval, maintaining the top half of the ingot in the liquid form to heat treat the bottom half of the solidified ingot. In situheat treatment process was employed to promote recrystallization in the bottom half of the ingot and achieve a near-equiaxed microstructure. Following solidification, the buttons were hot isostatically pressed (HIP) at 1850 °C for 4 hr in an Ar atmosphere (Fig. However, even after the HIP treatment ( Fig. 1a), the microstructure did not recrystallize and consisted of columnar and equiaxed regions like a cast material (Fig. The HIPed buttons were sectioned using a slow-speed cutter and then mounted in an epoxy resin to evaluate the microstructure. The mounted specimens were first mechanically polished using emery paper and then in a vibromat using a colloidal silica solution of particle size ⁓0.04 µm to achieve a mirror finish. S3a). From the equiaxed section of the HIPed buttons, dog-bone specimens of gauge length, width, and thickness ⁓3 × 1.4 × 1 mm 3were machined for the tensile tests (Fig. The specimens were mechanically polished before tensile and compression tests to remove the oxide layers formed on the surface during the EDM process. The specimens were kept at the testing temperature for 20 min before starting the tests. A constant stream of Ar gas was maintained through a steel tube inserted around the fixtures to minimize oxidation during the tests. The flow of Ar gas was also maintained during the cooling process to prevent the oxidation of the fractured surfaces of the specimens. The microstructures of the specimens exposed to high temperature were also investigated post facto. The deformed microstructure was evaluated by focused ion beam (FIB) lift-outs of microscale specimens after the compression tests at 1200 °C using 30 kV Ga-ion followed by 5 kV and 2 kV polishing. The composition variation along the grain boundaries in these samples was characterized using an EDS line scan on an FEI TitanX at an operating voltage of 300 kV. Additional FIB lift-outs were performed to prepare lamellae with grain boundary oxides that were then transferred to a Protochip heating E-chip. In situheating experiments were carried out at 800 °C in the same TEM using a Protochip heating holder with a heating rate of 20 °C/s.

The alloy prepared using vacuum arc melting was obtained from Sophisticated Alloys, Inc. The cast samples were hot-rolled to 30% thickness reduction at 1150 °C, and then cold-rolled to achieve an additional 30% thickness reduction. In the first route, homogenization at 1100 °C for 10 min followed by water quenching results in what is referred to as the homogenized (AH) condition. In the second route, the cold-rolled + homogenized material was subsequently annealed at 580 °C for 24 h to form L1 2precipitates, which henceforth are denoted as as-homogenized + low-temperature annealing (AH + LTA) condition.

The alloys ingots, with a nominal composition of Fe 55Co 15Cr 10Al 8Ni 12-xSi x(x = 0, 3 at. %), are produced in a vacuum arc furnace that is protected by argon gas. The ingots are turned and remelted five times and then suction-cast into water-cooled copper molds with dimensions of 100 mm × 11 mm × 8 mm. Subsequently, a homogenization heat treatment at 1100 °C in an argon atmosphere is conducted, followed by rolling at room temperature to achieve a thickness of about 1.8 mm. The cold-rolled plate then undergoes annealing heat treatment at 800 °C for 10 min, with all the above heat treatment utilizing water quenching.

This study introduces a method for in-situ tailoring of microstructure and properties of high entropy alloys (HEAs) by modulating the micrometer-scale elemental mixing through altering laser processing parameters. The influence of laser processing parameters in the laser-powder bed fusion (PBF-LB) process on the microstructure and properties of alloys prepared through in-situ alloying of AlSi10Mg and FeCoCrNi mixed powders was investigated. In this work, gas-atomized FeCoCrNi alloy powder and AlSi10Mg alloy powder were employed. A mixture of the two powders with an Al content of about 10 at% was blended for 10 h using a three-dimensional powder mixer and then dried in a vacuum oven at 100°C for 4 h. The in-situ alloying process was conducted on a commercial PBF-LB system (Renishaw RenAM 500E) equipped with a 500 W fiber laser (beam size of 80 μm), utilizing a 316 L stainless steel substrate. In this study, we manufactured the NiCoCr medium-entropy alloy (MEA) for the first time with controlled interstitial C content of 0.25 at% and 0.75 at% (0. Moreover, an attempt was made to manufacture an i-MEA using L-PBF type SLM technology to improve the properties and manufacture net-shape parts. The pre-alloyed powders were processed using SLM. Bar type bulk samples sized 85 mm × 10 mm × 12 mm were prepared under the optimal process conditions to evaluate the microstructural and mechanical properties of the two alloys ( Fig. 2(a)). To investigate the effect of interstitial carbon on the tensile properties of SLM-built MEA, we manufactured tensile samples with a gauge length of 12 mm, a gauge width of 3 mm, and a gauge thickness of 1.5 mm in the scanning direction (SD). We then conducted a room temperature tensile test of a plate-shaped tensile specimen with an initial strain rate of 10 −3/s (model: MTS 810, MTS systems, USA).

The EHEA with a nominal composition of Al 21Co 19. 5Fe 9. 5Ni 50was prepared by arc-melting a mixture of constituent elements with a purity higher than 99.99 wt.% in a high-purity argon atmosphere. Before the melting process, the surfaces of each metal block were mechanically cleaned to remove surface oxides. Each alloy sample was melted five times for one minute and flipped over each melting to ensure complete mixing and chemical homogeneity. In order to regulate the phase precipitation and substructure features as well as obtain a homogeneous microstructure, the as-cast EHEA is subjected to solid-solution treatments at 900 and 1100 °C followed by different cooling methods. After solid-solution treatments at 900 °C for 1 h, the samples were cooled to room temperature using three different cooling methods: furnace cooling (at a rate of 5 °C min -1), air cooling, and water quenching. This study presents the innovative development and characterization of lightweight multi-component alloys (MCAs), specifically MgAlCuZnGd alloys, fabricated using a novel high-throughput gradient continuous casting method. This study presents the innovative development and characterization of lightweight multi-component alloys (MCAs), specifically MgAlCuZnGd alloys, fabricated using a novel high-throughput gradient continuous casting method. Utilizing an advanced high-throughput multi-component axial functional gradient-material equipment, this work focuses on fabricating the MgAlCuZnGd MCAs rod with diverse chemical compositions. Accordingly, in this work, lightweight MgAlCuZnGd MCAs with component gradient were prepared by gradient continuous casting method. Each of these materials had a purity level of at least 99.9 % and a particle size within the range of 1-2 mm. Throughout the experimental process, argon gas was used to create a protective atmosphere, ensuring the integrity of the materials. In the preparation stage, metal particles consisting of Al, Zn, Mg, Gd, and Cu were individually placed into five separate containers. These containers were then methodically fed into the particle mixing chamber. The flow rates were carefully controlled to align with the desired compositions for the experiment. Once mixed, the combined particles of Al, Zn, Mg, Gd, and Cu were transported through a spiral feeding rod to the heating unit. This step initiated the casting process. The resultant MgAlCuZnGd MCA rod, featuring a gradient of chemical compositions, emerged from the lower end of the equipment. This process involved melting, casting, and solidifying the materials. To prepare the samples for elemental analysis, each region underwent a meticulous grinding process. This process utilized silicon carbide sandpaper, progressing from coarse to fine grades, followed by a final polish using a 0.5 μm silica suspension. Each of these materials had a purity level of at least 99.9 % and a particle size within the range of 1-2 mm. Throughout the experimental process, argon gas was used to create a protective atmosphere, ensuring the integrity of the materials. In the preparation stage, metal particles consisting of Al, Zn, Mg, Gd, and Cu were individually placed into five separate containers. These containers were then methodically fed into the particle mixing chamber. The flow rates were carefully controlled to align with the desired compositions for the experiment. Once mixed, the combined particles of Al, Zn, Mg, Gd, and Cu were transported through a spiral feeding rod to the heating unit. This step initiated the casting process. The resultant MgAlCuZnGd MCA rod, featuring a gradient of chemical compositions, emerged from the lower end of the equipment. This process involved melting, casting, and solidifying the materials. To prepare the samples for elemental analysis, each region underwent a meticulous grinding process. This process utilized silicon carbide sandpaper, progressing from coarse to fine grades, followed by a final polish using a 0.5 μm silica suspension. Additionally, precise machining of samples from these eight regions was conducted to facilitate the subsequent tests. For the OM studies, samples from different regions of the MCA rod underwent a preparation process involving grinding, polishing, and etching. The etching solution comprised 4.2 g of picric acid ((NO 2) 3C 6H 2OH), 10 mL of CH 3COOH, 10 mL of H 2O, and 90 mL of CH 5OH, and the samples were etched for 16-20 seconds. Experiments were performed with a three-electrode electrochemical cell comprising a saturated calomel electrode (SCE) as the reference electrode, a platinum mesh as the counter electrode, and the specimen itself as the working electrode. Square specimens, each 10 mm in length and 2 mm in height, were prepared from different regions of the as-received MgAlCuZnGd MCA rod after grinding and polishing.

The equiatomic CuFeMn and non-equiatomic Al 15(CuFeMn) 85(at%) IMMEAs were produced with high-purity (99.99%) element pellets by vacuum induction melting (VTC200, Indutherm, Germany). The ingots were homogenized at 1073 K for 6 h followed by water quenching [ 1, 9]. Then, cold rolling at ambient temperature reduced the thickness of the ingots from 23 mm to 11 mm (reduction ratio: 52.2%) to break the cast coarse microstructures. The as-rolled samples were annealed at 1073 K for 1 h and immediately water-quenched [ 1, 9].

Initially, the alloys were melted in a vacuum induction furnace and cast into 50 kg ingots. After riser removal, each ingot was sectioned into four parts and forged into billets measuring cross-sectional size of 40 × 100 mm. To ensure compositional and microstructural homogeneity, the billets underwent a solid solution treatment at 1100 °C for 12 h in an air furnace before hot rolling. Hot rolling commenced at 1150 °C and concluded at 1000 °C, achieving a maximum cumulative reduction of 88 % and a final plate thickness of 5 mm. The plates were then immediately quenched to ambient temperature using an ultra-fast cooling device. Final processing involved cold rolling to a total cumulative reduction of 80 % using a four-high reversible cold rolling mill, followed by recrystallization annealing at 900 °C for 5 min in an argon atmosphere. Finally, the samples were water-quenched to ambient temperature.

The FSW experiment was performed by a homemade FSW1609K machine equipped with a threaded cylindrical tool that consisted of a shoulder in 20 mm diameter and a 9.6 mm length pin with 10 mm diameter. The traverse speed, the rotational speed and the tilt angle of the tool were 200 mm/min, 700 rpm and 3 o, respectively. In addition, the plunge depth of shoulder was 0.3 mm. During this creep ageing process, the specimens were firstly heated to the target temperature and then quickly loaded to the target stress. Besides, the TEM samples cut from the middle part of creep aged specimens were mechanically thinned to about 80 μm and punched into 3 mm diameter, and then twin-jet electropolished by a Struers A2 device in a mixture solution (nitric acid: methanol = 3:7) at 15 V and -25°C.

This study investigates the microstructures and mechanical properties of FCC-based CoCrFeNi2Mox HEAs with varying Mo contents (x = 0, 0.25, 0.5, and 1) fabricated via laser melting deposition (LMD) additive manufacturing. The CoCrFeNi 2Mo x(x = 0,0.25,0.5,1) high entropy alloy powders (HEA-Mo x) for laser melting deposition were blended in a planetary ball mill at 100 rpm for 3 h to ensure homogenization. The HEA-Mo xbulk samples were fabricated employing a coaxial powder feeding laser system in an Ar atmosphere. To mitigate the risk of sample cracking, an inductive heating unit was employed to maintain the substrate at 300 °C throughout the manufacturing process. The following printing parameters were used: laser power of 800 W, scanning speed of 5 mm/s, powder feeding rate of 5 L/min, and overlap ratio of 50 %. A scanning pattern with a 90° angle rotation between two consecutive deposition layers was applied.

Laser-based directed energy deposition (DED) technique provides new opportunities for fabricating eutectic high entropy alloys (EHEAs) with directional nanolamellar structures that exhibit superior mechanical properties. Here we employ in situsynchrotron-based high-energy X-ray diffraction and X-ray tomography to study a DED-fabricated nanolamellar AlCoCrFeNi 2.1that is comprised of face-centered cubic (fcc) and ordered body-centered cubic (B2) phases. The EHEA samples were fabricated using a 4-kW DED system equipped with a coaxial powder delivery system ( Fig. 1(a)). The samples were produced in a chamber that was purged with Ar gas to maintain an oxygen content of less than 50 ppm (See details in the Supplementary Information). After the built plate was fabricated, we machined three types of tensile samples for tensile tests: The samples were oriented 0°, 45°, and 90° to the building direction (Z axis) and labeled as HEA0, HEA45, and HEA90, respectively ( Fig. 1(a)).

The EHEA samples were fabricated using a 4-kW DED system equipped with a coaxial powder delivery system ( Fig. 1(a)). The samples were produced in a chamber that was purged with Ar gas to maintain an oxygen content of less than 50 ppm (See details in the Supplementary Information). After the built plate was fabricated, we machined three types of tensile samples for tensile tests: The samples were oriented 0°, 45°, and 90° to the building direction (Z axis) and labeled as HEA0, HEA45, and HEA90, respectively ( Fig. 1(a)).

In the present study, the FeCoCrNiMn HEACs reinforced with TiC particles were fabricated using the SLM technique. During the powders mixing process, FeCoCrNiMn powder was blended with 2.5 wt%, 5 wt%, and 7.5 wt% of TiC particles in a planetary ball mill. The milling operation was conducted at a speed of 400 rpm for 4 h, with a ball-to-powder weight ratio of 1:1. To avoid container overheating, the ball mill operation was paused for 10 min after every 20 min milling, and the rotation direction was then altered. For the 3D printing process, 25 cubic samples with dimensions of 5 mm × 5 mm × 5 mm were printed using an SLM machine (FORWEDO LM-120, Forwedo). To minimize the thermal stress of the printed sample on the building plane (X and Y directions), we employed a scanning strategy where the laser scanning was rotated 90° between adjacent layers, as shown in Fig. 2b. The highest relative density of 99.0% was achieved with a specific energy density of 150 J/mm 3( P= 300 W, v= 400 mm/s). In this study, we have successfully manufactured TiC-reinforced FeCoCrNiMn HEACs with superior yield strength and toughness via SLM.

In this work, the nano-twin/γʹ precipitate microstructure was achieved in the NiCoCr-based medium entropy alloy (MEA) via rolling at ambient temperature and subsequent ageing treatments. 5Al 1alloy ingot obtained by induction melting was homogenized at 1200 °C and then hot-forged to a bar with a diameter of 50 mm. Prior to rolling, the material was solution treated at 1150 °C for 30 min followed by water quenching. Subsequently, the material was rolled to a 50% reduction in thickness to achieve the high density of nano-twins in grain interiors. The rolled sample was then annealed at 700 °C for 8, 50, 100 and 300 h, respectively. The superior combination of strength and uniform elongation for the aged-50 h sample essentially evolves from the dynamic balance achieved between the softening effect resulted from nano-twin thickening and hardening effect induced by the precipitation of γ′ phase. Rolling introduced high densities of nano-twins in the NiCoCr-based MEA. Following ageing treatment at 700 °C induced the rapid precipitation in the rolled sample.

Subsequently, the material was rolled to a 50% reduction in thickness to achieve the high density of nano-twins in grain interiors. The rolled sample was then annealed at 700 °C for 8, 50, 100 and 300 h, respectively. The superior combination of strength and uniform elongation for the aged-50 h sample essentially evolves from the dynamic balance achieved between the softening effect resulted from nano-twin thickening and hardening effect induced by the precipitation of γ′ phase. Rolling introduced high densities of nano-twins in the NiCoCr-based MEA. Following ageing treatment at 700 °C induced the rapid precipitation in the rolled sample.

3Ni 33.3was produced by powder metallurgy (PM) using pure elements Fe, Cr and Ni (purity >99.9%) as raw materials. To obtain the required spherical powder, the raw material was firstly melted and then dropped into a ceramic tube in a high purity Argon atmosphere with 4 MPa atomization pressure, followed by cooling and solidification. After atomization, the spherical powder was sealed, degassed and pre-heated at 1150 °C for 1 h in a 45# steel tank with an inner diameter of 50 mm and a length of 150 mm. Finally, a rod-like material was taken out by hot extrusion with a ratio of 7:1 and a velocity of ∼10 mm/s on a 2500 T hydraulic press, following which the rod-like material was cooled to room temperature in air.

The material used in this study was commercially multipass hot-rolled Inconel 625 alloy plate (Xiong FengFa Special Metals Ltd), which was annealed at 980 °C for 30 min. For the scanning electron microscope (SEM) and electron back-scattered diffraction (EBSD) characterizations, the samples were metallographically prepared by fine grinding followed by polishing on a vibratory polisher (UNIPOL V1200) using a colloidal silica suspension (particle size 50 nm). Round discs with a diameter of 3 mm were punched out of these foils and electropolished in a double jet polishing system (TJ100-SE, LEBO Science, China) using an electrolyte consisting of 96% ethanol and 4% perchloric acid at a temperature of - 30 °C and an applied voltage of 30 V. In this work, the hot-rolled Inconel 625 alloy was annealed at 980 °C for 30 mins.

1CoCrFeNi HEA ingots were prepared by arc-melting a mixture of pure metals with purity over 99.9 wt% under argon atmosphere. To ensure homogeneity, the ingots were remelted at least five times and then drop-casted into a 10 × 10 × 30 mm 3copper mold. The cast plates were cold-rolled from 10 mm to 2.5 mm (75 % thickness reduction). The cold-rolled (CR) plates were annealed at 600 °C for 1 h (H600-1), 3 h (H600-3), 6 h (H600-6), 12 h (H600-12), and 120 h (H600-120) to generate different fractions of recrystallization, respectively, followed by water quenching. Afterward, electrochemical polishing was carried out on the polished specimens in a mixture of HClO 4:C 2H 6O = 1:9 (v/v) at 25 V to remove residual stress.

This study investigates the synthesis of a FeCoCrNi high-entropy alloy (HEA) containing 1.5 at. % Si in situusing selective laser melting (SLM). % Si. The raw materials were mixed in a three-dimensional mixer for 5 h at a spindle speed of 30 r/min. The powder blends were composed of spherical Fe, Co, Ni and 50CrNi (Ni 47Cr 50Si 3, commonly used in thermal spray and powder metallurgy) powders (>99 % purity). The particle diameter of each powder ranged from 15 to 53 μm. The SLM samples with a layer thickness of 40 μm were fabricated using a Renishaw AM-400 AM system (UK). The composition of the deposited material was homogenized by remelting each layer after its initial laser scanning. Process optimization based on a polynomial regression model (see S1 in Supplementary Material for process optimization details) was used to select the optimal parameter combinations for the first scanning, remelting, and resulting product density ( Table 1). The same optimization was applied to FeCoCrNi alloy control samples without Si addition. Remelting was not required in the control samples because the chemical composition of the alloy powder was already evenly distributed (see S2 in Supplementary Material for optimization and printing of control samples). Remelting was conducted immediately after the first melt at a lower laser power and wider hatch spacing. Therefore, the VED of the remelting procedure was much lower than the first melt and the center of the laser beam was deviated ( Fig. 13e). The convection area was shallow, allowing for the targeting of inhomogeneous areas near the surface. Greater mixing of the unevenly distributed components occurred, where the composition of the remelted samples exhibited a more uniform distribution ( Fig. 13f).

Spherical-shaped (CoCrFeMnNi) 99C 1(at%) powders with a particle size in the range of 10-55 µm produced by gas atomization (Hot gas atomization system, PSI Ltd.) were used as a raw material for the SLM process. The cuboidal samples of 15 × 15 × 15 mm 3were fabricated with a meander scanning pattern using a commercial SLM machine (Mlab, Concept Laser GmbH, Germany). The SLM samples were built with laser power of 90 W, hatch space of 80 µm, and layer thickness of 25 µm. Two post-SLM heat treatments were performed on the as-built samples: annealing at 800 °C and 900 °C for 10 min, followed by water quenching. The annealed samples are denoted as A800 and A900, corresponding to the annealing temperatures of 800 °C and 900 °C, respectively.

The ingots with nominal compositions of Al x(MoV) 100-x(x = 0, 15, 33, and 50 at%, henceforth denoted as Al0, Al15, Al33, and Al50, respectively) were fabricated using vacuum arc melting (VAR). The VAR process was conducted under a Ti-gettered Ar atmosphere, followed by rapid quenching in a water-cooled copper mold. To enhance chemical homogeneity, each ingot underwent a series of flipping and remelting at least 5 times. By employing a reverse alloy design strategy based on thermodynamic calculations, we developed the Al-Mo-V alloys.

The studied alloy with a nominal composition of AlCoCrFeNi 2.1(atomic percent, at%, hereinafter referred to as Ni 2.1) was prepared, using arc-melting elemental ingredients with a purity >99.95% (weight percent, wt. The alloy was remelted at least five times to promote the chemical homogeneity in a Ti-gettered high-purity argon atmosphere. The molten alloy was cast into a water-cooled copper mould to form a plate ingot with a length of 110 mm, a width of 40 mm, and a thickness of 10 mm. The rods with the dimension of 9.8 mm in diameter and 110 mm in length were cut from the ingot through wire electro-discharge machining. The heating procedure employed was described as follows: heating from room temperature to 800 °C over 30 min, holding for 20 min, then further heating for 40 min to reach 1410 °C, followed by a 30-min hold to ensure complete alloy melting. After that, the crucible was pulled into the liquid Ga-In-Sn alloy with different growth velocities, respectively.

The molten alloy was cast into a water-cooled copper mould to form a plate ingot with a length of 110 mm, a width of 40 mm, and a thickness of 10 mm. The rods with the dimension of 9.8 mm in diameter and 110 mm in length were cut from the ingot through wire electro-discharge machining. The heating procedure employed was described as follows: heating from room temperature to 800 °C over 30 min, holding for 20 min, then further heating for 40 min to reach 1410 °C, followed by a 30-min hold to ensure complete alloy melting. After that, the crucible was pulled into the liquid Ga-In-Sn alloy with different growth velocities, respectively.

FeCoCrNiMn pre-alloyed powder with a particle size of 50-110 µm was prepared by electrode induction melting gas atomization (EIGA). The thin-wall shaped bulk HEAs (40 mm × 2 mm × 70 mm) were fabricated on a FeCoCrNiMn HEA substrate by a coaxial powder feeding DED system equipped with ytterbium fiber laser, and the deposition process was carried out in a cavity filled with high-purity Ar gas. For comparison, a bulk FeCoCrNiMn HEA was also fabricated by vacuum arc melting and water-cooling copper mold suction casting, which can also obtain extremely fast cooling rates. The samples for EBSD and XRD detection were electropolished at −30 °C and 25 V with 7% perchloric acid and 93% ethanol solution for 40 s. The thin film samples used for TEM were prepared by twin-jet electronic polishing method at −25 °C with 7% perchloric acid and 93% ethanol solution.

The chemical composition of the Al-Cu-Mg alloy was: Cu 3.5 wt%, Mg 1.4 wt%, Mn 0.4 wt%, impurity elements ∼0.2 wt%, with the balance being Al. After solution treatment at 520 °C for 1 h, an Al-Cu-Mg alloy plate (thickness: 1.5 mm) was quenched in water to room temperature, then aged at 180 °C for 24 h, and recorded as sample SA. Al-Cu-Mg alloy plates with a thickness of 3 mm were cold-rolled after the same solution treatment, with rolling reductions of 40 % (strain rate ∼4.4 s⁻¹) or 50 % (strain rate ∼4.92 s⁻¹). One set was aged at 180 °C for 24 h and recorded as SRA-40 (40 % rolling reduction) or SRA-50 (50 % rolling reduction). The other set was undergoing cryogenic treatment in liquid nitrogen at -196 °C, followed by aging at 180 °C for 24 h, and was recorded as SRCA-40 or SRCA-50.

The arc melting was repeated 8 times to ensure the chemical uniformity. The ingot was cut into cubes using electrical discharge machining (EDM) and then vacuum-sealed with quartz tubes. All the samples were water quenched.

The aim of this study is to improve the comprehensive properties of CoCrFeNiCu high entropy alloy coating (HEAc) prepared by induction cladding by means of ultrasonic impact treatment (UIT). In our previous work, induction cladding technology was applied to HEAc preparation for the first time [21], and CoCrFeNiCu HEAc was successfully prepared on the surface of Q235 steel. The powders were put into a planetary ball mill for mechanical alloying with a ball material ratio of 15:1, a rotational speed of 350 rpm and a time of 30 h. Before induction cladding, the substrate was polished and cleaned, and the alloyed powder was mixed with liquid sodium silicate as binder and laid flat on the substrate, and then dried at 60 °C for 2 h. The cladding specimen was placed in the induction cladding equipment (HR-BF-120) and heated for 12 s under the protection of argon with an output current of 400 A. The surface of HEAc prepared by induction cladding were polished with sandpaper with grit sizes from 150 to 2000 and then placed on the CNC machine for ultrasonic impact treatment.

A recently developed class is the Si-containing MPEAs (labeled Si-containing HEAs in this paper), which exhibit excellent oxidation, corrosion, and wear resistance as well as mechanical properties [13-16]. In the as-cast state, the addition of alloying elements is an effective approach for refining the as-cast features such as the dendrite arm spacing (DAS), as recently shown by Karimzadeh et al.[86]for the CoCrFeNi alloy ( Fig. 9). Cold deformation and annealing (as well as hot working) is another major method for grain refinement of HEAs [88-90], where processes such as reversion of martensite to austenite in metastable HEAs, recrystallization of deformed austenite, and grain growth are responsible for determining the grain size. This method has been used for obtaining various grain sizes in Fig. 8b. On the other hand, severe plastic deformation (SPD) processes are frequently used for extreme grain refinement of HEAs; among them, equal-channel angular pressing (ECAP) [91,92], high-pressure torsion (HPT) [93-95], friction stir processing (FSP) [96,97], multidirectional forging (MDF) [98]are the most widely used ones. Grain size refinement and increasing the deformation temperature often weaken the TWIP effect [121-123,128-130]. Regarding the chemical composition, Fig. 17presents a remarkable example, in which, by decreasing the amount of Mn in the Fe 80-xMn xCo 10Cr 10alloy, the sequence of plasticity mechanisms is as follows: TWIP → TRIP → DP-TRIP [112]. Regarding the effect of grain size, grain refinement generally increases the stability of the austenite phase toward suppressing the TRIP effect, as shown in Fig. In fact, the development of a dual-phase microstructure (interface hardening) and the occurrence of strain-induced martensitic transformation (transformation-induced hardening) in metastable HEAs allow for the overcoming of the strength-ductility trade-off [48,139]. Besides the FCC → HCP transformation, another important TRIP mechanism is the FCC → BCC transformation [143], typically in the Fe-rich HEAs and especially at cryogenic deformation temperatures [50,134,50]. As shown in Fig. 20, the FCC → BCC transformation happens mostly along grain boundaries (GBs) at the early stage of deformation. Concurrently, within FCC grains, a large number of deformation-induced shear bands (SBs) with stacking faults associated with the Shockley partials and thin HCP plates form. Subsequently, the BCC phase nucleates and grows at the intersections of SBs [50]. The formation of the BCC phase during deformation remarkably enhances the work-hardening rate toward improvement of the strength-ductility synergy, as shown in Fig. 21. This effect is intensified at cryogenic temperatures due to the enhanced metastability, as shown in Fig. 21, where a pronounced increment of work-hardening rate can be detected for the Fe 60Co 15Ni 15Cr 10alloy at 77 K. The Si-containing HEAs exhibit excellent oxidation, corrosion, and wear resistance, as well as excellent mechanical properties [13-16,144-147]. Before diving into the mechanical behavior, it is beneficial to take a look at the improvement of other properties of HEAs via Si addition.
