Precipitation strengthening from CP and DP can be estimated based on APT results. APT results reveal an L1 2fraction of approximately 12 % in CP regions, whereas it notably increases to around 33 % in DP areas. Assuming that precipitation strengthening results from dislocation shearing of the L1 2phase, its effect can be calculated as follows ( Gwalani et al. , 2021; Jung et al., 2024): σp=M·0.81(γAPB/2b)(3πf/8)1/2where the Taylor factor (M) for fcc polycrystalline materials was assumed to be 3.06, and the Burgers vector ( b) was obtained from XRD results as 2. 54 Å, respectively. The anti-phase boundary energy ( γAPB) was estimated to be approximately 140 mJ/m 2, taking an Fe-rich MEA as a reference ( Jung et al. , 2024). Based on the aforementioned equation, the calculated precipitation strengthening effects in the CP and DP regions are approximately 257 MPa and 426 MPa, respectively. This calculation confirms that fine grains with DP are considered a hard phase, and thus their contribution to strength is included in the HDI stress. Regarding dislocation strengthening, the influence of dislocations can be neglected in the annealing-aged samples. For the direct-aged sample, a dislocation strengthening value of 128 MPa was adopted, based on a reference to L-PBF L1 2-strengthened austenitic stainless steel aged at 700 °C for 2 h ( Hu et al. , 2025). The HDI stress values obtained from Fig. 17(b) are approximately 430 MPa for the AN 1200-AG sample, 552 MPa for the AN 1000-AG sample, and 630 MPa for the direct-aged sample. These results indicate that HDI strengthening is a significant contributor to the strength of the studied samples. In summary, the estimated YS, calculated by summing the individual contributions, are approximately 788 MPa, 906 MPa, and 1112 MPa for the AN1200-AG, AN1000-AG, and direct-aged samples, respectively. These calculated values show a slight deviation from the experimental yield strengths, which are approximately 845 MPa, 999 MPa, and 1139 MPa, respectively. In summary, different annealing treatments prior to identical aging were performed on an L1 2-strengthened Fe-rich MEA fabricated by L-PBF. These treatments resulted in distinct final microstructures characterized by either DP or CP dominance, accompanied by varied mechanical properties. The results indicate that the Fe-MEA fabricated via L-PBF may be a promising candidate for advanced structural applications, owing to its acceptable comprehensive mechanical properties and relatively low production cost. The present study clearly reveals that different post-printing heat treatments result in varied precipitation behavior dominated by either CP or DP. In L1 2-strengthened H/MEAs, the relationship between CP and DP is competitive and the reasons are listed below. According to the equilibrium phase diagram, the aging temperature is located within the fcc+L1 2dual-phase region. Therefore, during aging treatment, there is a thermodynamic driving force for L1 2precipitation from the supersaturated matrix of the as-built sample with a single fcc phase. Moreover, from a dynamic perspective, there are two pathways for L1 2precipitation, CP and DP. The consumption of L1 2-forming elements like Ni, Al, and Ti within matrix by CP ahead of the DP region greatly decreases the driving force for the DP growth, thereby suppressing the advancement of DP. Besides, the CP nanoparticles have a pinning effect to the moving grain boundaries driven by DP, thereby kinetically hindering the DP growth. Conversely, a slow formation of CP allows the matrix to maintain a high supersaturation of L1 2-forming elements, thereby increasing the chemical driving force for DP migration. Additionally, it results in a weaker pinning effect on grain boundary migration, dynamically favoring DP growth. This combination enhances the growth of DP into the supersaturated matrix ( Fang et al., 2022b). The competition between CP and DP in L1 2-strengthened H/MEAs is primarily influenced by factors such as aging temperature, grain size, and dislocation density ( Fang et al., 2022a, 2022b; Liu et al., 2022a). Since the aging temperature was consistent across all aged samples in the present study, its influence was not revealed in this work. Regarding grain size, finer grains are more likely to promote DP, owing to the increased density of grain boundaries that not only facilitates diffusion along these boundaries but also provides numerous sites for the nucleation of DP. In addition, the roles of high-density dislocation in the DP and CP are twofold. If the high-density dislocation is insufficient to trigger recrystallization, it promotes CP by enhancing bulk diffusion and providing an additional driving force for the nucleation of precipitates. Conversely, when the high-density dislocation induced recrystallization, the high mobility of recrystallized grain boundaries and the high-density grain boundaries of fine recrystallized grains promote DP ( Fan et al. , 2020; Fang et al., 2022a, 2022b). In the present study, the as-built samples are characterized by dominant coarse grains with a high density of dislocations. It is suggested that the dislocations, which are insufficient to trigger significant recrystallization of coarse grains, together with the dominant coarse grains, enhance CP and result in CP being dominant in the direct-aged sample. By contrast, annealing at 1000 °C for 1 h mainly leads to a reduction in dislocation density within the AN 1000 sample, thereby slowing CP within the coarse grains of the AN 1000-AG sample compared to the direct-aged sample. This, in turn, facilitates DP which preferentially initiate at the grain boundaries of fine grains, leading to DP dominance in the AN 1000-AG sample. The explanation for the microstructural evolution from the AN 1100 sample to the AN 1100-AG sample follows a similar rationale as that of the AN 1000 sample to the AN 1000-AG sample, due to their comparable initial microstructures. Annealing at 1200 °C not only significantly eliminates dislocations but also results in the formation of significantly coarse, nearly equiaxed grains with almost no fine grains. This makes DP less competitive, resulting in CP dominance in the AN 1200-AG sample. In addition to factors such as grain size and dislocation density, further examination of the microstructures in the AN 1000 sample has confirmed that elemental enrichment along cell walls has become negligible, accompanied by a reduction in dislocation density. These findings are illustrated in Supplementary Fig. S8. The enrichment of L1 2-forming elements such as Ni and Ti can enhance the chemical driving force. Consequently, in the direct-aged sample characterized by CP dominance, the elemental enrichment along cell walls should facilitate CP by increasing the local chemical driving force. Following annealing at temperatures of 1000 °C or higher, the elemental enrichment along cell walls becomes negligible, thereby slowing down CP within coarse grains. This deceleration subsequently could promote the formation of DP in the AN 1000-AG sample. Furthermore, it is proposed that the effect of limited L1 2precipitation in AN 1000 sample on subsequent aging could be negligible. Firstly, the L1 2precipitation in the AN 1000 sample appears to be very minimal, as suggested by a decrease in hardness compared to the as-built sample. Secondly, the AN 1100 sample without L1 2peaks, undergoes similar microstructural evolution to the AN 1000 sample during aging treatment. In the direct-aged sample, the formation mechanisms of fine grains may be debatable, although some researchers suggest that they form via recrystallization ( Huang et al. , 2024; Wang and Chan, 2023). This explanation could be reasonable since the as-built sample contains a high density of dislocations, which may trigger recrystallization during aging treatment. The high mobility of recrystallized grain boundaries favors the subsequent formation of DP. However, it is also possible that the formation of these fine grains is attributed to DP occurring within the initial fine microstructures. Given that the DP initiates via a supersaturated solid solution (α 0) transformed into a usually lamellar structure of a new phase (β) with solute enrichment, and a new phase (α) with solute depletion and the same crystal structure as α 0. With the reaction front advancing into the supersaturated matrix, the developed α lamellae maintains the same orientation as that of the initial α lamellae. Therefore, rather than resulting in a single grain after the DP reaction, there could be multiple grains corresponding to different growing colonies of the DP ( Han et al. , 2021; Kim et al. , 2024; Tałach-Dumańska et al. , 2003). It is also reported that DP can be effectively utilized to achieve grain refinement without any plastic deformation ( Tałach-Dumańska et al. , 2003). As a result, it is proposed that the roles of DP on the grain refinement should also be considered. For the AN 1000-AG and AN 1100-AG samples, it is intriguing that new fine grains formed after the annealing-aging treatment rather than after annealing alone. This phenomenon is unexpected since the dislocation density in the as-built samples is higher than those of annealed samples (Supplementary Fig. S3), which should result in more remarkable recrystallization and corresponding formation of fine grains in the direct-aged samples. Therefore, given that the driving force for recrystallization is diminished during high-temperature annealing, it is hypothesized that grain refinement may be linked to DP ( Han et al. , 2021; Tałach-Dumańska et al. , 2003). The initial fine-grain region plays a crucial role in enhancing DP which grows into coarse grains and correspondingly divides coarse grains into multiple finer grains. The abnormal grain refinement in the AN 1200-AG sample is still likely related to the DP ( Kim et al. , 2024). The SEM image and corresponding EBSD measurement of the YOZ plane for the AN 1200-AG sample further support that the grain refinement occurs through DP, as demonstrated in Supplementary Fig. S9. The AN 1200-AG sample exhibits DP regions with brighter contrast when compared to the CP regions. It is evident that the DP region is primarily located along the boundaries of the coarse grains. The corresponding EBSD IPF image clearly indicates that the fine grains are predominantly found within the DP region, while the CP region retains the coarse grain structure. Furthermore, the EBSD phase map exclusively displays the fcc structure due to the crystallographic similarity between the fcc and L1 2phases. This confirms that grain refinement is not caused by the formation of new phases that do not possess an fcc structure ( Chu et al. , 2024; Gwalani et al. , 2018). Moreover, the kernel average misorientation (KAM) map suggests an exceptionally low dislocation density in this area, indicating that the formation of new grains is not related to recrystallization. Additionally, the studied samples exhibit multiscale heterogenous microstructures, such as CP within coarse grains and DP within fine grains ( Fan et al. , 2022; Yang et al. , 2024). During the deformation of the heterostructure, geometrically necessary dislocations (GNDs) accumulate in the soft regions. The elastic field produced by these piled-up GNDs generates a force in the opposite direction to the applied stress on the soft domains. Consequently, a higher applied stress is required to deform the soft domains, resulting in the hardening effect known as HDI hardening ( Jung et al. , 2024; Kim et al. , 2024; Yang and Kim, 2024; Yang et al. , 2016; Zhu and Wu, 2019). To determine the contribution of HDI stress, LUR tests were conducted, as shown in Fig. 17(a). Furthermore, Fig. 17(b) illustrates the evolution of HDI stress as a function of true strain, measured from the hysteresis loops in Fig. 17(a) ( Yang et al. , 2016). At first, the HDI stress in the AN1000-AG sample is higher than that in the AN 1200-AG sample. Fine grains with DP are usually regarded as a hard phase, hence their contribution to strength is encompassed in HDI stress ( Kim et al. , 2024). The higher HDI stress in the AN 1000-AG sample can be attributed to its significantly higher fraction of fine grains with DP. However, the direct-aged sample with coarse grains and CP dominance still shows a slightly higher HDI stress compared to the AN 1000-AG sample. Considering the relatively low fraction of fine grains with DP, the high HDI stress observed in the direct-aged sample can also be attributed to its heterogeneous distribution of dislocations ( Wang et al., 2024a), which consists of hard cells with high local dislocation density and soft regions within cell interior. A simplified strengthening model was employed to calculate the various contributions to the differing YS of the studied samples. The YS can be divided into effective stress ( σ eff), arising from short-range interaction, and HDI stress ( σ HDI) which originates from long-range interaction. Therefore, the YS can be calculated using the following equation ( Jung et al. , 2024; Kim et al., 2024): σy=σeff+σHDIσeff=σ0+Δσss+Δσp+Δσρwhere σ 0, Δ σ ss, Δ σ p, and Δ σ ρrepresent friction stress, solid solution strengthening, precipitation strengthening, and dislocation strengthening, respectively. Given that the solid-solution strengthening can be integrated into the friction stress due to the difficulty in distinguishing between solvent and solute atoms, the friction stress value of an FeNiCrAlTi MEA (97 MPa) was adopted in this study ( Jung et al. , 2024; Wang et al., 2024a). Precipitation strengthening from CP and DP can be estimated based on APT results. APT results reveal an L1 2fraction of approximately 12 % in CP regions, whereas it notably increases to around 33 % in DP areas. Assuming that precipitation strengthening results from dislocation shearing of the L1 2phase, its effect can be calculated as follows ( Gwalani et al. , 2021; Jung et al., 2024): σp=M·0.81(γAPB/2b)(3πf/8)1/2where the Taylor factor (M) for fcc polycrystalline materials was assumed to be 3.06, and the Burgers vector ( b) was obtained from XRD results as 2. 54 Å, respectively. The anti-phase boundary energy ( γAPB) was estimated to be approximately 140 mJ/m 2, taking an Fe-rich MEA as a reference ( Jung et al. , 2024). Based on the aforementioned equation, the calculated precipitation strengthening effects in the CP and DP regions are approximately 257 MPa and 426 MPa, respectively. This calculation confirms that fine grains with DP are considered a hard phase, and thus their contribution to strength is included in the HDI stress. Regarding dislocation strengthening, the influence of dislocations can be neglected in the annealing-aged samples. For the direct-aged sample, a dislocation strengthening value of 128 MPa was adopted, based on a reference to L-PBF L1 2-strengthened austenitic stainless steel aged at 700 °C for 2 h ( Hu et al. , 2025). The HDI stress values obtained from Fig. 17(b) are approximately 430 MPa for the AN 1200-AG sample, 552 MPa for the AN 1000-AG sample, and 630 MPa for the direct-aged sample. These results indicate that HDI strengthening is a significant contributor to the strength of the studied samples. In summary, the estimated YS, calculated by summing the individual contributions, are approximately 788 MPa, 906 MPa, and 1112 MPa for the AN1200-AG, AN1000-AG, and direct-aged samples, respectively. These calculated values show a slight deviation from the experimental yield strengths, which are approximately 845 MPa, 999 MPa, and 1139 MPa, respectively. In summary, different annealing treatments prior to identical aging were performed on an L1 2-strengthened Fe-rich MEA fabricated by L-PBF. These treatments resulted in distinct final microstructures characterized by either DP or CP dominance, accompanied by varied mechanical properties. The detailed conclusions are as follows: 1The high-density dislocations and coarse grains induced by L-PBF promote CP. In contrast, the fine grains formed via L-PBF and the reduced dislocation density through annealing enhance DP, which in turn leads to grain refinement. 2The L-PBF Fe-MEA demonstrates acceptable printability, cost efficiency, and mechanical properties. Specifically, the direct-aged sample exhibits a YS of approximately 1. 1 GPa and a UE of around 11 %. The AN 1000-AG sample achieves a YS of about 1. 0 GPa and a UE of approximately 15 %. In the AN 1000-AG and AN 1200-AG samples, HDI strengthening primarily originates from the heterogeneous distribution of grains and precipitates. In contrast, the HDI strengthening in the direct-aged sample is attributed not only to the heterogeneous distribution of grains and precipitates but also to the heterogeneous dislocation structure. The present study clearly reveals that different post-printing heat treatments result in varied precipitation behavior dominated by either CP or DP. In L1 2-strengthened H/MEAs, the relationship between CP and DP is competitive and the reasons are listed below. According to the equilibrium phase diagram, the aging temperature is located within the fcc+L1 2dual-phase region. Therefore, during aging treatment, there is a thermodynamic driving force for L1 2precipitation from the supersaturated matrix of the as-built sample with a single fcc phase. Moreover, from a dynamic perspective, there are two pathways for L1 2precipitation, CP and DP. The consumption of L1 2-forming elements like Ni, Al, and Ti within matrix by CP ahead of the DP region greatly decreases the driving force for the DP growth, thereby suppressing the advancement of DP. Besides, the CP nanoparticles have a pinning effect to the moving grain boundaries driven by DP, thereby kinetically hindering the DP growth. Conversely, a slow formation of CP allows the matrix to maintain a high supersaturation of L1 2-forming elements, thereby increasing the chemical driving force for DP migration. Additionally, it results in a weaker pinning effect on grain boundary migration, dynamically favoring DP growth. This combination enhances the growth of DP into the supersaturated matrix ( Fang et al., 2022b). The competition between CP and DP in L1 2-strengthened H/MEAs is primarily influenced by factors such as aging temperature, grain size, and dislocation density ( Fang et al., 2022a, 2022b; Liu et al., 2022a). Since the aging temperature was consistent across all aged samples in the present study, its influence was not revealed in this work. Regarding grain size, finer grains are more likely to promote DP, owing to the increased density of grain boundaries that not only facilitates diffusion along these boundaries but also provides numerous sites for the nucleation of DP. In addition, the roles of high-density dislocation in the DP and CP are twofold. If the high-density dislocation is insufficient to trigger recrystallization, it promotes CP by enhancing bulk diffusion and providing an additional driving force for the nucleation of precipitates. Conversely, when the high-density dislocation induced recrystallization, the high mobility of recrystallized grain boundaries and the high-density grain boundaries of fine recrystallized grains promote DP ( Fan et al. , 2020; Fang et al., 2022a, 2022b). In the present study, the as-built samples are characterized by dominant coarse grains with a high density of dislocations. It is suggested that the dislocations, which are insufficient to trigger significant recrystallization of coarse grains, together with the dominant coarse grains, enhance CP and result in CP being dominant in the direct-aged sample. By contrast, annealing at 1000 °C for 1 h mainly leads to a reduction in dislocation density within the AN 1000 sample, thereby slowing CP within the coarse grains of the AN 1000-AG sample compared to the direct-aged sample. This, in turn, facilitates DP which preferentially initiate at the grain boundaries of fine grains, leading to DP dominance in the AN 1000-AG sample. The explanation for the microstructural evolution from the AN 1100 sample to the AN 1100-AG sample follows a similar rationale as that of the AN 1000 sample to the AN 1000-AG sample, due to their comparable initial microstructures. Annealing at 1200 °C not only significantly eliminates dislocations but also results in the formation of significantly coarse, nearly equiaxed grains with almost no fine grains. This makes DP less competitive, resulting in CP dominance in the AN 1200-AG sample. In addition to factors such as grain size and dislocation density, further examination of the microstructures in the AN 1000 sample has confirmed that elemental enrichment along cell walls has become negligible, accompanied by a reduction in dislocation density. These findings are illustrated in Supplementary Fig. S8. The enrichment of L1 2-forming elements such as Ni and Ti can enhance the chemical driving force. Consequently, in the direct-aged sample characterized by CP dominance, the elemental enrichment along cell walls should facilitate CP by increasing the local chemical driving force. Following annealing at temperatures of 1000 °C or higher, the elemental enrichment along cell walls becomes negligible, thereby slowing down CP within coarse grains. This deceleration subsequently could promote the formation of DP in the AN 1000-AG sample. Furthermore, it is proposed that the effect of limited L1 2precipitation in AN 1000 sample on subsequent aging could be negligible. Firstly, the L1 2precipitation in the AN 1000 sample appears to be very minimal, as suggested by a decrease in hardness compared to the as-built sample. Secondly, the AN 1100 sample without L1 2peaks, undergoes similar microstructural evolution to the AN 1000 sample during aging treatment. In the direct-aged sample, the formation mechanisms of fine grains may be debatable, although some researchers suggest that they form via recrystallization ( Huang et al. , 2024; Wang and Chan, 2023). This explanation could be reasonable since the as-built sample contains a high density of dislocations, which may trigger recrystallization during aging treatment. The high mobility of recrystallized grain boundaries favors the subsequent formation of DP. However, it is also possible that the formation of these fine grains is attributed to DP occurring within the initial fine microstructures. Given that the DP initiates via a supersaturated solid solution (α 0) transformed into a usually lamellar structure of a new phase (β) with solute enrichment, and a new phase (α) with solute depletion and the same crystal structure as α 0. With the reaction front advancing into the supersaturated matrix, the developed α lamellae maintains the same orientation as that of the initial α lamellae. Therefore, rather than resulting in a single grain after the DP reaction, there could be multiple grains corresponding to different growing colonies of the DP ( Han et al. , 2021; Kim et al. , 2024; Tałach-Dumańska et al. , 2003). It is also reported that DP can be effectively utilized to achieve grain refinement without any plastic deformation ( Tałach-Dumańska et al. , 2003). As a result, it is proposed that the roles of DP on the grain refinement should also be considered. For the AN 1000-AG and AN 1100-AG samples, it is intriguing that new fine grains formed after the annealing-aging treatment rather than after annealing alone. This phenomenon is unexpected since the dislocation density in the as-built samples is higher than those of annealed samples (Supplementary Fig. S3), which should result in more remarkable recrystallization and corresponding formation of fine grains in the direct-aged samples. Therefore, given that the driving force for recrystallization is diminished during high-temperature annealing, it is hypothesized that grain refinement may be linked to DP ( Han et al. , 2021; Tałach-Dumańska et al. , 2003). The initial fine-grain region plays a crucial role in enhancing DP which grows into coarse grains and correspondingly divides coarse grains into multiple finer grains. The abnormal grain refinement in the AN 1200-AG sample is still likely related to the DP ( Kim et al. , 2024). The SEM image and corresponding EBSD measurement of the YOZ plane for the AN 1200-AG sample further support that the grain refinement occurs through DP, as demonstrated in Supplementary Fig. S9. The AN 1200-AG sample exhibits DP regions with brighter contrast when compared to the CP regions. It is evident that the DP region is primarily located along the boundaries of the coarse grains. The corresponding EBSD IPF image clearly indicates that the fine grains are predominantly found within the DP region, while the CP region retains the coarse grain structure. Furthermore, the EBSD phase map exclusively displays the fcc structure due to the crystallographic similarity between the fcc and L1 2phases. This confirms that grain refinement is not caused by the formation of new phases that do not possess an fcc structure ( Chu et al. , 2024; Gwalani et al. , 2018). Moreover, the kernel average misorientation (KAM) map suggests an exceptionally low dislocation density in this area, indicating that the formation of new grains is not related to recrystallization. During the deformation of the heterostructure, geometrically necessary dislocations (GNDs) accumulate in the soft regions. The elastic field produced by these piled-up GNDs generates a force in the opposite direction to the applied stress on the soft domains. Consequently, a higher applied stress is required to deform the soft domains, resulting in the hardening effect known as HDI hardening ( Jung et al. , 2024; Kim et al. , 2024; Yang and Kim, 2024; Yang et al. , 2016; Zhu and Wu, 2019). To determine the contribution of HDI stress, LUR tests were conducted, as shown in Fig. 17(a). Furthermore, Fig. 17(b) illustrates the evolution of HDI stress as a function of true strain, measured from the hysteresis loops in Fig. 17(a) ( Yang et al. , 2016). At first, the HDI stress in the AN1000-AG sample is higher than that in the AN 1200-AG sample. Fine grains with DP are usually regarded as a hard phase, hence their contribution to strength is encompassed in HDI stress ( Kim et al. , 2024). The higher HDI stress in the AN 1000-AG sample can be attributed to its significantly higher fraction of fine grains with DP. However, the direct-aged sample with coarse grains and CP dominance still shows a slightly higher HDI stress compared to the AN 1000-AG sample. Considering the relatively low fraction of fine grains with DP, the high HDI stress observed in the direct-aged sample can also be attributed to its heterogeneous distribution of dislocations ( Wang et al., 2024a), which consists of hard cells with high local dislocation density and soft regions within cell interior. A simplified strengthening model was employed to calculate the various contributions to the differing YS of the studied samples. The YS can be divided into effective stress ( σ eff), arising from short-range interaction, and HDI stress ( σ HDI) which originates from long-range interaction. Therefore, the YS can be calculated using the following equation ( Jung et al. , 2024; Kim et al., 2024): σy=σeff+σHDIσeff=σ0+Δσss+Δσp+Δσρwhere σ 0, Δ σ ss, Δ σ p, and Δ σ ρrepresent friction stress, solid solution strengthening, precipitation strengthening, and dislocation strengthening, respectively. Given that the solid-solution strengthening can be integrated into the friction stress due to the difficulty in distinguishing between solvent and solute atoms, the friction stress value of an FeNiCrAlTi MEA (97 MPa) was adopted in this study ( Jung et al. , 2024; Wang et al., 2024a). Precipitation strengthening from CP and DP can be estimated based on APT results. The anti-phase boundary energy ( γAPB) was estimated to be approximately 140 mJ/m 2, taking an Fe-rich MEA as a reference ( Jung et al. , 2024). Based on the aforementioned equation, the calculated precipitation strengthening effects in the CP and DP regions are approximately 257 MPa and 426 MPa, respectively. This calculation confirms that fine grains with DP are considered a hard phase, and thus their contribution to strength is included in the HDI stress. Regarding dislocation strengthening, the influence of dislocations can be neglected in the annealing-aged samples. For the direct-aged sample, a dislocation strengthening value of 128 MPa was adopted, based on a reference to L-PBF L1 2-strengthened austenitic stainless steel aged at 700 °C for 2 h ( Hu et al. , 2025). These results indicate that HDI strengthening is a significant contributor to the strength of the studied samples. In summary, the estimated YS, calculated by summing the individual contributions, are approximately 788 MPa, 906 MPa, and 1112 MPa for the AN1200-AG, AN1000-AG, and direct-aged samples, respectively. The results indicate that the Fe-MEA fabricated via L-PBF may be a promising candidate for advanced structural applications, owing to its acceptable comprehensive mechanical properties and relatively low production cost. The present study clearly reveals that different post-printing heat treatments result in varied precipitation behavior dominated by either CP or DP. In L1 2-strengthened H/MEAs, the relationship between CP and DP is competitive and the reasons are listed below. According to the equilibrium phase diagram, the aging temperature is located within the fcc+L1 2dual-phase region. Therefore, during aging treatment, there is a thermodynamic driving force for L1 2precipitation from the supersaturated matrix of the as-built sample with a single fcc phase. Moreover, from a dynamic perspective, there are two pathways for L1 2precipitation, CP and DP. The consumption of L1 2-forming elements like Ni, Al, and Ti within matrix by CP ahead of the DP region greatly decreases the driving force for the DP growth, thereby suppressing the advancement of DP. Besides, the CP nanoparticles have a pinning effect to the moving grain boundaries driven by DP, thereby kinetically hindering the DP growth. Conversely, a slow formation of CP allows the matrix to maintain a high supersaturation of L1 2-forming elements, thereby increasing the chemical driving force for DP migration. Additionally, it results in a weaker pinning effect on grain boundary migration, dynamically favoring DP growth. This combination enhances the growth of DP into the supersaturated matrix ( Fang et al., 2022b). The competition between CP and DP in L1 2-strengthened H/MEAs is primarily influenced by factors such as aging temperature, grain size, and dislocation density ( Fang et al., 2022a, 2022b; Liu et al., 2022a). Since the aging temperature was consistent across all aged samples in the present study, its influence was not revealed in this work. Regarding grain size, finer grains are more likely to promote DP, owing to the increased density of grain boundaries that not only facilitates diffusion along these boundaries but also provides numerous sites for the nucleation of DP. In addition, the roles of high-density dislocation in the DP and CP are twofold. If the high-density dislocation is insufficient to trigger recrystallization, it promotes CP by enhancing bulk diffusion and providing an additional driving force for the nucleation of precipitates. Conversely, when the high-density dislocation induced recrystallization, the high mobility of recrystallized grain boundaries and the high-density grain boundaries of fine recrystallized grains promote DP ( Fan et al. , 2020; Fang et al., 2022a, 2022b). In the present study, the as-built samples are characterized by dominant coarse grains with a high density of dislocations. It is suggested that the dislocations, which are insufficient to trigger significant recrystallization of coarse grains, together with the dominant coarse grains, enhance CP and result in CP being dominant in the direct-aged sample. By contrast, annealing at 1000 °C for 1 h mainly leads to a reduction in dislocation density within the AN 1000 sample, thereby slowing CP within the coarse grains of the AN 1000-AG sample compared to the direct-aged sample. This, in turn, facilitates DP which preferentially initiate at the grain boundaries of fine grains, leading to DP dominance in the AN 1000-AG sample. The explanation for the microstructural evolution from the AN 1100 sample to the AN 1100-AG sample follows a similar rationale as that of the AN 1000 sample to the AN 1000-AG sample, due to their comparable initial microstructures. Annealing at 1200 °C not only significantly eliminates dislocations but also results in the formation of significantly coarse, nearly equiaxed grains with almost no fine grains. This makes DP less competitive, resulting in CP dominance in the AN 1200-AG sample. In addition to factors such as grain size and dislocation density, further examination of the microstructures in the AN 1000 sample has confirmed that elemental enrichment along cell walls has become negligible, accompanied by a reduction in dislocation density. These findings are illustrated in Supplementary Fig. S8. The enrichment of L1 2-forming elements such as Ni and Ti can enhance the chemical driving force. Consequently, in the direct-aged sample characterized by CP dominance, the elemental enrichment along cell walls should facilitate CP by increasing the local chemical driving force. Following annealing at temperatures of 1000 °C or higher, the elemental enrichment along cell walls becomes negligible, thereby slowing down CP within coarse grains. This deceleration subsequently could promote the formation of DP in the AN 1000-AG sample. Furthermore, it is proposed that the effect of limited L1 2precipitation in AN 1000 sample on subsequent aging could be negligible. Firstly, the L1 2precipitation in the AN 1000 sample appears to be very minimal, as suggested by a decrease in hardness compared to the as-built sample. Secondly, the AN 1100 sample without L1 2peaks, undergoes similar microstructural evolution to the AN 1000 sample during aging treatment. In the direct-aged sample, the formation mechanisms of fine grains may be debatable, although some researchers suggest that they form via recrystallization ( Huang et al. , 2024; Wang and Chan, 2023). This explanation could be reasonable since the as-built sample contains a high density of dislocations, which may trigger recrystallization during aging treatment. The high mobility of recrystallized grain boundaries favors the subsequent formation of DP. However, it is also possible that the formation of these fine grains is attributed to DP occurring within the initial fine microstructures. Given that the DP initiates via a supersaturated solid solution (α 0) transformed into a usually lamellar structure of a new phase (β) with solute enrichment, and a new phase (α) with solute depletion and the same crystal structure as α 0. With the reaction front advancing into the supersaturated matrix, the developed α lamellae maintains the same orientation as that of the initial α lamellae. Therefore, rather than resulting in a single grain after the DP reaction, there could be multiple grains corresponding to different growing colonies of the DP ( Han et al. , 2021; Kim et al. , 2024; Tałach-Dumańska et al. , 2003). It is also reported that DP can be effectively utilized to achieve grain refinement without any plastic deformation ( Tałach-Dumańska et al. , 2003). As a result, it is proposed that the roles of DP on the grain refinement should also be considered. For the AN 1000-AG and AN 1100-AG samples, it is intriguing that new fine grains formed after the annealing-aging treatment rather than after annealing alone. This phenomenon is unexpected since the dislocation density in the as-built samples is higher than those of annealed samples (Supplementary Fig. S3), which should result in more remarkable recrystallization and corresponding formation of fine grains in the direct-aged samples. Therefore, given that the driving force for recrystallization is diminished during high-temperature annealing, it is hypothesized that grain refinement may be linked to DP ( Han et al. , 2021; Tałach-Dumańska et al. , 2003). The initial fine-grain region plays a crucial role in enhancing DP which grows into coarse grains and correspondingly divides coarse grains into multiple finer grains. The abnormal grain refinement in the AN 1200-AG sample is still likely related to the DP ( Kim et al. , 2024). The SEM image and corresponding EBSD measurement of the YOZ plane for the AN 1200-AG sample further support that the grain refinement occurs through DP, as demonstrated in Supplementary Fig. S9. The AN 1200-AG sample exhibits DP regions with brighter contrast when compared to the CP regions. It is evident that the DP region is primarily located along the boundaries of the coarse grains. The corresponding EBSD IPF image clearly indicates that the fine grains are predominantly found within the DP region, while the CP region retains the coarse grain structure. Furthermore, the EBSD phase map exclusively displays the fcc structure due to the crystallographic similarity between the fcc and L1 2phases. This confirms that grain refinement is not caused by the formation of new phases that do not possess an fcc structure ( Chu et al. , 2024; Gwalani et al. , 2018). Moreover, the kernel average misorientation (KAM) map suggests an exceptionally low dislocation density in this area, indicating that the formation of new grains is not related to recrystallization. Additionally, the studied samples exhibit multiscale heterogenous microstructures, such as CP within coarse grains and DP within fine grains ( Fan et al. , 2022; Yang et al. , 2024). During the deformation of the heterostructure, geometrically necessary dislocations (GNDs) accumulate in the soft regions. The elastic field produced by these piled-up GNDs generates a force in the opposite direction to the applied stress on the soft domains. Consequently, a higher applied stress is required to deform the soft domains, resulting in the hardening effect known as HDI hardening ( Jung et al. , 2024; Kim et al. , 2024; Yang and Kim, 2024; Yang et al. , 2016; Zhu and Wu, 2019). To determine the contribution of HDI stress, LUR tests were conducted, as shown in Fig. 17(a). Furthermore, Fig. 17(b) illustrates the evolution of HDI stress as a function of true strain, measured from the hysteresis loops in Fig. 17(a) ( Yang et al. , 2016). At first, the HDI stress in the AN1000-AG sample is higher than that in the AN 1200-AG sample. Fine grains with DP are usually regarded as a hard phase, hence their contribution to strength is encompassed in HDI stress ( Kim et al. , 2024). The higher HDI stress in the AN 1000-AG sample can be attributed to its significantly higher fraction of fine grains with DP. However, the direct-aged sample with coarse grains and CP dominance still shows a slightly higher HDI stress compared to the AN 1000-AG sample. Considering the relatively low fraction of fine grains with DP, the high HDI stress observed in the direct-aged sample can also be attributed to its heterogeneous distribution of dislocations ( Wang et al., 2024a), which consists of hard cells with high local dislocation density and soft regions within cell interior. A simplified strengthening model was employed to calculate the various contributions to the differing YS of the studied samples. The YS can be divided into effective stress ( σ eff), arising from short-range interaction, and HDI stress ( σ HDI) which originates from long-range interaction. Therefore, the YS can be calculated using the following equation ( Jung et al. , 2024; Kim et al., 2024): σy=σeff+σHDIσeff=σ0+Δσss+Δσp+Δσρwhere σ 0, Δ σ ss, Δ σ p, and Δ σ ρrepresent friction stress, solid solution strengthening, precipitation strengthening, and dislocation strengthening, respectively. Given that the solid-solution strengthening can be integrated into the friction stress due to the difficulty in distinguishing between solvent and solute atoms, the friction stress value of an FeNiCrAlTi MEA (97 MPa) was adopted in this study ( Jung et al. , 2024; Wang et al., 2024a). Precipitation strengthening from CP and DP can be estimated based on APT results. APT results reveal an L1 2fraction of approximately 12 % in CP regions, whereas it notably increases to around 33 % in DP areas. Assuming that precipitation strengthening results from dislocation shearing of the L1 2phase, its effect can be calculated as follows ( Gwalani et al. , 2021; Jung et al., 2024): σp=M·0.81(γAPB/2b)(3πf/8)1/2where the Taylor factor (M) for fcc polycrystalline materials was assumed to be 3.06, and the Burgers vector ( b) was obtained from XRD results as 2. 54 Å, respectively. The anti-phase boundary energy ( γAPB) was estimated to be approximately 140 mJ/m 2, taking an Fe-rich MEA as a reference ( Jung et al. , 2024). Based on the aforementioned equation, the calculated precipitation strengthening effects in the CP and DP regions are approximately 257 MPa and 426 MPa, respectively. This calculation confirms that fine grains with DP are considered a hard phase, and thus their contribution to strength is included in the HDI stress. Regarding dislocation strengthening, the influence of dislocations can be neglected in the annealing-aged samples. For the direct-aged sample, a dislocation strengthening value of 128 MPa was adopted, based on a reference to L-PBF L1 2-strengthened austenitic stainless steel aged at 700 °C for 2 h ( Hu et al. , 2025). The HDI stress values obtained from Fig. 17(b) are approximately 430 MPa for the AN 1200-AG sample, 552 MPa for the AN 1000-AG sample, and 630 MPa for the direct-aged sample. These results indicate that HDI strengthening is a significant contributor to the strength of the studied samples. In summary, the estimated YS, calculated by summing the individual contributions, are approximately 788 MPa, 906 MPa, and 1112 MPa for the AN1200-AG, AN1000-AG, and direct-aged samples, respectively. These calculated values show a slight deviation from the experimental yield strengths, which are approximately 845 MPa, 999 MPa, and 1139 MPa, respectively. In summary, different annealing treatments prior to identical aging were performed on an L1 2-strengthened Fe-rich MEA fabricated by L-PBF. These treatments resulted in distinct final microstructures characterized by either DP or CP dominance, accompanied by varied mechanical properties. The detailed conclusions are as follows: 1The high-density dislocations and coarse grains induced by L-PBF promote CP. In contrast, the fine grains formed via L-PBF and the reduced dislocation density through annealing enhance DP, which in turn leads to grain refinement. 2The L-PBF Fe-MEA demonstrates acceptable printability, cost efficiency, and mechanical properties. Specifically, the direct-aged sample exhibits a YS of approximately 1. 1 GPa and a UE of around 11 %. The AN 1000-AG sample achieves a YS of about 1. 0 GPa and a UE of approximately 15 %. In the AN 1000-AG and AN 1200-AG samples, HDI strengthening primarily originates from the heterogeneous distribution of grains and precipitates. In contrast, the HDI strengthening in the direct-aged sample is attributed not only to the heterogeneous distribution of grains and precipitates but also to the heterogeneous dislocation structure. Dog-bone-shaped tensile specimens, with gauge dimensions of approximately 12 × 2.5 × 1.5 mm 3, were prepared along the X-axis direction using electrical-discharge machining and subsequently polished using 2000-grid SiC paper. The present study clearly reveals that different post-printing heat treatments result in varied precipitation behavior dominated by either CP or DP. In L1 2-strengthened H/MEAs, the relationship between CP and DP is competitive and the reasons are listed below. According to the equilibrium phase diagram, the aging temperature is located within the fcc+L1 2dual-phase region. Therefore, during aging treatment, there is a thermodynamic driving force for L1 2precipitation from the supersaturated matrix of the as-built sample with a single fcc phase. Moreover, from a dynamic perspective, there are two pathways for L1 2precipitation, CP and DP. The consumption of L1 2-forming elements like Ni, Al, and Ti within matrix by CP ahead of the DP region greatly decreases the driving force for the DP growth, thereby suppressing the advancement of DP. Besides, the CP nanoparticles have a pinning effect to the moving grain boundaries driven by DP, thereby kinetically hindering the DP growth. Conversely, a slow formation of CP allows the matrix to maintain a high supersaturation of L1 2-forming elements, thereby increasing the chemical driving force for DP migration. Additionally, it results in a weaker pinning effect on grain boundary migration, dynamically favoring DP growth. This combination enhances the growth of DP into the supersaturated matrix ( Fang et al., 2022b). The competition between CP and DP in L1 2-strengthened H/MEAs is primarily influenced by factors such as aging temperature, grain size, and dislocation density ( Fang et al., 2022a, 2022b; Liu et al., 2022a). Since the aging temperature was consistent across all aged samples in the present study, its influence was not revealed in this work. Regarding grain size, finer grains are more likely to promote DP, owing to the increased density of grain boundaries that not only facilitates diffusion along these boundaries but also provides numerous sites for the nucleation of DP. In addition, the roles of high-density dislocation in the DP and CP are twofold. If the high-density dislocation is insufficient to trigger recrystallization, it promotes CP by enhancing bulk diffusion and providing an additional driving force for the nucleation of precipitates. Conversely, when the high-density dislocation induced recrystallization, the high mobility of recrystallized grain boundaries and the high-density grain boundaries of fine recrystallized grains promote DP ( Fan et al. , 2020; Fang et al., 2022a, 2022b). In the present study, the as-built samples are characterized by dominant coarse grains with a high density of dislocations. It is suggested that the dislocations, which are insufficient to trigger significant recrystallization of coarse grains, together with the dominant coarse grains, enhance CP and result in CP being dominant in the direct-aged sample. By contrast, annealing at 1000 °C for 1 h mainly leads to a reduction in dislocation density within the AN 1000 sample, thereby slowing CP within the coarse grains of the AN 1000-AG sample compared to the direct-aged sample. This, in turn, facilitates DP which preferentially initiate at the grain boundaries of fine grains, leading to DP dominance in the AN 1000-AG sample. The explanation for the microstructural evolution from the AN 1100 sample to the AN 1100-AG sample follows a similar rationale as that of the AN 1000 sample to the AN 1000-AG sample, due to their comparable initial microstructures. Annealing at 1200 °C not only significantly eliminates dislocations but also results in the formation of significantly coarse, nearly equiaxed grains with almost no fine grains. This makes DP less competitive, resulting in CP dominance in the AN 1200-AG sample. In addition to factors such as grain size and dislocation density, further examination of the microstructures in the AN 1000 sample has confirmed that elemental enrichment along cell walls has become negligible, accompanied by a reduction in dislocation density. These findings are illustrated in Supplementary Fig. S8. The enrichment of L1 2-forming elements such as Ni and Ti can enhance the chemical driving force. Consequently, in the direct-aged sample characterized by CP dominance, the elemental enrichment along cell walls should facilitate CP by increasing the local chemical driving force. Following annealing at temperatures of 1000 °C or higher, the elemental enrichment along cell walls becomes negligible, thereby slowing down CP within coarse grains. This deceleration subsequently could promote the formation of DP in the AN 1000-AG sample. Furthermore, it is proposed that the effect of limited L1 2precipitation in AN 1000 sample on subsequent aging could be negligible. Firstly, the L1 2precipitation in the AN 1000 sample appears to be very minimal, as suggested by a decrease in hardness compared to the as-built sample. Secondly, the AN 1100 sample without L1 2peaks, undergoes similar microstructural evolution to the AN 1000 sample during aging treatment. In the direct-aged sample, the formation mechanisms of fine grains may be debatable, although some researchers suggest that they form via recrystallization ( Huang et al. , 2024; Wang and Chan, 2023). This explanation could be reasonable since the as-built sample contains a high density of dislocations, which may trigger recrystallization during aging treatment. The high mobility of recrystallized grain boundaries favors the subsequent formation of DP. However, it is also possible that the formation of these fine grains is attributed to DP occurring within the initial fine microstructures. Given that the DP initiates via a supersaturated solid solution (α 0) transformed into a usually lamellar structure of a new phase (β) with solute enrichment, and a new phase (α) with solute depletion and the same crystal structure as α 0. With the reaction front advancing into the supersaturated matrix, the developed α lamellae maintains the same orientation as that of the initial α lamellae. Therefore, rather than resulting in a single grain after the DP reaction, there could be multiple grains corresponding to different growing colonies of the DP ( Han et al. , 2021; Kim et al. , 2024; Tałach-Dumańska et al. , 2003). It is also reported that DP can be effectively utilized to achieve grain refinement without any plastic deformation ( Tałach-Dumańska et al. , 2003). As a result, it is proposed that the roles of DP on the grain refinement should also be considered. For the AN 1000-AG and AN 1100-AG samples, it is intriguing that new fine grains formed after the annealing-aging treatment rather than after annealing alone. This phenomenon is unexpected since the dislocation density in the as-built samples is higher than those of annealed samples (Supplementary Fig. S3), which should result in more remarkable recrystallization and corresponding formation of fine grains in the direct-aged samples. Therefore, given that the driving force for recrystallization is diminished during high-temperature annealing, it is hypothesized that grain refinement may be linked to DP ( Han et al. , 2021; Tałach-Dumańska et al. , 2003). The initial fine-grain region plays a crucial role in enhancing DP which grows into coarse grains and correspondingly divides coarse grains into multiple finer grains. The abnormal grain refinement in the AN 1200-AG sample is still likely related to the DP ( Kim et al. , 2024). The SEM image and corresponding EBSD measurement of the YOZ plane for the AN 1200-AG sample further support that the grain refinement occurs through DP, as demonstrated in Supplementary Fig. S9. The AN 1200-AG sample exhibits DP regions with brighter contrast when compared to the CP regions. It is evident that the DP region is primarily located along the boundaries of the coarse grains. The corresponding EBSD IPF image clearly indicates that the fine grains are predominantly found within the DP region, while the CP region retains the coarse grain structure. Furthermore, the EBSD phase map exclusively displays the fcc structure due to the crystallographic similarity between the fcc and L1 2phases. This confirms that grain refinement is not caused by the formation of new phases that do not possess an fcc structure ( Chu et al. , 2024; Gwalani et al. , 2018). Moreover, the kernel average misorientation (KAM) map suggests an exceptionally low dislocation density in this area, indicating that the formation of new grains is not related to recrystallization. Additionally, the studied samples exhibit multiscale heterogenous microstructures, such as CP within coarse grains and DP within fine grains ( Fan et al. , 2022; Yang et al. , 2024). During the deformation of the heterostructure, geometrically necessary dislocations (GNDs) accumulate in the soft regions. The elastic field produced by these piled-up GNDs generates a force in the opposite direction to the applied stress on the soft domains. Consequently, a higher applied stress is required to deform the soft domains, resulting in the hardening effect known as HDI hardening ( Jung et al. , 2024; Kim et al. , 2024; Yang and Kim, 2024; Yang et al. , 2016; Zhu and Wu, 2019). To determine the contribution of HDI stress, LUR tests were conducted, as shown in Fig. 17(a). Furthermore, Fig. 17(b) illustrates the evolution of HDI stress as a function of true strain, measured from the hysteresis loops in Fig. 17(a) ( Yang et al. , 2016). At first, the HDI stress in the AN1000-AG sample is higher than that in the AN 1200-AG sample. Fine grains with DP are usually regarded as a hard phase, hence their contribution to strength is encompassed in HDI stress ( Kim et al. , 2024). The higher HDI stress in the AN 1000-AG sample can be attributed to its significantly higher fraction of fine grains with DP. However, the direct-aged sample with coarse grains and CP dominance still shows a slightly higher HDI stress compared to the AN 1000-AG sample. Considering the relatively low fraction of fine grains with DP, the high HDI stress observed in the direct-aged sample can also be attributed to its heterogeneous distribution of dislocations ( Wang et al., 2024a), which consists of hard cells with high local dislocation density and soft regions within cell interior. A simplified strengthening model was employed to calculate the various contributions to the differing YS of the studied samples. The YS can be divided into effective stress ( σ eff), arising from short-range interaction, and HDI stress ( σ HDI) which originates from long-range interaction. Therefore, the YS can be calculated using the following equation ( Jung et al. , 2024; Kim et al., 2024): σy=σeff+σHDIσeff=σ0+Δσss+Δσp+Δσρwhere σ 0, Δ σ ss, Δ σ p, and Δ σ ρrepresent friction stress, solid solution strengthening, precipitation strengthening, and dislocation strengthening, respectively. Given that the solid-solution strengthening can be integrated into the friction stress due to the difficulty in distinguishing between solvent and solute atoms, the friction stress value of an FeNiCrAlTi MEA (97 MPa) was adopted in this study ( Jung et al. , 2024; Wang et al., 2024a). Precipitation strengthening from CP and DP can be estimated based on APT results. APT results reveal an L1 2fraction of approximately 12 % in CP regions, whereas it notably increases to around 33 % in DP areas. Assuming that precipitation strengthening results from dislocation shearing of the L1 2phase, its effect can be calculated as follows ( Gwalani et al. , 2021; Jung et al., 2024): σp=M·0.81(γAPB/2b)(3πf/8)1/2where the Taylor factor (M) for fcc polycrystalline materials was assumed to be 3.06, and the Burgers vector ( b) was obtained from XRD results as 2. 54 Å, respectively. The anti-phase boundary energy ( γAPB) was estimated to be approximately 140 mJ/m 2, taking an Fe-rich MEA as a reference ( Jung et al. , 2024). Based on the aforementioned equation, the calculated precipitation strengthening effects in the CP and DP regions are approximately 257 MPa and 426 MPa, respectively. This calculation confirms that fine grains with DP are considered a hard phase, and thus their contribution to strength is included in the HDI stress. Regarding dislocation strengthening, the influence of dislocations can be neglected in the annealing-aged samples. For the direct-aged sample, a dislocation strengthening value of 128 MPa was adopted, based on a reference to L-PBF L1 2-strengthened austenitic stainless steel aged at 700 °C for 2 h ( Hu et al. , 2025). The HDI stress values obtained from Fig. 17(b) are approximately 430 MPa for the AN 1200-AG sample, 552 MPa for the AN 1000-AG sample, and 630 MPa for the direct-aged sample. These results indicate that HDI strengthening is a significant contributor to the strength of the studied samples. In summary, the estimated YS, calculated by summing the individual contributions, are approximately 788 MPa, 906 MPa, and 1112 MPa for the AN1200-AG, AN1000-AG, and direct-aged samples, respectively. These calculated values show a slight deviation from the experimental yield strengths, which are approximately 845 MPa, 999 MPa, and 1139 MPa, respectively. These treatments resulted in distinct final microstructures characterized by either DP or CP dominance, accompanied by varied mechanical properties. The results indicate that the Fe-MEA fabricated via L-PBF may be a promising candidate for advanced structural applications, owing to its acceptable comprehensive mechanical properties and relatively low production cost. The present study clearly reveals that different post-printing heat treatments result in varied precipitation behavior dominated by either CP or DP. In L1 2-strengthened H/MEAs, the relationship between CP and DP is competitive and the reasons are listed below. According to the equilibrium phase diagram, the aging temperature is located within the fcc+L1 2dual-phase region. Therefore, during aging treatment, there is a thermodynamic driving force for L1 2precipitation from the supersaturated matrix of the as-built sample with a single fcc phase. Moreover, from a dynamic perspective, there are two pathways for L1 2precipitation, CP and DP. The consumption of L1 2-forming elements like Ni, Al, and Ti within matrix by CP ahead of the DP region greatly decreases the driving force for the DP growth, thereby suppressing the advancement of DP. Besides, the CP nanoparticles have a pinning effect to the moving grain boundaries driven by DP, thereby kinetically hindering the DP growth. Conversely, a slow formation of CP allows the matrix to maintain a high supersaturation of L1 2-forming elements, thereby increasing the chemical driving force for DP migration. Additionally, it results in a weaker pinning effect on grain boundary migration, dynamically favoring DP growth. This combination enhances the growth of DP into the supersaturated matrix ( Fang et al., 2022b). The competition between CP and DP in L1 2-strengthened H/MEAs is primarily influenced by factors such as aging temperature, grain size, and dislocation density ( Fang et al., 2022a, 2022b; Liu et al., 2022a). Since the aging temperature was consistent across all aged samples in the present study, its influence was not revealed in this work. Regarding grain size, finer grains are more likely to promote DP, owing to the increased density of grain boundaries that not only facilitates diffusion along these boundaries but also provides numerous sites for the nucleation of DP. In addition, the roles of high-density dislocation in the DP and CP are twofold. If the high-density dislocation is insufficient to trigger recrystallization, it promotes CP by enhancing bulk diffusion and providing an additional driving force for the nucleation of precipitates. Conversely, when the high-density dislocation induced recrystallization, the high mobility of recrystallized grain boundaries and the high-density grain boundaries of fine recrystallized grains promote DP ( Fan et al. , 2020; Fang et al., 2022a, 2022b). In the present study, the as-built samples are characterized by dominant coarse grains with a high density of dislocations. It is suggested that the dislocations, which are insufficient to trigger significant recrystallization of coarse grains, together with the dominant coarse grains, enhance CP and result in CP being dominant in the direct-aged sample. By contrast, annealing at 1000 °C for 1 h mainly leads to a reduction in dislocation density within the AN 1000 sample, thereby slowing CP within the coarse grains of the AN 1000-AG sample compared to the direct-aged sample. This, in turn, facilitates DP which preferentially initiate at the grain boundaries of fine grains, leading to DP dominance in the AN 1000-AG sample. The explanation for the microstructural evolution from the AN 1100 sample to the AN 1100-AG sample follows a similar rationale as that of the AN 1000 sample to the AN 1000-AG sample, due to their comparable initial microstructures. Annealing at 1200 °C not only significantly eliminates dislocations but also results in the formation of significantly coarse, nearly equiaxed grains with almost no fine grains. This makes DP less competitive, resulting in CP dominance in the AN 1200-AG sample. In addition to factors such as grain size and dislocation density, further examination of the microstructures in the AN 1000 sample has confirmed that elemental enrichment along cell walls has become negligible, accompanied by a reduction in dislocation density. These findings are illustrated in Supplementary Fig. S8. The enrichment of L1 2-forming elements such as Ni and Ti can enhance the chemical driving force. Consequently, in the direct-aged sample characterized by CP dominance, the elemental enrichment along cell walls should facilitate CP by increasing the local chemical driving force. Following annealing at temperatures of 1000 °C or higher, the elemental enrichment along cell walls becomes negligible, thereby slowing down CP within coarse grains. This deceleration subsequently could promote the formation of DP in the AN 1000-AG sample. Furthermore, it is proposed that the effect of limited L1 2precipitation in AN 1000 sample on subsequent aging could be negligible. Firstly, the L1 2precipitation in the AN 1000 sample appears to be very minimal, as suggested by a decrease in hardness compared to the as-built sample. Secondly, the AN 1100 sample without L1 2peaks, undergoes similar microstructural evolution to the AN 1000 sample during aging treatment. In the direct-aged sample, the formation mechanisms of fine grains may be debatable, although some researchers suggest that they form via recrystallization ( Huang et al. , 2024; Wang and Chan, 2023). This explanation could be reasonable since the as-built sample contains a high density of dislocations, which may trigger recrystallization during aging treatment. The high mobility of recrystallized grain boundaries favors the subsequent formation of DP. However, it is also possible that the formation of these fine grains is attributed to DP occurring within the initial fine microstructures. Given that the DP initiates via a supersaturated solid solution (α 0) transformed into a usually lamellar structure of a new phase (β) with solute enrichment, and a new phase (α) with solute depletion and the same crystal structure as α 0. With the reaction front advancing into the supersaturated matrix, the developed α lamellae maintains the same orientation as that of the initial α lamellae. Therefore, rather than resulting in a single grain after the DP reaction, there could be multiple grains corresponding to different growing colonies of the DP ( Han et al. , 2021; Kim et al. , 2024; Tałach-Dumańska et al. , 2003). It is also reported that DP can be effectively utilized to achieve grain refinement without any plastic deformation ( Tałach-Dumańska et al. , 2003). As a result, it is proposed that the roles of DP on the grain refinement should also be considered. For the AN 1000-AG and AN 1100-AG samples, it is intriguing that new fine grains formed after the annealing-aging treatment rather than after annealing alone. This phenomenon is unexpected since the dislocation density in the as-built samples is higher than those of annealed samples (Supplementary Fig. S3), which should result in more remarkable recrystallization and corresponding formation of fine grains in the direct-aged samples. Therefore, given that the driving force for recrystallization is diminished during high-temperature annealing, it is hypothesized that grain refinement may be linked to DP ( Han et al. , 2021; Tałach-Dumańska et al. , 2003). The initial fine-grain region plays a crucial role in enhancing DP which grows into coarse grains and correspondingly divides coarse grains into multiple finer grains. The abnormal grain refinement in the AN 1200-AG sample is still likely related to the DP ( Kim et al. , 2024). The SEM image and corresponding EBSD measurement of the YOZ plane for the AN 1200-AG sample further support that the grain refinement occurs through DP, as demonstrated in Supplementary Fig. S9. The AN 1200-AG sample exhibits DP regions with brighter contrast when compared to the CP regions. It is evident that the DP region is primarily located along the boundaries of the coarse grains. The corresponding EBSD IPF image clearly indicates that the fine grains are predominantly found within the DP region, while the CP region retains the coarse grain structure. Furthermore, the EBSD phase map exclusively displays the fcc structure due to the crystallographic similarity between the fcc and L1 2phases. This confirms that grain refinement is not caused by the formation of new phases that do not possess an fcc structure ( Chu et al. , 2024; Gwalani et al. , 2018). Moreover, the kernel average misorientation (KAM) map suggests an exceptionally low dislocation density in this area, indicating that the formation of new grains is not related to recrystallization. Additionally, the studied samples exhibit multiscale heterogenous microstructures, such as CP within coarse grains and DP within fine grains ( Fan et al. , 2022; Yang et al. , 2024). During the deformation of the heterostructure, geometrically necessary dislocations (GNDs) accumulate in the soft regions. The elastic field produced by these piled-up GNDs generates a force in the opposite direction to the applied stress on the soft domains. Consequently, a higher applied stress is required to deform the soft domains, resulting in the hardening effect known as HDI hardening ( Jung et al. , 2024; Kim et al. , 2024; Yang and Kim, 2024; Yang et al. , 2016; Zhu and Wu, 2019). To determine the contribution of HDI stress, LUR tests were conducted, as shown in Fig. 17(a). Furthermore, Fig. 17(b) illustrates the evolution of HDI stress as a function of true strain, measured from the hysteresis loops in Fig. 17(a) ( Yang et al. , 2016). At first, the HDI stress in the AN1000-AG sample is higher than that in the AN 1200-AG sample. Fine grains with DP are usually regarded as a hard phase, hence their contribution to strength is encompassed in HDI stress ( Kim et al. , 2024). The higher HDI stress in the AN 1000-AG sample can be attributed to its significantly higher fraction of fine grains with DP. However, the direct-aged sample with coarse grains and CP dominance still shows a slightly higher HDI stress compared to the AN 1000-AG sample. Considering the relatively low fraction of fine grains with DP, the high HDI stress observed in the direct-aged sample can also be attributed to its heterogeneous distribution of dislocations ( Wang et al., 2024a), which consists of hard cells with high local dislocation density and soft regions within cell interior. A simplified strengthening model was employed to calculate the various contributions to the differing YS of the studied samples. The YS can be divided into effective stress ( σ eff), arising from short-range interaction, and HDI stress ( σ HDI) which originates from long-range interaction. Therefore, the YS can be calculated using the following equation ( Jung et al. , 2024; Kim et al., 2024): σy=σeff+σHDIσeff=σ0+Δσss+Δσp+Δσρwhere σ 0, Δ σ ss, Δ σ p, and Δ σ ρrepresent friction stress, solid solution strengthening, precipitation strengthening, and dislocation strengthening, respectively. Given that the solid-solution strengthening can be integrated into the friction stress due to the difficulty in distinguishing between solvent and solute atoms, the friction stress value of an FeNiCrAlTi MEA (97 MPa) was adopted in this study ( Jung et al. , 2024; Wang et al., 2024a). Precipitation strengthening from CP and DP can be estimated based on APT results. APT results reveal an L1 2fraction of approximately 12 % in CP regions, whereas it notably increases to around 33 % in DP areas. Assuming that precipitation strengthening results from dislocation shearing of the L1 2phase, its effect can be calculated as follows ( Gwalani et al. , 2021; Jung et al., 2024): σp=M·0.81(γAPB/2b)(3πf/8)1/2where the Taylor factor (M) for fcc polycrystalline materials was assumed to be 3.06, and the Burgers vector ( b) was obtained from XRD results as 2. 54 Å, respectively. The anti-phase boundary energy ( γAPB) was estimated to be approximately 140 mJ/m 2, taking an Fe-rich MEA as a reference ( Jung et al. , 2024). Based on the aforementioned equation, the calculated precipitation strengthening effects in the CP and DP regions are approximately 257 MPa and 426 MPa, respectively. This calculation confirms that fine grains with DP are considered a hard phase, and thus their contribution to strength is included in the HDI stress. Regarding dislocation strengthening, the influence of dislocations can be neglected in the annealing-aged samples. For the direct-aged sample, a dislocation strengthening value of 128 MPa was adopted, based on a reference to L-PBF L1 2-strengthened austenitic stainless steel aged at 700 °C for 2 h ( Hu et al. , 2025). The HDI stress values obtained from Fig. 17(b) are approximately 430 MPa for the AN 1200-AG sample, 552 MPa for the AN 1000-AG sample, and 630 MPa for the direct-aged sample. These results indicate that HDI strengthening is a significant contributor to the strength of the studied samples. In summary, the estimated YS, calculated by summing the individual contributions, are approximately 788 MPa, 906 MPa, and 1112 MPa for the AN1200-AG, AN1000-AG, and direct-aged samples, respectively. These calculated values show a slight deviation from the experimental yield strengths, which are approximately 845 MPa, 999 MPa, and 1139 MPa, respectively. The present study clearly reveals that different post-printing heat treatments result in varied precipitation behavior dominated by either CP or DP. In L1 2-strengthened H/MEAs, the relationship between CP and DP is competitive and the reasons are listed below. According to the equilibrium phase diagram, the aging temperature is located within the fcc+L1 2dual-phase region. Therefore, during aging treatment, there is a thermodynamic driving force for L1 2precipitation from the supersaturated matrix of the as-built sample with a single fcc phase. Moreover, from a dynamic perspective, there are two pathways for L1 2precipitation, CP and DP. The consumption of L1 2-forming elements like Ni, Al, and Ti within matrix by CP ahead of the DP region greatly decreases the driving force for the DP growth, thereby suppressing the advancement of DP. Besides, the CP nanoparticles have a pinning effect to the moving grain boundaries driven by DP, thereby kinetically hindering the DP growth. Conversely, a slow formation of CP allows the matrix to maintain a high supersaturation of L1 2-forming elements, thereby increasing the chemical driving force for DP migration. Additionally, it results in a weaker pinning effect on grain boundary migration, dynamically favoring DP growth. This combination enhances the growth of DP into the supersaturated matrix ( Fang et al., 2022b). The competition between CP and DP in L1 2-strengthened H/MEAs is primarily influenced by factors such as aging temperature, grain size, and dislocation density ( Fang et al., 2022a, 2022b; Liu et al., 2022a). Since the aging temperature was consistent across all aged samples in the present study, its influence was not revealed in this work. Regarding grain size, finer grains are more likely to promote DP, owing to the increased density of grain boundaries that not only facilitates diffusion along these boundaries but also provides numerous sites for the nucleation of DP. In addition, the roles of high-density dislocation in the DP and CP are twofold. If the high-density dislocation is insufficient to trigger recrystallization, it promotes CP by enhancing bulk diffusion and providing an additional driving force for the nucleation of precipitates. Conversely, when the high-density dislocation induced recrystallization, the high mobility of recrystallized grain boundaries and the high-density grain boundaries of fine recrystallized grains promote DP ( Fan et al. , 2020; Fang et al., 2022a, 2022b). In the present study, the as-built samples are characterized by dominant coarse grains with a high density of dislocations. It is suggested that the dislocations, which are insufficient to trigger significant recrystallization of coarse grains, together with the dominant coarse grains, enhance CP and result in CP being dominant in the direct-aged sample. By contrast, annealing at 1000 °C for 1 h mainly leads to a reduction in dislocation density within the AN 1000 sample, thereby slowing CP within the coarse grains of the AN 1000-AG sample compared to the direct-aged sample. This, in turn, facilitates DP which preferentially initiate at the grain boundaries of fine grains, leading to DP dominance in the AN 1000-AG sample. The explanation for the microstructural evolution from the AN 1100 sample to the AN 1100-AG sample follows a similar rationale as that of the AN 1000 sample to the AN 1000-AG sample, due to their comparable initial microstructures. Annealing at 1200 °C not only significantly eliminates dislocations but also results in the formation of significantly coarse, nearly equiaxed grains with almost no fine grains. This makes DP less competitive, resulting in CP dominance in the AN 1200-AG sample. In addition to factors such as grain size and dislocation density, further examination of the microstructures in the AN 1000 sample has confirmed that elemental enrichment along cell walls has become negligible, accompanied by a reduction in dislocation density. These findings are illustrated in Supplementary Fig. S8. The enrichment of L1 2-forming elements such as Ni and Ti can enhance the chemical driving force. Consequently, in the direct-aged sample characterized by CP dominance, the elemental enrichment along cell walls should facilitate CP by increasing the local chemical driving force. Following annealing at temperatures of 1000 °C or higher, the elemental enrichment along cell walls becomes negligible, thereby slowing down CP within coarse grains. This deceleration subsequently could promote the formation of DP in the AN 1000-AG sample. Furthermore, it is proposed that the effect of limited L1 2precipitation in AN 1000 sample on subsequent aging could be negligible. Firstly, the L1 2precipitation in the AN 1000 sample appears to be very minimal, as suggested by a decrease in hardness compared to the as-built sample. Secondly, the AN 1100 sample without L1 2peaks, undergoes similar microstructural evolution to the AN 1000 sample during aging treatment. In the direct-aged sample, the formation mechanisms of fine grains may be debatable, although some researchers suggest that they form via recrystallization ( Huang et al. , 2024; Wang and Chan, 2023). This explanation could be reasonable since the as-built sample contains a high density of dislocations, which may trigger recrystallization during aging treatment. The high mobility of recrystallized grain boundaries favors the subsequent formation of DP. However, it is also possible that the formation of these fine grains is attributed to DP occurring within the initial fine microstructures. Given that the DP initiates via a supersaturated solid solution (α 0) transformed into a usually lamellar structure of a new phase (β) with solute enrichment, and a new phase (α) with solute depletion and the same crystal structure as α 0. With the reaction front advancing into the supersaturated matrix, the developed α lamellae maintains the same orientation as that of the initial α lamellae. Therefore, rather than resulting in a single grain after the DP reaction, there could be multiple grains corresponding to different growing colonies of the DP ( Han et al. , 2021; Kim et al. , 2024; Tałach-Dumańska et al. , 2003). It is also reported that DP can be effectively utilized to achieve grain refinement without any plastic deformation ( Tałach-Dumańska et al. , 2003). As a result, it is proposed that the roles of DP on the grain refinement should also be considered. For the AN 1000-AG and AN 1100-AG samples, it is intriguing that new fine grains formed after the annealing-aging treatment rather than after annealing alone. This phenomenon is unexpected since the dislocation density in the as-built samples is higher than those of annealed samples (Supplementary Fig. S3), which should result in more remarkable recrystallization and corresponding formation of fine grains in the direct-aged samples. Therefore, given that the driving force for recrystallization is diminished during high-temperature annealing, it is hypothesized that grain refinement may be linked to DP ( Han et al. , 2021; Tałach-Dumańska et al. , 2003). The initial fine-grain region plays a crucial role in enhancing DP which grows into coarse grains and correspondingly divides coarse grains into multiple finer grains. The abnormal grain refinement in the AN 1200-AG sample is still likely related to the DP ( Kim et al. , 2024). The SEM image and corresponding EBSD measurement of the YOZ plane for the AN 1200-AG sample further support that the grain refinement occurs through DP, as demonstrated in Supplementary Fig. S9. The AN 1200-AG sample exhibits DP regions with brighter contrast when compared to the CP regions. It is evident that the DP region is primarily located along the boundaries of the coarse grains. The corresponding EBSD IPF image clearly indicates that the fine grains are predominantly found within the DP region, while the CP region retains the coarse grain structure. Furthermore, the EBSD phase map exclusively displays the fcc structure due to the crystallographic similarity between the fcc and L1 2phases. This confirms that grain refinement is not caused by the formation of new phases that do not possess an fcc structure ( Chu et al. , 2024; Gwalani et al. , 2018). Moreover, the kernel average misorientation (KAM) map suggests an exceptionally low dislocation density in this area, indicating that the formation of new grains is not related to recrystallization.
