Additionally, the studied samples exhibit multiscale heterogenous microstructures, such as CP within coarse grains and DP within fine grains ( Fan et al. , 2022; Yang et al. , 2024). During the deformation of the heterostructure, geometrically necessary dislocations (GNDs) accumulate in the soft regions. The elastic field produced by these piled-up GNDs generates a force in the opposite direction to the applied stress on the soft domains. Consequently, a higher applied stress is required to deform the soft domains, resulting in the hardening effect known as HDI hardening ( Jung et al. , 2024; Kim et al. , 2024; Yang and Kim, 2024; Yang et al. , 2016; Zhu and Wu, 2019). To determine the contribution of HDI stress, LUR tests were conducted, as shown in Fig. 17(a). Furthermore, Fig. 17(b) illustrates the evolution of HDI stress as a function of true strain, measured from the hysteresis loops in Fig. 17(a) ( Yang et al. , 2016). At first, the HDI stress in the AN1000-AG sample is higher than that in the AN 1200-AG sample. Fine grains with DP are usually regarded as a hard phase, hence their contribution to strength is encompassed in HDI stress ( Kim et al. , 2024). The higher HDI stress in the AN 1000-AG sample can be attributed to its significantly higher fraction of fine grains with DP. However, the direct-aged sample with coarse grains and CP dominance still shows a slightly higher HDI stress compared to the AN 1000-AG sample. Considering the relatively low fraction of fine grains with DP, the high HDI stress observed in the direct-aged sample can also be attributed to its heterogeneous distribution of dislocations ( Wang et al., 2024a), which consists of hard cells with high local dislocation density and soft regions within cell interior. A simplified strengthening model was employed to calculate the various contributions to the differing YS of the studied samples. The YS can be divided into effective stress ( σ eff), arising from short-range interaction, and HDI stress ( σ HDI) which originates from long-range interaction. Therefore, the YS can be calculated using the following equation ( Jung et al. , 2024; Kim et al., 2024): σy=σeff+σHDIσeff=σ0+Δσss+Δσp+Δσρwhere σ 0, Δ σ ss, Δ σ p, and Δ σ ρrepresent friction stress, solid solution strengthening, precipitation strengthening, and dislocation strengthening, respectively. Given that the solid-solution strengthening can be integrated into the friction stress due to the difficulty in distinguishing between solvent and solute atoms, the friction stress value of an FeNiCrAlTi MEA (97 MPa) was adopted in this study ( Jung et al. , 2024; Wang et al., 2024a). Precipitation strengthening from CP and DP can be estimated based on APT results. APT results reveal an L1 2fraction of approximately 12 % in CP regions, whereas it notably increases to around 33 % in DP areas. Assuming that precipitation strengthening results from dislocation shearing of the L1 2phase, its effect can be calculated as follows ( Gwalani et al. , 2021; Jung et al., 2024): σp=M·0.81(γAPB/2b)(3πf/8)1/2where the Taylor factor (M) for fcc polycrystalline materials was assumed to be 3.06, and the Burgers vector ( b) was obtained from XRD results as 2. 54 Å, respectively. The anti-phase boundary energy ( γAPB) was estimated to be approximately 140 mJ/m 2, taking an Fe-rich MEA as a reference ( Jung et al. , 2024). Based on the aforementioned equation, the calculated precipitation strengthening effects in the CP and DP regions are approximately 257 MPa and 426 MPa, respectively. This calculation confirms that fine grains with DP are considered a hard phase, and thus their contribution to strength is included in the HDI stress. Regarding dislocation strengthening, the influence of dislocations can be neglected in the annealing-aged samples. For the direct-aged sample, a dislocation strengthening value of 128 MPa was adopted, based on a reference to L-PBF L1 2-strengthened austenitic stainless steel aged at 700 °C for 2 h ( Hu et al. , 2025). The HDI stress values obtained from Fig. 17(b) are approximately 430 MPa for the AN 1200-AG sample, 552 MPa for the AN 1000-AG sample, and 630 MPa for the direct-aged sample. These results indicate that HDI strengthening is a significant contributor to the strength of the studied samples. In summary, the estimated YS, calculated by summing the individual contributions, are approximately 788 MPa, 906 MPa, and 1112 MPa for the AN1200-AG, AN1000-AG, and direct-aged samples, respectively. These calculated values show a slight deviation from the experimental yield strengths, which are approximately 845 MPa, 999 MPa, and 1139 MPa, respectively. The results indicate that the Fe-MEA fabricated via L-PBF may be a promising candidate for advanced structural applications, owing to its acceptable comprehensive mechanical properties and relatively low production cost. The present study clearly reveals that different post-printing heat treatments result in varied precipitation behavior dominated by either CP or DP. In L1 2-strengthened H/MEAs, the relationship between CP and DP is competitive and the reasons are listed below. According to the equilibrium phase diagram, the aging temperature is located within the fcc+L1 2dual-phase region. Therefore, during aging treatment, there is a thermodynamic driving force for L1 2precipitation from the supersaturated matrix of the as-built sample with a single fcc phase. Moreover, from a dynamic perspective, there are two pathways for L1 2precipitation, CP and DP. The consumption of L1 2-forming elements like Ni, Al, and Ti within matrix by CP ahead of the DP region greatly decreases the driving force for the DP growth, thereby suppressing the advancement of DP. Besides, the CP nanoparticles have a pinning effect to the moving grain boundaries driven by DP, thereby kinetically hindering the DP growth. Conversely, a slow formation of CP allows the matrix to maintain a high supersaturation of L1 2-forming elements, thereby increasing the chemical driving force for DP migration. Additionally, it results in a weaker pinning effect on grain boundary migration, dynamically favoring DP growth. This combination enhances the growth of DP into the supersaturated matrix ( Fang et al., 2022b). The competition between CP and DP in L1 2-strengthened H/MEAs is primarily influenced by factors such as aging temperature, grain size, and dislocation density ( Fang et al., 2022a, 2022b; Liu et al., 2022a). Since the aging temperature was consistent across all aged samples in the present study, its influence was not revealed in this work. Regarding grain size, finer grains are more likely to promote DP, owing to the increased density of grain boundaries that not only facilitates diffusion along these boundaries but also provides numerous sites for the nucleation of DP. In addition, the roles of high-density dislocation in the DP and CP are twofold. If the high-density dislocation is insufficient to trigger recrystallization, it promotes CP by enhancing bulk diffusion and providing an additional driving force for the nucleation of precipitates. Conversely, when the high-density dislocation induced recrystallization, the high mobility of recrystallized grain boundaries and the high-density grain boundaries of fine recrystallized grains promote DP ( Fan et al. , 2020; Fang et al., 2022a, 2022b). In the present study, the as-built samples are characterized by dominant coarse grains with a high density of dislocations. It is suggested that the dislocations, which are insufficient to trigger significant recrystallization of coarse grains, together with the dominant coarse grains, enhance CP and result in CP being dominant in the direct-aged sample. By contrast, annealing at 1000 °C for 1 h mainly leads to a reduction in dislocation density within the AN 1000 sample, thereby slowing CP within the coarse grains of the AN 1000-AG sample compared to the direct-aged sample. This, in turn, facilitates DP which preferentially initiate at the grain boundaries of fine grains, leading to DP dominance in the AN 1000-AG sample. The explanation for the microstructural evolution from the AN 1100 sample to the AN 1100-AG sample follows a similar rationale as that of the AN 1000 sample to the AN 1000-AG sample, due to their comparable initial microstructures. Annealing at 1200 °C not only significantly eliminates dislocations but also results in the formation of significantly coarse, nearly equiaxed grains with almost no fine grains. This makes DP less competitive, resulting in CP dominance in the AN 1200-AG sample. In addition to factors such as grain size and dislocation density, further examination of the microstructures in the AN 1000 sample has confirmed that elemental enrichment along cell walls has become negligible, accompanied by a reduction in dislocation density. These findings are illustrated in Supplementary Fig. S8. The enrichment of L1 2-forming elements such as Ni and Ti can enhance the chemical driving force. Consequently, in the direct-aged sample characterized by CP dominance, the elemental enrichment along cell walls should facilitate CP by increasing the local chemical driving force. Following annealing at temperatures of 1000 °C or higher, the elemental enrichment along cell walls becomes negligible, thereby slowing down CP within coarse grains. This deceleration subsequently could promote the formation of DP in the AN 1000-AG sample. Furthermore, it is proposed that the effect of limited L1 2precipitation in AN 1000 sample on subsequent aging could be negligible. Firstly, the L1 2precipitation in the AN 1000 sample appears to be very minimal, as suggested by a decrease in hardness compared to the as-built sample. Secondly, the AN 1100 sample without L1 2peaks, undergoes similar microstructural evolution to the AN 1000 sample during aging treatment. In the direct-aged sample, the formation mechanisms of fine grains may be debatable, although some researchers suggest that they form via recrystallization ( Huang et al. , 2024; Wang and Chan, 2023). This explanation could be reasonable since the as-built sample contains a high density of dislocations, which may trigger recrystallization during aging treatment. The high mobility of recrystallized grain boundaries favors the subsequent formation of DP. However, it is also possible that the formation of these fine grains is attributed to DP occurring within the initial fine microstructures. Given that the DP initiates via a supersaturated solid solution (α 0) transformed into a usually lamellar structure of a new phase (β) with solute enrichment, and a new phase (α) with solute depletion and the same crystal structure as α 0. With the reaction front advancing into the supersaturated matrix, the developed α lamellae maintains the same orientation as that of the initial α lamellae. Therefore, rather than resulting in a single grain after the DP reaction, there could be multiple grains corresponding to different growing colonies of the DP ( Han et al. , 2021; Kim et al. , 2024; Tałach-Dumańska et al. , 2003). It is also reported that DP can be effectively utilized to achieve grain refinement without any plastic deformation ( Tałach-Dumańska et al. , 2003). As a result, it is proposed that the roles of DP on the grain refinement should also be considered. For the AN 1000-AG and AN 1100-AG samples, it is intriguing that new fine grains formed after the annealing-aging treatment rather than after annealing alone. This phenomenon is unexpected since the dislocation density in the as-built samples is higher than those of annealed samples (Supplementary Fig. S3), which should result in more remarkable recrystallization and corresponding formation of fine grains in the direct-aged samples. Therefore, given that the driving force for recrystallization is diminished during high-temperature annealing, it is hypothesized that grain refinement may be linked to DP ( Han et al. , 2021; Tałach-Dumańska et al. , 2003). The initial fine-grain region plays a crucial role in enhancing DP which grows into coarse grains and correspondingly divides coarse grains into multiple finer grains. The abnormal grain refinement in the AN 1200-AG sample is still likely related to the DP ( Kim et al. , 2024). The SEM image and corresponding EBSD measurement of the YOZ plane for the AN 1200-AG sample further support that the grain refinement occurs through DP, as demonstrated in Supplementary Fig. S9. The AN 1200-AG sample exhibits DP regions with brighter contrast when compared to the CP regions. It is evident that the DP region is primarily located along the boundaries of the coarse grains. The corresponding EBSD IPF image clearly indicates that the fine grains are predominantly found within the DP region, while the CP region retains the coarse grain structure. Furthermore, the EBSD phase map exclusively displays the fcc structure due to the crystallographic similarity between the fcc and L1 2phases. This confirms that grain refinement is not caused by the formation of new phases that do not possess an fcc structure ( Chu et al. , 2024; Gwalani et al. , 2018). Moreover, the kernel average misorientation (KAM) map suggests an exceptionally low dislocation density in this area, indicating that the formation of new grains is not related to recrystallization. Therefore, the SFE of the fcc matrix in the direct-aged sample could be sufficiently low to facilitate the formation of deformation-induced twinning and SFs in both CP and DP regions. The formation of SFs in both CP (Supplementary Fig. S11) and DP (Supplementary Fig. S12) regions of the AN 1000-AG sample was also revealed, indicating that both the CP and DP regions exhibit good deformation capacity. Additionally, the studied samples exhibit multiscale heterogenous microstructures, such as CP within coarse grains and DP within fine grains ( Fan et al. , 2022; Yang et al. , 2024). During the deformation of the heterostructure, geometrically necessary dislocations (GNDs) accumulate in the soft regions. The elastic field produced by these piled-up GNDs generates a force in the opposite direction to the applied stress on the soft domains. Consequently, a higher applied stress is required to deform the soft domains, resulting in the hardening effect known as HDI hardening ( Jung et al. , 2024; Kim et al. , 2024; Yang and Kim, 2024; Yang et al. , 2016; Zhu and Wu, 2019). To determine the contribution of HDI stress, LUR tests were conducted, as shown in Fig. 17(a). Furthermore, Fig. 17(b) illustrates the evolution of HDI stress as a function of true strain, measured from the hysteresis loops in Fig. 17(a) ( Yang et al. , 2016). At first, the HDI stress in the AN1000-AG sample is higher than that in the AN 1200-AG sample. Fine grains with DP are usually regarded as a hard phase, hence their contribution to strength is encompassed in HDI stress ( Kim et al. , 2024). The higher HDI stress in the AN 1000-AG sample can be attributed to its significantly higher fraction of fine grains with DP. However, the direct-aged sample with coarse grains and CP dominance still shows a slightly higher HDI stress compared to the AN 1000-AG sample. Considering the relatively low fraction of fine grains with DP, the high HDI stress observed in the direct-aged sample can also be attributed to its heterogeneous distribution of dislocations ( Wang et al., 2024a), which consists of hard cells with high local dislocation density and soft regions within cell interior. A simplified strengthening model was employed to calculate the various contributions to the differing YS of the studied samples. The YS can be divided into effective stress ( σ eff), arising from short-range interaction, and HDI stress ( σ HDI) which originates from long-range interaction. Therefore, the YS can be calculated using the following equation ( Jung et al. , 2024; Kim et al., 2024): σy=σeff+σHDIσeff=σ0+Δσss+Δσp+Δσρwhere σ 0, Δ σ ss, Δ σ p, and Δ σ ρrepresent friction stress, solid solution strengthening, precipitation strengthening, and dislocation strengthening, respectively. Given that the solid-solution strengthening can be integrated into the friction stress due to the difficulty in distinguishing between solvent and solute atoms, the friction stress value of an FeNiCrAlTi MEA (97 MPa) was adopted in this study ( Jung et al. , 2024; Wang et al., 2024a). Precipitation strengthening from CP and DP can be estimated based on APT results. APT results reveal an L1 2fraction of approximately 12 % in CP regions, whereas it notably increases to around 33 % in DP areas. Assuming that precipitation strengthening results from dislocation shearing of the L1 2phase, its effect can be calculated as follows ( Gwalani et al. , 2021; Jung et al., 2024): σp=M·0.81(γAPB/2b)(3πf/8)1/2where the Taylor factor (M) for fcc polycrystalline materials was assumed to be 3.06, and the Burgers vector ( b) was obtained from XRD results as 2. 54 Å, respectively. The anti-phase boundary energy ( γAPB) was estimated to be approximately 140 mJ/m 2, taking an Fe-rich MEA as a reference ( Jung et al. , 2024). Based on the aforementioned equation, the calculated precipitation strengthening effects in the CP and DP regions are approximately 257 MPa and 426 MPa, respectively. This calculation confirms that fine grains with DP are considered a hard phase, and thus their contribution to strength is included in the HDI stress. Regarding dislocation strengthening, the influence of dislocations can be neglected in the annealing-aged samples. For the direct-aged sample, a dislocation strengthening value of 128 MPa was adopted, based on a reference to L-PBF L1 2-strengthened austenitic stainless steel aged at 700 °C for 2 h ( Hu et al. , 2025). The HDI stress values obtained from Fig. 17(b) are approximately 430 MPa for the AN 1200-AG sample, 552 MPa for the AN 1000-AG sample, and 630 MPa for the direct-aged sample. These results indicate that HDI strengthening is a significant contributor to the strength of the studied samples. In summary, the estimated YS, calculated by summing the individual contributions, are approximately 788 MPa, 906 MPa, and 1112 MPa for the AN1200-AG, AN1000-AG, and direct-aged samples, respectively. These calculated values show a slight deviation from the experimental yield strengths, which are approximately 845 MPa, 999 MPa, and 1139 MPa, respectively. In summary, different annealing treatments prior to identical aging were performed on an L1 2-strengthened Fe-rich MEA fabricated by L-PBF. These treatments resulted in distinct final microstructures characterized by either DP or CP dominance, accompanied by varied mechanical properties. The present study clearly reveals that different post-printing heat treatments result in varied precipitation behavior dominated by either CP or DP. In L1 2-strengthened H/MEAs, the relationship between CP and DP is competitive and the reasons are listed below. According to the equilibrium phase diagram, the aging temperature is located within the fcc+L1 2dual-phase region. Therefore, during aging treatment, there is a thermodynamic driving force for L1 2precipitation from the supersaturated matrix of the as-built sample with a single fcc phase. Moreover, from a dynamic perspective, there are two pathways for L1 2precipitation, CP and DP. The consumption of L1 2-forming elements like Ni, Al, and Ti within matrix by CP ahead of the DP region greatly decreases the driving force for the DP growth, thereby suppressing the advancement of DP. Besides, the CP nanoparticles have a pinning effect to the moving grain boundaries driven by DP, thereby kinetically hindering the DP growth. Conversely, a slow formation of CP allows the matrix to maintain a high supersaturation of L1 2-forming elements, thereby increasing the chemical driving force for DP migration. Additionally, it results in a weaker pinning effect on grain boundary migration, dynamically favoring DP growth. This combination enhances the growth of DP into the supersaturated matrix ( Fang et al., 2022b). The competition between CP and DP in L1 2-strengthened H/MEAs is primarily influenced by factors such as aging temperature, grain size, and dislocation density ( Fang et al., 2022a, 2022b; Liu et al., 2022a). Since the aging temperature was consistent across all aged samples in the present study, its influence was not revealed in this work. Regarding grain size, finer grains are more likely to promote DP, owing to the increased density of grain boundaries that not only facilitates diffusion along these boundaries but also provides numerous sites for the nucleation of DP. In addition, the roles of high-density dislocation in the DP and CP are twofold. If the high-density dislocation is insufficient to trigger recrystallization, it promotes CP by enhancing bulk diffusion and providing an additional driving force for the nucleation of precipitates. Conversely, when the high-density dislocation induced recrystallization, the high mobility of recrystallized grain boundaries and the high-density grain boundaries of fine recrystallized grains promote DP ( Fan et al. , 2020; Fang et al., 2022a, 2022b). In the present study, the as-built samples are characterized by dominant coarse grains with a high density of dislocations. It is suggested that the dislocations, which are insufficient to trigger significant recrystallization of coarse grains, together with the dominant coarse grains, enhance CP and result in CP being dominant in the direct-aged sample. By contrast, annealing at 1000 °C for 1 h mainly leads to a reduction in dislocation density within the AN 1000 sample, thereby slowing CP within the coarse grains of the AN 1000-AG sample compared to the direct-aged sample. This, in turn, facilitates DP which preferentially initiate at the grain boundaries of fine grains, leading to DP dominance in the AN 1000-AG sample. The explanation for the microstructural evolution from the AN 1100 sample to the AN 1100-AG sample follows a similar rationale as that of the AN 1000 sample to the AN 1000-AG sample, due to their comparable initial microstructures. Annealing at 1200 °C not only significantly eliminates dislocations but also results in the formation of significantly coarse, nearly equiaxed grains with almost no fine grains. This makes DP less competitive, resulting in CP dominance in the AN 1200-AG sample. In addition to factors such as grain size and dislocation density, further examination of the microstructures in the AN 1000 sample has confirmed that elemental enrichment along cell walls has become negligible, accompanied by a reduction in dislocation density. These findings are illustrated in Supplementary Fig. S8. The enrichment of L1 2-forming elements such as Ni and Ti can enhance the chemical driving force. Consequently, in the direct-aged sample characterized by CP dominance, the elemental enrichment along cell walls should facilitate CP by increasing the local chemical driving force. Following annealing at temperatures of 1000 °C or higher, the elemental enrichment along cell walls becomes negligible, thereby slowing down CP within coarse grains. This deceleration subsequently could promote the formation of DP in the AN 1000-AG sample. Furthermore, it is proposed that the effect of limited L1 2precipitation in AN 1000 sample on subsequent aging could be negligible. Firstly, the L1 2precipitation in the AN 1000 sample appears to be very minimal, as suggested by a decrease in hardness compared to the as-built sample. Secondly, the AN 1100 sample without L1 2peaks, undergoes similar microstructural evolution to the AN 1000 sample during aging treatment. In the direct-aged sample, the formation mechanisms of fine grains may be debatable, although some researchers suggest that they form via recrystallization ( Huang et al. , 2024; Wang and Chan, 2023). This explanation could be reasonable since the as-built sample contains a high density of dislocations, which may trigger recrystallization during aging treatment. The high mobility of recrystallized grain boundaries favors the subsequent formation of DP. However, it is also possible that the formation of these fine grains is attributed to DP occurring within the initial fine microstructures. Given that the DP initiates via a supersaturated solid solution (α 0) transformed into a usually lamellar structure of a new phase (β) with solute enrichment, and a new phase (α) with solute depletion and the same crystal structure as α 0. With the reaction front advancing into the supersaturated matrix, the developed α lamellae maintains the same orientation as that of the initial α lamellae. Therefore, rather than resulting in a single grain after the DP reaction, there could be multiple grains corresponding to different growing colonies of the DP ( Han et al. , 2021; Kim et al. , 2024; Tałach-Dumańska et al. , 2003). It is also reported that DP can be effectively utilized to achieve grain refinement without any plastic deformation ( Tałach-Dumańska et al. , 2003). As a result, it is proposed that the roles of DP on the grain refinement should also be considered. For the AN 1000-AG and AN 1100-AG samples, it is intriguing that new fine grains formed after the annealing-aging treatment rather than after annealing alone. This phenomenon is unexpected since the dislocation density in the as-built samples is higher than those of annealed samples (Supplementary Fig. S3), which should result in more remarkable recrystallization and corresponding formation of fine grains in the direct-aged samples. Therefore, given that the driving force for recrystallization is diminished during high-temperature annealing, it is hypothesized that grain refinement may be linked to DP ( Han et al. , 2021; Tałach-Dumańska et al. , 2003). The initial fine-grain region plays a crucial role in enhancing DP which grows into coarse grains and correspondingly divides coarse grains into multiple finer grains. The abnormal grain refinement in the AN 1200-AG sample is still likely related to the DP ( Kim et al. , 2024). The SEM image and corresponding EBSD measurement of the YOZ plane for the AN 1200-AG sample further support that the grain refinement occurs through DP, as demonstrated in Supplementary Fig. S9. The AN 1200-AG sample exhibits DP regions with brighter contrast when compared to the CP regions. It is evident that the DP region is primarily located along the boundaries of the coarse grains. The corresponding EBSD IPF image clearly indicates that the fine grains are predominantly found within the DP region, while the CP region retains the coarse grain structure. Furthermore, the EBSD phase map exclusively displays the fcc structure due to the crystallographic similarity between the fcc and L1 2phases. This confirms that grain refinement is not caused by the formation of new phases that do not possess an fcc structure ( Chu et al. , 2024; Gwalani et al. , 2018). Moreover, the kernel average misorientation (KAM) map suggests an exceptionally low dislocation density in this area, indicating that the formation of new grains is not related to recrystallization. Additionally, the studied samples exhibit multiscale heterogenous microstructures, such as CP within coarse grains and DP within fine grains ( Fan et al. , 2022; Yang et al. , 2024). During the deformation of the heterostructure, geometrically necessary dislocations (GNDs) accumulate in the soft regions. The elastic field produced by these piled-up GNDs generates a force in the opposite direction to the applied stress on the soft domains. Consequently, a higher applied stress is required to deform the soft domains, resulting in the hardening effect known as HDI hardening ( Jung et al. , 2024; Kim et al. , 2024; Yang and Kim, 2024; Yang et al. , 2016; Zhu and Wu, 2019). To determine the contribution of HDI stress, LUR tests were conducted, as shown in Fig. 17(a). Furthermore, Fig. 17(b) illustrates the evolution of HDI stress as a function of true strain, measured from the hysteresis loops in Fig. 17(a) ( Yang et al. , 2016). At first, the HDI stress in the AN1000-AG sample is higher than that in the AN 1200-AG sample. Fine grains with DP are usually regarded as a hard phase, hence their contribution to strength is encompassed in HDI stress ( Kim et al. , 2024). The higher HDI stress in the AN 1000-AG sample can be attributed to its significantly higher fraction of fine grains with DP. However, the direct-aged sample with coarse grains and CP dominance still shows a slightly higher HDI stress compared to the AN 1000-AG sample. Considering the relatively low fraction of fine grains with DP, the high HDI stress observed in the direct-aged sample can also be attributed to its heterogeneous distribution of dislocations ( Wang et al., 2024a), which consists of hard cells with high local dislocation density and soft regions within cell interior. A simplified strengthening model was employed to calculate the various contributions to the differing YS of the studied samples. The YS can be divided into effective stress ( σ eff), arising from short-range interaction, and HDI stress ( σ HDI) which originates from long-range interaction. Therefore, the YS can be calculated using the following equation ( Jung et al. , 2024; Kim et al., 2024): σy=σeff+σHDIσeff=σ0+Δσss+Δσp+Δσρwhere σ 0, Δ σ ss, Δ σ p, and Δ σ ρrepresent friction stress, solid solution strengthening, precipitation strengthening, and dislocation strengthening, respectively. Given that the solid-solution strengthening can be integrated into the friction stress due to the difficulty in distinguishing between solvent and solute atoms, the friction stress value of an FeNiCrAlTi MEA (97 MPa) was adopted in this study ( Jung et al. , 2024; Wang et al., 2024a). Precipitation strengthening from CP and DP can be estimated based on APT results. APT results reveal an L1 2fraction of approximately 12 % in CP regions, whereas it notably increases to around 33 % in DP areas. Assuming that precipitation strengthening results from dislocation shearing of the L1 2phase, its effect can be calculated as follows ( Gwalani et al. , 2021; Jung et al., 2024): σp=M·0.81(γAPB/2b)(3πf/8)1/2where the Taylor factor (M) for fcc polycrystalline materials was assumed to be 3.06, and the Burgers vector ( b) was obtained from XRD results as 2. 54 Å, respectively. The anti-phase boundary energy ( γAPB) was estimated to be approximately 140 mJ/m 2, taking an Fe-rich MEA as a reference ( Jung et al. , 2024). Based on the aforementioned equation, the calculated precipitation strengthening effects in the CP and DP regions are approximately 257 MPa and 426 MPa, respectively. This calculation confirms that fine grains with DP are considered a hard phase, and thus their contribution to strength is included in the HDI stress. Regarding dislocation strengthening, the influence of dislocations can be neglected in the annealing-aged samples. For the direct-aged sample, a dislocation strengthening value of 128 MPa was adopted, based on a reference to L-PBF L1 2-strengthened austenitic stainless steel aged at 700 °C for 2 h ( Hu et al. , 2025). The HDI stress values obtained from Fig. 17(b) are approximately 430 MPa for the AN 1200-AG sample, 552 MPa for the AN 1000-AG sample, and 630 MPa for the direct-aged sample. These results indicate that HDI strengthening is a significant contributor to the strength of the studied samples. In summary, the estimated YS, calculated by summing the individual contributions, are approximately 788 MPa, 906 MPa, and 1112 MPa for the AN1200-AG, AN1000-AG, and direct-aged samples, respectively. These calculated values show a slight deviation from the experimental yield strengths, which are approximately 845 MPa, 999 MPa, and 1139 MPa, respectively. In summary, different annealing treatments prior to identical aging were performed on an L1 2-strengthened Fe-rich MEA fabricated by L-PBF. These treatments resulted in distinct final microstructures characterized by either DP or CP dominance, accompanied by varied mechanical properties. The results indicate that the Fe-MEA fabricated via L-PBF may be a promising candidate for advanced structural applications, owing to its acceptable comprehensive mechanical properties and relatively low production cost. The present study clearly reveals that different post-printing heat treatments result in varied precipitation behavior dominated by either CP or DP. In L1 2-strengthened H/MEAs, the relationship between CP and DP is competitive and the reasons are listed below. According to the equilibrium phase diagram, the aging temperature is located within the fcc+L1 2dual-phase region. Therefore, during aging treatment, there is a thermodynamic driving force for L1 2precipitation from the supersaturated matrix of the as-built sample with a single fcc phase. Moreover, from a dynamic perspective, there are two pathways for L1 2precipitation, CP and DP. The consumption of L1 2-forming elements like Ni, Al, and Ti within matrix by CP ahead of the DP region greatly decreases the driving force for the DP growth, thereby suppressing the advancement of DP. Besides, the CP nanoparticles have a pinning effect to the moving grain boundaries driven by DP, thereby kinetically hindering the DP growth. Conversely, a slow formation of CP allows the matrix to maintain a high supersaturation of L1 2-forming elements, thereby increasing the chemical driving force for DP migration. Additionally, it results in a weaker pinning effect on grain boundary migration, dynamically favoring DP growth. This combination enhances the growth of DP into the supersaturated matrix ( Fang et al., 2022b). The competition between CP and DP in L1 2-strengthened H/MEAs is primarily influenced by factors such as aging temperature, grain size, and dislocation density ( Fang et al., 2022a, 2022b; Liu et al., 2022a). Since the aging temperature was consistent across all aged samples in the present study, its influence was not revealed in this work. Regarding grain size, finer grains are more likely to promote DP, owing to the increased density of grain boundaries that not only facilitates diffusion along these boundaries but also provides numerous sites for the nucleation of DP. In addition, the roles of high-density dislocation in the DP and CP are twofold. If the high-density dislocation is insufficient to trigger recrystallization, it promotes CP by enhancing bulk diffusion and providing an additional driving force for the nucleation of precipitates. Conversely, when the high-density dislocation induced recrystallization, the high mobility of recrystallized grain boundaries and the high-density grain boundaries of fine recrystallized grains promote DP ( Fan et al. , 2020; Fang et al., 2022a, 2022b). In the present study, the as-built samples are characterized by dominant coarse grains with a high density of dislocations. It is suggested that the dislocations, which are insufficient to trigger significant recrystallization of coarse grains, together with the dominant coarse grains, enhance CP and result in CP being dominant in the direct-aged sample. By contrast, annealing at 1000 °C for 1 h mainly leads to a reduction in dislocation density within the AN 1000 sample, thereby slowing CP within the coarse grains of the AN 1000-AG sample compared to the direct-aged sample. This, in turn, facilitates DP which preferentially initiate at the grain boundaries of fine grains, leading to DP dominance in the AN 1000-AG sample. The explanation for the microstructural evolution from the AN 1100 sample to the AN 1100-AG sample follows a similar rationale as that of the AN 1000 sample to the AN 1000-AG sample, due to their comparable initial microstructures. Annealing at 1200 °C not only significantly eliminates dislocations but also results in the formation of significantly coarse, nearly equiaxed grains with almost no fine grains. This makes DP less competitive, resulting in CP dominance in the AN 1200-AG sample. In addition to factors such as grain size and dislocation density, further examination of the microstructures in the AN 1000 sample has confirmed that elemental enrichment along cell walls has become negligible, accompanied by a reduction in dislocation density. These findings are illustrated in Supplementary Fig. S8. The enrichment of L1 2-forming elements such as Ni and Ti can enhance the chemical driving force. Consequently, in the direct-aged sample characterized by CP dominance, the elemental enrichment along cell walls should facilitate CP by increasing the local chemical driving force. Following annealing at temperatures of 1000 °C or higher, the elemental enrichment along cell walls becomes negligible, thereby slowing down CP within coarse grains. This deceleration subsequently could promote the formation of DP in the AN 1000-AG sample. Furthermore, it is proposed that the effect of limited L1 2precipitation in AN 1000 sample on subsequent aging could be negligible. Firstly, the L1 2precipitation in the AN 1000 sample appears to be very minimal, as suggested by a decrease in hardness compared to the as-built sample. Secondly, the AN 1100 sample without L1 2peaks, undergoes similar microstructural evolution to the AN 1000 sample during aging treatment. In the direct-aged sample, the formation mechanisms of fine grains may be debatable, although some researchers suggest that they form via recrystallization ( Huang et al. , 2024; Wang and Chan, 2023). This explanation could be reasonable since the as-built sample contains a high density of dislocations, which may trigger recrystallization during aging treatment. The high mobility of recrystallized grain boundaries favors the subsequent formation of DP. However, it is also possible that the formation of these fine grains is attributed to DP occurring within the initial fine microstructures. Given that the DP initiates via a supersaturated solid solution (α 0) transformed into a usually lamellar structure of a new phase (β) with solute enrichment, and a new phase (α) with solute depletion and the same crystal structure as α 0. With the reaction front advancing into the supersaturated matrix, the developed α lamellae maintains the same orientation as that of the initial α lamellae. Therefore, rather than resulting in a single grain after the DP reaction, there could be multiple grains corresponding to different growing colonies of the DP ( Han et al. , 2021; Kim et al. , 2024; Tałach-Dumańska et al. , 2003). It is also reported that DP can be effectively utilized to achieve grain refinement without any plastic deformation ( Tałach-Dumańska et al. , 2003). As a result, it is proposed that the roles of DP on the grain refinement should also be considered. For the AN 1000-AG and AN 1100-AG samples, it is intriguing that new fine grains formed after the annealing-aging treatment rather than after annealing alone. This phenomenon is unexpected since the dislocation density in the as-built samples is higher than those of annealed samples (Supplementary Fig. S3), which should result in more remarkable recrystallization and corresponding formation of fine grains in the direct-aged samples. Therefore, given that the driving force for recrystallization is diminished during high-temperature annealing, it is hypothesized that grain refinement may be linked to DP ( Han et al. , 2021; Tałach-Dumańska et al. , 2003). The initial fine-grain region plays a crucial role in enhancing DP which grows into coarse grains and correspondingly divides coarse grains into multiple finer grains. The abnormal grain refinement in the AN 1200-AG sample is still likely related to the DP ( Kim et al. , 2024). The SEM image and corresponding EBSD measurement of the YOZ plane for the AN 1200-AG sample further support that the grain refinement occurs through DP, as demonstrated in Supplementary Fig. S9. The AN 1200-AG sample exhibits DP regions with brighter contrast when compared to the CP regions. It is evident that the DP region is primarily located along the boundaries of the coarse grains. The corresponding EBSD IPF image clearly indicates that the fine grains are predominantly found within the DP region, while the CP region retains the coarse grain structure. Furthermore, the EBSD phase map exclusively displays the fcc structure due to the crystallographic similarity between the fcc and L1 2phases. This confirms that grain refinement is not caused by the formation of new phases that do not possess an fcc structure ( Chu et al. , 2024; Gwalani et al. , 2018). Moreover, the kernel average misorientation (KAM) map suggests an exceptionally low dislocation density in this area, indicating that the formation of new grains is not related to recrystallization. The elastic field produced by these piled-up GNDs generates a force in the opposite direction to the applied stress on the soft domains. Consequently, a higher applied stress is required to deform the soft domains, resulting in the hardening effect known as HDI hardening ( Jung et al. , 2024; Kim et al. , 2024; Yang and Kim, 2024; Yang et al. , 2016; Zhu and Wu, 2019). To determine the contribution of HDI stress, LUR tests were conducted, as shown in Fig. 17(a). Fine grains with DP are usually regarded as a hard phase, hence their contribution to strength is encompassed in HDI stress ( Kim et al. , 2024). The higher HDI stress in the AN 1000-AG sample can be attributed to its significantly higher fraction of fine grains with DP. However, the direct-aged sample with coarse grains and CP dominance still shows a slightly higher HDI stress compared to the AN 1000-AG sample. Considering the relatively low fraction of fine grains with DP, the high HDI stress observed in the direct-aged sample can also be attributed to its heterogeneous distribution of dislocations ( Wang et al., 2024a), which consists of hard cells with high local dislocation density and soft regions within cell interior. A simplified strengthening model was employed to calculate the various contributions to the differing YS of the studied samples. The YS can be divided into effective stress ( σ eff), arising from short-range interaction, and HDI stress ( σ HDI) which originates from long-range interaction. This calculation confirms that fine grains with DP are considered a hard phase, and thus their contribution to strength is included in the HDI stress. Regarding dislocation strengthening, the influence of dislocations can be neglected in the annealing-aged samples. For the direct-aged sample, a dislocation strengthening value of 128 MPa was adopted, based on a reference to L-PBF L1 2-strengthened austenitic stainless steel aged at 700 °C for 2 h ( Hu et al. , 2025). The HDI stress values obtained from Fig. 17(b) are approximately 430 MPa for the AN 1200-AG sample, 552 MPa for the AN 1000-AG sample, and 630 MPa for the direct-aged sample. These results indicate that HDI strengthening is a significant contributor to the strength of the studied samples. In summary, the estimated YS, calculated by summing the individual contributions, are approximately 788 MPa, 906 MPa, and 1112 MPa for the AN1200-AG, AN1000-AG, and direct-aged samples, respectively. These calculated values show a slight deviation from the experimental yield strengths, which are approximately 845 MPa, 999 MPa, and 1139 MPa, respectively. In summary, different annealing treatments prior to identical aging were performed on an L1 2-strengthened Fe-rich MEA fabricated by L-PBF. These treatments resulted in distinct final microstructures characterized by either DP or CP dominance, accompanied by varied mechanical properties. The detailed conclusions are as follows: 1The high-density dislocations and coarse grains induced by L-PBF promote CP. In contrast, the fine grains formed via L-PBF and the reduced dislocation density through annealing enhance DP, which in turn leads to grain refinement. 2The L-PBF Fe-MEA demonstrates acceptable printability, cost efficiency, and mechanical properties. Specifically, the direct-aged sample exhibits a YS of approximately 1. 1 GPa and a UE of around 11 %. The AN 1000-AG sample achieves a YS of about 1. 0 GPa and a UE of approximately 15 %. The AN 1200-AG sample exhibits a YS of approximately 0. 8 GPa and a UE of around 21 %. 3The SFE of the fcc matrix in both the CP and DP regions of the direct-aged sample is sufficiently low to facilitate the formation of deformation-induced twinning and SFs, indicating that both the CP and DP regions exhibit good deformation capacity. 4HDI strengthening is a significant contributor to the strength of the studied samples. In contrast, the HDI strengthening in the direct-aged sample is attributed not only to the heterogeneous distribution of grains and precipitates but also to the heterogeneous dislocation structure. After homogenization at 1100 °C for 24 h, the ingot was directly cold rolled to a thickness of ∼ 2 mm.

Partial recrystallization during annealing at 600 °C for 15 min results in a good combination of a yield strength of 875 MPa and ductility improved to 30 %. This study examines changes in the microstructure and mechanical properties during annealing of a heavily rolled Co 40(CrFeNi) 60FCC alloy with an emphasis on three key aspects: (i) characterization of the deformed microstructure; (ii) quantitative analysis of recrystallization; and (iii) evaluation of effects of partial recrystallization on strength and ductility. Disk-shaped ingots of the Co 40(CrFeNi) 60alloy with a thickness of 10 mm and a diameter of ∼ 40 mm were produced in a vacuum arc melter. Each ingot was flipped and re-melted five times to improve the chemical homogeneity. The as-cast ingots were trimmed to obtain samples with parallel sides along an intended rolling direction (RD), after which the samples were cold-rolled 80 %. Several tensile specimens and specimens for microstructural examinations were annealed at 600 °C for 15 min, 1 h and 10 h to produce material at different stages of recrystallization. Due to a high stored energy in shear bands and layers of mixed orientations, these regions become preferential nucleation sites for recrystallized grains during annealing ( Fig. 2a,b). To enable direct comparison of properties in this sample and in a partially recrystallized material with a lower Co content, a sample of the CoCrFeNi alloy cold-rolled to 80 % was annealed at 600 °C for 15 min, followed by microstructural characterization and tensile testing. The microstructure and mechanical properties have been investigated in a Co 40(CrFeNi) 60alloy annealed after 80 % cold rolling. Good combinations of strength (YS=875 MPa, UTS=1057 MPa) and ductility ( ε f= 30 %) are achieved in a partially recrystallized sample obtained by annealing at 600 °C for 15 min.

The high-entropy alloy (HEA) FeCoCrNiMn has been extensively studied due to its excellent mechanical properties and stability [ 19, 20]. However, due to the single face-centered cubic (FCC) phase and high phase stability of FeCoCrNiMn, the preparation of heterostructured FeCoCrNiMn alloys is limited to grain boundary engineering, cell/columnar substructure, etc. [ 21, 22], while it is difficult to fabricate poly-phases heterogeneous alloy. To explore the phase transition of FeCoCrNiMn, Park et al. [ 23] changed the Fe content in FeCoCrNiMn, and found that the increase of Fe content reduces the stability of the alloy system and produce body-centered cubic (BCC) phase, while the deformation mechanism will change from twinning induced plasticity (TWIP) to transition induces plasticity (TRIP). In addition, studies on changing the content of Co, Cr, Mn have also been reported [ 24-26]. However, the strength promotion often comes at the expense of ductility. In order to systematically explore the influence of element content on the microscopic morphology and mechanical properties of FeCoCrNiMn, alloys with different Fe content were prepared by mixing different proportions of Fe powder and FeCoCrNiMn powder for in-situLPBF in previous studies [ 27, 28]. On the one hand, LPBF has a broad combination of process methods which is sufficient to debug the best processing parameters; On the other hand, the Fe content can be freely customized by changing the powder ratio without additional custom pre-alloyed powder. Spherical powders of pure Fe and pre-alloyed FeCoCrNiMn HEA with particle diameters ranging between 15 and 53 μm (average diameters of 31 and 37 μm, respectively) were prepared by gas atomization, as shown in Fig. 1a-d. To ensure homogeneous powder distribution while preserving powder flowability, the two powders were mixed in 1:3 and 3:1 ratio respectively by using a planetary ball mill without adding ceramic balls (NanDa Instrument QM-3SP4) at 300 rpm/min for 6 h. The yield strength (YS), ultimate tensile strength (UTS) and elongation were determined for all tested samples. The loading-unloading-reloading tensile tests were performed on all samples to investigate the evolution of hetero-deformation induced (HDI) stresses during tensile straining. Moreover, the phase diagram was carried out by the CALPHAD calculation though graphical mode by the Thermo-Calc 2023a software coupled with TCHEA4 database, on basis of the global minimization of the Gibbs energy of the system. The XRD patterns of alloys with different proportions of Fe elements addition are exhibited in Fig. 2a. The FeCoCrNiMn and Fe40 samples show diffraction peaks with FCC crystal structure. FeCoCrNiMn has a yield strength (YS) of 490 MPa, an ultimate tensile strength (UTS) of 554 MPa and an elongation of 20 %.

On the one hand, LPBF has a broad combination of process methods which is sufficient to debug the best processing parameters; On the other hand, the Fe content can be freely customized by changing the powder ratio without additional custom pre-alloyed powder. In other words, it is only necessary to adjust the powder ratio to manufacture materials with diametrically opposite mechanical properties through LPBF. Spherical powders of pure Fe and pre-alloyed FeCoCrNiMn HEA with particle diameters ranging between 15 and 53 μm (average diameters of 31 and 37 μm, respectively) were prepared by gas atomization, as shown in Fig. 1a-d. To ensure homogeneous powder distribution while preserving powder flowability, the two powders were mixed in 1:3 and 3:1 ratio respectively by using a planetary ball mill without adding ceramic balls (NanDa Instrument QM-3SP4) at 300 rpm/min for 6 h. The resulting homogeneous mixed powders have Fe contents of 40 % and 80 % (hereafter named Fe40 and Fe80, respectively), as shown in Fig. 1e and f. The loading-unloading-reloading tensile tests were performed on all samples to investigate the evolution of hetero-deformation induced (HDI) stresses during tensile straining. Moreover, the phase diagram was carried out by the CALPHAD calculation though graphical mode by the Thermo-Calc 2023a software coupled with TCHEA4 database, on basis of the global minimization of the Gibbs energy of the system. The XRD patterns of alloys with different proportions of Fe elements addition are exhibited in Fig. 2a. The FeCoCrNiMn and Fe40 samples show diffraction peaks with FCC crystal structure. The pseudo-3D OM images of Fe40, Fe80 and LHA samples are shown in Fig. 3a-d and g, respectively. The top surface of Fe40 exhibits a distinct checkboard shape with columnar crystals on the side, which grow epitaxially through the molten tracks, as shown in Fig. 3a. Especially, as shown in Fig. 3b, melt pools and grains are filled with columnar/cellular substructures. Those substructures grow along the maximum thermal gradient and typically undergoes a 90° deflection at the melt tracks or grain boundaries [ 34]. Due to the influence of the viewing angle, the substructures are cellular-like on the front and columnar-like on the side ( Fig. 3c). Fig. 4a and b depicts the inverse pole figure (IPF) and phase distribution of the Fe40 sample, which indicates that coarse columnar grains with <001> orientation parallel to the BD, with FCC structural composition and almost no BCC phase. Due to the preferential growth orientation of FCC structural materials is the <001> orientation, the <001> orientation grows epitaxally along the direction of the maximum thermal gradient (usually BD) during solidification and competes for the growth space of other grain orientations [ 37]. Tensile testing was performed on Fe40, Fe80 and LHA specimens to understand the mechanical response of the material. Fig. 6a and b presents the engineering tensile stress-strain curves and the work hardening rate (WHR) curves for all those specimens, respectively. FeCoCrNiMn has a yield strength (YS) of 490 MPa, an ultimate tensile strength (UTS) of 554 MPa and an elongation of 20 %. The pure Fe obtained by LPBF has YS and UTS of 381Mpa and 457Mpa, respectively, accompanied by 20.1 % elongation. Compared with the base material (FeCoCrNiMn and pure Fe, Fig. 6a), Fe40 sacrifices a small amount of strength (YS of 410 MPa an UTS of 536 MPa) for a large increase in ductility (∼35 %). Fig. 7depicts the fracture morphology of Fe40, LHA and Fe80 samples after tensile deformation. The extensive dimple structure accompanied by slip lines in the Fe40 sample, as shown in Fig. 7a 1and a 2, was a classical fracture mode of ductility. Fe80 exhibited small and shallow dimple, while wide range of brittle cleavage planes are also present, indicating the primary fracture mode of brittleness, as shown in Fig. 7c 1and c 2. To better understand the manufacturing mechanism of FEL with ultrafine grains and BCC structure, single laser track experiments were performed, as shown in Fig. 8. According to Fig. 8a1, laser melts the 1st layer of Fe80 powder on the surface of the Fe40 matrix, leaving a hill-like melt pool, which has a height of about 30 μm. It is important to note that although nonuniform distributions of Fe elements are observed at the bottom of the melt pool ( Fig. 8a3, white arrows), only a single FCC phase was observed in and around the melt pool. A small amount of heterostructure ( Fig. 8b1, black arrows) was observed in the 2nd layer of the melt cross section, accompanied by the overall grain refinement of the fuse, as shown in Fig. 8b1. The phase distribution ( Fig. 8b2) and EDS map ( Fig. 8b3) indicate BCC phase and higher Fe content in those heterostructured region. In addition, those heterostructures have a vortex shape and are close to the melt pool boundary ( Fig. 8b2). Usually, due to the flow effect of Marangoni effect under the LPBF processing, particles, such as pure Fe powders, are dragged into the melt pool to enhance elemental diffusion [ 57]. However, although powder physical mixing tends to homogenize the melt, full homogenization requires sufficient mutual diffusion between the two powder elements [ 58], which is difficult to achieve in LPBF processes characterized by rapid solidification [ 59]. The melting point of Fe powder is 1808. 15 K [ 60], and the corresponding melting point of FeCoCrNiMn is 1607 K [ 61]. In other words, under the same VED, it is more difficult for Fe to completely melt than FeCoCrNiMn, which promotes the uneven distribution of elements. Notably, In-situalloying of equiatomic FeCoCrNiMn HEA using LPBF process was previously investigated by Karimi et al. [ 62], which also showed a non-uniform distribution of Fe elements with vortex shape. The 3rd and 4th layer of the melt cross sections present roughly similar features with the 2nd layer ( Fig. 8c1-3 and d1-3). With the number of layers stacking, the BCC phase content inside the melt pool significantly increased. After laser scanning of the 4th layer, only 23. 8 % BCC content was observed at the melt cross sections ( Fig. 8d2), which could not form the layered features shown in Fig. 4e. However, as shown in Fig. 8e2, the 5th layer showed a sharp increase in the content of the BCC phase (68.1 %), which was observed in several repeated experiments rather than by chance. According to Fig. 8e1, it can be observed that the ultra-fine BCC grains with random orientation are distributed in the melt cross section, while the EDS mapping ( Fig. 8e3) suggest a uniform Fe content distribution. EDS line scanning were adopted to determine the chemical composition of the melt cross sections with 1-5 layers, as shown in Fig. 9a-e. According to Fig. 9a, the Fe element in the melt cross section of the 1st layer remains about 40.5 % on average, containing 8.1 % fluctuation. With the number of layers stacking, the average Fe content increased from 50.4 % to 74.3 %, while the fluctuation decreased from 10.3 % to 6. 2 %. That is to say, under the addition of new powder and remelting of the laser, the Fe content of the melt cross section tends to increase and homogenize. The results of Ondicho et al. indicated that the increase in Fe content will reduce the stability of the FCC phase in the alloy system, especially when the Fe content is higher than 60 %, the BCC phase will be dominated [ 63]. In this research, the average Fe content of the 5th layer (74.3 %) is higher than 60 %, while the fluctuation (6.2 %) is smaller than other layers, which provides important conditions for the formation of stable BCC phase. Fig. 5f-h are the IPF, KAM and phase distribution of the magnified 5th layer cross section, respectively. Importantly, there is an unmelted powder around the melt cross section (yellow dotted region, Fig. 9f-h), which indicated to be Fe powder according to the EDS mapping in Fig. 8e3. It is worth noting that the unmelted powder has a BCC structure with a grain size which coarser than the other BCC phases within the melt pool. In addition, the KAM distribution within the unmelt powder is much lower than the other BCC phases in the melt cross section, as shown in Fig. 9g. In fact, the difference between the two kinds of BCC structures already suggests that the fine-grained BCC phase is formed during the LPBF process, while the coarse-grained BCC phase is the original structure. To explore the origin of grain refinement, we characterized the fine-grained BCC phase with EBSD at higher magnification, as shown in Fig. 9j and k. The band contrast (BC) image indicates that numbers of nano-sized grains are present in the fine-grained BCC phase, and the corresponding KAM image ( Fig. 9i) also demonstrated that high KAM regions are mainly observed between grain boundaries, which also contain sub-grain boundaries ( Fig. 9k). Fig. 10a illustrates the phase diagram calculated from the change of Fe content in the Fe-Co-Cr-Ni-Mn alloy system. Notably, FCC remains a high-temperature stable phase even if the Fe content is higher than 80 %. However, the effect on the stable phase is highlighted by the modification of Fe content with decreasing temperature. According to Fig. 10a, when the Fe content is lower than 44.5 %, even the segregation phase of MnNi (MnNi_L10, [ 64]) will appear. However, the high cooling rate of LPBF avoids the formation of such a phase, so this structure was not found in the Fe40 sample. Similarly, the Cr-rich σ phase is inhibited due to the high cooling rate that inhibits segregation formation [ 65]. In addition, the increase of Fe content will also inhibit the production of σ phase [ 66]. That is to say, under the fabrication conditions of LPBF, FCC and BCC are the predominant phases. The calculated result indicates that 60 % is the split point at which FCC and BCC occupy the main phase at lower temperatures. Therefore, two basic conclusions can be obtained: Ⅰ: At low Fe content, the stable phase is FCC phase at both high and low temperatures; Ⅱ: At high Fe content, the stable phase at high and low temperatures are dominated by FCC and BCC, respectively. By referring to the thermal cycle history of stainless steel during LPBF processing [ 67], schematic diagrams of the thermal history of FDL and FEL were drew, as shown in Fig. 10b and c, respectively. Since the stable phase has not changed, FDL did not involve the phase transition during heating-cooling-heating process, hence it formed the microscopic morphology of classical columnar epitaxial growth and has larger grain size, as shown in Fig. 10d. However, FEL contained multiple phase transitions during thermal cycling, according to Fig. 10a and c, while it is also worth noting that the size and structure of the grains also changed significantly after fabrication ( Fig. 9f-k). This fine structure also appears in the LPBF study of pure iron by Lejček et al. [ 38], which was attributed to the α-γ-α phase transition. Similarly, a phase transition from FCC to BCC will be experienced during solidification when the Fe content is sufficiently high [ 68], as shown in Fig. 10e. The phase transition can be achieved by local shuffling [ 69] or dislocation slip [ 38] during rapid heating or cooling, which is characterized by non-diffusion [ 70, 71]. Since the lattice difference between FCC and BCC is close to 26 % [ 39], the process of phase transition contains volume changes, resulting in an increase of internal stress. Thus, the stress inside the final sample is partially released by the mechanism of dislocation slip. Eventually resulting in a morphology with ultra-fine grains and high KAM. Interestingly, previous studies have shown that alloys with 40 % Fe content (Fe: FeCoCrNiMn = 1:3) showing FCC structure and excellent ductility, while alloys with 80 % Fe content (Fe: FeCoCrNiMn = 3:1) showing BCC structure and higher strength. In other words, it is only necessary to adjust the powder ratio to manufacture materials with diametrically opposite mechanical properties through LPBF. Spherical powders of pure Fe and pre-alloyed FeCoCrNiMn HEA with particle diameters ranging between 15 and 53 μm (average diameters of 31 and 37 μm, respectively) were prepared by gas atomization, as shown in Fig. 1a-d. To ensure homogeneous powder distribution while preserving powder flowability, the two powders were mixed in 1:3 and 3:1 ratio respectively by using a planetary ball mill without adding ceramic balls (NanDa Instrument QM-3SP4) at 300 rpm/min for 6 h. The resulting homogeneous mixed powders have Fe contents of 40 % and 80 % (hereafter named Fe40 and Fe80, respectively), as shown in Fig. 1e and f. The yield strength (YS), ultimate tensile strength (UTS) and elongation were determined for all tested samples. The loading-unloading-reloading tensile tests were performed on all samples to investigate the evolution of hetero-deformation induced (HDI) stresses during tensile straining. Moreover, the phase diagram was carried out by the CALPHAD calculation though graphical mode by the Thermo-Calc 2023a software coupled with TCHEA4 database, on basis of the global minimization of the Gibbs energy of the system. The top surface of Fe40 exhibits a distinct checkboard shape with columnar crystals on the side, which grow epitaxially through the molten tracks, as shown in Fig. 3a. Especially, as shown in Fig. 3b, melt pools and grains are filled with columnar/cellular substructures. That is to say, under the addition of new powder and remelting of the laser, the Fe content of the melt cross section tends to increase and homogenize. Recently, heterostructured materials offers a novel strategy for solving the longstanding dilemma of strength-ductility trade-off of metallic materials, that is, soft and hard domains with significant rheological stress difference are used as the basic units to orderly construct the heterostructure [ 1, 2]. Then, the strength-ductility synergy is obtained by additional strain hardening induced by the heterogeneous deformation [ 3]. Apparently, the heterostructure, such as gradient structure [ 4], bimodal structure [ 5] or layered structure [ 6], etc., should be controlled by appropriate methods for the desired size and architecture to obtain the satisfactory properties. To date, there are "top-down" [ 7] and "bottom-up" [ 8] routes for the fabrication of heterostructured materials. The former is mainly through mechanical deformation, for instance, surface mechanical grinding [ 9], ultrasonic surface rolling [ 10] or asynchronous rolling [ 7], etc., so as to achieve heterostructure. While the latter mainly involves the formation of multi-scale distribution of grains or phase components achieved through composition or architectural design [ 8]. Layered heterostructure possesses more architectural parameters, e.g., layer space, thickness, hardness and proportion of layers, etc., tailoring strength or plasticity across a wide range [ 11]. With the advancement of additive manufacturing (AM), the "layer-by-layer" approach inherently provides an advantage in the direct fabrication of layer heterostructured materials [ 12]. In these cases, the heterostructure should be mainly understood as the AM of multi-materials, such as CuSn10/SS316L [ 12], Al 2O 3/Ti [ 13], SS321/Ti6Al4V [ 14], Ti64/Ti64 + MEA [ 15] etc. However, due to variations in thermophysical properties, these heterogeneous materials exhibited some shortcomings, including low compatibility, interface defects, chemical reactions, etc. Recently, some researchers fabricated materials with layered distribution of grain sizes [ 16, 17] and phases [ 18] by AM combined with rolling methods, avoiding the problem of incompatibility between the heterogeneous materials, but this undoubtedly decreases the engineering applications of AM. Therefore, how to accurately control the phase ratio or grain size to achieve high quality layered heterostructure still remain as a problem. Given the above, if heterostructure composed of FCC and BCC phases with layered architecture is produced in the FeCoCrNiMn, taking advantage of the “layer-by-layer” manner of LPBF process, synergistic combination of strength and ductility might be expected. In this study, we demonstrated an interesting scheme for alloy preparation of dual powder-source alloy system based on the LPBF process. The as-built samples exhibit excellent strength-ductility balance, which attributes to the well-architectured layered heterostructure. Such dual-phase microstructure are rarely deployed in CoCrFeMnNi-based alloys, and the corresponding strain hardening mechanism for alloys with such layered structures has not been explored. Based on the preparation method and mechanical properties, two issues need to be clarified: How does the microstructure of the layered heterostructure with dual phase formed? Secondly, the deformation mechanisms of heterostructure alloys during tensile deformation process. Hard BCC layer also changed from the elastic stage to the elastoplastic stage, while the back stress induced by GNDs failed to completely offset the normal stress, and finally causing HDI strengthening [ 87]. In stage II, further deformation at the interface results in severe local shear strain, and DTs begin to produce and proliferate at these sites. Simultaneously, dislocations also start to produce within the hard BCC domain to coordinate the plastic deformation. These SFs and DTs hinder further dislocation motion, and the synergistic effect of HDI stress, resulting in additional hardening mechanism, which slows down the decrease of WHR. In stage III, as a result of the overall extensive deformation, dislocations, SFs, and DTs disperse throughout the entire FCC layer. The severe shear strain at the interface leads to the formation of nano-sized HCP phase and stronger HDI stress, which can effectively suppress the formation of necking and micro-cracks. In conclusion, the presence of SFs, DTs, NTs and nano-HCP phase adapts to the strain gradient at the interface and ultimately coordinates the overall deformation. Recently, heterostructured materials offers a novel strategy for solving the longstanding dilemma of strength-ductility trade-off of metallic materials, that is, soft and hard domains with significant rheological stress difference are used as the basic units to orderly construct the heterostructure [ 1, 2]. Then, the strength-ductility synergy is obtained by additional strain hardening induced by the heterogeneous deformation [ 3]. Apparently, the heterostructure, such as gradient structure [ 4], bimodal structure [ 5] or layered structure [ 6], etc., should be controlled by appropriate methods for the desired size and architecture to obtain the satisfactory properties. To date, there are "top-down" [ 7] and "bottom-up" [ 8] routes for the fabrication of heterostructured materials. The former is mainly through mechanical deformation, for instance, surface mechanical grinding [ 9], ultrasonic surface rolling [ 10] or asynchronous rolling [ 7], etc., so as to achieve heterostructure. While the latter mainly involves the formation of multi-scale distribution of grains or phase components achieved through composition or architectural design [ 8]. Layered heterostructure possesses more architectural parameters, e.g., layer space, thickness, hardness and proportion of layers, etc., tailoring strength or plasticity across a wide range [ 11]. With the advancement of additive manufacturing (AM), the "layer-by-layer" approach inherently provides an advantage in the direct fabrication of layer heterostructured materials [ 12]. In these cases, the heterostructure should be mainly understood as the AM of multi-materials, such as CuSn10/SS316L [ 12], Al 2O 3/Ti [ 13], SS321/Ti6Al4V [ 14], Ti64/Ti64 + MEA [ 15] etc. However, due to variations in thermophysical properties, these heterogeneous materials exhibited some shortcomings, including low compatibility, interface defects, chemical reactions, etc. Recently, some researchers fabricated materials with layered distribution of grain sizes [ 16, 17] and phases [ 18] by AM combined with rolling methods, avoiding the problem of incompatibility between the heterogeneous materials, but this undoubtedly decreases the engineering applications of AM. Therefore, how to accurately control the phase ratio or grain size to achieve high quality layered heterostructure still remain as a problem. Given the above, if heterostructure composed of FCC and BCC phases with layered architecture is produced in the FeCoCrNiMn, taking advantage of the “layer-by-layer” manner of LPBF process, synergistic combination of strength and ductility might be expected. In this study, we demonstrated an interesting scheme for alloy preparation of dual powder-source alloy system based on the LPBF process. The as-built samples exhibit excellent strength-ductility balance, which attributes to the well-architectured layered heterostructure. Such dual-phase microstructure are rarely deployed in CoCrFeMnNi-based alloys, and the corresponding strain hardening mechanism for alloys with such layered structures has not been explored. Based on the preparation method and mechanical properties, two issues need to be clarified: How does the microstructure of the layered heterostructure with dual phase formed? Secondly, the deformation mechanisms of heterostructure alloys during tensile deformation process. In the following, the fabrication, microstructure, mechanical properties and deformation mechanism of the CoCrFeMnNi-based alloy system fabricated by LPBF were reported and analyzed through the combination of crystal plasticity finite element method (CPFEM) and experiment characterization. The DiMetal- 100H (Laser Additive Manufacturing GmbH, Guangzhou, China) was adopted for LPBF manufacturing, while the layered heterostructured alloys (LHA) were fabricated by melting three layers of Fe40 powder and five layers of Fe80 powder in a cycle along the build direction (BD), as described in Fig. 1g. All the layers were processed in orthogonal scan mode using the optimized parameters. i.e., laser power of 200 W, scanning speed of 800 mm/s, layer thickness of 30 μm and hatching space of 70 μm, respectively. The cuboid samples were processed into thin slices of dog bone-shaped tensile samples along the normal direction (ND) or transverse direction (TD) with a thickness of 1 mm by wire cutting ( Fig. 1h). In addition, the width of the corresponding gauge section is 2 mm and the length is 8 mm. The samples for microstructural analysis were sandpapered (200#-3000#) and polished using diamond suspension with particle size of 1 μm. The yield strength (YS), ultimate tensile strength (UTS) and elongation were determined for all tested samples. The loading-unloading-reloading tensile tests were performed on all samples to investigate the evolution of hetero-deformation induced (HDI) stresses during tensile straining. Moreover, the phase diagram was carried out by the CALPHAD calculation though graphical mode by the Thermo-Calc 2023a software coupled with TCHEA4 database, on basis of the global minimization of the Gibbs energy of the system. Finite Element Method (FEM) with crystal plasticity as constitutive model were performed to access the information of stress/strain evolution and slip activity for different layer in LHA. The basic principle of crystal plasticity is induced in Refs. [ 29, 30]. The shear strain rate formula based on the energy criterion which proposed by Hutchinson [ 31] was adopted. Since the different layers in LHA have significant differences in grain size, phase and orientation, a simple layered heterogeneous model was constructed by Neper [ 32] and given the corresponding random orientation. Finally, the simulation was carried out in ABAQUS/STANDARD®. The schematic diagram of enhanced strength-ductility trade-off of LHA are summarized in Fig. 17. According to the WHR, the deformation of LHA can be divided into three stages. In stage I, due to the large activation of dislocations and the reduced rate of dislocation storage, the WHR exhibits a rapid decrease. GNDs and SFs were generated inside the soft domain (FCC) around the interface to coordinate the local strain gradient. Hard BCC layer also changed from the elastic stage to the elastoplastic stage, while the back stress induced by GNDs failed to completely offset the normal stress, and finally causing HDI strengthening [ 87]. In stage II, further deformation at the interface results in severe local shear strain, and DTs begin to produce and proliferate at these sites. Simultaneously, dislocations also start to produce within the hard BCC domain to coordinate the plastic deformation. These SFs and DTs hinder further dislocation motion, and the synergistic effect of HDI stress, resulting in additional hardening mechanism, which slows down the decrease of WHR. In stage III, as a result of the overall extensive deformation, dislocations, SFs, and DTs disperse throughout the entire FCC layer. The severe shear strain at the interface leads to the formation of nano-sized HCP phase and stronger HDI stress, which can effectively suppress the formation of necking and micro-cracks. In conclusion, the presence of SFs, DTs, NTs and nano-HCP phase adapts to the strain gradient at the interface and ultimately coordinates the overall deformation. In addition, the dislocation occlusion and back stress were the main mechanisms of HDI strengthening, which were the main reasons for the elevation of WHR.
