Recently, heterostructured materials offers a novel strategy for solving the longstanding dilemma of strength-ductility trade-off of metallic materials, that is, soft and hard domains with significant rheological stress difference are used as the basic units to orderly construct the heterostructure [ 1, 2]. Then, the strength-ductility synergy is obtained by additional strain hardening induced by the heterogeneous deformation [ 3]. Apparently, the heterostructure, such as gradient structure [ 4], bimodal structure [ 5] or layered structure [ 6], etc., should be controlled by appropriate methods for the desired size and architecture to obtain the satisfactory properties. To date, there are "top-down" [ 7] and "bottom-up" [ 8] routes for the fabrication of heterostructured materials. The former is mainly through mechanical deformation, for instance, surface mechanical grinding [ 9], ultrasonic surface rolling [ 10] or asynchronous rolling [ 7], etc., so as to achieve heterostructure. While the latter mainly involves the formation of multi-scale distribution of grains or phase components achieved through composition or architectural design [ 8]. Layered heterostructure possesses more architectural parameters, e.g., layer space, thickness, hardness and proportion of layers, etc., tailoring strength or plasticity across a wide range [ 11]. With the advancement of additive manufacturing (AM), the "layer-by-layer" approach inherently provides an advantage in the direct fabrication of layer heterostructured materials [ 12]. In these cases, the heterostructure should be mainly understood as the AM of multi-materials, such as CuSn10/SS316L [ 12], Al 2O 3/Ti [ 13], SS321/Ti6Al4V [ 14], Ti64/Ti64 + MEA [ 15] etc. However, due to variations in thermophysical properties, these heterogeneous materials exhibited some shortcomings, including low compatibility, interface defects, chemical reactions, etc. Recently, some researchers fabricated materials with layered distribution of grain sizes [ 16, 17] and phases [ 18] by AM combined with rolling methods, avoiding the problem of incompatibility between the heterogeneous materials, but this undoubtedly decreases the engineering applications of AM. Therefore, how to accurately control the phase ratio or grain size to achieve high quality layered heterostructure still remain as a problem. Given the above, if heterostructure composed of FCC and BCC phases with layered architecture is produced in the FeCoCrNiMn, taking advantage of the “layer-by-layer” manner of LPBF process, synergistic combination of strength and ductility might be expected. In this study, we demonstrated an interesting scheme for alloy preparation of dual powder-source alloy system based on the LPBF process. The as-built samples exhibit excellent strength-ductility balance, which attributes to the well-architectured layered heterostructure. Such dual-phase microstructure are rarely deployed in CoCrFeMnNi-based alloys, and the corresponding strain hardening mechanism for alloys with such layered structures has not been explored. Based on the preparation method and mechanical properties, two issues need to be clarified: How does the microstructure of the layered heterostructure with dual phase formed? Secondly, the deformation mechanisms of heterostructure alloys during tensile deformation process. In the following, the fabrication, microstructure, mechanical properties and deformation mechanism of the CoCrFeMnNi-based alloy system fabricated by LPBF were reported and analyzed through the combination of crystal plasticity finite element method (CPFEM) and experiment characterization. The DiMetal- 100H (Laser Additive Manufacturing GmbH, Guangzhou, China) was adopted for LPBF manufacturing, while the layered heterostructured alloys (LHA) were fabricated by melting three layers of Fe40 powder and five layers of Fe80 powder in a cycle along the build direction (BD), as described in Fig. 1g. All the layers were processed in orthogonal scan mode using the optimized parameters. i.e., laser power of 200 W, scanning speed of 800 mm/s, layer thickness of 30 μm and hatching space of 70 μm, respectively. The cuboid samples were processed into thin slices of dog bone-shaped tensile samples along the normal direction (ND) or transverse direction (TD) with a thickness of 1 mm by wire cutting ( Fig. 1h). In addition, the width of the corresponding gauge section is 2 mm and the length is 8 mm. The samples for microstructural analysis were sandpapered (200#-3000#) and polished using diamond suspension with particle size of 1 μm. The yield strength (YS), ultimate tensile strength (UTS) and elongation were determined for all tested samples. The loading-unloading-reloading tensile tests were performed on all samples to investigate the evolution of hetero-deformation induced (HDI) stresses during tensile straining. Moreover, the phase diagram was carried out by the CALPHAD calculation though graphical mode by the Thermo-Calc 2023a software coupled with TCHEA4 database, on basis of the global minimization of the Gibbs energy of the system. Finite Element Method (FEM) with crystal plasticity as constitutive model were performed to access the information of stress/strain evolution and slip activity for different layer in LHA. The basic principle of crystal plasticity is induced in Refs. [ 29, 30]. The shear strain rate formula based on the energy criterion which proposed by Hutchinson [ 31] was adopted. Since the different layers in LHA have significant differences in grain size, phase and orientation, a simple layered heterogeneous model was constructed by Neper [ 32] and given the corresponding random orientation. Finally, the simulation was carried out in ABAQUS/STANDARD®. For better presentation, the details of the model including the main parameters will be expressed in the discussion section together with the results. Tensile testing was performed on Fe40, Fe80 and LHA specimens to understand the mechanical response of the material. Fig. 6a and b presents the engineering tensile stress-strain curves and the work hardening rate (WHR) curves for all those specimens, respectively. FeCoCrNiMn has a yield strength (YS) of 490 MPa, an ultimate tensile strength (UTS) of 554 MPa and an elongation of 20 %. The pure Fe obtained by LPBF has YS and UTS of 381Mpa and 457Mpa, respectively, accompanied by 20.1 % elongation. Compared with the base material (FeCoCrNiMn and pure Fe, Fig. 6a), Fe40 sacrifices a small amount of strength (YS of 410 MPa an UTS of 536 MPa) for a large increase in ductility (∼35 %). The Fe80 has the highest YS and UTS, 813 and 912 MPa, while it is poor in the elongation (9. 9 %). In contrast, the YS, UTS and elongation of the LHA are 581 MPa, 757 MPa and 22.8 %, respectively, which achieved satisfactory strength-ductility balance. Notably, the WHR curves of all specimens showed a monotonically decreasing trend. Among them, the Fe40 undergoes a stable but low WHR after a rapid decline, and Fe80 displays a sharp drop in WHR. In contrast, the LHA maintains the highest hardening rate during the stable plastic deformation stage ( Fig. 6b). The rapid decline of the WHR curves generally occurs at the beginning stage of the deformation (the first stage), and the deformation is dominated by dislocation slip at the moment [ 41]. Subsequently, when the dislocations become saturated, the storage rate of dislocations decreases, while the emergence of strengthening mechanisms (such as twins, phase transition, etc.) causes WHR to enter a slow downward phase (the second stage) [ 42]. Here, Fe80 has almost no second stage of WHR, in contrast to Fe40, which has a significantly lower WHR than LHA. In other words, LHA has a more efficient strengthening mechanism during the stable plastic deformation stage, which providing extra strengthening and ensuring plastic flow. Compared to FeCoCrNiMn that were processed by other methods (LPBF [ 21, 43-45], As-cast [ 46-49] and Particle reinforcement engineering [ 50-53]), LHA also exhibits much better synergy in strength and ductility, which is summarized in Fig. 6c. In general, due to different crystal structures and chemical compositions, FDL and FEL of LHA exhibit different mechanisms during deformation, respectively. FEL is dominated by dislocation slip, while FDL contains a large amount of DTs in addition to dislocation. Two factors are responsible for the premature DT behavior in the LHA, i.e. (i) Increasing Fe content in FeCoCrNiMn system results in significant decrease of stacking fault energy (SFE) [ 89]. (ii) Strain gradient induced by the heterostructured incompatibility during tensile deformation results in significant shear stress concentration at the layer interfaces [ 42]. The back stress exerted on the soft domain elevates the nominal stress beyond the loading stress. Ultimately, the local shear stress surpasses the threshold of the critical stress for twinning nucleation, resulting in the formation of DTs [ 90]. The appearance of high-density DTs introduce new interfaces to reduce the dislocation mean free path [ 91], and high-density GNDs aggregate at the BCC/FCC interface, resulting in superior hardening capacity ( Fig. 6b). In general, the HCP phase is considered to be the transition phase from the TRIP process of FCC-BCC, which also known as the ε-martensite phase transition [ 23, 97]. However, the elongated HCP phase clearly does not fit the characteristics of the ε-martensitic phase transition. Owing to the intense shear strain at the layer interface, continuous slip of SFs within the FCC matrix could potentially result in the formation of a nano-sized HCP phase [ 98]. In other words, two plane-thickness (n = 2) stacking layers of dislocation act as HCP embryos [ 99], which typically occur in materials with low SFE [ 23]. Like SFs and DTs, the formation of those HCP phase is beneficial to alleviate the local stress concentration, thereby providing better ductility [ 100]. The schematic diagram of enhanced strength-ductility trade-off of LHA are summarized in Fig. 17. According to the WHR, the deformation of LHA can be divided into three stages. In stage I, due to the large activation of dislocations and the reduced rate of dislocation storage, the WHR exhibits a rapid decrease. GNDs and SFs were generated inside the soft domain (FCC) around the interface to coordinate the local strain gradient. Hard BCC layer also changed from the elastic stage to the elastoplastic stage, while the back stress induced by GNDs failed to completely offset the normal stress, and finally causing HDI strengthening [ 87]. In stage II, further deformation at the interface results in severe local shear strain, and DTs begin to produce and proliferate at these sites. Simultaneously, dislocations also start to produce within the hard BCC domain to coordinate the plastic deformation. These SFs and DTs hinder further dislocation motion, and the synergistic effect of HDI stress, resulting in additional hardening mechanism, which slows down the decrease of WHR. In stage III, as a result of the overall extensive deformation, dislocations, SFs, and DTs disperse throughout the entire FCC layer. The severe shear strain at the interface leads to the formation of nano-sized HCP phase and stronger HDI stress, which can effectively suppress the formation of necking and micro-cracks. In conclusion, the presence of SFs, DTs, NTs and nano-HCP phase adapts to the strain gradient at the interface and ultimately coordinates the overall deformation. In addition, the dislocation occlusion and back stress were the main mechanisms of HDI strengthening, which were the main reasons for the elevation of WHR. Recently, heterostructured materials offers a novel strategy for solving the longstanding dilemma of strength-ductility trade-off of metallic materials, that is, soft and hard domains with significant rheological stress difference are used as the basic units to orderly construct the heterostructure [ 1, 2]. Then, the strength-ductility synergy is obtained by additional strain hardening induced by the heterogeneous deformation [ 3]. Apparently, the heterostructure, such as gradient structure [ 4], bimodal structure [ 5] or layered structure [ 6], etc., should be controlled by appropriate methods for the desired size and architecture to obtain the satisfactory properties. To date, there are "top-down" [ 7] and "bottom-up" [ 8] routes for the fabrication of heterostructured materials. The former is mainly through mechanical deformation, for instance, surface mechanical grinding [ 9], ultrasonic surface rolling [ 10] or asynchronous rolling [ 7], etc., so as to achieve heterostructure. While the latter mainly involves the formation of multi-scale distribution of grains or phase components achieved through composition or architectural design [ 8]. Layered heterostructure possesses more architectural parameters, e.g., layer space, thickness, hardness and proportion of layers, etc., tailoring strength or plasticity across a wide range [ 11]. With the advancement of additive manufacturing (AM), the "layer-by-layer" approach inherently provides an advantage in the direct fabrication of layer heterostructured materials [ 12]. In these cases, the heterostructure should be mainly understood as the AM of multi-materials, such as CuSn10/SS316L [ 12], Al 2O 3/Ti [ 13], SS321/Ti6Al4V [ 14], Ti64/Ti64 + MEA [ 15] etc. However, due to variations in thermophysical properties, these heterogeneous materials exhibited some shortcomings, including low compatibility, interface defects, chemical reactions, etc. Recently, some researchers fabricated materials with layered distribution of grain sizes [ 16, 17] and phases [ 18] by AM combined with rolling methods, avoiding the problem of incompatibility between the heterogeneous materials, but this undoubtedly decreases the engineering applications of AM. Therefore, how to accurately control the phase ratio or grain size to achieve high quality layered heterostructure still remain as a problem. Given the above, if heterostructure composed of FCC and BCC phases with layered architecture is produced in the FeCoCrNiMn, taking advantage of the “layer-by-layer” manner of LPBF process, synergistic combination of strength and ductility might be expected. In this study, we demonstrated an interesting scheme for alloy preparation of dual powder-source alloy system based on the LPBF process. The as-built samples exhibit excellent strength-ductility balance, which attributes to the well-architectured layered heterostructure. Such dual-phase microstructure are rarely deployed in CoCrFeMnNi-based alloys, and the corresponding strain hardening mechanism for alloys with such layered structures has not been explored. Based on the preparation method and mechanical properties, two issues need to be clarified: How does the microstructure of the layered heterostructure with dual phase formed? Secondly, the deformation mechanisms of heterostructure alloys during tensile deformation process. In the following, the fabrication, microstructure, mechanical properties and deformation mechanism of the CoCrFeMnNi-based alloy system fabricated by LPBF were reported and analyzed through the combination of crystal plasticity finite element method (CPFEM) and experiment characterization. The DiMetal- 100H (Laser Additive Manufacturing GmbH, Guangzhou, China) was adopted for LPBF manufacturing, while the layered heterostructured alloys (LHA) were fabricated by melting three layers of Fe40 powder and five layers of Fe80 powder in a cycle along the build direction (BD), as described in Fig. 1g. All the layers were processed in orthogonal scan mode using the optimized parameters. i.e., laser power of 200 W, scanning speed of 800 mm/s, layer thickness of 30 μm and hatching space of 70 μm, respectively. The cuboid samples were processed into thin slices of dog bone-shaped tensile samples along the normal direction (ND) or transverse direction (TD) with a thickness of 1 mm by wire cutting ( Fig. 1h). In addition, the width of the corresponding gauge section is 2 mm and the length is 8 mm. The samples for microstructural analysis were sandpapered (200#-3000#) and polished using diamond suspension with particle size of 1 μm. The yield strength (YS), ultimate tensile strength (UTS) and elongation were determined for all tested samples. The loading-unloading-reloading tensile tests were performed on all samples to investigate the evolution of hetero-deformation induced (HDI) stresses during tensile straining. Moreover, the phase diagram was carried out by the CALPHAD calculation though graphical mode by the Thermo-Calc 2023a software coupled with TCHEA4 database, on basis of the global minimization of the Gibbs energy of the system. Finite Element Method (FEM) with crystal plasticity as constitutive model were performed to access the information of stress/strain evolution and slip activity for different layer in LHA. The basic principle of crystal plasticity is induced in Refs. [ 29, 30]. The shear strain rate formula based on the energy criterion which proposed by Hutchinson [ 31] was adopted. Since the different layers in LHA have significant differences in grain size, phase and orientation, a simple layered heterogeneous model was constructed by Neper [ 32] and given the corresponding random orientation. Finally, the simulation was carried out in ABAQUS/STANDARD®. For better presentation, the details of the model including the main parameters will be expressed in the discussion section together with the results. Due to the mismatch between strength and plastic deformation ability, the layer interface is the main stress concentration area during deformation [ 85], where the soft layer (FDL) generates back stress and the hard layer (FEL) generates normal stress [ 86]. Back and normal stresses do not cancel each other out overall, and together they produce HDI reinforcement to improve YS [ 87], while the higher KAM values at the interface in LHA indicate the presence of strengthening. In general, due to different crystal structures and chemical compositions, FDL and FEL of LHA exhibit different mechanisms during deformation, respectively. FEL is dominated by dislocation slip, while FDL contains a large amount of DTs in addition to dislocation. Two factors are responsible for the premature DT behavior in the LHA, i.e. (i) Increasing Fe content in FeCoCrNiMn system results in significant decrease of stacking fault energy (SFE) [ 89]. (ii) Strain gradient induced by the heterostructured incompatibility during tensile deformation results in significant shear stress concentration at the layer interfaces [ 42]. The back stress exerted on the soft domain elevates the nominal stress beyond the loading stress. Ultimately, the local shear stress surpasses the threshold of the critical stress for twinning nucleation, resulting in the formation of DTs [ 90]. The appearance of high-density DTs introduce new interfaces to reduce the dislocation mean free path [ 91], and high-density GNDs aggregate at the BCC/FCC interface, resulting in superior hardening capacity ( Fig. 6b). At this stage, dislocations can nucleate at the twin interface and slip parallel to the twin plane, which avoiding stress concentration caused by dislocation stacking and thus improving ductility [ 42]. In general, the HCP phase is considered to be the transition phase from the TRIP process of FCC-BCC, which also known as the ε-martensite phase transition [ 23, 97]. However, the elongated HCP phase clearly does not fit the characteristics of the ε-martensitic phase transition. Owing to the intense shear strain at the layer interface, continuous slip of SFs within the FCC matrix could potentially result in the formation of a nano-sized HCP phase [ 98]. In other words, two plane-thickness (n = 2) stacking layers of dislocation act as HCP embryos [ 99], which typically occur in materials with low SFE [ 23]. Like SFs and DTs, the formation of those HCP phase is beneficial to alleviate the local stress concentration, thereby providing better ductility [ 100]. The schematic diagram of enhanced strength-ductility trade-off of LHA are summarized in Fig. 17. According to the WHR, the deformation of LHA can be divided into three stages. In stage I, due to the large activation of dislocations and the reduced rate of dislocation storage, the WHR exhibits a rapid decrease. GNDs and SFs were generated inside the soft domain (FCC) around the interface to coordinate the local strain gradient. Hard BCC layer also changed from the elastic stage to the elastoplastic stage, while the back stress induced by GNDs failed to completely offset the normal stress, and finally causing HDI strengthening [ 87]. In stage II, further deformation at the interface results in severe local shear strain, and DTs begin to produce and proliferate at these sites. Simultaneously, dislocations also start to produce within the hard BCC domain to coordinate the plastic deformation. These SFs and DTs hinder further dislocation motion, and the synergistic effect of HDI stress, resulting in additional hardening mechanism, which slows down the decrease of WHR. In stage III, as a result of the overall extensive deformation, dislocations, SFs, and DTs disperse throughout the entire FCC layer. The severe shear strain at the interface leads to the formation of nano-sized HCP phase and stronger HDI stress, which can effectively suppress the formation of necking and micro-cracks. In conclusion, the presence of SFs, DTs, NTs and nano-HCP phase adapts to the strain gradient at the interface and ultimately coordinates the overall deformation. In addition, the dislocation occlusion and back stress were the main mechanisms of HDI strengthening, which were the main reasons for the elevation of WHR. Recently, heterostructured materials offers a novel strategy for solving the longstanding dilemma of strength-ductility trade-off of metallic materials, that is, soft and hard domains with significant rheological stress difference are used as the basic units to orderly construct the heterostructure [ 1, 2]. Then, the strength-ductility synergy is obtained by additional strain hardening induced by the heterogeneous deformation [ 3]. Apparently, the heterostructure, such as gradient structure [ 4], bimodal structure [ 5] or layered structure [ 6], etc., should be controlled by appropriate methods for the desired size and architecture to obtain the satisfactory properties. To date, there are "top-down" [ 7] and "bottom-up" [ 8] routes for the fabrication of heterostructured materials. The former is mainly through mechanical deformation, for instance, surface mechanical grinding [ 9], ultrasonic surface rolling [ 10] or asynchronous rolling [ 7], etc., so as to achieve heterostructure. While the latter mainly involves the formation of multi-scale distribution of grains or phase components achieved through composition or architectural design [ 8]. Layered heterostructure possesses more architectural parameters, e.g., layer space, thickness, hardness and proportion of layers, etc., tailoring strength or plasticity across a wide range [ 11]. With the advancement of additive manufacturing (AM), the "layer-by-layer" approach inherently provides an advantage in the direct fabrication of layer heterostructured materials [ 12]. In these cases, the heterostructure should be mainly understood as the AM of multi-materials, such as CuSn10/SS316L [ 12], Al 2O 3/Ti [ 13], SS321/Ti6Al4V [ 14], Ti64/Ti64 + MEA [ 15] etc. However, due to variations in thermophysical properties, these heterogeneous materials exhibited some shortcomings, including low compatibility, interface defects, chemical reactions, etc. Recently, some researchers fabricated materials with layered distribution of grain sizes [ 16, 17] and phases [ 18] by AM combined with rolling methods, avoiding the problem of incompatibility between the heterogeneous materials, but this undoubtedly decreases the engineering applications of AM. Therefore, how to accurately control the phase ratio or grain size to achieve high quality layered heterostructure still remain as a problem. Given the above, if heterostructure composed of FCC and BCC phases with layered architecture is produced in the FeCoCrNiMn, taking advantage of the “layer-by-layer” manner of LPBF process, synergistic combination of strength and ductility might be expected. In this study, we demonstrated an interesting scheme for alloy preparation of dual powder-source alloy system based on the LPBF process. The as-built samples exhibit excellent strength-ductility balance, which attributes to the well-architectured layered heterostructure. Such dual-phase microstructure are rarely deployed in CoCrFeMnNi-based alloys, and the corresponding strain hardening mechanism for alloys with such layered structures has not been explored. Based on the preparation method and mechanical properties, two issues need to be clarified: How does the microstructure of the layered heterostructure with dual phase formed? Secondly, the deformation mechanisms of heterostructure alloys during tensile deformation process. In the following, the fabrication, microstructure, mechanical properties and deformation mechanism of the CoCrFeMnNi-based alloy system fabricated by LPBF were reported and analyzed through the combination of crystal plasticity finite element method (CPFEM) and experiment characterization. The DiMetal- 100H (Laser Additive Manufacturing GmbH, Guangzhou, China) was adopted for LPBF manufacturing, while the layered heterostructured alloys (LHA) were fabricated by melting three layers of Fe40 powder and five layers of Fe80 powder in a cycle along the build direction (BD), as described in Fig. 1g. All the layers were processed in orthogonal scan mode using the optimized parameters. i.e., laser power of 200 W, scanning speed of 800 mm/s, layer thickness of 30 μm and hatching space of 70 μm, respectively. The cuboid samples were processed into thin slices of dog bone-shaped tensile samples along the normal direction (ND) or transverse direction (TD) with a thickness of 1 mm by wire cutting ( Fig. 1h). In addition, the width of the corresponding gauge section is 2 mm and the length is 8 mm. The samples for microstructural analysis were sandpapered (200#-3000#) and polished using diamond suspension with particle size of 1 μm. The yield strength (YS), ultimate tensile strength (UTS) and elongation were determined for all tested samples. The loading-unloading-reloading tensile tests were performed on all samples to investigate the evolution of hetero-deformation induced (HDI) stresses during tensile straining. Moreover, the phase diagram was carried out by the CALPHAD calculation though graphical mode by the Thermo-Calc 2023a software coupled with TCHEA4 database, on basis of the global minimization of the Gibbs energy of the system. Finite Element Method (FEM) with crystal plasticity as constitutive model were performed to access the information of stress/strain evolution and slip activity for different layer in LHA. The basic principle of crystal plasticity is induced in Refs. [ 29, 30]. The shear strain rate formula based on the energy criterion which proposed by Hutchinson [ 31] was adopted. Since the different layers in LHA have significant differences in grain size, phase and orientation, a simple layered heterogeneous model was constructed by Neper [ 32] and given the corresponding random orientation. Finally, the simulation was carried out in ABAQUS/STANDARD®. For better presentation, the details of the model including the main parameters will be expressed in the discussion section together with the results. Hard BCC layer also changed from the elastic stage to the elastoplastic stage, while the back stress induced by GNDs failed to completely offset the normal stress, and finally causing HDI strengthening [ 87]. In stage II, further deformation at the interface results in severe local shear strain, and DTs begin to produce and proliferate at these sites. Simultaneously, dislocations also start to produce within the hard BCC domain to coordinate the plastic deformation. These SFs and DTs hinder further dislocation motion, and the synergistic effect of HDI stress, resulting in additional hardening mechanism, which slows down the decrease of WHR. In stage III, as a result of the overall extensive deformation, dislocations, SFs, and DTs disperse throughout the entire FCC layer. The severe shear strain at the interface leads to the formation of nano-sized HCP phase and stronger HDI stress, which can effectively suppress the formation of necking and micro-cracks. In conclusion, the presence of SFs, DTs, NTs and nano-HCP phase adapts to the strain gradient at the interface and ultimately coordinates the overall deformation. Recently, heterostructured materials offers a novel strategy for solving the longstanding dilemma of strength-ductility trade-off of metallic materials, that is, soft and hard domains with significant rheological stress difference are used as the basic units to orderly construct the heterostructure [ 1, 2]. Then, the strength-ductility synergy is obtained by additional strain hardening induced by the heterogeneous deformation [ 3]. Apparently, the heterostructure, such as gradient structure [ 4], bimodal structure [ 5] or layered structure [ 6], etc., should be controlled by appropriate methods for the desired size and architecture to obtain the satisfactory properties. To date, there are "top-down" [ 7] and "bottom-up" [ 8] routes for the fabrication of heterostructured materials. The former is mainly through mechanical deformation, for instance, surface mechanical grinding [ 9], ultrasonic surface rolling [ 10] or asynchronous rolling [ 7], etc., so as to achieve heterostructure. While the latter mainly involves the formation of multi-scale distribution of grains or phase components achieved through composition or architectural design [ 8]. Layered heterostructure possesses more architectural parameters, e.g., layer space, thickness, hardness and proportion of layers, etc., tailoring strength or plasticity across a wide range [ 11]. With the advancement of additive manufacturing (AM), the "layer-by-layer" approach inherently provides an advantage in the direct fabrication of layer heterostructured materials [ 12]. In these cases, the heterostructure should be mainly understood as the AM of multi-materials, such as CuSn10/SS316L [ 12], Al 2O 3/Ti [ 13], SS321/Ti6Al4V [ 14], Ti64/Ti64 + MEA [ 15] etc. However, due to variations in thermophysical properties, these heterogeneous materials exhibited some shortcomings, including low compatibility, interface defects, chemical reactions, etc. Recently, some researchers fabricated materials with layered distribution of grain sizes [ 16, 17] and phases [ 18] by AM combined with rolling methods, avoiding the problem of incompatibility between the heterogeneous materials, but this undoubtedly decreases the engineering applications of AM. Therefore, how to accurately control the phase ratio or grain size to achieve high quality layered heterostructure still remain as a problem. Given the above, if heterostructure composed of FCC and BCC phases with layered architecture is produced in the FeCoCrNiMn, taking advantage of the “layer-by-layer” manner of LPBF process, synergistic combination of strength and ductility might be expected. In this study, we demonstrated an interesting scheme for alloy preparation of dual powder-source alloy system based on the LPBF process. The as-built samples exhibit excellent strength-ductility balance, which attributes to the well-architectured layered heterostructure. Such dual-phase microstructure are rarely deployed in CoCrFeMnNi-based alloys, and the corresponding strain hardening mechanism for alloys with such layered structures has not been explored. Based on the preparation method and mechanical properties, two issues need to be clarified: How does the microstructure of the layered heterostructure with dual phase formed? Secondly, the deformation mechanisms of heterostructure alloys during tensile deformation process. In the following, the fabrication, microstructure, mechanical properties and deformation mechanism of the CoCrFeMnNi-based alloy system fabricated by LPBF were reported and analyzed through the combination of crystal plasticity finite element method (CPFEM) and experiment characterization. The DiMetal- 100H (Laser Additive Manufacturing GmbH, Guangzhou, China) was adopted for LPBF manufacturing, while the layered heterostructured alloys (LHA) were fabricated by melting three layers of Fe40 powder and five layers of Fe80 powder in a cycle along the build direction (BD), as described in Fig. 1g. All the layers were processed in orthogonal scan mode using the optimized parameters. i.e., laser power of 200 W, scanning speed of 800 mm/s, layer thickness of 30 μm and hatching space of 70 μm, respectively. The cuboid samples were processed into thin slices of dog bone-shaped tensile samples along the normal direction (ND) or transverse direction (TD) with a thickness of 1 mm by wire cutting ( Fig. 1h). In addition, the width of the corresponding gauge section is 2 mm and the length is 8 mm. The samples for microstructural analysis were sandpapered (200#-3000#) and polished using diamond suspension with particle size of 1 μm. The yield strength (YS), ultimate tensile strength (UTS) and elongation were determined for all tested samples. The loading-unloading-reloading tensile tests were performed on all samples to investigate the evolution of hetero-deformation induced (HDI) stresses during tensile straining. Moreover, the phase diagram was carried out by the CALPHAD calculation though graphical mode by the Thermo-Calc 2023a software coupled with TCHEA4 database, on basis of the global minimization of the Gibbs energy of the system. Finite Element Method (FEM) with crystal plasticity as constitutive model were performed to access the information of stress/strain evolution and slip activity for different layer in LHA. The basic principle of crystal plasticity is induced in Refs. [ 29, 30]. The shear strain rate formula based on the energy criterion which proposed by Hutchinson [ 31] was adopted. Since the different layers in LHA have significant differences in grain size, phase and orientation, a simple layered heterogeneous model was constructed by Neper [ 32] and given the corresponding random orientation. Finally, the simulation was carried out in ABAQUS/STANDARD®. The schematic diagram of enhanced strength-ductility trade-off of LHA are summarized in Fig. 17. According to the WHR, the deformation of LHA can be divided into three stages. In stage I, due to the large activation of dislocations and the reduced rate of dislocation storage, the WHR exhibits a rapid decrease. GNDs and SFs were generated inside the soft domain (FCC) around the interface to coordinate the local strain gradient. Hard BCC layer also changed from the elastic stage to the elastoplastic stage, while the back stress induced by GNDs failed to completely offset the normal stress, and finally causing HDI strengthening [ 87]. In stage II, further deformation at the interface results in severe local shear strain, and DTs begin to produce and proliferate at these sites. Simultaneously, dislocations also start to produce within the hard BCC domain to coordinate the plastic deformation. These SFs and DTs hinder further dislocation motion, and the synergistic effect of HDI stress, resulting in additional hardening mechanism, which slows down the decrease of WHR. In stage III, as a result of the overall extensive deformation, dislocations, SFs, and DTs disperse throughout the entire FCC layer. The severe shear strain at the interface leads to the formation of nano-sized HCP phase and stronger HDI stress, which can effectively suppress the formation of necking and micro-cracks. In conclusion, the presence of SFs, DTs, NTs and nano-HCP phase adapts to the strain gradient at the interface and ultimately coordinates the overall deformation. In addition, the dislocation occlusion and back stress were the main mechanisms of HDI strengthening, which were the main reasons for the elevation of WHR. Recently, heterostructured materials offers a novel strategy for solving the longstanding dilemma of strength-ductility trade-off of metallic materials, that is, soft and hard domains with significant rheological stress difference are used as the basic units to orderly construct the heterostructure [ 1, 2]. Then, the strength-ductility synergy is obtained by additional strain hardening induced by the heterogeneous deformation [ 3]. Apparently, the heterostructure, such as gradient structure [ 4], bimodal structure [ 5] or layered structure [ 6], etc., should be controlled by appropriate methods for the desired size and architecture to obtain the satisfactory properties. To date, there are "top-down" [ 7] and "bottom-up" [ 8] routes for the fabrication of heterostructured materials. The former is mainly through mechanical deformation, for instance, surface mechanical grinding [ 9], ultrasonic surface rolling [ 10] or asynchronous rolling [ 7], etc., so as to achieve heterostructure. While the latter mainly involves the formation of multi-scale distribution of grains or phase components achieved through composition or architectural design [ 8]. Layered heterostructure possesses more architectural parameters, e.g., layer space, thickness, hardness and proportion of layers, etc., tailoring strength or plasticity across a wide range [ 11]. With the advancement of additive manufacturing (AM), the "layer-by-layer" approach inherently provides an advantage in the direct fabrication of layer heterostructured materials [ 12]. In these cases, the heterostructure should be mainly understood as the AM of multi-materials, such as CuSn10/SS316L [ 12], Al 2O 3/Ti [ 13], SS321/Ti6Al4V [ 14], Ti64/Ti64 + MEA [ 15] etc. However, due to variations in thermophysical properties, these heterogeneous materials exhibited some shortcomings, including low compatibility, interface defects, chemical reactions, etc. Recently, some researchers fabricated materials with layered distribution of grain sizes [ 16, 17] and phases [ 18] by AM combined with rolling methods, avoiding the problem of incompatibility between the heterogeneous materials, but this undoubtedly decreases the engineering applications of AM. Therefore, how to accurately control the phase ratio or grain size to achieve high quality layered heterostructure still remain as a problem. Given the above, if heterostructure composed of FCC and BCC phases with layered architecture is produced in the FeCoCrNiMn, taking advantage of the “layer-by-layer” manner of LPBF process, synergistic combination of strength and ductility might be expected. In this study, we demonstrated an interesting scheme for alloy preparation of dual powder-source alloy system based on the LPBF process. The as-built samples exhibit excellent strength-ductility balance, which attributes to the well-architectured layered heterostructure. Such dual-phase microstructure are rarely deployed in CoCrFeMnNi-based alloys, and the corresponding strain hardening mechanism for alloys with such layered structures has not been explored. Based on the preparation method and mechanical properties, two issues need to be clarified: How does the microstructure of the layered heterostructure with dual phase formed? Secondly, the deformation mechanisms of heterostructure alloys during tensile deformation process. In the following, the fabrication, microstructure, mechanical properties and deformation mechanism of the CoCrFeMnNi-based alloy system fabricated by LPBF were reported and analyzed through the combination of crystal plasticity finite element method (CPFEM) and experiment characterization. The DiMetal- 100H (Laser Additive Manufacturing GmbH, Guangzhou, China) was adopted for LPBF manufacturing, while the layered heterostructured alloys (LHA) were fabricated by melting three layers of Fe40 powder and five layers of Fe80 powder in a cycle along the build direction (BD), as described in Fig. 1g. All the layers were processed in orthogonal scan mode using the optimized parameters. i.e., laser power of 200 W, scanning speed of 800 mm/s, layer thickness of 30 μm and hatching space of 70 μm, respectively. The cuboid samples were processed into thin slices of dog bone-shaped tensile samples along the normal direction (ND) or transverse direction (TD) with a thickness of 1 mm by wire cutting ( Fig. 1h). In addition, the width of the corresponding gauge section is 2 mm and the length is 8 mm. The samples for microstructural analysis were sandpapered (200#-3000#) and polished using diamond suspension with particle size of 1 μm. The yield strength (YS), ultimate tensile strength (UTS) and elongation were determined for all tested samples. The schematic diagram of enhanced strength-ductility trade-off of LHA are summarized in Fig. 17. According to the WHR, the deformation of LHA can be divided into three stages. In stage I, due to the large activation of dislocations and the reduced rate of dislocation storage, the WHR exhibits a rapid decrease. GNDs and SFs were generated inside the soft domain (FCC) around the interface to coordinate the local strain gradient. Hard BCC layer also changed from the elastic stage to the elastoplastic stage, while the back stress induced by GNDs failed to completely offset the normal stress, and finally causing HDI strengthening [ 87]. In stage II, further deformation at the interface results in severe local shear strain, and DTs begin to produce and proliferate at these sites. Simultaneously, dislocations also start to produce within the hard BCC domain to coordinate the plastic deformation. These SFs and DTs hinder further dislocation motion, and the synergistic effect of HDI stress, resulting in additional hardening mechanism, which slows down the decrease of WHR. In stage III, as a result of the overall extensive deformation, dislocations, SFs, and DTs disperse throughout the entire FCC layer. The severe shear strain at the interface leads to the formation of nano-sized HCP phase and stronger HDI stress, which can effectively suppress the formation of necking and micro-cracks. Recently, heterostructured materials offers a novel strategy for solving the longstanding dilemma of strength-ductility trade-off of metallic materials, that is, soft and hard domains with significant rheological stress difference are used as the basic units to orderly construct the heterostructure [ 1, 2]. Then, the strength-ductility synergy is obtained by additional strain hardening induced by the heterogeneous deformation [ 3]. Apparently, the heterostructure, such as gradient structure [ 4], bimodal structure [ 5] or layered structure [ 6], etc., should be controlled by appropriate methods for the desired size and architecture to obtain the satisfactory properties. To date, there are "top-down" [ 7] and "bottom-up" [ 8] routes for the fabrication of heterostructured materials. The former is mainly through mechanical deformation, for instance, surface mechanical grinding [ 9], ultrasonic surface rolling [ 10] or asynchronous rolling [ 7], etc., so as to achieve heterostructure. While the latter mainly involves the formation of multi-scale distribution of grains or phase components achieved through composition or architectural design [ 8]. Layered heterostructure possesses more architectural parameters, e.g., layer space, thickness, hardness and proportion of layers, etc., tailoring strength or plasticity across a wide range [ 11]. With the advancement of additive manufacturing (AM), the "layer-by-layer" approach inherently provides an advantage in the direct fabrication of layer heterostructured materials [ 12]. In these cases, the heterostructure should be mainly understood as the AM of multi-materials, such as CuSn10/SS316L [ 12], Al 2O 3/Ti [ 13], SS321/Ti6Al4V [ 14], Ti64/Ti64 + MEA [ 15] etc. However, due to variations in thermophysical properties, these heterogeneous materials exhibited some shortcomings, including low compatibility, interface defects, chemical reactions, etc. Recently, some researchers fabricated materials with layered distribution of grain sizes [ 16, 17] and phases [ 18] by AM combined with rolling methods, avoiding the problem of incompatibility between the heterogeneous materials, but this undoubtedly decreases the engineering applications of AM. Therefore, how to accurately control the phase ratio or grain size to achieve high quality layered heterostructure still remain as a problem. Given the above, if heterostructure composed of FCC and BCC phases with layered architecture is produced in the FeCoCrNiMn, taking advantage of the “layer-by-layer” manner of LPBF process, synergistic combination of strength and ductility might be expected. In this study, we demonstrated an interesting scheme for alloy preparation of dual powder-source alloy system based on the LPBF process. The as-built samples exhibit excellent strength-ductility balance, which attributes to the well-architectured layered heterostructure. Such dual-phase microstructure are rarely deployed in CoCrFeMnNi-based alloys, and the corresponding strain hardening mechanism for alloys with such layered structures has not been explored. Based on the preparation method and mechanical properties, two issues need to be clarified: How does the microstructure of the layered heterostructure with dual phase formed? Secondly, the deformation mechanisms of heterostructure alloys during tensile deformation process. In the following, the fabrication, microstructure, mechanical properties and deformation mechanism of the CoCrFeMnNi-based alloy system fabricated by LPBF were reported and analyzed through the combination of crystal plasticity finite element method (CPFEM) and experiment characterization. The DiMetal- 100H (Laser Additive Manufacturing GmbH, Guangzhou, China) was adopted for LPBF manufacturing, while the layered heterostructured alloys (LHA) were fabricated by melting three layers of Fe40 powder and five layers of Fe80 powder in a cycle along the build direction (BD), as described in Fig. 1g. All the layers were processed in orthogonal scan mode using the optimized parameters. i.e., laser power of 200 W, scanning speed of 800 mm/s, layer thickness of 30 μm and hatching space of 70 μm, respectively. The cuboid samples were processed into thin slices of dog bone-shaped tensile samples along the normal direction (ND) or transverse direction (TD) with a thickness of 1 mm by wire cutting ( Fig. 1h). In addition, the width of the corresponding gauge section is 2 mm and the length is 8 mm. The samples for microstructural analysis were sandpapered (200#-3000#) and polished using diamond suspension with particle size of 1 μm. The yield strength (YS), ultimate tensile strength (UTS) and elongation were determined for all tested samples. The loading-unloading-reloading tensile tests were performed on all samples to investigate the evolution of hetero-deformation induced (HDI) stresses during tensile straining. Moreover, the phase diagram was carried out by the CALPHAD calculation though graphical mode by the Thermo-Calc 2023a software coupled with TCHEA4 database, on basis of the global minimization of the Gibbs energy of the system. Finite Element Method (FEM) with crystal plasticity as constitutive model were performed to access the information of stress/strain evolution and slip activity for different layer in LHA. The basic principle of crystal plasticity is induced in Refs. [ 29, 30]. The shear strain rate formula based on the energy criterion which proposed by Hutchinson [ 31] was adopted. Since the different layers in LHA have significant differences in grain size, phase and orientation, a simple layered heterogeneous model was constructed by Neper [ 32] and given the corresponding random orientation. Finally, the simulation was carried out in ABAQUS/STANDARD®. For better presentation, the details of the model including the main parameters will be expressed in the discussion section together with the results. The GND density of FDL increased from 1.56 × 10 14m −2to 2.71 × 10 14m −2under different strains (0 %-15 %), indicating a slow upward trend, as shown in Fig. 15b. However, the GND density of FEL has more than doubled from 4.51 × 10 14m −2to 9.68 × 10 14m −2, indicating that FEL was the main stress-bearing layer in deformation, while the main role of FDL was to coordinate deformation. In addition, it is worth noting that the width of the low KAM (original FDL) layer narrowed from 170 μm to 135 μm after deformation, and high KAM regions were observed at the layer interface, as shown by the dotted line in Fig. 15a 1and a 4. Due to the mismatch between strength and plastic deformation ability, the layer interface is the main stress concentration area during deformation [ 85], where the soft layer (FDL) generates back stress and the hard layer (FEL) generates normal stress [ 86]. Back and normal stresses do not cancel each other out overall, and together they produce HDI reinforcement to improve YS [ 87], while the higher KAM values at the interface in LHA indicate the presence of strengthening. To characterize the evolution of deformation twins (DTs) in LHA, high-magnification EBSD characterization of the layer boundary was implemented, as shown in Fig. 15d 1-d 3. Interestingly, DTs were formed in the FCC matrix even if at strain of 5 %. For comparison, no DT behavior was observed in Fe40 (with the same chemical composition with the FDL in LHA sample) even if at strain of 10 % ( Fig. 11b), while the excessively fine grains within the Fe80 sample also prevented the generation of DT ( Fig. 11d) [ 88]. With the increase of strain, the proportion of DT boundaries in the FCC matrix (FDL) increase from 32.2 % at the 5 % strain to 56.9 % at the 15 % strain, as shown in Fig. 15e. As shown in Fig. 15e, by observing the grain morphology and IPF of the individual grains in the FDL, the grain not only produces twirling, but also undergoes a deflective orientation. In general, due to different crystal structures and chemical compositions, FDL and FEL of LHA exhibit different mechanisms during deformation, respectively. FEL is dominated by dislocation slip, while FDL contains a large amount of DTs in addition to dislocation. Two factors are responsible for the premature DT behavior in the LHA, i.e. (i) Increasing Fe content in FeCoCrNiMn system results in significant decrease of stacking fault energy (SFE) [ 89]. (ii) Strain gradient induced by the heterostructured incompatibility during tensile deformation results in significant shear stress concentration at the layer interfaces [ 42]. The back stress exerted on the soft domain elevates the nominal stress beyond the loading stress. Ultimately, the local shear stress surpasses the threshold of the critical stress for twinning nucleation, resulting in the formation of DTs [ 90]. The appearance of high-density DTs introduce new interfaces to reduce the dislocation mean free path [ 91], and high-density GNDs aggregate at the BCC/FCC interface, resulting in superior hardening capacity ( Fig. 6b). Therefore, based on the above results and analysis, it can be considered that the difference between the CPFEM curve in Fig. 13and the experimental results is due to additional hardening mechanisms such as DT and GND strengthening, which were not considered in the simulation. The region of interest of the fractured LHA (strain = 22 %) sample was selected for further observations, and a typically interface region was shown in Fig. 16a-c. According to Fig. 14a, the morphology of grains in FEL changes after deformation, indicating severe plastic deformation, while FDL presents a large number of DTs. As special grain boundaries, the formation of DTs releases local non-uniform stress, while also hindering dislocation slip, which require a larger driving force to cross the boundary [ 92]. Therefore, it can be assumed that this local twinning induced plasticity (TWIP) phenomenon at the interface increases the overall strength while also hindering the crack nucleation to improve the toughness. Interestingly, unlike the previous inter-layer difference ( Fig. 15a), the KAM distribution depicted in Fig. 16c indicates that the values within FDL and FEL are almost identical, and the quantitative calculation results are 9.27 × 10 14m −2and 1.25 × 10 15m −2, respectively. That is to say, in the final stage of deformation, the differences between FDL and FEL tend to be consistent, which is reflected in the fact that as a soft phase, FDL continuously generates GND through dislocations and DTs to adapt to the overall deformation [ 93, 94]. Subsequently, TEM was employed to explore the coordinated deformation behavior. Nano-twinning (NT) bundles were observed, as shown in Fig. 16d. These NTs are still in the propagation stage, intermediate between nucleation and thickening [ 95]. At this stage, dislocations can nucleate at the twin interface and slip parallel to the twin plane, which avoiding stress concentration caused by dislocation stacking and thus improving ductility [ 42]. Stacking faults were observed in the FCC phase, as shown in Fig. 16e. In addition, Lomer-Cottrell (L-C) lock could form when shockley partial dislocations cross along the same slip system, which were also observed in Fig. 16e. L-C locks not only act as a strong barrier to effectively immobilize dislocation motion, but can also act as a Frank-Read source for dislocation multiplication, leading to stable and progressive work hardening, which benefits UTS and plasticity [ 96]. In contrast, FEL with BCC phase was surrounded by dislocation forest and no other deformation mechanism was found, as depicted in Fig. 16f. Fig. 16g depicts the interface of the FCC and BCC phases, while the Kurdjumov-Sachs (KS) orientation relationship comprises a transition of [110]-FCC zone into [111]-BCC zone. Interestingly, nano-sized hexagonal close-packed (HCP) phase with width of 13.1 nm was observed, as shown in Fig. 16h and i. In general, the HCP phase is considered to be the transition phase from the TRIP process of FCC-BCC, which also known as the ε-martensite phase transition [ 23, 97]. However, the elongated HCP phase clearly does not fit the characteristics of the ε-martensitic phase transition. Owing to the intense shear strain at the layer interface, continuous slip of SFs within the FCC matrix could potentially result in the formation of a nano-sized HCP phase [ 98]. In other words, two plane-thickness (n = 2) stacking layers of dislocation act as HCP embryos [ 99], which typically occur in materials with low SFE [ 23]. Like SFs and DTs, the formation of those HCP phase is beneficial to alleviate the local stress concentration, thereby providing better ductility [ 100]. The schematic diagram of enhanced strength-ductility trade-off of LHA are summarized in Fig. 17. According to the WHR, the deformation of LHA can be divided into three stages. In stage I, due to the large activation of dislocations and the reduced rate of dislocation storage, the WHR exhibits a rapid decrease. GNDs and SFs were generated inside the soft domain (FCC) around the interface to coordinate the local strain gradient. Hard BCC layer also changed from the elastic stage to the elastoplastic stage, while the back stress induced by GNDs failed to completely offset the normal stress, and finally causing HDI strengthening [ 87]. In stage II, further deformation at the interface results in severe local shear strain, and DTs begin to produce and proliferate at these sites. Simultaneously, dislocations also start to produce within the hard BCC domain to coordinate the plastic deformation. These SFs and DTs hinder further dislocation motion, and the synergistic effect of HDI stress, resulting in additional hardening mechanism, which slows down the decrease of WHR. In stage III, as a result of the overall extensive deformation, dislocations, SFs, and DTs disperse throughout the entire FCC layer. The severe shear strain at the interface leads to the formation of nano-sized HCP phase and stronger HDI stress, which can effectively suppress the formation of necking and micro-cracks. In conclusion, the presence of SFs, DTs, NTs and nano-HCP phase adapts to the strain gradient at the interface and ultimately coordinates the overall deformation. In addition, the dislocation occlusion and back stress were the main mechanisms of HDI strengthening, which were the main reasons for the elevation of WHR. Recently, heterostructured materials offers a novel strategy for solving the longstanding dilemma of strength-ductility trade-off of metallic materials, that is, soft and hard domains with significant rheological stress difference are used as the basic units to orderly construct the heterostructure [ 1, 2]. Then, the strength-ductility synergy is obtained by additional strain hardening induced by the heterogeneous deformation [ 3]. Apparently, the heterostructure, such as gradient structure [ 4], bimodal structure [ 5] or layered structure [ 6], etc., should be controlled by appropriate methods for the desired size and architecture to obtain the satisfactory properties. To date, there are "top-down" [ 7] and "bottom-up" [ 8] routes for the fabrication of heterostructured materials. The former is mainly through mechanical deformation, for instance, surface mechanical grinding [ 9], ultrasonic surface rolling [ 10] or asynchronous rolling [ 7], etc., so as to achieve heterostructure. While the latter mainly involves the formation of multi-scale distribution of grains or phase components achieved through composition or architectural design [ 8]. Layered heterostructure possesses more architectural parameters, e.g., layer space, thickness, hardness and proportion of layers, etc., tailoring strength or plasticity across a wide range [ 11]. With the advancement of additive manufacturing (AM), the "layer-by-layer" approach inherently provides an advantage in the direct fabrication of layer heterostructured materials [ 12]. In these cases, the heterostructure should be mainly understood as the AM of multi-materials, such as CuSn10/SS316L [ 12], Al 2O 3/Ti [ 13], SS321/Ti6Al4V [ 14], Ti64/Ti64 + MEA [ 15] etc. However, due to variations in thermophysical properties, these heterogeneous materials exhibited some shortcomings, including low compatibility, interface defects, chemical reactions, etc. Recently, some researchers fabricated materials with layered distribution of grain sizes [ 16, 17] and phases [ 18] by AM combined with rolling methods, avoiding the problem of incompatibility between the heterogeneous materials, but this undoubtedly decreases the engineering applications of AM. Therefore, how to accurately control the phase ratio or grain size to achieve high quality layered heterostructure still remain as a problem. Given the above, if heterostructure composed of FCC and BCC phases with layered architecture is produced in the FeCoCrNiMn, taking advantage of the “layer-by-layer” manner of LPBF process, synergistic combination of strength and ductility might be expected. In this study, we demonstrated an interesting scheme for alloy preparation of dual powder-source alloy system based on the LPBF process. The as-built samples exhibit excellent strength-ductility balance, which attributes to the well-architectured layered heterostructure. Such dual-phase microstructure are rarely deployed in CoCrFeMnNi-based alloys, and the corresponding strain hardening mechanism for alloys with such layered structures has not been explored. Based on the preparation method and mechanical properties, two issues need to be clarified: How does the microstructure of the layered heterostructure with dual phase formed? Secondly, the deformation mechanisms of heterostructure alloys during tensile deformation process. In the following, the fabrication, microstructure, mechanical properties and deformation mechanism of the CoCrFeMnNi-based alloy system fabricated by LPBF were reported and analyzed through the combination of crystal plasticity finite element method (CPFEM) and experiment characterization. The DiMetal- 100H (Laser Additive Manufacturing GmbH, Guangzhou, China) was adopted for LPBF manufacturing, while the layered heterostructured alloys (LHA) were fabricated by melting three layers of Fe40 powder and five layers of Fe80 powder in a cycle along the build direction (BD), as described in Fig. 1g. All the layers were processed in orthogonal scan mode using the optimized parameters. i.e., laser power of 200 W, scanning speed of 800 mm/s, layer thickness of 30 μm and hatching space of 70 μm, respectively. The cuboid samples were processed into thin slices of dog bone-shaped tensile samples along the normal direction (ND) or transverse direction (TD) with a thickness of 1 mm by wire cutting ( Fig. 1h). In addition, the width of the corresponding gauge section is 2 mm and the length is 8 mm. The samples for microstructural analysis were sandpapered (200#-3000#) and polished using diamond suspension with particle size of 1 μm. The yield strength (YS), ultimate tensile strength (UTS) and elongation were determined for all tested samples. The loading-unloading-reloading tensile tests were performed on all samples to investigate the evolution of hetero-deformation induced (HDI) stresses during tensile straining. Moreover, the phase diagram was carried out by the CALPHAD calculation though graphical mode by the Thermo-Calc 2023a software coupled with TCHEA4 database, on basis of the global minimization of the Gibbs energy of the system. Finite Element Method (FEM) with crystal plasticity as constitutive model were performed to access the information of stress/strain evolution and slip activity for different layer in LHA. The basic principle of crystal plasticity is induced in Refs. [ 29, 30]. The shear strain rate formula based on the energy criterion which proposed by Hutchinson [ 31] was adopted. Since the different layers in LHA have significant differences in grain size, phase and orientation, a simple layered heterogeneous model was constructed by Neper [ 32] and given the corresponding random orientation. Finally, the simulation was carried out in ABAQUS/STANDARD®. For better presentation, the details of the model including the main parameters will be expressed in the discussion section together with the results. Hard BCC layer also changed from the elastic stage to the elastoplastic stage, while the back stress induced by GNDs failed to completely offset the normal stress, and finally causing HDI strengthening [ 87]. In stage II, further deformation at the interface results in severe local shear strain, and DTs begin to produce and proliferate at these sites. Simultaneously, dislocations also start to produce within the hard BCC domain to coordinate the plastic deformation. These SFs and DTs hinder further dislocation motion, and the synergistic effect of HDI stress, resulting in additional hardening mechanism, which slows down the decrease of WHR. In stage III, as a result of the overall extensive deformation, dislocations, SFs, and DTs disperse throughout the entire FCC layer. The severe shear strain at the interface leads to the formation of nano-sized HCP phase and stronger HDI stress, which can effectively suppress the formation of necking and micro-cracks. Recently, heterostructured materials offers a novel strategy for solving the longstanding dilemma of strength-ductility trade-off of metallic materials, that is, soft and hard domains with significant rheological stress difference are used as the basic units to orderly construct the heterostructure [ 1, 2]. Then, the strength-ductility synergy is obtained by additional strain hardening induced by the heterogeneous deformation [ 3]. Apparently, the heterostructure, such as gradient structure [ 4], bimodal structure [ 5] or layered structure [ 6], etc., should be controlled by appropriate methods for the desired size and architecture to obtain the satisfactory properties. To date, there are "top-down" [ 7] and "bottom-up" [ 8] routes for the fabrication of heterostructured materials. The former is mainly through mechanical deformation, for instance, surface mechanical grinding [ 9], ultrasonic surface rolling [ 10] or asynchronous rolling [ 7], etc., so as to achieve heterostructure. While the latter mainly involves the formation of multi-scale distribution of grains or phase components achieved through composition or architectural design [ 8]. Layered heterostructure possesses more architectural parameters, e.g., layer space, thickness, hardness and proportion of layers, etc., tailoring strength or plasticity across a wide range [ 11]. With the advancement of additive manufacturing (AM), the "layer-by-layer" approach inherently provides an advantage in the direct fabrication of layer heterostructured materials [ 12]. In these cases, the heterostructure should be mainly understood as the AM of multi-materials, such as CuSn10/SS316L [ 12], Al 2O 3/Ti [ 13], SS321/Ti6Al4V [ 14], Ti64/Ti64 + MEA [ 15] etc. However, due to variations in thermophysical properties, these heterogeneous materials exhibited some shortcomings, including low compatibility, interface defects, chemical reactions, etc. Recently, some researchers fabricated materials with layered distribution of grain sizes [ 16, 17] and phases [ 18] by AM combined with rolling methods, avoiding the problem of incompatibility between the heterogeneous materials, but this undoubtedly decreases the engineering applications of AM. Therefore, how to accurately control the phase ratio or grain size to achieve high quality layered heterostructure still remain as a problem. Given the above, if heterostructure composed of FCC and BCC phases with layered architecture is produced in the FeCoCrNiMn, taking advantage of the “layer-by-layer” manner of LPBF process, synergistic combination of strength and ductility might be expected. In this study, we demonstrated an interesting scheme for alloy preparation of dual powder-source alloy system based on the LPBF process. The as-built samples exhibit excellent strength-ductility balance, which attributes to the well-architectured layered heterostructure. Such dual-phase microstructure are rarely deployed in CoCrFeMnNi-based alloys, and the corresponding strain hardening mechanism for alloys with such layered structures has not been explored. Based on the preparation method and mechanical properties, two issues need to be clarified: How does the microstructure of the layered heterostructure with dual phase formed? Secondly, the deformation mechanisms of heterostructure alloys during tensile deformation process. In the following, the fabrication, microstructure, mechanical properties and deformation mechanism of the CoCrFeMnNi-based alloy system fabricated by LPBF were reported and analyzed through the combination of crystal plasticity finite element method (CPFEM) and experiment characterization. The DiMetal- 100H (Laser Additive Manufacturing GmbH, Guangzhou, China) was adopted for LPBF manufacturing, while the layered heterostructured alloys (LHA) were fabricated by melting three layers of Fe40 powder and five layers of Fe80 powder in a cycle along the build direction (BD), as described in Fig. 1g. All the layers were processed in orthogonal scan mode using the optimized parameters. i.e., laser power of 200 W, scanning speed of 800 mm/s, layer thickness of 30 μm and hatching space of 70 μm, respectively. The cuboid samples were processed into thin slices of dog bone-shaped tensile samples along the normal direction (ND) or transverse direction (TD) with a thickness of 1 mm by wire cutting ( Fig. 1h). In addition, the width of the corresponding gauge section is 2 mm and the length is 8 mm. The samples for microstructural analysis were sandpapered (200#-3000#) and polished using diamond suspension with particle size of 1 μm. The yield strength (YS), ultimate tensile strength (UTS) and elongation were determined for all tested samples. The loading-unloading-reloading tensile tests were performed on all samples to investigate the evolution of hetero-deformation induced (HDI) stresses during tensile straining. Moreover, the phase diagram was carried out by the CALPHAD calculation though graphical mode by the Thermo-Calc 2023a software coupled with TCHEA4 database, on basis of the global minimization of the Gibbs energy of the system. Finite Element Method (FEM) with crystal plasticity as constitutive model were performed to access the information of stress/strain evolution and slip activity for different layer in LHA. The basic principle of crystal plasticity is induced in Refs. [ 29, 30]. The shear strain rate formula based on the energy criterion which proposed by Hutchinson [ 31] was adopted. Since the different layers in LHA have significant differences in grain size, phase and orientation, a simple layered heterogeneous model was constructed by Neper [ 32] and given the corresponding random orientation. Finally, the simulation was carried out in ABAQUS/STANDARD®. In stage I, due to the large activation of dislocations and the reduced rate of dislocation storage, the WHR exhibits a rapid decrease. GNDs and SFs were generated inside the soft domain (FCC) around the interface to coordinate the local strain gradient. Hard BCC layer also changed from the elastic stage to the elastoplastic stage, while the back stress induced by GNDs failed to completely offset the normal stress, and finally causing HDI strengthening [ 87]. In stage II, further deformation at the interface results in severe local shear strain, and DTs begin to produce and proliferate at these sites. Simultaneously, dislocations also start to produce within the hard BCC domain to coordinate the plastic deformation. These SFs and DTs hinder further dislocation motion, and the synergistic effect of HDI stress, resulting in additional hardening mechanism, which slows down the decrease of WHR. In stage III, as a result of the overall extensive deformation, dislocations, SFs, and DTs disperse throughout the entire FCC layer. The severe shear strain at the interface leads to the formation of nano-sized HCP phase and stronger HDI stress, which can effectively suppress the formation of necking and micro-cracks. In conclusion, the presence of SFs, DTs, NTs and nano-HCP phase adapts to the strain gradient at the interface and ultimately coordinates the overall deformation. Recently, heterostructured materials offers a novel strategy for solving the longstanding dilemma of strength-ductility trade-off of metallic materials, that is, soft and hard domains with significant rheological stress difference are used as the basic units to orderly construct the heterostructure [ 1, 2]. Then, the strength-ductility synergy is obtained by additional strain hardening induced by the heterogeneous deformation [ 3]. Apparently, the heterostructure, such as gradient structure [ 4], bimodal structure [ 5] or layered structure [ 6], etc., should be controlled by appropriate methods for the desired size and architecture to obtain the satisfactory properties. To date, there are "top-down" [ 7] and "bottom-up" [ 8] routes for the fabrication of heterostructured materials. The former is mainly through mechanical deformation, for instance, surface mechanical grinding [ 9], ultrasonic surface rolling [ 10] or asynchronous rolling [ 7], etc., so as to achieve heterostructure. While the latter mainly involves the formation of multi-scale distribution of grains or phase components achieved through composition or architectural design [ 8]. Layered heterostructure possesses more architectural parameters, e.g., layer space, thickness, hardness and proportion of layers, etc., tailoring strength or plasticity across a wide range [ 11]. With the advancement of additive manufacturing (AM), the "layer-by-layer" approach inherently provides an advantage in the direct fabrication of layer heterostructured materials [ 12]. In these cases, the heterostructure should be mainly understood as the AM of multi-materials, such as CuSn10/SS316L [ 12], Al 2O 3/Ti [ 13], SS321/Ti6Al4V [ 14], Ti64/Ti64 + MEA [ 15] etc. However, due to variations in thermophysical properties, these heterogeneous materials exhibited some shortcomings, including low compatibility, interface defects, chemical reactions, etc. Recently, some researchers fabricated materials with layered distribution of grain sizes [ 16, 17] and phases [ 18] by AM combined with rolling methods, avoiding the problem of incompatibility between the heterogeneous materials, but this undoubtedly decreases the engineering applications of AM. Therefore, how to accurately control the phase ratio or grain size to achieve high quality layered heterostructure still remain as a problem. Given the above, if heterostructure composed of FCC and BCC phases with layered architecture is produced in the FeCoCrNiMn, taking advantage of the “layer-by-layer” manner of LPBF process, synergistic combination of strength and ductility might be expected. In this study, we demonstrated an interesting scheme for alloy preparation of dual powder-source alloy system based on the LPBF process. The as-built samples exhibit excellent strength-ductility balance, which attributes to the well-architectured layered heterostructure. Such dual-phase microstructure are rarely deployed in CoCrFeMnNi-based alloys, and the corresponding strain hardening mechanism for alloys with such layered structures has not been explored. Based on the preparation method and mechanical properties, two issues need to be clarified: How does the microstructure of the layered heterostructure with dual phase formed? Secondly, the deformation mechanisms of heterostructure alloys during tensile deformation process. In the following, the fabrication, microstructure, mechanical properties and deformation mechanism of the CoCrFeMnNi-based alloy system fabricated by LPBF were reported and analyzed through the combination of crystal plasticity finite element method (CPFEM) and experiment characterization. The DiMetal- 100H (Laser Additive Manufacturing GmbH, Guangzhou, China) was adopted for LPBF manufacturing, while the layered heterostructured alloys (LHA) were fabricated by melting three layers of Fe40 powder and five layers of Fe80 powder in a cycle along the build direction (BD), as described in Fig. 1g. All the layers were processed in orthogonal scan mode using the optimized parameters. i.e., laser power of 200 W, scanning speed of 800 mm/s, layer thickness of 30 μm and hatching space of 70 μm, respectively. The cuboid samples were processed into thin slices of dog bone-shaped tensile samples along the normal direction (ND) or transverse direction (TD) with a thickness of 1 mm by wire cutting ( Fig. 1h). In addition, the width of the corresponding gauge section is 2 mm and the length is 8 mm. The samples for microstructural analysis were sandpapered (200#-3000#) and polished using diamond suspension with particle size of 1 μm. The yield strength (YS), ultimate tensile strength (UTS) and elongation were determined for all tested samples. The loading-unloading-reloading tensile tests were performed on all samples to investigate the evolution of hetero-deformation induced (HDI) stresses during tensile straining. Moreover, the phase diagram was carried out by the CALPHAD calculation though graphical mode by the Thermo-Calc 2023a software coupled with TCHEA4 database, on basis of the global minimization of the Gibbs energy of the system. Finite Element Method (FEM) with crystal plasticity as constitutive model were performed to access the information of stress/strain evolution and slip activity for different layer in LHA. The basic principle of crystal plasticity is induced in Refs. [ 29, 30]. The shear strain rate formula based on the energy criterion which proposed by Hutchinson [ 31] was adopted. Since the different layers in LHA have significant differences in grain size, phase and orientation, a simple layered heterogeneous model was constructed by Neper [ 32] and given the corresponding random orientation. Finally, the simulation was carried out in ABAQUS/STANDARD®. For better presentation, the details of the model including the main parameters will be expressed in the discussion section together with the results. The schematic diagram of enhanced strength-ductility trade-off of LHA are summarized in Fig. 17. According to the WHR, the deformation of LHA can be divided into three stages. In stage I, due to the large activation of dislocations and the reduced rate of dislocation storage, the WHR exhibits a rapid decrease. GNDs and SFs were generated inside the soft domain (FCC) around the interface to coordinate the local strain gradient. Hard BCC layer also changed from the elastic stage to the elastoplastic stage, while the back stress induced by GNDs failed to completely offset the normal stress, and finally causing HDI strengthening [ 87]. In stage II, further deformation at the interface results in severe local shear strain, and DTs begin to produce and proliferate at these sites. Simultaneously, dislocations also start to produce within the hard BCC domain to coordinate the plastic deformation. These SFs and DTs hinder further dislocation motion, and the synergistic effect of HDI stress, resulting in additional hardening mechanism, which slows down the decrease of WHR. In stage III, as a result of the overall extensive deformation, dislocations, SFs, and DTs disperse throughout the entire FCC layer. The severe shear strain at the interface leads to the formation of nano-sized HCP phase and stronger HDI stress, which can effectively suppress the formation of necking and micro-cracks. In conclusion, the presence of SFs, DTs, NTs and nano-HCP phase adapts to the strain gradient at the interface and ultimately coordinates the overall deformation. In addition, the dislocation occlusion and back stress were the main mechanisms of HDI strengthening, which were the main reasons for the elevation of WHR. In this work, we take advantages of Fe and LPBF to regulate grain size and phase composition of the Fe-Co-Cr-Ni-Mn alloy systems to fabricated periodically layered materials, which can enhance strength-ductility trade-off at a controllable procedure. The following conclusions can be obtained. 1)Layered heterostructure alloys can be prepared through changing the ratio of Fe and FeCoCrNiMn in the mixed powder. Under low Fe content, the prepared samples had FCC structure with coarser grains and lower hardness. By contrast, samples at high Fe content will convert to BCC structure and are characterized by ultrafine grains with an average diameter of 4.24 μm. 2)During the preparation of LHA, the BCC phase began to appear in the 2nd layer of the FEL, while the 5th layer completes the mutation of BCC phase content.
