Recently, heterostructured materials offers a novel strategy for solving the longstanding dilemma of strength-ductility trade-off of metallic materials, that is, soft and hard domains with significant rheological stress difference are used as the basic units to orderly construct the heterostructure [ 1, 2]. Then, the strength-ductility synergy is obtained by additional strain hardening induced by the heterogeneous deformation [ 3]. Apparently, the heterostructure, such as gradient structure [ 4], bimodal structure [ 5] or layered structure [ 6], etc., should be controlled by appropriate methods for the desired size and architecture to obtain the satisfactory properties. To date, there are "top-down" [ 7] and "bottom-up" [ 8] routes for the fabrication of heterostructured materials. The former is mainly through mechanical deformation, for instance, surface mechanical grinding [ 9], ultrasonic surface rolling [ 10] or asynchronous rolling [ 7], etc., so as to achieve heterostructure. While the latter mainly involves the formation of multi-scale distribution of grains or phase components achieved through composition or architectural design [ 8]. Layered heterostructure possesses more architectural parameters, e.g., layer space, thickness, hardness and proportion of layers, etc., tailoring strength or plasticity across a wide range [ 11]. With the advancement of additive manufacturing (AM), the "layer-by-layer" approach inherently provides an advantage in the direct fabrication of layer heterostructured materials [ 12]. In these cases, the heterostructure should be mainly understood as the AM of multi-materials, such as CuSn10/SS316L [ 12], Al 2O 3/Ti [ 13], SS321/Ti6Al4V [ 14], Ti64/Ti64 + MEA [ 15] etc. However, due to variations in thermophysical properties, these heterogeneous materials exhibited some shortcomings, including low compatibility, interface defects, chemical reactions, etc. Recently, some researchers fabricated materials with layered distribution of grain sizes [ 16, 17] and phases [ 18] by AM combined with rolling methods, avoiding the problem of incompatibility between the heterogeneous materials, but this undoubtedly decreases the engineering applications of AM. Therefore, how to accurately control the phase ratio or grain size to achieve high quality layered heterostructure still remain as a problem. Given the above, if heterostructure composed of FCC and BCC phases with layered architecture is produced in the FeCoCrNiMn, taking advantage of the “layer-by-layer” manner of LPBF process, synergistic combination of strength and ductility might be expected. In this study, we demonstrated an interesting scheme for alloy preparation of dual powder-source alloy system based on the LPBF process. The as-built samples exhibit excellent strength-ductility balance, which attributes to the well-architectured layered heterostructure. Such dual-phase microstructure are rarely deployed in CoCrFeMnNi-based alloys, and the corresponding strain hardening mechanism for alloys with such layered structures has not been explored. Based on the preparation method and mechanical properties, two issues need to be clarified: How does the microstructure of the layered heterostructure with dual phase formed? Secondly, the deformation mechanisms of heterostructure alloys during tensile deformation process. In the following, the fabrication, microstructure, mechanical properties and deformation mechanism of the CoCrFeMnNi-based alloy system fabricated by LPBF were reported and analyzed through the combination of crystal plasticity finite element method (CPFEM) and experiment characterization. The DiMetal- 100H (Laser Additive Manufacturing GmbH, Guangzhou, China) was adopted for LPBF manufacturing, while the layered heterostructured alloys (LHA) were fabricated by melting three layers of Fe40 powder and five layers of Fe80 powder in a cycle along the build direction (BD), as described in Fig. 1g. All the layers were processed in orthogonal scan mode using the optimized parameters. i.e., laser power of 200 W, scanning speed of 800 mm/s, layer thickness of 30 μm and hatching space of 70 μm, respectively. The cuboid samples were processed into thin slices of dog bone-shaped tensile samples along the normal direction (ND) or transverse direction (TD) with a thickness of 1 mm by wire cutting ( Fig. 1h). In addition, the width of the corresponding gauge section is 2 mm and the length is 8 mm. The samples for microstructural analysis were sandpapered (200#-3000#) and polished using diamond suspension with particle size of 1 μm. The yield strength (YS), ultimate tensile strength (UTS) and elongation were determined for all tested samples. The loading-unloading-reloading tensile tests were performed on all samples to investigate the evolution of hetero-deformation induced (HDI) stresses during tensile straining. Moreover, the phase diagram was carried out by the CALPHAD calculation though graphical mode by the Thermo-Calc 2023a software coupled with TCHEA4 database, on basis of the global minimization of the Gibbs energy of the system. Finite Element Method (FEM) with crystal plasticity as constitutive model were performed to access the information of stress/strain evolution and slip activity for different layer in LHA. The basic principle of crystal plasticity is induced in Refs. [ 29, 30]. The shear strain rate formula based on the energy criterion which proposed by Hutchinson [ 31] was adopted. Since the different layers in LHA have significant differences in grain size, phase and orientation, a simple layered heterogeneous model was constructed by Neper [ 32] and given the corresponding random orientation. Finally, the simulation was carried out in ABAQUS/STANDARD®. For better presentation, the details of the model including the main parameters will be expressed in the discussion section together with the results. For comparison, no DT behavior was observed in Fe40 (with the same chemical composition with the FDL in LHA sample) even if at strain of 10 % ( Fig. 11b), while the excessively fine grains within the Fe80 sample also prevented the generation of DT ( Fig. 11d) [ 88]. With the increase of strain, the proportion of DT boundaries in the FCC matrix (FDL) increase from 32.2 % at the 5 % strain to 56.9 % at the 15 % strain, as shown in Fig. 15e. As shown in Fig. 15e, by observing the grain morphology and IPF of the individual grains in the FDL, the grain not only produces twirling, but also undergoes a deflective orientation. In general, due to different crystal structures and chemical compositions, FDL and FEL of LHA exhibit different mechanisms during deformation, respectively. FEL is dominated by dislocation slip, while FDL contains a large amount of DTs in addition to dislocation. Two factors are responsible for the premature DT behavior in the LHA, i.e. (i) Increasing Fe content in FeCoCrNiMn system results in significant decrease of stacking fault energy (SFE) [ 89]. (ii) Strain gradient induced by the heterostructured incompatibility during tensile deformation results in significant shear stress concentration at the layer interfaces [ 42]. The back stress exerted on the soft domain elevates the nominal stress beyond the loading stress. Ultimately, the local shear stress surpasses the threshold of the critical stress for twinning nucleation, resulting in the formation of DTs [ 90]. The appearance of high-density DTs introduce new interfaces to reduce the dislocation mean free path [ 91], and high-density GNDs aggregate at the BCC/FCC interface, resulting in superior hardening capacity ( Fig. 6b). Therefore, based on the above results and analysis, it can be considered that the difference between the CPFEM curve in Fig. 13and the experimental results is due to additional hardening mechanisms such as DT and GND strengthening, which were not considered in the simulation. According to Fig. 14a, the morphology of grains in FEL changes after deformation, indicating severe plastic deformation, while FDL presents a large number of DTs. As special grain boundaries, the formation of DTs releases local non-uniform stress, while also hindering dislocation slip, which require a larger driving force to cross the boundary [ 92]. Therefore, it can be assumed that this local twinning induced plasticity (TWIP) phenomenon at the interface increases the overall strength while also hindering the crack nucleation to improve the toughness. Interestingly, unlike the previous inter-layer difference ( Fig. 15a), the KAM distribution depicted in Fig. 16c indicates that the values within FDL and FEL are almost identical, and the quantitative calculation results are 9.27 × 10 14m −2and 1.25 × 10 15m −2, respectively. That is to say, in the final stage of deformation, the differences between FDL and FEL tend to be consistent, which is reflected in the fact that as a soft phase, FDL continuously generates GND through dislocations and DTs to adapt to the overall deformation [ 93, 94]. Subsequently, TEM was employed to explore the coordinated deformation behavior. Nano-twinning (NT) bundles were observed, as shown in Fig. 16d. These NTs are still in the propagation stage, intermediate between nucleation and thickening [ 95]. At this stage, dislocations can nucleate at the twin interface and slip parallel to the twin plane, which avoiding stress concentration caused by dislocation stacking and thus improving ductility [ 42]. Stacking faults were observed in the FCC phase, as shown in Fig. 16e. In addition, Lomer-Cottrell (L-C) lock could form when shockley partial dislocations cross along the same slip system, which were also observed in Fig. 16e. L-C locks not only act as a strong barrier to effectively immobilize dislocation motion, but can also act as a Frank-Read source for dislocation multiplication, leading to stable and progressive work hardening, which benefits UTS and plasticity [ 96]. In contrast, FEL with BCC phase was surrounded by dislocation forest and no other deformation mechanism was found, as depicted in Fig. 16f. Fig. 16g depicts the interface of the FCC and BCC phases, while the Kurdjumov-Sachs (KS) orientation relationship comprises a transition of [110]-FCC zone into [111]-BCC zone. Interestingly, nano-sized hexagonal close-packed (HCP) phase with width of 13.1 nm was observed, as shown in Fig. 16h and i. In general, the HCP phase is considered to be the transition phase from the TRIP process of FCC-BCC, which also known as the ε-martensite phase transition [ 23, 97]. However, the elongated HCP phase clearly does not fit the characteristics of the ε-martensitic phase transition. Owing to the intense shear strain at the layer interface, continuous slip of SFs within the FCC matrix could potentially result in the formation of a nano-sized HCP phase [ 98]. In other words, two plane-thickness (n = 2) stacking layers of dislocation act as HCP embryos [ 99], which typically occur in materials with low SFE [ 23]. Like SFs and DTs, the formation of those HCP phase is beneficial to alleviate the local stress concentration, thereby providing better ductility [ 100]. The schematic diagram of enhanced strength-ductility trade-off of LHA are summarized in Fig. 17. According to the WHR, the deformation of LHA can be divided into three stages. In stage I, due to the large activation of dislocations and the reduced rate of dislocation storage, the WHR exhibits a rapid decrease. GNDs and SFs were generated inside the soft domain (FCC) around the interface to coordinate the local strain gradient. Hard BCC layer also changed from the elastic stage to the elastoplastic stage, while the back stress induced by GNDs failed to completely offset the normal stress, and finally causing HDI strengthening [ 87]. In stage II, further deformation at the interface results in severe local shear strain, and DTs begin to produce and proliferate at these sites. Simultaneously, dislocations also start to produce within the hard BCC domain to coordinate the plastic deformation. These SFs and DTs hinder further dislocation motion, and the synergistic effect of HDI stress, resulting in additional hardening mechanism, which slows down the decrease of WHR. In stage III, as a result of the overall extensive deformation, dislocations, SFs, and DTs disperse throughout the entire FCC layer. The severe shear strain at the interface leads to the formation of nano-sized HCP phase and stronger HDI stress, which can effectively suppress the formation of necking and micro-cracks. In conclusion, the presence of SFs, DTs, NTs and nano-HCP phase adapts to the strain gradient at the interface and ultimately coordinates the overall deformation. In addition, the dislocation occlusion and back stress were the main mechanisms of HDI strengthening, which were the main reasons for the elevation of WHR. Recently, heterostructured materials offers a novel strategy for solving the longstanding dilemma of strength-ductility trade-off of metallic materials, that is, soft and hard domains with significant rheological stress difference are used as the basic units to orderly construct the heterostructure [ 1, 2]. Then, the strength-ductility synergy is obtained by additional strain hardening induced by the heterogeneous deformation [ 3]. Apparently, the heterostructure, such as gradient structure [ 4], bimodal structure [ 5] or layered structure [ 6], etc., should be controlled by appropriate methods for the desired size and architecture to obtain the satisfactory properties. To date, there are "top-down" [ 7] and "bottom-up" [ 8] routes for the fabrication of heterostructured materials. The former is mainly through mechanical deformation, for instance, surface mechanical grinding [ 9], ultrasonic surface rolling [ 10] or asynchronous rolling [ 7], etc., so as to achieve heterostructure. While the latter mainly involves the formation of multi-scale distribution of grains or phase components achieved through composition or architectural design [ 8]. Layered heterostructure possesses more architectural parameters, e.g., layer space, thickness, hardness and proportion of layers, etc., tailoring strength or plasticity across a wide range [ 11]. With the advancement of additive manufacturing (AM), the "layer-by-layer" approach inherently provides an advantage in the direct fabrication of layer heterostructured materials [ 12]. In these cases, the heterostructure should be mainly understood as the AM of multi-materials, such as CuSn10/SS316L [ 12], Al 2O 3/Ti [ 13], SS321/Ti6Al4V [ 14], Ti64/Ti64 + MEA [ 15] etc. However, due to variations in thermophysical properties, these heterogeneous materials exhibited some shortcomings, including low compatibility, interface defects, chemical reactions, etc. Recently, some researchers fabricated materials with layered distribution of grain sizes [ 16, 17] and phases [ 18] by AM combined with rolling methods, avoiding the problem of incompatibility between the heterogeneous materials, but this undoubtedly decreases the engineering applications of AM. Therefore, how to accurately control the phase ratio or grain size to achieve high quality layered heterostructure still remain as a problem. Given the above, if heterostructure composed of FCC and BCC phases with layered architecture is produced in the FeCoCrNiMn, taking advantage of the “layer-by-layer” manner of LPBF process, synergistic combination of strength and ductility might be expected. In this study, we demonstrated an interesting scheme for alloy preparation of dual powder-source alloy system based on the LPBF process. The as-built samples exhibit excellent strength-ductility balance, which attributes to the well-architectured layered heterostructure. Such dual-phase microstructure are rarely deployed in CoCrFeMnNi-based alloys, and the corresponding strain hardening mechanism for alloys with such layered structures has not been explored. Based on the preparation method and mechanical properties, two issues need to be clarified: How does the microstructure of the layered heterostructure with dual phase formed? Secondly, the deformation mechanisms of heterostructure alloys during tensile deformation process. In the following, the fabrication, microstructure, mechanical properties and deformation mechanism of the CoCrFeMnNi-based alloy system fabricated by LPBF were reported and analyzed through the combination of crystal plasticity finite element method (CPFEM) and experiment characterization. The DiMetal- 100H (Laser Additive Manufacturing GmbH, Guangzhou, China) was adopted for LPBF manufacturing, while the layered heterostructured alloys (LHA) were fabricated by melting three layers of Fe40 powder and five layers of Fe80 powder in a cycle along the build direction (BD), as described in Fig. 1g. All the layers were processed in orthogonal scan mode using the optimized parameters. i.e., laser power of 200 W, scanning speed of 800 mm/s, layer thickness of 30 μm and hatching space of 70 μm, respectively. The cuboid samples were processed into thin slices of dog bone-shaped tensile samples along the normal direction (ND) or transverse direction (TD) with a thickness of 1 mm by wire cutting ( Fig. 1h). In addition, the width of the corresponding gauge section is 2 mm and the length is 8 mm. The samples for microstructural analysis were sandpapered (200#-3000#) and polished using diamond suspension with particle size of 1 μm. The yield strength (YS), ultimate tensile strength (UTS) and elongation were determined for all tested samples. The loading-unloading-reloading tensile tests were performed on all samples to investigate the evolution of hetero-deformation induced (HDI) stresses during tensile straining. Moreover, the phase diagram was carried out by the CALPHAD calculation though graphical mode by the Thermo-Calc 2023a software coupled with TCHEA4 database, on basis of the global minimization of the Gibbs energy of the system. Finite Element Method (FEM) with crystal plasticity as constitutive model were performed to access the information of stress/strain evolution and slip activity for different layer in LHA. The basic principle of crystal plasticity is induced in Refs. [ 29, 30]. The shear strain rate formula based on the energy criterion which proposed by Hutchinson [ 31] was adopted. Since the different layers in LHA have significant differences in grain size, phase and orientation, a simple layered heterogeneous model was constructed by Neper [ 32] and given the corresponding random orientation. Finally, the simulation was carried out in ABAQUS/STANDARD®. For better presentation, the details of the model including the main parameters will be expressed in the discussion section together with the results. Hard BCC layer also changed from the elastic stage to the elastoplastic stage, while the back stress induced by GNDs failed to completely offset the normal stress, and finally causing HDI strengthening [ 87]. In stage II, further deformation at the interface results in severe local shear strain, and DTs begin to produce and proliferate at these sites. Simultaneously, dislocations also start to produce within the hard BCC domain to coordinate the plastic deformation. These SFs and DTs hinder further dislocation motion, and the synergistic effect of HDI stress, resulting in additional hardening mechanism, which slows down the decrease of WHR. In stage III, as a result of the overall extensive deformation, dislocations, SFs, and DTs disperse throughout the entire FCC layer. The severe shear strain at the interface leads to the formation of nano-sized HCP phase and stronger HDI stress, which can effectively suppress the formation of necking and micro-cracks. Recently, heterostructured materials offers a novel strategy for solving the longstanding dilemma of strength-ductility trade-off of metallic materials, that is, soft and hard domains with significant rheological stress difference are used as the basic units to orderly construct the heterostructure [ 1, 2]. Then, the strength-ductility synergy is obtained by additional strain hardening induced by the heterogeneous deformation [ 3]. Apparently, the heterostructure, such as gradient structure [ 4], bimodal structure [ 5] or layered structure [ 6], etc., should be controlled by appropriate methods for the desired size and architecture to obtain the satisfactory properties. To date, there are "top-down" [ 7] and "bottom-up" [ 8] routes for the fabrication of heterostructured materials. The former is mainly through mechanical deformation, for instance, surface mechanical grinding [ 9], ultrasonic surface rolling [ 10] or asynchronous rolling [ 7], etc., so as to achieve heterostructure. While the latter mainly involves the formation of multi-scale distribution of grains or phase components achieved through composition or architectural design [ 8]. Layered heterostructure possesses more architectural parameters, e.g., layer space, thickness, hardness and proportion of layers, etc., tailoring strength or plasticity across a wide range [ 11]. With the advancement of additive manufacturing (AM), the "layer-by-layer" approach inherently provides an advantage in the direct fabrication of layer heterostructured materials [ 12]. In these cases, the heterostructure should be mainly understood as the AM of multi-materials, such as CuSn10/SS316L [ 12], Al 2O 3/Ti [ 13], SS321/Ti6Al4V [ 14], Ti64/Ti64 + MEA [ 15] etc. However, due to variations in thermophysical properties, these heterogeneous materials exhibited some shortcomings, including low compatibility, interface defects, chemical reactions, etc. Recently, some researchers fabricated materials with layered distribution of grain sizes [ 16, 17] and phases [ 18] by AM combined with rolling methods, avoiding the problem of incompatibility between the heterogeneous materials, but this undoubtedly decreases the engineering applications of AM. Therefore, how to accurately control the phase ratio or grain size to achieve high quality layered heterostructure still remain as a problem. Given the above, if heterostructure composed of FCC and BCC phases with layered architecture is produced in the FeCoCrNiMn, taking advantage of the “layer-by-layer” manner of LPBF process, synergistic combination of strength and ductility might be expected. In this study, we demonstrated an interesting scheme for alloy preparation of dual powder-source alloy system based on the LPBF process. The as-built samples exhibit excellent strength-ductility balance, which attributes to the well-architectured layered heterostructure. Such dual-phase microstructure are rarely deployed in CoCrFeMnNi-based alloys, and the corresponding strain hardening mechanism for alloys with such layered structures has not been explored. Based on the preparation method and mechanical properties, two issues need to be clarified: How does the microstructure of the layered heterostructure with dual phase formed? Secondly, the deformation mechanisms of heterostructure alloys during tensile deformation process. In the following, the fabrication, microstructure, mechanical properties and deformation mechanism of the CoCrFeMnNi-based alloy system fabricated by LPBF were reported and analyzed through the combination of crystal plasticity finite element method (CPFEM) and experiment characterization. The DiMetal- 100H (Laser Additive Manufacturing GmbH, Guangzhou, China) was adopted for LPBF manufacturing, while the layered heterostructured alloys (LHA) were fabricated by melting three layers of Fe40 powder and five layers of Fe80 powder in a cycle along the build direction (BD), as described in Fig. 1g. All the layers were processed in orthogonal scan mode using the optimized parameters. i.e., laser power of 200 W, scanning speed of 800 mm/s, layer thickness of 30 μm and hatching space of 70 μm, respectively. The cuboid samples were processed into thin slices of dog bone-shaped tensile samples along the normal direction (ND) or transverse direction (TD) with a thickness of 1 mm by wire cutting ( Fig. 1h). In addition, the width of the corresponding gauge section is 2 mm and the length is 8 mm. The samples for microstructural analysis were sandpapered (200#-3000#) and polished using diamond suspension with particle size of 1 μm. The yield strength (YS), ultimate tensile strength (UTS) and elongation were determined for all tested samples. The loading-unloading-reloading tensile tests were performed on all samples to investigate the evolution of hetero-deformation induced (HDI) stresses during tensile straining. Moreover, the phase diagram was carried out by the CALPHAD calculation though graphical mode by the Thermo-Calc 2023a software coupled with TCHEA4 database, on basis of the global minimization of the Gibbs energy of the system. Finite Element Method (FEM) with crystal plasticity as constitutive model were performed to access the information of stress/strain evolution and slip activity for different layer in LHA. The basic principle of crystal plasticity is induced in Refs. [ 29, 30]. The shear strain rate formula based on the energy criterion which proposed by Hutchinson [ 31] was adopted. Since the different layers in LHA have significant differences in grain size, phase and orientation, a simple layered heterogeneous model was constructed by Neper [ 32] and given the corresponding random orientation. Finally, the simulation was carried out in ABAQUS/STANDARD®. For better presentation, the details of the model including the main parameters will be expressed in the discussion section together with the results. Hard BCC layer also changed from the elastic stage to the elastoplastic stage, while the back stress induced by GNDs failed to completely offset the normal stress, and finally causing HDI strengthening [ 87]. In stage II, further deformation at the interface results in severe local shear strain, and DTs begin to produce and proliferate at these sites. Simultaneously, dislocations also start to produce within the hard BCC domain to coordinate the plastic deformation. These SFs and DTs hinder further dislocation motion, and the synergistic effect of HDI stress, resulting in additional hardening mechanism, which slows down the decrease of WHR. In stage III, as a result of the overall extensive deformation, dislocations, SFs, and DTs disperse throughout the entire FCC layer. The severe shear strain at the interface leads to the formation of nano-sized HCP phase and stronger HDI stress, which can effectively suppress the formation of necking and micro-cracks. In conclusion, the presence of SFs, DTs, NTs and nano-HCP phase adapts to the strain gradient at the interface and ultimately coordinates the overall deformation. Recently, heterostructured materials offers a novel strategy for solving the longstanding dilemma of strength-ductility trade-off of metallic materials, that is, soft and hard domains with significant rheological stress difference are used as the basic units to orderly construct the heterostructure [ 1, 2]. Then, the strength-ductility synergy is obtained by additional strain hardening induced by the heterogeneous deformation [ 3]. Apparently, the heterostructure, such as gradient structure [ 4], bimodal structure [ 5] or layered structure [ 6], etc., should be controlled by appropriate methods for the desired size and architecture to obtain the satisfactory properties. To date, there are "top-down" [ 7] and "bottom-up" [ 8] routes for the fabrication of heterostructured materials. The former is mainly through mechanical deformation, for instance, surface mechanical grinding [ 9], ultrasonic surface rolling [ 10] or asynchronous rolling [ 7], etc., so as to achieve heterostructure. While the latter mainly involves the formation of multi-scale distribution of grains or phase components achieved through composition or architectural design [ 8]. Layered heterostructure possesses more architectural parameters, e.g., layer space, thickness, hardness and proportion of layers, etc., tailoring strength or plasticity across a wide range [ 11]. With the advancement of additive manufacturing (AM), the "layer-by-layer" approach inherently provides an advantage in the direct fabrication of layer heterostructured materials [ 12]. In these cases, the heterostructure should be mainly understood as the AM of multi-materials, such as CuSn10/SS316L [ 12], Al 2O 3/Ti [ 13], SS321/Ti6Al4V [ 14], Ti64/Ti64 + MEA [ 15] etc. However, due to variations in thermophysical properties, these heterogeneous materials exhibited some shortcomings, including low compatibility, interface defects, chemical reactions, etc. Recently, some researchers fabricated materials with layered distribution of grain sizes [ 16, 17] and phases [ 18] by AM combined with rolling methods, avoiding the problem of incompatibility between the heterogeneous materials, but this undoubtedly decreases the engineering applications of AM. Therefore, how to accurately control the phase ratio or grain size to achieve high quality layered heterostructure still remain as a problem. Given the above, if heterostructure composed of FCC and BCC phases with layered architecture is produced in the FeCoCrNiMn, taking advantage of the “layer-by-layer” manner of LPBF process, synergistic combination of strength and ductility might be expected. In this study, we demonstrated an interesting scheme for alloy preparation of dual powder-source alloy system based on the LPBF process. The as-built samples exhibit excellent strength-ductility balance, which attributes to the well-architectured layered heterostructure. Such dual-phase microstructure are rarely deployed in CoCrFeMnNi-based alloys, and the corresponding strain hardening mechanism for alloys with such layered structures has not been explored. Based on the preparation method and mechanical properties, two issues need to be clarified: How does the microstructure of the layered heterostructure with dual phase formed? Secondly, the deformation mechanisms of heterostructure alloys during tensile deformation process. In the following, the fabrication, microstructure, mechanical properties and deformation mechanism of the CoCrFeMnNi-based alloy system fabricated by LPBF were reported and analyzed through the combination of crystal plasticity finite element method (CPFEM) and experiment characterization. The DiMetal- 100H (Laser Additive Manufacturing GmbH, Guangzhou, China) was adopted for LPBF manufacturing, while the layered heterostructured alloys (LHA) were fabricated by melting three layers of Fe40 powder and five layers of Fe80 powder in a cycle along the build direction (BD), as described in Fig. 1g. All the layers were processed in orthogonal scan mode using the optimized parameters. i.e., laser power of 200 W, scanning speed of 800 mm/s, layer thickness of 30 μm and hatching space of 70 μm, respectively. The cuboid samples were processed into thin slices of dog bone-shaped tensile samples along the normal direction (ND) or transverse direction (TD) with a thickness of 1 mm by wire cutting ( Fig. 1h). In addition, the width of the corresponding gauge section is 2 mm and the length is 8 mm. The samples for microstructural analysis were sandpapered (200#-3000#) and polished using diamond suspension with particle size of 1 μm. The yield strength (YS), ultimate tensile strength (UTS) and elongation were determined for all tested samples. The loading-unloading-reloading tensile tests were performed on all samples to investigate the evolution of hetero-deformation induced (HDI) stresses during tensile straining. Moreover, the phase diagram was carried out by the CALPHAD calculation though graphical mode by the Thermo-Calc 2023a software coupled with TCHEA4 database, on basis of the global minimization of the Gibbs energy of the system. Finite Element Method (FEM) with crystal plasticity as constitutive model were performed to access the information of stress/strain evolution and slip activity for different layer in LHA. The basic principle of crystal plasticity is induced in Refs. [ 29, 30]. The shear strain rate formula based on the energy criterion which proposed by Hutchinson [ 31] was adopted. Since the different layers in LHA have significant differences in grain size, phase and orientation, a simple layered heterogeneous model was constructed by Neper [ 32] and given the corresponding random orientation. Finally, the simulation was carried out in ABAQUS/STANDARD®. In stage I, due to the large activation of dislocations and the reduced rate of dislocation storage, the WHR exhibits a rapid decrease. GNDs and SFs were generated inside the soft domain (FCC) around the interface to coordinate the local strain gradient. Hard BCC layer also changed from the elastic stage to the elastoplastic stage, while the back stress induced by GNDs failed to completely offset the normal stress, and finally causing HDI strengthening [ 87]. In stage II, further deformation at the interface results in severe local shear strain, and DTs begin to produce and proliferate at these sites. Simultaneously, dislocations also start to produce within the hard BCC domain to coordinate the plastic deformation. These SFs and DTs hinder further dislocation motion, and the synergistic effect of HDI stress, resulting in additional hardening mechanism, which slows down the decrease of WHR. In stage III, as a result of the overall extensive deformation, dislocations, SFs, and DTs disperse throughout the entire FCC layer. The severe shear strain at the interface leads to the formation of nano-sized HCP phase and stronger HDI stress, which can effectively suppress the formation of necking and micro-cracks. In conclusion, the presence of SFs, DTs, NTs and nano-HCP phase adapts to the strain gradient at the interface and ultimately coordinates the overall deformation. Recently, heterostructured materials offers a novel strategy for solving the longstanding dilemma of strength-ductility trade-off of metallic materials, that is, soft and hard domains with significant rheological stress difference are used as the basic units to orderly construct the heterostructure [ 1, 2]. Then, the strength-ductility synergy is obtained by additional strain hardening induced by the heterogeneous deformation [ 3]. Apparently, the heterostructure, such as gradient structure [ 4], bimodal structure [ 5] or layered structure [ 6], etc., should be controlled by appropriate methods for the desired size and architecture to obtain the satisfactory properties. To date, there are "top-down" [ 7] and "bottom-up" [ 8] routes for the fabrication of heterostructured materials. The former is mainly through mechanical deformation, for instance, surface mechanical grinding [ 9], ultrasonic surface rolling [ 10] or asynchronous rolling [ 7], etc., so as to achieve heterostructure. While the latter mainly involves the formation of multi-scale distribution of grains or phase components achieved through composition or architectural design [ 8]. Layered heterostructure possesses more architectural parameters, e.g., layer space, thickness, hardness and proportion of layers, etc., tailoring strength or plasticity across a wide range [ 11]. With the advancement of additive manufacturing (AM), the "layer-by-layer" approach inherently provides an advantage in the direct fabrication of layer heterostructured materials [ 12]. In these cases, the heterostructure should be mainly understood as the AM of multi-materials, such as CuSn10/SS316L [ 12], Al 2O 3/Ti [ 13], SS321/Ti6Al4V [ 14], Ti64/Ti64 + MEA [ 15] etc. However, due to variations in thermophysical properties, these heterogeneous materials exhibited some shortcomings, including low compatibility, interface defects, chemical reactions, etc. Recently, some researchers fabricated materials with layered distribution of grain sizes [ 16, 17] and phases [ 18] by AM combined with rolling methods, avoiding the problem of incompatibility between the heterogeneous materials, but this undoubtedly decreases the engineering applications of AM. Therefore, how to accurately control the phase ratio or grain size to achieve high quality layered heterostructure still remain as a problem. Given the above, if heterostructure composed of FCC and BCC phases with layered architecture is produced in the FeCoCrNiMn, taking advantage of the “layer-by-layer” manner of LPBF process, synergistic combination of strength and ductility might be expected. In this study, we demonstrated an interesting scheme for alloy preparation of dual powder-source alloy system based on the LPBF process. The as-built samples exhibit excellent strength-ductility balance, which attributes to the well-architectured layered heterostructure. Such dual-phase microstructure are rarely deployed in CoCrFeMnNi-based alloys, and the corresponding strain hardening mechanism for alloys with such layered structures has not been explored. Based on the preparation method and mechanical properties, two issues need to be clarified: How does the microstructure of the layered heterostructure with dual phase formed? Secondly, the deformation mechanisms of heterostructure alloys during tensile deformation process. In the following, the fabrication, microstructure, mechanical properties and deformation mechanism of the CoCrFeMnNi-based alloy system fabricated by LPBF were reported and analyzed through the combination of crystal plasticity finite element method (CPFEM) and experiment characterization. The DiMetal- 100H (Laser Additive Manufacturing GmbH, Guangzhou, China) was adopted for LPBF manufacturing, while the layered heterostructured alloys (LHA) were fabricated by melting three layers of Fe40 powder and five layers of Fe80 powder in a cycle along the build direction (BD), as described in Fig. 1g. All the layers were processed in orthogonal scan mode using the optimized parameters. i.e., laser power of 200 W, scanning speed of 800 mm/s, layer thickness of 30 μm and hatching space of 70 μm, respectively. The cuboid samples were processed into thin slices of dog bone-shaped tensile samples along the normal direction (ND) or transverse direction (TD) with a thickness of 1 mm by wire cutting ( Fig. 1h). In addition, the width of the corresponding gauge section is 2 mm and the length is 8 mm. The samples for microstructural analysis were sandpapered (200#-3000#) and polished using diamond suspension with particle size of 1 μm. The yield strength (YS), ultimate tensile strength (UTS) and elongation were determined for all tested samples. The loading-unloading-reloading tensile tests were performed on all samples to investigate the evolution of hetero-deformation induced (HDI) stresses during tensile straining. Moreover, the phase diagram was carried out by the CALPHAD calculation though graphical mode by the Thermo-Calc 2023a software coupled with TCHEA4 database, on basis of the global minimization of the Gibbs energy of the system. Finite Element Method (FEM) with crystal plasticity as constitutive model were performed to access the information of stress/strain evolution and slip activity for different layer in LHA. The basic principle of crystal plasticity is induced in Refs. [ 29, 30]. The shear strain rate formula based on the energy criterion which proposed by Hutchinson [ 31] was adopted. Since the different layers in LHA have significant differences in grain size, phase and orientation, a simple layered heterogeneous model was constructed by Neper [ 32] and given the corresponding random orientation. Finally, the simulation was carried out in ABAQUS/STANDARD®. For better presentation, the details of the model including the main parameters will be expressed in the discussion section together with the results. The appearance of high-density DTs introduce new interfaces to reduce the dislocation mean free path [ 91], and high-density GNDs aggregate at the BCC/FCC interface, resulting in superior hardening capacity ( Fig. 6b). Therefore, based on the above results and analysis, it can be considered that the difference between the CPFEM curve in Fig. 13and the experimental results is due to additional hardening mechanisms such as DT and GND strengthening, which were not considered in the simulation. The region of interest of the fractured LHA (strain = 22 %) sample was selected for further observations, and a typically interface region was shown in Fig. 16a-c. According to Fig. 14a, the morphology of grains in FEL changes after deformation, indicating severe plastic deformation, while FDL presents a large number of DTs. As special grain boundaries, the formation of DTs releases local non-uniform stress, while also hindering dislocation slip, which require a larger driving force to cross the boundary [ 92]. Therefore, it can be assumed that this local twinning induced plasticity (TWIP) phenomenon at the interface increases the overall strength while also hindering the crack nucleation to improve the toughness. Interestingly, unlike the previous inter-layer difference ( Fig. 15a), the KAM distribution depicted in Fig. 16c indicates that the values within FDL and FEL are almost identical, and the quantitative calculation results are 9.27 × 10 14m −2and 1.25 × 10 15m −2, respectively. That is to say, in the final stage of deformation, the differences between FDL and FEL tend to be consistent, which is reflected in the fact that as a soft phase, FDL continuously generates GND through dislocations and DTs to adapt to the overall deformation [ 93, 94]. Subsequently, TEM was employed to explore the coordinated deformation behavior. Nano-twinning (NT) bundles were observed, as shown in Fig. 16d. These NTs are still in the propagation stage, intermediate between nucleation and thickening [ 95]. At this stage, dislocations can nucleate at the twin interface and slip parallel to the twin plane, which avoiding stress concentration caused by dislocation stacking and thus improving ductility [ 42]. Stacking faults were observed in the FCC phase, as shown in Fig. 16e. In addition, Lomer-Cottrell (L-C) lock could form when shockley partial dislocations cross along the same slip system, which were also observed in Fig. 16e. L-C locks not only act as a strong barrier to effectively immobilize dislocation motion, but can also act as a Frank-Read source for dislocation multiplication, leading to stable and progressive work hardening, which benefits UTS and plasticity [ 96]. In contrast, FEL with BCC phase was surrounded by dislocation forest and no other deformation mechanism was found, as depicted in Fig. 16f. Fig. 16g depicts the interface of the FCC and BCC phases, while the Kurdjumov-Sachs (KS) orientation relationship comprises a transition of [110]-FCC zone into [111]-BCC zone. Interestingly, nano-sized hexagonal close-packed (HCP) phase with width of 13.1 nm was observed, as shown in Fig. 16h and i. In general, the HCP phase is considered to be the transition phase from the TRIP process of FCC-BCC, which also known as the ε-martensite phase transition [ 23, 97]. However, the elongated HCP phase clearly does not fit the characteristics of the ε-martensitic phase transition. Owing to the intense shear strain at the layer interface, continuous slip of SFs within the FCC matrix could potentially result in the formation of a nano-sized HCP phase [ 98]. In other words, two plane-thickness (n = 2) stacking layers of dislocation act as HCP embryos [ 99], which typically occur in materials with low SFE [ 23]. Like SFs and DTs, the formation of those HCP phase is beneficial to alleviate the local stress concentration, thereby providing better ductility [ 100]. The schematic diagram of enhanced strength-ductility trade-off of LHA are summarized in Fig. 17. According to the WHR, the deformation of LHA can be divided into three stages. In stage I, due to the large activation of dislocations and the reduced rate of dislocation storage, the WHR exhibits a rapid decrease. GNDs and SFs were generated inside the soft domain (FCC) around the interface to coordinate the local strain gradient. Hard BCC layer also changed from the elastic stage to the elastoplastic stage, while the back stress induced by GNDs failed to completely offset the normal stress, and finally causing HDI strengthening [ 87]. In stage II, further deformation at the interface results in severe local shear strain, and DTs begin to produce and proliferate at these sites. Simultaneously, dislocations also start to produce within the hard BCC domain to coordinate the plastic deformation. These SFs and DTs hinder further dislocation motion, and the synergistic effect of HDI stress, resulting in additional hardening mechanism, which slows down the decrease of WHR. In stage III, as a result of the overall extensive deformation, dislocations, SFs, and DTs disperse throughout the entire FCC layer. The severe shear strain at the interface leads to the formation of nano-sized HCP phase and stronger HDI stress, which can effectively suppress the formation of necking and micro-cracks. In conclusion, the presence of SFs, DTs, NTs and nano-HCP phase adapts to the strain gradient at the interface and ultimately coordinates the overall deformation. In addition, the dislocation occlusion and back stress were the main mechanisms of HDI strengthening, which were the main reasons for the elevation of WHR. Recently, heterostructured materials offers a novel strategy for solving the longstanding dilemma of strength-ductility trade-off of metallic materials, that is, soft and hard domains with significant rheological stress difference are used as the basic units to orderly construct the heterostructure [ 1, 2]. Then, the strength-ductility synergy is obtained by additional strain hardening induced by the heterogeneous deformation [ 3]. Apparently, the heterostructure, such as gradient structure [ 4], bimodal structure [ 5] or layered structure [ 6], etc., should be controlled by appropriate methods for the desired size and architecture to obtain the satisfactory properties. To date, there are "top-down" [ 7] and "bottom-up" [ 8] routes for the fabrication of heterostructured materials. The former is mainly through mechanical deformation, for instance, surface mechanical grinding [ 9], ultrasonic surface rolling [ 10] or asynchronous rolling [ 7], etc., so as to achieve heterostructure. While the latter mainly involves the formation of multi-scale distribution of grains or phase components achieved through composition or architectural design [ 8]. Layered heterostructure possesses more architectural parameters, e.g., layer space, thickness, hardness and proportion of layers, etc., tailoring strength or plasticity across a wide range [ 11]. With the advancement of additive manufacturing (AM), the "layer-by-layer" approach inherently provides an advantage in the direct fabrication of layer heterostructured materials [ 12]. In these cases, the heterostructure should be mainly understood as the AM of multi-materials, such as CuSn10/SS316L [ 12], Al 2O 3/Ti [ 13], SS321/Ti6Al4V [ 14], Ti64/Ti64 + MEA [ 15] etc. However, due to variations in thermophysical properties, these heterogeneous materials exhibited some shortcomings, including low compatibility, interface defects, chemical reactions, etc. Recently, some researchers fabricated materials with layered distribution of grain sizes [ 16, 17] and phases [ 18] by AM combined with rolling methods, avoiding the problem of incompatibility between the heterogeneous materials, but this undoubtedly decreases the engineering applications of AM. Therefore, how to accurately control the phase ratio or grain size to achieve high quality layered heterostructure still remain as a problem. Given the above, if heterostructure composed of FCC and BCC phases with layered architecture is produced in the FeCoCrNiMn, taking advantage of the “layer-by-layer” manner of LPBF process, synergistic combination of strength and ductility might be expected. In this study, we demonstrated an interesting scheme for alloy preparation of dual powder-source alloy system based on the LPBF process. The as-built samples exhibit excellent strength-ductility balance, which attributes to the well-architectured layered heterostructure. Such dual-phase microstructure are rarely deployed in CoCrFeMnNi-based alloys, and the corresponding strain hardening mechanism for alloys with such layered structures has not been explored. Based on the preparation method and mechanical properties, two issues need to be clarified: How does the microstructure of the layered heterostructure with dual phase formed? Secondly, the deformation mechanisms of heterostructure alloys during tensile deformation process. In the following, the fabrication, microstructure, mechanical properties and deformation mechanism of the CoCrFeMnNi-based alloy system fabricated by LPBF were reported and analyzed through the combination of crystal plasticity finite element method (CPFEM) and experiment characterization. The DiMetal- 100H (Laser Additive Manufacturing GmbH, Guangzhou, China) was adopted for LPBF manufacturing, while the layered heterostructured alloys (LHA) were fabricated by melting three layers of Fe40 powder and five layers of Fe80 powder in a cycle along the build direction (BD), as described in Fig. 1g. All the layers were processed in orthogonal scan mode using the optimized parameters. i.e., laser power of 200 W, scanning speed of 800 mm/s, layer thickness of 30 μm and hatching space of 70 μm, respectively. The cuboid samples were processed into thin slices of dog bone-shaped tensile samples along the normal direction (ND) or transverse direction (TD) with a thickness of 1 mm by wire cutting ( Fig. 1h). In addition, the width of the corresponding gauge section is 2 mm and the length is 8 mm. The samples for microstructural analysis were sandpapered (200#-3000#) and polished using diamond suspension with particle size of 1 μm. The yield strength (YS), ultimate tensile strength (UTS) and elongation were determined for all tested samples. The loading-unloading-reloading tensile tests were performed on all samples to investigate the evolution of hetero-deformation induced (HDI) stresses during tensile straining. Moreover, the phase diagram was carried out by the CALPHAD calculation though graphical mode by the Thermo-Calc 2023a software coupled with TCHEA4 database, on basis of the global minimization of the Gibbs energy of the system. Finite Element Method (FEM) with crystal plasticity as constitutive model were performed to access the information of stress/strain evolution and slip activity for different layer in LHA. The basic principle of crystal plasticity is induced in Refs. [ 29, 30]. The shear strain rate formula based on the energy criterion which proposed by Hutchinson [ 31] was adopted. Since the different layers in LHA have significant differences in grain size, phase and orientation, a simple layered heterogeneous model was constructed by Neper [ 32] and given the corresponding random orientation. Finally, the simulation was carried out in ABAQUS/STANDARD®. For better presentation, the details of the model including the main parameters will be expressed in the discussion section together with the results. Based on the grain size distribution of LHA in Fig. 4f, a simplified layered heterostructured polycrystalline model with a size of 700 × 500 μm 2was developed, as shown in Fig. 13a. A polycrystalline representative volume cell (RVE) with 610 grains, consisting of 14,000 plane-strain finite elements (CPE4), was used in the simulations. In addition, the coarse-grained and fine-grained layers are defined as FCC and BCC structures, which correspond to FDL and FEL of LHA, respectively. To prevent rigid body displacement, the upper part of the model was fixed and a uniform tensile load was applied below. Homogeneous Fe40 and Fe80 models with corresponding grain size and structure were built prior to LHA implementation of tensile, and parameters were obtained by trial and error on the basis of FeCoCrNiMn [ 74] and pure Fe [ 75], respectively, as shown in Table 2, where C11, C12, C44, γ˙0, h0, τ0, τsand qare elastic constants, reference strain rate, initial hardening moduli, initial critical resolved shear stress (CRSS), saturation stress and hardening coefficient, respectively. Fig. 13b shows the comparison of simulation and experimental tensile data at the strain rate of 0.001/s. Among them, the simulation and experimental comparison results of Fe40 and Fe80 achieved satisfactory agreement. Since damage was not considered, the strain hardening of Fe80 was not attenuated at higher strains. However, the strength and hardening obtained by assigning the parameters of Fe40 and Fe80 to the LHA model were still lower than the experimental results, even though the damage of Fe80 was not considered. Considering that other deformation mechanisms such as DT, HDI strengthening, etc. are not considered in the simulation, the above reasons will be explained in the follow-up. Here, we only research the stress and strain distributions under layered heterostructure for subsequent discussion. Fig. 13c 1-e 1present the Von Mises stress distribution from 5 % to 15 % strain. As hard layer, the FEL bears the main stress [ 76], whereas depending on the crystal orientation, the Mises stress is not uniform within the FEL [ 77, 78]. With the increase of macroscopic strain, the high-stress region in the FEL gradually increased, while the stress in the FDL was significantly different from that in the FEL. In addition, microscopic strain localizations occurred with the increasing of strain, resulting in many dispersed and crossed strain bands. Those discrete shear bands were developed at about 45° to the tensile direction and present like the shape of "X", as shown in Fig. 13c 2-e 2. Such high-density and tightly spaced X-shaped shear bands occurred in many metal-layered composite materials [ 79-81]. The hardening behavior of different layers during deformation leads to local necking and eventually induces strain redistribution (X-shaped shear bands) [ 82], which can effectively delay the macroscopic strain concentration [ 83]. For further insight into the inter-layer hardening mechanism of LHA under tensile loading, a quasi-in situ laser confocal characterization was performed and the results are shown in Fig. 14. Fig. 14a 1-c 1indicates that hard layers (FEL) in LHA sample gradually protruded, while the height difference between FEL and FDL expanded with the increase of tensile strain (5 %-15 %). The average height difference expanded from 4.2 μm at 5 % to 26.7 μm at 15 %. In addition, the high magnification confocal gray-scale images indicate that the slip lines were already present even at 5 % strain and further proliferated with strain increasing, as shown in Fig. 14a 2-c 2. For an accessible description of the stress and strain distribution during plastic deformation of LHA, Fig. 14d 1shows the simplest model of a laminate structure with a soft layer sandwiched between two hard layers. During plastic deformation, the hard layer (FEL) bearing the stress and shrinking faster than the soft layer [ 84]. That is, the soft layer (FDL) needs to support the unstable FEL by generating higher strain hardening through its own deformation, which manifests as a large number of proliferating slip lines, as shown in Fig. 14d 2. Thus, the FEL is subjected to the normal tensile (positive) stress in the X direction, while the FDL is the normal compressive (negative) stress, which forms the interlayer deformation incompatibility, manifested as the protrusion of the FEL and further plastic deformation of the FDL. The above simulation and experiment results have shown that stress and strain incompatibility does occur during the tensile strain of LHA. For more microscopic deformation mechanism, quasi in-situEBSD analyses were performed at the same location on the gauge plane of LHA tensile samples subjected to strains of 0 %, 5 %, 10 % and 15 %, as depicted in Fig. 15. The EBSD-KAM images ( Fig. 15a 1-a 4) corresponding to different strains exhibited the increasing KAM value with tensile strains, suggesting an accumulation of geometrically necessary dislocations (GNDs). With increasing strain, the region with high KAM gradually spreads towards the layer interfaces, and finally penetrates into the low-strength FCC layer when ε = 15 % ( Fig. 15 a 4). The GND density of FDL increased from 1.56 × 10 14m −2to 2.71 × 10 14m −2under different strains (0 %-15 %), indicating a slow upward trend, as shown in Fig. 15b. However, the GND density of FEL has more than doubled from 4.51 × 10 14m −2to 9.68 × 10 14m −2, indicating that FEL was the main stress-bearing layer in deformation, while the main role of FDL was to coordinate deformation. In addition, it is worth noting that the width of the low KAM (original FDL) layer narrowed from 170 μm to 135 μm after deformation, and high KAM regions were observed at the layer interface, as shown by the dotted line in Fig. 15a 1and a 4. Due to the mismatch between strength and plastic deformation ability, the layer interface is the main stress concentration area during deformation [ 85], where the soft layer (FDL) generates back stress and the hard layer (FEL) generates normal stress [ 86]. Back and normal stresses do not cancel each other out overall, and together they produce HDI reinforcement to improve YS [ 87], while the higher KAM values at the interface in LHA indicate the presence of strengthening. To characterize the evolution of deformation twins (DTs) in LHA, high-magnification EBSD characterization of the layer boundary was implemented, as shown in Fig. 15d 1-d 3. Interestingly, DTs were formed in the FCC matrix even if at strain of 5 %. For comparison, no DT behavior was observed in Fe40 (with the same chemical composition with the FDL in LHA sample) even if at strain of 10 % ( Fig. 11b), while the excessively fine grains within the Fe80 sample also prevented the generation of DT ( Fig. 11d) [ 88]. With the increase of strain, the proportion of DT boundaries in the FCC matrix (FDL) increase from 32.2 % at the 5 % strain to 56.9 % at the 15 % strain, as shown in Fig. 15e. As shown in Fig. 15e, by observing the grain morphology and IPF of the individual grains in the FDL, the grain not only produces twirling, but also undergoes a deflective orientation. In general, due to different crystal structures and chemical compositions, FDL and FEL of LHA exhibit different mechanisms during deformation, respectively. FEL is dominated by dislocation slip, while FDL contains a large amount of DTs in addition to dislocation. Two factors are responsible for the premature DT behavior in the LHA, i.e. (i) Increasing Fe content in FeCoCrNiMn system results in significant decrease of stacking fault energy (SFE) [ 89]. (ii) Strain gradient induced by the heterostructured incompatibility during tensile deformation results in significant shear stress concentration at the layer interfaces [ 42]. The back stress exerted on the soft domain elevates the nominal stress beyond the loading stress. Ultimately, the local shear stress surpasses the threshold of the critical stress for twinning nucleation, resulting in the formation of DTs [ 90]. The appearance of high-density DTs introduce new interfaces to reduce the dislocation mean free path [ 91], and high-density GNDs aggregate at the BCC/FCC interface, resulting in superior hardening capacity ( Fig. 6b). Therefore, based on the above results and analysis, it can be considered that the difference between the CPFEM curve in Fig. 13and the experimental results is due to additional hardening mechanisms such as DT and GND strengthening, which were not considered in the simulation. The region of interest of the fractured LHA (strain = 22 %) sample was selected for further observations, and a typically interface region was shown in Fig. 16a-c. According to Fig. 14a, the morphology of grains in FEL changes after deformation, indicating severe plastic deformation, while FDL presents a large number of DTs. As special grain boundaries, the formation of DTs releases local non-uniform stress, while also hindering dislocation slip, which require a larger driving force to cross the boundary [ 92]. Therefore, it can be assumed that this local twinning induced plasticity (TWIP) phenomenon at the interface increases the overall strength while also hindering the crack nucleation to improve the toughness. Interestingly, unlike the previous inter-layer difference ( Fig. 15a), the KAM distribution depicted in Fig. 16c indicates that the values within FDL and FEL are almost identical, and the quantitative calculation results are 9.27 × 10 14m −2and 1.25 × 10 15m −2, respectively. That is to say, in the final stage of deformation, the differences between FDL and FEL tend to be consistent, which is reflected in the fact that as a soft phase, FDL continuously generates GND through dislocations and DTs to adapt to the overall deformation [ 93, 94]. Subsequently, TEM was employed to explore the coordinated deformation behavior. Nano-twinning (NT) bundles were observed, as shown in Fig. 16d. These NTs are still in the propagation stage, intermediate between nucleation and thickening [ 95]. At this stage, dislocations can nucleate at the twin interface and slip parallel to the twin plane, which avoiding stress concentration caused by dislocation stacking and thus improving ductility [ 42]. Stacking faults were observed in the FCC phase, as shown in Fig. 16e. In addition, Lomer-Cottrell (L-C) lock could form when shockley partial dislocations cross along the same slip system, which were also observed in Fig. 16e. L-C locks not only act as a strong barrier to effectively immobilize dislocation motion, but can also act as a Frank-Read source for dislocation multiplication, leading to stable and progressive work hardening, which benefits UTS and plasticity [ 96]. In contrast, FEL with BCC phase was surrounded by dislocation forest and no other deformation mechanism was found, as depicted in Fig. 16f. Fig. 16g depicts the interface of the FCC and BCC phases, while the Kurdjumov-Sachs (KS) orientation relationship comprises a transition of [110]-FCC zone into [111]-BCC zone. Interestingly, nano-sized hexagonal close-packed (HCP) phase with width of 13.1 nm was observed, as shown in Fig. 16h and i. In general, the HCP phase is considered to be the transition phase from the TRIP process of FCC-BCC, which also known as the ε-martensite phase transition [ 23, 97]. However, the elongated HCP phase clearly does not fit the characteristics of the ε-martensitic phase transition. Owing to the intense shear strain at the layer interface, continuous slip of SFs within the FCC matrix could potentially result in the formation of a nano-sized HCP phase [ 98]. In other words, two plane-thickness (n = 2) stacking layers of dislocation act as HCP embryos [ 99], which typically occur in materials with low SFE [ 23]. Like SFs and DTs, the formation of those HCP phase is beneficial to alleviate the local stress concentration, thereby providing better ductility [ 100]. The schematic diagram of enhanced strength-ductility trade-off of LHA are summarized in Fig. 17. According to the WHR, the deformation of LHA can be divided into three stages. In stage I, due to the large activation of dislocations and the reduced rate of dislocation storage, the WHR exhibits a rapid decrease. GNDs and SFs were generated inside the soft domain (FCC) around the interface to coordinate the local strain gradient. Hard BCC layer also changed from the elastic stage to the elastoplastic stage, while the back stress induced by GNDs failed to completely offset the normal stress, and finally causing HDI strengthening [ 87]. In stage II, further deformation at the interface results in severe local shear strain, and DTs begin to produce and proliferate at these sites. Simultaneously, dislocations also start to produce within the hard BCC domain to coordinate the plastic deformation. These SFs and DTs hinder further dislocation motion, and the synergistic effect of HDI stress, resulting in additional hardening mechanism, which slows down the decrease of WHR. In stage III, as a result of the overall extensive deformation, dislocations, SFs, and DTs disperse throughout the entire FCC layer. The severe shear strain at the interface leads to the formation of nano-sized HCP phase and stronger HDI stress, which can effectively suppress the formation of necking and micro-cracks. In conclusion, the presence of SFs, DTs, NTs and nano-HCP phase adapts to the strain gradient at the interface and ultimately coordinates the overall deformation. In addition, the dislocation occlusion and back stress were the main mechanisms of HDI strengthening, which were the main reasons for the elevation of WHR. In this work, we take advantages of Fe and LPBF to regulate grain size and phase composition of the Fe-Co-Cr-Ni-Mn alloy systems to fabricated periodically layered materials, which can enhance strength-ductility trade-off at a controllable procedure. The following conclusions can be obtained. 1)Layered heterostructure alloys can be prepared through changing the ratio of Fe and FeCoCrNiMn in the mixed powder. Under low Fe content, the prepared samples had FCC structure with coarser grains and lower hardness. By contrast, samples at high Fe content will convert to BCC structure and are characterized by ultrafine grains with an average diameter of 4.24 μm. 2)During the preparation of LHA, the BCC phase began to appear in the 2nd layer of the FEL, while the 5th layer completes the mutation of BCC phase content. The whole process is essentially the consequence of the increasement and homogenization of the Fe element content. 3)CPFEM simulations and quasi in-situlaser confocal experiments indicated that the LHA has stress/strain incompatibility during tensile deformation, in which the FEL bears the stress and the FDL support the unstable FEL through plastic deformation. 4)The YS, UTS and elongation of the LHA are 581 MPa, 757 MPa and 22.8 %, respectively, achieved satisfactory strength-ductility balance. The mismatch of plastic deformation allows FDL and FEL to generate back and normal stresses, respectively, which induces a series of strengthening mechanisms (dislocations, SFs, DTs and nano-HCP transition). Ultimately, Finally, the GND density difference between the soft and hard phase tends to be consistent through the above hardening mechanism. The MEC 0, MEC 7.5and MEC 15were prepared from pure elements of Fe, Co, Ni, and Nb powders with purity >99.7 wt% and particle size <45 μm through mechanical alloying followed by spark plasma sintering. Cyclohexane (C 6H 12) was introduced as the process control agent (PCA) to prevent powder agglomeration and oxidation during milling process. The MA process was conducted on a high energy QM-3SP4 planetary mill (Nanda Instrument Plant, China) for 60 h at 300 rpm. Then, the as-milled powders were dried in a vacuum chamber at 60 °C and subsequently sieved by 300-mesh sieve before spark plasma sintering. The sieved powders were consolidated using a Dr. Sinter SPS-825 Apparatus (Sumitomo Coal Mining Co. Ltd. , Japan) at a temperature/pressure of 1000 °C/30 MPa for a holding time of 10 min under vacuum condition (< 10 Pa).

The ingot was fabricated by vacuum induction melting (under Ar atmosphere) a mixture of pure metals Fe, Mn, Co, Cr (purity > 99.9 wt%) and compounds of MnN and CrN. Following hot forging at 1200 °C, the alloy underwent multi-pass hot rolling to achieve a total reduction of 50 % (initial and terminal rolling temperatures are 1050 °C and 900 °C, respectively). Subsequently, homogenization treatment was conducted at 1200 °C for 2 h to obtain the homogenized (HOMO) material. Finally, the HOMO material underwent multi-passes cold rolling (CR), achieving an overall thickness reduction of 60 %, and the CR sheet was used for LAG processing. A three-dimensional coordinate system is established based on the CR sheet geometry: rolling direction (RD), transverse direction (TD) and normal direction (ND). LAG was performed on the RD-TD plane of the N1-CR sheet using a hydraulic surface grinding machine (MY250). A continuous laser with the power of 600 W was incident from one side and formed a laser heating (LH) zone with a diameter of 5 mm on the experimental platform. The N1-CR sheet workpiece passed through the laser heating zone and grinding processing zone in order along RD at a feed rate of 5 mm/s. Micro lubrication water cooling was used during grinding. For comparison, the N1-CR sheet that only passed through LH zone without grinding was also prepared, and hereafter denoted as the N1-LH material. The characteristics of the gradient structure have been detailed and analyzed in the previous section. Here the average grain sizes at distances of 100 μm (RX layer) and 800 μm (PRX layer) along ND from the surface of the N1-LH material are 38 μm and 5 μm, respectively ( Fig. 2(b) and (e)). Subsequently, the N1-LH material was grinded and a work hardening layer was formed on the grinding surface ( Fig. 2(d)), then the N1-LAG material with good machining surface quality was prepared. It is noticed that the average grain sizes at distances of 100 μm (RX layer) and 800 μm (PRX layer) along ND from the surface of the material are 41 μm and 9.5 μm, respectively ( Fig. 2(b) and (e)). The results show that the grain size of the same regions in this material is larger than that in the N1-LH material, indicating that the grinding heat will cause grain growth in the RX and PRX layers [ 58, 59].

In this study, we firstly prepared the Fe 1+2xCo 1-xNi 1-xCr (x = 0, 0.1 and 0.2 in molar ratio) HEAs by melting the high purity metal particles (Fe, Co, Ni and Cr > 99.9 %) under an Ar atmosphere through vacuum induction melting. Firstly, commercial high purity Fe, Ti and C (size from 0 to 50 μm) powders were weighted and followed mechanically mixed using a planetary ball milling machine. For mechanical alloying, the rotational speed was maintained at 250 r/min, the ball-to-materials ratio was closed to 10:1 and the milling time was set to 8 h. The homogeneous mixed powders were dried in a vacuum drying oven at 110 °C for 90 min, and subsequently shaped into a thin block using a hydraulic press at 15 MPa. The thin block was mixed with Ni, Co and Cr metal particles in a ceramic crucible and then put them into the smelting furnace. As the mixture become melted solution, poured it into a water-cooled copper crucible and cooled in the furnace.

A CoFeNi-based HEA with a hierarchical structure with heterogeneous microstructure, consisting of body-centered cubic (BCC) bands, ultra-fine grained dual-phase and non-recrystallized lamellae (NRL) zones containing a high-density of nanoprecipitates, was fabricated and finely tuned by cold rolling (CR) and annealing. Plates (100 × 10 × 10 mm 3) of the designed alloy were prepared by arc melting and suction casting into a water-cooled Cu mold under argon atmosphere. The plates were 80% cold rolled along the longitudinal direction. The rolled sheets were subsequently annealed for 1 h at 650 °C, 750 °C, 850 °C and 950 °C (labelled as HEA-650, HEA-750, HEA-850 and HEA-950, respectively).

The HEA used in this study was processed by arc-melting a mixture of pure metals with a nominal composition Cr 20Mn 20Fe 20Co 20Ni 20(at%) in a high purity argon atmosphere. The ingot was remelted at least five times to ensure homogeneity before it was drop-cast into a rectangular-cross-section copper mould. The as-cast ingot was cold rolled by 70% reduction in thickness. Recrystallization at 820 °C for 1 h resulted in an equiaxed grain structure with an average grain size of 8 µm ( Fig. 1a). Hydrogen was introduced into the tensile specimens using a cathodic electrochemical charging technique in a 0.5 mol/L H 2SO 4+ 1 g/L CH 4N 2S (thiourea) solution with constant current density of 20 mA/cm 2at room temperature.

5HEA was fabricated in vacuum arc-melting with argon atmosphere, using raw metals of Ni, Cr, Co, Fe, Mo, Al, and Ti with purity >99.5 wt%. To mitigate burning loss of Al and Cr, an additional 1.5 wt% of Al and Cr was added. To ensure compositional homogeneity and consistency, the ingots were melted, solidified, and flipped five times before being poured into a fluted copper mold with dimension of approximately Φ50 × 130 mm 3. Subsequently, the as-cast ingots homogenized at 1120 ℃ for 8 hours Then, the homogenized samples were cold-rolled by 80 % reduction. The cold-rolled alloys were recrystallized at 1100 ℃ for 1 min, 1100 ℃ for 5 min, and 1100 ℃ for 60 min, respectively, to obtain different grain sizes. The recrystallized alloys（1100 ℃-1 min）were selected for aging at 700 ℃ for 1.5 h to induce the formation of L1 2precipitates. Samples were dropped into water in the end of all the heat treatment.

Laser powder bed fusion (LPBF) was explored to produce CoCrNi medium entropy alloys (MEAs) from pre-alloyed powder with a relatively high oxygen concentration (870 ppm). Before LPBF, a BZF-50 dryer was used to bake the powder in the air for 2 hours to make it drier and have better fluidity, and at the same time, try to introduce some oxygen into the powder. CoCrNi MEAs specimens of dimensions 10×10×10 mm were prepared using an SP100-3D printer. A scanning strategy of 67° laser rotation per printing layer was adopted to minimize defects in the alloys. Non-equiatomic ratio (TiZrNb-based) 100-xO x( x= 0, 2 at%) RHEAs were prepared by vacuum induction melting in argon atmosphere in a water-cooled copper crucible. The ingot is remelted at least three times to guarantee its chemical homogeneity. Then, the as-cast alloys were homogenized at 1100 ℃ for 2 h and forged on a hot press with a deformation of 50 %. Then, repeat the heat treatment and forging process. The forged sample was recrystallized and annealed at 800℃ for 2 h, and then the O0 and O2 RHEAs were water-quench (named O0-WQ and O2-WQ, respectively). In addition, after recrystallization and water-quench treatment, the RHEAs were isothermally annealed at the temperature ranging from 500℃ to 700℃ for 1 h, 2 h, 4 h, 10 h and 24 h.

The constraints applied in this study included that each element must be present in ≥10 at %concentration to achieve a high entropy of mixing, and additionally, Co and Ni were constrained to have maximum concentrations of 15 and 20 at %, respectively, in order to reduce associated cost. The selected alloy was produced via arc melting and vacuum casting into a 15 × 15 mmsquare copper mould, under a protective Ar atmosphere with high purity elements (≥99. 99%). The cast ingot was homogenised in two stages, firstly it was hot rolled at 950 °C to a reduction of 65% to consolidate the casting by minimising porosity and breaking down the cast and dendritic structure. Secondly, the rolled ingot was subsequently heat treated at 950 °C for 6 h and water quenched to produce an equiaxed structure. Lamella samples were prepared by sectioning a 10 × 1 μm rectangle at a depth of 5 μm. The lift-out was progressively ion polished down to <100 nm thickness with the final polish using a beam energy of 5 kV and beam current of 10 pA to remove any amorphous layer.

Outstanding High-temperature performance CoCrFeNiW0.8 were prepared by ultrasonic-assisted laser cladding (UALC), which are promising candidates for extreme environment. The raw materials included spherical pre-alloyed CoCrFeNi powder (prepared by vacuum atomization) and tungsten (W) powder with a purity exceeding 99. Subsequently, the mixed powder was dried at 80 °C for 8 h to ensure flowability. The processing parameters for laser cladding were as follows: powder feeding rate of 15.8 g/min, laser power of 2000 W, scanning speed of 3 mm/s, and overlap rate of 30 %. The ultrasonic operation parameters were as follows: defocus distance of 57 mm, tilt angle of 30°, and amplitudes of 0 %, 40 % (8 μm), 50 % (10 μm), 60 % (12 μm), and 70 % (14 μm), the schematic diagram of preparation is shown in Fig. 1(c). During the laser scanning process, the mechanical alloy powder is melted, creating a molten pool. In this study, CoCrFeNiW 0.8strengthening layers were successfully fabricated using ultrasonic-assisted laser cladding (UALC) with varying ultrasonic amplitudes, and their microstructure, high-temperature tensile, and high-temperature wear behavior were thoroughly investigated.

ODS-NbTaTiV RHEAs were prepared utilizing powder metallurgy (P/M) method with high-purity elemental powder (Nb, Ta, Ti, V, >99.5%, <45 μm, equiatomic) and Y 2O 3powder (30-50 nm, 0.35 wt%). The powders were ground in a planetary ball mill (MITR-YXQM-4 L) at 250 rpm for 20 h. Tungsten carbide vials and balls were used as milling media with the ball-to-powder mass ratio of 10:1. The miller was interrupted and reversed every 5 min, and then stopped for another 5 min to avoid overheating. Then, the milled powders were consolidated via spark plasma sintering (SPS, LABOX-325R) at 1300 °C, 1400 °C, and 1500 °C to produce the cylindrical bulks (Φ 20 × 10 mm) with a heating rate of 100 °C/min and a pressure of 40 MPa for 10 min. In summary, an ODS-NbTaTiV RHEA reinforced with multiscale oxides was successfully synthesized. The following conclusions were reached: (1)Novel ODS-NbTaTiV RHEAs with multiscale oxides were synthesized through the in-situ precipitation method. The Ti-(O, N) precipitates undergo dissolution and reprecipitation during the milling and sintering process.

First, submicron-sized HEAps were synthesized via the thermal plasma processing of mechanically alloyed HEAps. Milling was performed at 500 rpm for 24 h under an argon atmosphere. Stainless steel balls (diameter:5 mm) were employed as milling media with a ball-to-powder ratio of 10:1. They were then subjected to a thermal plasma process (PL-35LSm, TEKNA plasma system) to reduce their sizes from hundreds to submicron-sized. The as-milled HEAps were injected into the plasma torch with argon carrier gas using a water-cooled probe. Ar gas was injected into the torch at a flow rate of 15 L/min, and the plasma was ignited and stabilized at a power of 28 kW. Next, a high-energy attrition mill was used to disperse 2 vol% of submicron-sized HEAps into Al powder. Secondary milling was performed at 500 rpm for 12 h under an argon atmosphere. After that, the composite powder and monolithic Al powder were processed via hot-rolling at 480 °C with a 5% reduction of up to 1.4 mm in thickness to produce the composite sheet. A copper tube heat-treated at 500 °C for 12 h was used for powder packing and sealed using a cold press machine.
