The CoCrNiFeMn HEA powder was fabricated via gas atomization, with detailed chemical and microstructural information reported in our previous investigation [ 31]. The HEA samples were produced using a ProX 300 LPBF system. The LPBF printing parameters included a laser beam diameter of 75 µm, a layer thickness of 40 µm, a hatching space of 50 µm, a laser power ranging from 160 to 290 W, and a scanning speed of 2000 mm s −1. Cubic samples with dimensions of 10 mm × 10 mm × 6 mm were additively manufactured to investigate thermal stability under various heat treatment conditions. The as-built samples were isochronally annealed in a furnace under an Ar atmosphere at temperatures of 673, 773, 873, 973, 1073, and 1173 K for 60 min each. Additionally, isothermal heat treatment was conducted at 1173 K for durations of 10, 30, 60, 120, 240, and 480 min. Following air cooling, the samples were mechanically ground sequentially using 400 to 4000 grit SiC papers to achieve a flat and smooth surface, followed by polishing with diamond suspensions and finally with an oxide polishing suspension (OPS) containing silica particles of about 40 nm to remove the strained layer caused by mechanical polishing. To assess the mechanical performance of the LPBF-printed CoCrNiFeMn HEA across a range of temperatures, flat dog-bone tensile specimens with gauge dimensions of 10 mm × 2 mm × 2.5 mm were fabricated. All surfaces of the specimens were mechanically polished using 1200 grit SiC paper before testing.

In this work, a non-equimolar CoCrNiTi medium-entropy alloy was successfully prepared using dual-wire arc additive manufacturing, and the Ni/Ti-rich η and γ′ phase size and distribution were adjusted by heat treatment to enhance the mechanical properties. In this study, a non-equimolar CoCrNiTi MEA was successfully prepared via dual-wire arc additive manufacturing (D-WAAM). In this work,D-WAAM was used to fabricate a non-equimolar CoCrNiTi MEA. In addition, the deposited samples (labeled as As-built) were placed in a heat treatment furnace and heated to 1050 °C and 1150 °C at a heating rate of 10 °C/min and held for 2 h. Finally, the samples were cooled to room temperature in the heat treatment furnace (labeled as HT-1050 and HT-1150, respectively).

The alloy underwent T651 heat treatment and was subsequently naturally aged at room temperature for one month to stabilize its material properties. Before obtaining the pre-strain Al alloy specimen, the Al alloy sheet was cut to the required thickness for the specimen, aligning the cutting direction with the rolling direction. Afterward, the Al alloy plates underwent pre-strain tension of 2% and 4% using a universal tensile testing machine. Tensile specimens, labeled as 0%P, 2%P, and 4%P, were cut from both the base material and the Al alloy plates subjected to 2% and 4% pre-strain treatments, respectively, using wire electrical discharge machining. Al alloys underwent electrochemical hydrogen charging using a 0.1 mol/L NaOH solution.

Inspired by the rigid-flexible coupled (RFC) structure of bamboo, 316L/FeCoCrNiMn bionic gradient heterostructured material was prepared by laser-directed energy deposition (LDED) technology. Layers G2 and G3 were created by thoroughly mixing the two types of powders in proportion using a planetary ball mill. To minimize the risk of oxidation or excessive moisture accumulation in the powders before printing, all materials underwent 12 h vacuum drying prior to further processing. After multiple rounds of experimental adjustment and optimization, it was found that both 316L and FeCoCrNiMn materials could be completely melted at a laser power of 650 W. Therefore, a laser power of 650 W was selected as the energy source. To maintain thermal input balance, a powder feeding rate of 2.5 r was combined with a scanning speed of 350 mm/s.

A series of Al x(HfNbTiZr) 100- x( x= 0, 3, 5, 7, 10 and12 in atomic percent, denoted as A-0, A-3, A-5, A-7, A-10 and A-12, respectively, in the following context for simplicity) refractory HEAs were prepared by arc-melting mixture of pure metals (the purities are higher than 99.9% for these metals) under argon atmosphere. To ensure compositional homogeneity, the ingots were turned over and re-melted five times, and electromagnetic stirring was conducted during the melting process. The melted alloys were finally drop-cast into a water-cooled copper mold with a dimension of 10 × 10 × 50 mm 3. As-cast bars were then cold-rolled by 80% reduction in thickness. After removing surface contamination by abrasive paper, the cold-rolled plates were encapsulated in evacuated argon-backfilled quartz ampoules for following heat treatment. In order to obtain uniform microstructure and investigate phase stability, two kinds of heat treatment processing were conducted. The first treatment was solid-solution treated at 1273 K for 0.5 h (depicted as SST in the following context), and the other process was solid-solution treated at 1273 K for 0.5 h, followed by aging at 873 K for 100 h (depicted as STA in the following context). After solid solution and aging processes, the specimens were quenched in water.

Subsequently, the cast ingots underwent a homogenization treatment at 1473 K for 10 h, followed by a multi-pass rolling with a total thickness reduction of 80 % (Al6Ta2 and Al4Ta ingots were cold rolled at room temperature, while Al2Ta6 ingot was hot rolled at 1273 K). In this study, CoCrNi medium entropy alloys strengthened with iron-based amorphous materials were fabricated using Selective Laser Melting (SLM) technology, with established gradients at 0, 3, 5, and 7 wt%. The CoCrNi powder and iron-based amorphous powder were subjected to a mixing process exceeding 2 h utilizing a three-dimensional motion mixer (GH-17 L, NanFang Powder Equipment Factory, Wenling, China). The experimental samples were fabricated utilizing an SLM 125HL machine (SLM Solutions, Lübeck, Germany) outfitted with a single-beam IPG fiber laser exhibiting a spot diameter between 70 and 100 μm. The printing process was executed in a 99.9 % high-purity argon environment to mitigate oxidation of the material during printing. Preliminary experiments established the optimal printing parameters: laser power of 250W, scanning speed of 800 mm/s, scanning spacing of 0.12 mm, layer thickness of 0.03 mm, and interlayer rotation angle of 67°. Concurrently, the elevated mixing entropy within the CoCrNi medium entropy alloy influences the glass-forming ability (GFA), by the Adam-Gibbs equation [ 32]. CoCrNi alloys, possessing a face-centered cubic (FCC) structure, display a propensity for growth into columnar crystals along the <100> direction [ 27, 40]. Fig. 9(a) depicts the room-temperature tensile performance curves for both Pure CoCrNi and iron-based amorphous-doped enhanced samples. Fig. 11(a) presents the stress-strain curves for the CoCrNi and iron-doped amorphous-strengthened specimens fabricated using Selective Laser Melting (SLM) at a low temperature of 200K, with detailed results elucidated in Table 4. This study employed Selective Laser Melting (SLM) technology to fabricate CoCrNi medium entropy alloys reinforced with 3 %, 5 %, and 7 % mass fractions of iron-based amorphous material. The samples were then compared with pure CoCrNi samples prepared using the same SLM technique.

The CoCrNi powder and iron-based amorphous powder were subjected to a mixing process exceeding 2 h utilizing a three-dimensional motion mixer (GH-17 L, NanFang Powder Equipment Factory, Wenling, China). The experimental samples were fabricated utilizing an SLM 125HL machine (SLM Solutions, Lübeck, Germany) outfitted with a single-beam IPG fiber laser exhibiting a spot diameter between 70 and 100 μm. The printing process was executed in a 99.9 % high-purity argon environment to mitigate oxidation of the material during printing. Preliminary experiments established the optimal printing parameters: laser power of 250W, scanning speed of 800 mm/s, scanning spacing of 0.12 mm, layer thickness of 0.03 mm, and interlayer rotation angle of 67°.

To prepare the equiatomic Ti-V-Zr-Nb and (Ti1. 5V) xZrNb ( x= 1-5) high-entropy alloys, high-purity (> 99.95%) constituent metals including titanium, vanadium, zirconium, and niobium were weighed according to the designed compositions. The pure metals were first arc-melted under a high-purity argon atmosphere to allow for thorough intermixing and alloying. To ensure chemical homogeneity, the molten master alloys were flipped and re-melted at least 5 times before they were drop-cast into a water-cooled copper mold to obtain plates measuring 10 × 80 × 5 mm. The as-cast alloy plates were cold rolled at room temperature in a two-high rolling mill through consecutive passes, achieving a total thickness reduction of approximately 80% in a laboratory-scale two-high rolling machine.

2 Zn (wt.%) sheets of ∼5 mm were employed, which were homogenized at 693 K for 1.5 h and then quenched in water. The one-pass rolling bonding process was assisted by two hard plates. Before rolling, surface treatment was performed on the slabs according to the following procedures: (i) use alcohol to clean the surfaces, (ii) polish the surfaces with angle grinder to remove impurities and expose the fresh layer, and (iii) clean the surfaces with acetone to remove oil stains. Subsequently, two slabs (4 mm thick) wrapped between two hard plates (1 mm thick) were heated together at 583 K for 15 min, followed by one-pass rolling with a thickness-reduction of ∼81%, to obtain a sample with a thickness of ∼1.5 mm. For the rolling process, two rollers with a diameter of 155 mm were heated to 373 K and rotated at 50 rpm. The as-rolled samples were annealed at 583 K for ∼5 min.

The preparation of FeCoCrNiMo high-entropy alloy (HEA) particle-reinforced aluminum matrix composites using multi-pass equal-diameter angular extrusion is an effective approach to address the application limitations related to strength and toughness. In this study, the composite materials were prepared by multi-pass equal-diameter angular extrusion. FeCoCrNiMo powder is mixed with 5083 Al matrix powder with a TC-2 V-type blender at a rotation speed of 20 r/min for 10 h. The mixed powder is then pre-pressed with a LDJ200/600-300 cold isostatic press, under 300 MPa rated working pressure and Φ200 mm × 600 mm cavity dimension. The pre-formed blank of the composite is placed in a custom-made die for isostatic angular extrusion at 400 °C. Hot extrusion forming is conducted with a YJ32-315A vertical four-column hydraulic press, which has a maximum downward pressure of 3150 kN. The preparation of FeCoCrNiMo high-entropy alloy (HEA) particle-reinforced aluminum matrix composites using multi-pass equal-diameter angular extrusion is an effective approach to address the application limitations related to strength and toughness. In this study, the composite materials were prepared by multi-pass equal-diameter angular extrusion. The present study involves the fabrication of high-strength and corrosion-resistant 15vol%FeCoCrNiMo/5083 Al composite through multi-pass channel angular extrusion. The conclusions drawn are as follows: (1)The properties of the composites with 15 % HEA content continuously improve with an increasing number of extrusion passes.

FeCoCrNiMo powder is mixed with 5083 Al matrix powder with a TC-2 V-type blender at a rotation speed of 20 r/min for 10 h. The mixed powder is then pre-pressed with a LDJ200/600-300 cold isostatic press, under 300 MPa rated working pressure and Φ200 mm × 600 mm cavity dimension. The pre-formed blank of the composite is placed in a custom-made die for isostatic angular extrusion at 400 °C. Hot extrusion forming is conducted with a YJ32-315A vertical four-column hydraulic press, which has a maximum downward pressure of 3150 kN. The preparation of FeCoCrNiMo high-entropy alloy (HEA) particle-reinforced aluminum matrix composites using multi-pass equal-diameter angular extrusion is an effective approach to address the application limitations related to strength and toughness. In this study, the composite materials were prepared by multi-pass equal-diameter angular extrusion. The present study involves the fabrication of high-strength and corrosion-resistant 15vol%FeCoCrNiMo/5083 Al composite through multi-pass channel angular extrusion. The conclusions drawn are as follows: (1)The properties of the composites with 15 % HEA content continuously improve with an increasing number of extrusion passes.

In this study, a set of CrFeNi -based medium-entropy alloys (MEAs) with varying carbon contents were prepared by spark plasm sintering (SPS) using atomized alloy powders as raw material. Herein, we investigate the practicability of fabricating (CrFeNi) 100-xC x(x = 0,4,8) MEAs through PM, specifically by consolidating gas-atomized (CrFeNi) 100-xC xpre-alloy powders using spark plasma sintering (SPS). The three different C-content powders were fabricated by gas atomization: CrFeNi, (CrFeNi) 96C 4and (CrFeNi) 92C 8(all in at. %), referred to as CFN0, CFN4, and CFN8, respectively. In order to prepare bulk materials, powders were consolidated through SPS (FCT HP D 25/3, German) in a 30 mm-inner-diameter graphite die at 1150 °C for 10 min. The sintering was carried out at 40 MPa under vacuum (<10 Pa).

42Al 3Ti 3MEA were repeatedly melted under protection of argon atmosphere in an induction melting furnace to reach chemical homogeneity. The as-received ingots were homogenized under a very high temperature of 1423 K to achieve composition homogeneity, and then hot-forged into plates with thickness of 18 mm. The plates were homogenized again under 1423 K, followed by water quenching. These 18 mm thick homogenized plates were then cold-rolled (CR) by multi-passes (0.1 mm thickness reduction per pass) into plates with thickness of about 1.5 mm. The CR plates were annealed at a selected temperature of 1273 K for 1 h followed by water quenching, to obtain a coarse-grained (CG) structure with single FCC phase. Single-graded structure was obtained by SMGT processing on the CG plates. The single-grade structure was aged at 973 K for varying times (10, 30, 120, 240 min) to obtain different dual-graded structures (hereafter referred as DG_10, DG_30, DG_120 and DG_240).

In this study, we present an ultra-strong and highly ductile CrCoNi MEA additively manufactured via in-situ alloying with nanoscale TiC particles. We incorporated nano-sized TiC particles (mean size ∼50 nm) with a 4 wt% fraction into CrCoNi MEA powder (particle size ranging from 15 to 50 μm) and blended the mixture for 4 h. The powder was then prepared using the ball milling method. As shown in Fig. 1(a), the blended powder was milled for 120 min using a ball-milling machine operating at 300 rpm. After ball milling, TiC particles were well attached on the surface of the CrCoNi MEA powder, as confirmed by EDS mapping ( Fig. 1(b-g)). The ball-milled MEA + TiC powder was subsequently processed in an LPBF machine. Dog-bone-shaped samples with gauge lengths and widths of 10 mm and 2 mm, respectively, were fabricated on a substrate made of 304 stainless steel. High-purity argon served as the shielding gas to protect the melt pool from oxidation. During AM, the rotation angle between adjacent layers was set to 67°, while the hatching space and layer thickness were maintained at 70 μm and 30 μm, respectively. The laser power and scanning speed were varied to identify the optimal AM parameters. The dog-bone samples were cut using electric discharge machining and subsequently ground with sandpapers to achieve a smooth surface.

We have previously shown that it is possible to make a spherical Ti-6Al-4 V(TC4)-B pre-alloyed powder [ 25, 32] through a melting-forging-atomization preparation technique. Here, spherical TC4-B pre-alloyed powder is used as the raw material, for EB-PBF additive manufacture (AM) and in-situ heat treatment to prepare TC4-B alloy samples. Firstly, sponge titanium with a purity of 99. 9%, Al, AlV, and 3.0wt. %TiB 2(5.1vol%TiB, purity of 99.9%) are mixed and compressed into electrodes. Secondly, to ensure a complete reaction between TiB 2and Ti, the electrode is vacuum arc melted twice and cast into ingots. Subsequently, the ingot is forged into a rod with a diameter of 45 mm at 950 °C using a rapid forging machine. Finally, it is processed into a cylindrical bar (dimensions: ⌀41 mm × 500 mm) to be used as raw material for powder preparation via Electrode Inert Gas Atomization (EIGA). Bulk TC4 alloy and TC4-TiBw samples were built with dimensions of 70 mm × 10 mm × 20 mm on a 316 L substrate.

Electron beam powder bed fusion (EB-PBF) is advantageous for preparing fine-grained Ti alloys [ 26] and the formation of nano TiBw, owing to preheating at approximately 800 °C and high cooling rates (10 4-10 6K/s) [ 25, 27]. As an effective, a new printing strategy been developed using pre-alloyed powder as the raw [ 25] (such as: Al/TiB 2[ 29], Fe/TiB 2[ 30], Ti/Fe/B [ 31], Ti/B [ 21, 32]). In this respect, the generation of nano-TiBw on the phase/grain boundaries from pre-alloyed powder through EB-PBF with an associated in-situ heat treatment is an attractive means of improving the high-temperature mechanical properties of the titanium alloys. We have previously shown that it is possible to make a spherical Ti-6Al-4 V(TC4)-B pre-alloyed powder [ 25, 32] through a melting-forging-atomization preparation technique. Here, spherical TC4-B pre-alloyed powder is used as the raw material, for EB-PBF additive manufacture (AM) and in-situ heat treatment to prepare TC4-B alloy samples. In this way, it has been possible to fabricate Ti alloys with 5.1 vol% nano TiBw located at the grain boundaries. Firstly, sponge titanium with a purity of 99. 9%, Al, AlV, and 3.0wt. %TiB 2(5.1vol%TiB, purity of 99.9%) are mixed and compressed into electrodes. Secondly, to ensure a complete reaction between TiB 2and Ti, the electrode is vacuum arc melted twice and cast into ingots. Subsequently, the ingot is forged into a rod with a diameter of 45 mm at 950 °C using a rapid forging machine. Finally, it is processed into a cylindrical bar (dimensions: ⌀41 mm × 500 mm) to be used as raw material for powder preparation via Electrode Inert Gas Atomization (EIGA). The prepared powder is sieved to obtain 75-120 μm TC4-TiBw pre-alloy powder for the AM process. The optimized process parameters are used for AM: beam spot size = 200 μm; preheating beam current = 40 mA; substrate preheating temperature = 800 °C to release residual stress during the AM process; printing beam current =16.5 mA; scanning speed = 5.8 m·s −1; layer thickness = 50 μm. Bulk TC4 alloy and TC4-TiBw samples were built with dimensions of 70 mm × 10 mm × 20 mm on a 316 L substrate.

The as-cast sample was homogenized at 1000 °C for 2 h and subsequently quenched in water. Then, the sample was cold-rolled with a total thickness reduction of 85%, and subsequently annealed in a box furnace at 850 °C for 15 min, followed by water cooling. To reveal the order-disorder transition and segregation behavior due to the formation of Cu-rich phase, the Metropolis MC calculations between 100 K and 1500 K for 1536 atoms were conducted with the CE Hamiltonian [53]. The structures annealed at various temperatures (100 K, 500 K and 900 K) were obtained using simulated annealing method [55].

The ingots of Fe 27Ni 28Mn 27Cr 18and Fe 25Co 25Cr 25Ni 25were prepared by arc melting of pure metal mixture (purity>99.95 wt%) in a high-purity argon atmosphere. All alloys were re-melted at least four times to ensure the uniformity of chemical compositions. The prepared alloys were cut by wire electrical discharge machining with size of 10 × 10 × 1 mm 3. To eliminate the primary defects and obtain uniform grain size, all alloys were annealed at 1200 °C for 48 h. The samples were ground with silicon carbide sandpaper through 7000 grit and polished on a polishing machine with polishing pastes with grit sizes of 7, 5, 3.5, 2.5, 1.5 and 0.5 µm, respectively. It was then further polished to a mirror surface with a 0.25 µm SiO 2suspension on a vibratory polisher. The platinum plate was used as the positive electrode and the cathode was connected to the samples. Electrochemical deuterium charging experiments were carried out in a heavy aqueous solution containing 0.5 g/L CH 4N 2S and 0.1 mol/L NaOH, and the samples were charged at a constant current of 50 mA/cm 2for 6 h. The flat dog-bone-like tensile samples with dimensions of 4 mm (width) × 10 mm (length) × 1 mm (thickness) were machined by electrical discharge machining, as shown in Fig. 1(b). All tensile samples were mechanically ground (grain size to 7000 mesh) with SiC sandpaper.

In this study, N microalloying was achieved by adding varying amounts of MnN as a raw material, and a series of Fe 50-xMn 30Co 10Cr 10N x(at. %, x= 0, 0.5, 1.0, 1.8) alloys were designed and fabricated. First, high-purity Fe, Mn, Co, Cr (≥99.9 wt. %), and MnN were placed in a vacuum induction furnace and melted under a protective argon atmosphere to obtain ingots. The ingots were then hot-rolled with a 50 % reduction (initial rolling temperature: 1050 °C, final rolling temperature: 900 °C) to produce hot-rolled plates with a final thickness of 5 mm. Subsequently, the hot-rolled plates were homogenized at 1200 °C for 2 h followed by water quenching. Multi-pass cold rolling with a total reduction of 60 % was then performed to obtain cold-rolled sheets with a thickness of 2 mm. Finally, the cold-rolled alloys underwent a short-time salt bath treatment at 900 °C for 3 min, followed by water quenching to achieve a fully recrystallized (FRX) state.

The ingots were then hot-rolled with a 50 % reduction (initial rolling temperature: 1050 °C, final rolling temperature: 900 °C) to produce hot-rolled plates with a final thickness of 5 mm. Subsequently, the hot-rolled plates were homogenized at 1200 °C for 2 h followed by water quenching. Multi-pass cold rolling with a total reduction of 60 % was then performed to obtain cold-rolled sheets with a thickness of 2 mm. Finally, the cold-rolled alloys underwent a short-time salt bath treatment at 900 °C for 3 min, followed by water quenching to achieve a fully recrystallized (FRX) state.

Based on the above strategies, we prepared a novel supersaturated Fe-30Cr-30Ni-8Mo (namely 30308 for short) super stainless high-entropy steel (SSHS) with significantly higher Cr and Mo contents than traditional austenitic stainless alloys, such as 316L SS and 7Mo SASS, by the laser-based powder bed fusion (PBF-LB/M) method. To prepare the 30308 SSHS, the pre-alloyed powders were prepared by gas atomization. The atomization gas and pressure are high-purity nitrogen and 4 MPa, respectively. The pre-alloyed powders have a near-spherical morphology, and the average powder size is ∼18 µm ( Fig. Then, fully dense sheet-shaped 30308 SSHS samples (12 mm × 12 mm × 50 mm) were prepared by Farsoon's FS271M machine. The laser spot size, laser power, scanning speed, hatching space, layer thickness, and scanning rotation angle are 90 µm, 350 W, 700 mm s −1, 110 µm, 50 µm, and 67°, respectively. Finally, the as-built 30308 SSHS samples were annealed at 400 °C for 3 h followed by a furnace cool to release residual stresses.

In this study, triple-wire plasma arc additive manufacturing (TW-PAAM) method was used to prepare MEAs. Non-equiatomic Alx-Cr-Fe-Ni MEAs (where x is the feeding speed of Al wire) were prepared using three commercial wires (ER1070, ER304L, and Ni80Cr20 wire). For each deposited layer, the sample was remelted while traversing the return path. The Al content of the samples was varied by changing the feeding speed of the Al wire. As shown in Fig. 1(b), thick-walled samples with approximate dimensions of 120 (length) × 15 (width) × 23 (height) mm were fabricated using a TW-PAAM system. They melt after entering the center of the plasma arc and form a single droplet ( Fig. 8(a) ). The various metals mixed under the impulsive force of the plasma arc. When the deposition of this layer was completed, the welding torch moved in the opposite direction for remelting ( Fig. 8(c) and (d)). Due to the absence of wire feeding, the alloy reformed in the molten pool under the action of the plasma arc and was stirred.

The ODS alloys are typically prepared using mechanical alloying (MA) followed by hot consolidation, which is also the method employed for the investigated ODS HEAs in this study. The process of MA usually leads to a significant level of plastic deformation, thereby inducing the generation of numerous lattice defects, such as vacancies, in the milled alloy powders [27]. The first principle density-functional calculation study conducted by Fu et al. previously reported a significantly high binding energy of ∼ 1.5 eV between O atoms in octahedral position sites and vacancies, leading to a notable reduction in the formation energy (i.e., increased solubility) of O in the Fe matrix [65]. This finding indicates that a high concentration of vacancies induced by MA exhibits a strong affinity with O atoms, resulting in the formation of O-Vacancy (abbreviated as O-V) pairs [65,66]. The release of O charge confinement through electron delocalization into the newly created O-V pair has been identified as a significant contributing source in establishing the exceptionally strong binding between O and vacancies [65]. Furthermore, the calculations also demonstrated that the binding energy can be further enhanced by attracting neighboring atoms with a high affinity for O (e.g. , Ti and Y) to O-V pairs, resulting in the formation of large clusters composed of O-V-Ti (or Y). The binding energies in the energy-optimized configuration of these clusters were calculated to be 2.45 for O-V-Ti and 3.35 eV for O-V-Y [67]. Moreover, the coexistence of both Ti and Y results in a further increase in the binding energy of O-V-Ti-Y cluster, reaching a high value of 4.1 eV [67]. Consequently, the O-V-Ti-Y clusters, characterized by their highest binding energy, exhibit superior thermal stability compared to other potential clusters. Therefore, these clusters can serve as ideal nucleation sites for the precipitation of Y-Ti-O enriched nanoparticles during sintering or heat treatment at elevated temperatures of milled powders. The ODS alloys are typically prepared using mechanical alloying (MA) followed by hot consolidation, which is also the method employed for the investigated ODS HEAs in this study. The process of MA usually leads to a significant level of plastic deformation, thereby inducing the generation of numerous lattice defects, such as vacancies, in the milled alloy powders [27]. The first principle density-functional calculation study conducted by Fu et al. previously reported a significantly high binding energy of ∼ 1.5 eV between O atoms in octahedral position sites and vacancies, leading to a notable reduction in the formation energy (i.e., increased solubility) of O in the Fe matrix [65]. This finding indicates that a high concentration of vacancies induced by MA exhibits a strong affinity with O atoms, resulting in the formation of O-Vacancy (abbreviated as O-V) pairs [65,66]. The release of O charge confinement through electron delocalization into the newly created O-V pair has been identified as a significant contributing source in establishing the exceptionally strong binding between O and vacancies [65]. Furthermore, the calculations also demonstrated that the binding energy can be further enhanced by attracting neighboring atoms with a high affinity for O (e.g. , Ti and Y) to O-V pairs, resulting in the formation of large clusters composed of O-V-Ti (or Y). The binding energies in the energy-optimized configuration of these clusters were calculated to be 2.45 for O-V-Ti and 3.35 eV for O-V-Y [67]. Moreover, the coexistence of both Ti and Y results in a further increase in the binding energy of O-V-Ti-Y cluster, reaching a high value of 4.1 eV [67]. Consequently, the O-V-Ti-Y clusters, characterized by their highest binding energy, exhibit superior thermal stability compared to other potential clusters. Therefore, these clusters can serve as ideal nucleation sites for the precipitation of Y-Ti-O enriched nanoparticles during sintering or heat treatment at elevated temperatures of milled powders. The ODS alloys are typically prepared using mechanical alloying (MA) followed by hot consolidation, which is also the method employed for the investigated ODS HEAs in this study. The process of MA usually leads to a significant level of plastic deformation, thereby inducing the generation of numerous lattice defects, such as vacancies, in the milled alloy powders [27]. The first principle density-functional calculation study conducted by Fu et al. previously reported a significantly high binding energy of ∼ 1.5 eV between O atoms in octahedral position sites and vacancies, leading to a notable reduction in the formation energy (i.e., increased solubility) of O in the Fe matrix [65]. This finding indicates that a high concentration of vacancies induced by MA exhibits a strong affinity with O atoms, resulting in the formation of O-Vacancy (abbreviated as O-V) pairs [65,66]. The release of O charge confinement through electron delocalization into the newly created O-V pair has been identified as a significant contributing source in establishing the exceptionally strong binding between O and vacancies [65]. Furthermore, the calculations also demonstrated that the binding energy can be further enhanced by attracting neighboring atoms with a high affinity for O (e.g. , Ti and Y) to O-V pairs, resulting in the formation of large clusters composed of O-V-Ti (or Y). The binding energies in the energy-optimized configuration of these clusters were calculated to be 2.45 for O-V-Ti and 3.35 eV for O-V-Y [67]. Moreover, the coexistence of both Ti and Y results in a further increase in the binding energy of O-V-Ti-Y cluster, reaching a high value of 4.1 eV [67]. Consequently, the O-V-Ti-Y clusters, characterized by their highest binding energy, exhibit superior thermal stability compared to other potential clusters. Therefore, these clusters can serve as ideal nucleation sites for the precipitation of Y-Ti-O enriched nanoparticles during sintering or heat treatment at elevated temperatures of milled powders. The ODS alloys are typically prepared using mechanical alloying (MA) followed by hot consolidation, which is also the method employed for the investigated ODS HEAs in this study. The process of MA usually leads to a significant level of plastic deformation, thereby inducing the generation of numerous lattice defects, such as vacancies, in the milled alloy powders [27]. The first principle density-functional calculation study conducted by Fu et al. previously reported a significantly high binding energy of ∼ 1.5 eV between O atoms in octahedral position sites and vacancies, leading to a notable reduction in the formation energy (i.e., increased solubility) of O in the Fe matrix [65]. This finding indicates that a high concentration of vacancies induced by MA exhibits a strong affinity with O atoms, resulting in the formation of O-Vacancy (abbreviated as O-V) pairs [65,66]. The release of O charge confinement through electron delocalization into the newly created O-V pair has been identified as a significant contributing source in establishing the exceptionally strong binding between O and vacancies [65]. Furthermore, the calculations also demonstrated that the binding energy can be further enhanced by attracting neighboring atoms with a high affinity for O (e.g. , Ti and Y) to O-V pairs, resulting in the formation of large clusters composed of O-V-Ti (or Y). The binding energies in the energy-optimized configuration of these clusters were calculated to be 2.45 for O-V-Ti and 3.35 eV for O-V-Y [67]. Moreover, the coexistence of both Ti and Y results in a further increase in the binding energy of O-V-Ti-Y cluster, reaching a high value of 4.1 eV [67]. Consequently, the O-V-Ti-Y clusters, characterized by their highest binding energy, exhibit superior thermal stability compared to other potential clusters. Therefore, these clusters can serve as ideal nucleation sites for the precipitation of Y-Ti-O enriched nanoparticles during sintering or heat treatment at elevated temperatures of milled powders. The ODS alloys are typically prepared using mechanical alloying (MA) followed by hot consolidation, which is also the method employed for the investigated ODS HEAs in this study. The process of MA usually leads to a significant level of plastic deformation, thereby inducing the generation of numerous lattice defects, such as vacancies, in the milled alloy powders [27]. The first principle density-functional calculation study conducted by Fu et al. previously reported a significantly high binding energy of ∼ 1.5 eV between O atoms in octahedral position sites and vacancies, leading to a notable reduction in the formation energy (i.e., increased solubility) of O in the Fe matrix [65]. This finding indicates that a high concentration of vacancies induced by MA exhibits a strong affinity with O atoms, resulting in the formation of O-Vacancy (abbreviated as O-V) pairs [65,66]. The release of O charge confinement through electron delocalization into the newly created O-V pair has been identified as a significant contributing source in establishing the exceptionally strong binding between O and vacancies [65]. Furthermore, the calculations also demonstrated that the binding energy can be further enhanced by attracting neighboring atoms with a high affinity for O (e.g. , Ti and Y) to O-V pairs, resulting in the formation of large clusters composed of O-V-Ti (or Y). The binding energies in the energy-optimized configuration of these clusters were calculated to be 2.45 for O-V-Ti and 3.35 eV for O-V-Y [67]. Moreover, the coexistence of both Ti and Y results in a further increase in the binding energy of O-V-Ti-Y cluster, reaching a high value of 4.1 eV [67]. Consequently, the O-V-Ti-Y clusters, characterized by their highest binding energy, exhibit superior thermal stability compared to other potential clusters. Therefore, these clusters can serve as ideal nucleation sites for the precipitation of Y-Ti-O enriched nanoparticles during sintering or heat treatment at elevated temperatures of milled powders. The ODS alloys are typically prepared using mechanical alloying (MA) followed by hot consolidation, which is also the method employed for the investigated ODS HEAs in this study. The process of MA usually leads to a significant level of plastic deformation, thereby inducing the generation of numerous lattice defects, such as vacancies, in the milled alloy powders [27]. The first principle density-functional calculation study conducted by Fu et al. previously reported a significantly high binding energy of ∼ 1.5 eV between O atoms in octahedral position sites and vacancies, leading to a notable reduction in the formation energy (i.e., increased solubility) of O in the Fe matrix [65]. This finding indicates that a high concentration of vacancies induced by MA exhibits a strong affinity with O atoms, resulting in the formation of O-Vacancy (abbreviated as O-V) pairs [65,66]. The release of O charge confinement through electron delocalization into the newly created O-V pair has been identified as a significant contributing source in establishing the exceptionally strong binding between O and vacancies [65]. Furthermore, the calculations also demonstrated that the binding energy can be further enhanced by attracting neighboring atoms with a high affinity for O (e.g. , Ti and Y) to O-V pairs, resulting in the formation of large clusters composed of O-V-Ti (or Y). The binding energies in the energy-optimized configuration of these clusters were calculated to be 2.45 for O-V-Ti and 3.35 eV for O-V-Y [67]. Moreover, the coexistence of both Ti and Y results in a further increase in the binding energy of O-V-Ti-Y cluster, reaching a high value of 4.1 eV [67]. Consequently, the O-V-Ti-Y clusters, characterized by their highest binding energy, exhibit superior thermal stability compared to other potential clusters. Therefore, these clusters can serve as ideal nucleation sites for the precipitation of Y-Ti-O enriched nanoparticles during sintering or heat treatment at elevated temperatures of milled powders. The ODS alloys are typically prepared using mechanical alloying (MA) followed by hot consolidation, which is also the method employed for the investigated ODS HEAs in this study. The process of MA usually leads to a significant level of plastic deformation, thereby inducing the generation of numerous lattice defects, such as vacancies, in the milled alloy powders [27]. The first principle density-functional calculation study conducted by Fu et al. previously reported a significantly high binding energy of ∼ 1.5 eV between O atoms in octahedral position sites and vacancies, leading to a notable reduction in the formation energy (i.e., increased solubility) of O in the Fe matrix [65]. This finding indicates that a high concentration of vacancies induced by MA exhibits a strong affinity with O atoms, resulting in the formation of O-Vacancy (abbreviated as O-V) pairs [65,66]. The release of O charge confinement through electron delocalization into the newly created O-V pair has been identified as a significant contributing source in establishing the exceptionally strong binding between O and vacancies [65]. Furthermore, the calculations also demonstrated that the binding energy can be further enhanced by attracting neighboring atoms with a high affinity for O (e.g. , Ti and Y) to O-V pairs, resulting in the formation of large clusters composed of O-V-Ti (or Y). The binding energies in the energy-optimized configuration of these clusters were calculated to be 2.45 for O-V-Ti and 3.35 eV for O-V-Y [67]. Moreover, the coexistence of both Ti and Y results in a further increase in the binding energy of O-V-Ti-Y cluster, reaching a high value of 4.1 eV [67]. Consequently, the O-V-Ti-Y clusters, characterized by their highest binding energy, exhibit superior thermal stability compared to other potential clusters. Therefore, these clusters can serve as ideal nucleation sites for the precipitation of Y-Ti-O enriched nanoparticles during sintering or heat treatment at elevated temperatures of milled powders. The ODS alloys are typically prepared using mechanical alloying (MA) followed by hot consolidation, which is also the method employed for the investigated ODS HEAs in this study. The process of MA usually leads to a significant level of plastic deformation, thereby inducing the generation of numerous lattice defects, such as vacancies, in the milled alloy powders [27]. The first principle density-functional calculation study conducted by Fu et al. previously reported a significantly high binding energy of ∼ 1.5 eV between O atoms in octahedral position sites and vacancies, leading to a notable reduction in the formation energy (i.e., increased solubility) of O in the Fe matrix [65]. This finding indicates that a high concentration of vacancies induced by MA exhibits a strong affinity with O atoms, resulting in the formation of O-Vacancy (abbreviated as O-V) pairs [65,66]. The release of O charge confinement through electron delocalization into the newly created O-V pair has been identified as a significant contributing source in establishing the exceptionally strong binding between O and vacancies [65]. Furthermore, the calculations also demonstrated that the binding energy can be further enhanced by attracting neighboring atoms with a high affinity for O (e.g. , Ti and Y) to O-V pairs, resulting in the formation of large clusters composed of O-V-Ti (or Y). The binding energies in the energy-optimized configuration of these clusters were calculated to be 2.45 for O-V-Ti and 3.35 eV for O-V-Y [67]. Moreover, the coexistence of both Ti and Y results in a further increase in the binding energy of O-V-Ti-Y cluster, reaching a high value of 4.1 eV [67]. Consequently, the O-V-Ti-Y clusters, characterized by their highest binding energy, exhibit superior thermal stability compared to other potential clusters. Therefore, these clusters can serve as ideal nucleation sites for the precipitation of Y-Ti-O enriched nanoparticles during sintering or heat treatment at elevated temperatures of milled powders. The first principle density-functional calculation study conducted by Fu et al. previously reported a significantly high binding energy of ∼ 1.5 eV between O atoms in octahedral position sites and vacancies, leading to a notable reduction in the formation energy (i.e., increased solubility) of O in the Fe matrix [65]. This finding indicates that a high concentration of vacancies induced by MA exhibits a strong affinity with O atoms, resulting in the formation of O-Vacancy (abbreviated as O-V) pairs [65,66]. The release of O charge confinement through electron delocalization into the newly created O-V pair has been identified as a significant contributing source in establishing the exceptionally strong binding between O and vacancies [65]. Furthermore, the calculations also demonstrated that the binding energy can be further enhanced by attracting neighboring atoms with a high affinity for O (e.g. , Ti and Y) to O-V pairs, resulting in the formation of large clusters composed of O-V-Ti (or Y). The binding energies in the energy-optimized configuration of these clusters were calculated to be 2.45 for O-V-Ti and 3.35 eV for O-V-Y [67]. Moreover, the coexistence of both Ti and Y results in a further increase in the binding energy of O-V-Ti-Y cluster, reaching a high value of 4.1 eV [67]. Consequently, the O-V-Ti-Y clusters, characterized by their highest binding energy, exhibit superior thermal stability compared to other potential clusters. The ODS alloys are typically prepared using mechanical alloying (MA) followed by hot consolidation, which is also the method employed for the investigated ODS HEAs in this study. The process of MA usually leads to a significant level of plastic deformation, thereby inducing the generation of numerous lattice defects, such as vacancies, in the milled alloy powders [27]. The first principle density-functional calculation study conducted by Fu et al. previously reported a significantly high binding energy of ∼ 1.5 eV between O atoms in octahedral position sites and vacancies, leading to a notable reduction in the formation energy (i.e., increased solubility) of O in the Fe matrix [65]. This finding indicates that a high concentration of vacancies induced by MA exhibits a strong affinity with O atoms, resulting in the formation of O-Vacancy (abbreviated as O-V) pairs [65,66]. The release of O charge confinement through electron delocalization into the newly created O-V pair has been identified as a significant contributing source in establishing the exceptionally strong binding between O and vacancies [65]. Furthermore, the calculations also demonstrated that the binding energy can be further enhanced by attracting neighboring atoms with a high affinity for O (e.g. , Ti and Y) to O-V pairs, resulting in the formation of large clusters composed of O-V-Ti (or Y). The binding energies in the energy-optimized configuration of these clusters were calculated to be 2.45 for O-V-Ti and 3.35 eV for O-V-Y [67]. Moreover, the coexistence of both Ti and Y results in a further increase in the binding energy of O-V-Ti-Y cluster, reaching a high value of 4.1 eV [67]. Consequently, the O-V-Ti-Y clusters, characterized by their highest binding energy, exhibit superior thermal stability compared to other potential clusters. Therefore, these clusters can serve as ideal nucleation sites for the precipitation of Y-Ti-O enriched nanoparticles during sintering or heat treatment at elevated temperatures of milled powders. The ODS alloys are typically prepared using mechanical alloying (MA) followed by hot consolidation, which is also the method employed for the investigated ODS HEAs in this study. The process of MA usually leads to a significant level of plastic deformation, thereby inducing the generation of numerous lattice defects, such as vacancies, in the milled alloy powders [27]. This finding indicates that a high concentration of vacancies induced by MA exhibits a strong affinity with O atoms, resulting in the formation of O-Vacancy (abbreviated as O-V) pairs [65,66]. The release of O charge confinement through electron delocalization into the newly created O-V pair has been identified as a significant contributing source in establishing the exceptionally strong binding between O and vacancies [65]. Furthermore, the calculations also demonstrated that the binding energy can be further enhanced by attracting neighboring atoms with a high affinity for O (e.g. , Ti and Y) to O-V pairs, resulting in the formation of large clusters composed of O-V-Ti (or Y). Moreover, the coexistence of both Ti and Y results in a further increase in the binding energy of O-V-Ti-Y cluster, reaching a high value of 4.1 eV [67]. Consequently, the O-V-Ti-Y clusters, characterized by their highest binding energy, exhibit superior thermal stability compared to other potential clusters. The ODS alloys are typically prepared using mechanical alloying (MA) followed by hot consolidation, which is also the method employed for the investigated ODS HEAs in this study. The process of MA usually leads to a significant level of plastic deformation, thereby inducing the generation of numerous lattice defects, such as vacancies, in the milled alloy powders [27]. The ODS alloys are typically prepared using mechanical alloying (MA) followed by hot consolidation, which is also the method employed for the investigated ODS HEAs in this study. The process of MA usually leads to a significant level of plastic deformation, thereby inducing the generation of numerous lattice defects, such as vacancies, in the milled alloy powders [27]. The first principle density-functional calculation study conducted by Fu et al. previously reported a significantly high binding energy of ∼ 1.5 eV between O atoms in octahedral position sites and vacancies, leading to a notable reduction in the formation energy (i.e., increased solubility) of O in the Fe matrix [65]. This finding indicates that a high concentration of vacancies induced by MA exhibits a strong affinity with O atoms, resulting in the formation of O-Vacancy (abbreviated as O-V) pairs [65,66]. The release of O charge confinement through electron delocalization into the newly created O-V pair has been identified as a significant contributing source in establishing the exceptionally strong binding between O and vacancies [65]. Furthermore, the calculations also demonstrated that the binding energy can be further enhanced by attracting neighboring atoms with a high affinity for O (e.g. , Ti and Y) to O-V pairs, resulting in the formation of large clusters composed of O-V-Ti (or Y). Consequently, the O-V-Ti-Y clusters, characterized by their highest binding energy, exhibit superior thermal stability compared to other potential clusters. The ODS alloys are typically prepared using mechanical alloying (MA) followed by hot consolidation, which is also the method employed for the investigated ODS HEAs in this study. The process of MA usually leads to a significant level of plastic deformation, thereby inducing the generation of numerous lattice defects, such as vacancies, in the milled alloy powders [27]. The first principle density-functional calculation study conducted by Fu et al. previously reported a significantly high binding energy of ∼ 1.5 eV between O atoms in octahedral position sites and vacancies, leading to a notable reduction in the formation energy (i.e., increased solubility) of O in the Fe matrix [65]. This finding indicates that a high concentration of vacancies induced by MA exhibits a strong affinity with O atoms, resulting in the formation of O-Vacancy (abbreviated as O-V) pairs [65,66]. The release of O charge confinement through electron delocalization into the newly created O-V pair has been identified as a significant contributing source in establishing the exceptionally strong binding between O and vacancies [65]. Furthermore, the calculations also demonstrated that the binding energy can be further enhanced by attracting neighboring atoms with a high affinity for O (e.g. , Ti and Y) to O-V pairs, resulting in the formation of large clusters composed of O-V-Ti (or Y). The binding energies in the energy-optimized configuration of these clusters were calculated to be 2.45 for O-V-Ti and 3.35 eV for O-V-Y [67]. Moreover, the coexistence of both Ti and Y results in a further increase in the binding energy of O-V-Ti-Y cluster, reaching a high value of 4.1 eV [67]. Consequently, the O-V-Ti-Y clusters, characterized by their highest binding energy, exhibit superior thermal stability compared to other potential clusters. Therefore, these clusters can serve as ideal nucleation sites for the precipitation of Y-Ti-O enriched nanoparticles during sintering or heat treatment at elevated temperatures of milled powders. This difference can be ascribed to the following reasons: Compared to T4-0. 7Y alloy, (1) ‘T4’-‘0. 7Y’ alloy exhibits a finer grain structure in the matrix phase, leading to reduced mobility and storage capacity of dislocations; (2) ‘T4’-‘0. 7Y’ alloy demonstrates a higher density of pre-existing dislocations (as described in Section 4.2.1), which have prematurely exhausted its ability for forest hardening during subsequent plastic deformation; (3) a notable reduction in the fraction of coarser MGs within the bimodal microstructure of ‘T4’-‘0. 7Y’ alloy (as illustrated in Table 3) may potentially result in a decline in the occurrence of deformation-induced nano-twins, thereby compromising the effectiveness of twinning-induced plasticity (TWIP) in this alloy. The ODS alloys are typically prepared using mechanical alloying (MA) followed by hot consolidation, which is also the method employed for the investigated ODS HEAs in this study. The process of MA usually leads to a significant level of plastic deformation, thereby inducing the generation of numerous lattice defects, such as vacancies, in the milled alloy powders [27]. The first principle density-functional calculation study conducted by Fu et al. previously reported a significantly high binding energy of ∼ 1.5 eV between O atoms in octahedral position sites and vacancies, leading to a notable reduction in the formation energy (i.e., increased solubility) of O in the Fe matrix [65]. This finding indicates that a high concentration of vacancies induced by MA exhibits a strong affinity with O atoms, resulting in the formation of O-Vacancy (abbreviated as O-V) pairs [65,66]. The release of O charge confinement through electron delocalization into the newly created O-V pair has been identified as a significant contributing source in establishing the exceptionally strong binding between O and vacancies [65]. Furthermore, the calculations also demonstrated that the binding energy can be further enhanced by attracting neighboring atoms with a high affinity for O (e.g. , Ti and Y) to O-V pairs, resulting in the formation of large clusters composed of O-V-Ti (or Y). The binding energies in the energy-optimized configuration of these clusters were calculated to be 2.45 for O-V-Ti and 3.35 eV for O-V-Y [67]. Moreover, the coexistence of both Ti and Y results in a further increase in the binding energy of O-V-Ti-Y cluster, reaching a high value of 4.1 eV [67]. Consequently, the O-V-Ti-Y clusters, characterized by their highest binding energy, exhibit superior thermal stability compared to other potential clusters. Therefore, these clusters can serve as ideal nucleation sites for the precipitation of Y-Ti-O enriched nanoparticles during sintering or heat treatment at elevated temperatures of milled powders. The ODS alloys are typically prepared using mechanical alloying (MA) followed by hot consolidation, which is also the method employed for the investigated ODS HEAs in this study. The process of MA usually leads to a significant level of plastic deformation, thereby inducing the generation of numerous lattice defects, such as vacancies, in the milled alloy powders [27]. The first principle density-functional calculation study conducted by Fu et al. previously reported a significantly high binding energy of ∼ 1.5 eV between O atoms in octahedral position sites and vacancies, leading to a notable reduction in the formation energy (i.e., increased solubility) of O in the Fe matrix [65]. This finding indicates that a high concentration of vacancies induced by MA exhibits a strong affinity with O atoms, resulting in the formation of O-Vacancy (abbreviated as O-V) pairs [65,66]. The release of O charge confinement through electron delocalization into the newly created O-V pair has been identified as a significant contributing source in establishing the exceptionally strong binding between O and vacancies [65]. Furthermore, the calculations also demonstrated that the binding energy can be further enhanced by attracting neighboring atoms with a high affinity for O (e.g. , Ti and Y) to O-V pairs, resulting in the formation of large clusters composed of O-V-Ti (or Y). The binding energies in the energy-optimized configuration of these clusters were calculated to be 2.45 for O-V-Ti and 3.35 eV for O-V-Y [67]. Moreover, the coexistence of both Ti and Y results in a further increase in the binding energy of O-V-Ti-Y cluster, reaching a high value of 4.1 eV [67]. Consequently, the O-V-Ti-Y clusters, characterized by their highest binding energy, exhibit superior thermal stability compared to other potential clusters. Therefore, these clusters can serve as ideal nucleation sites for the precipitation of Y-Ti-O enriched nanoparticles during sintering or heat treatment at elevated temperatures of milled powders. The ODS alloys are typically prepared using mechanical alloying (MA) followed by hot consolidation, which is also the method employed for the investigated ODS HEAs in this study. The process of MA usually leads to a significant level of plastic deformation, thereby inducing the generation of numerous lattice defects, such as vacancies, in the milled alloy powders [27]. The first principle density-functional calculation study conducted by Fu et al. previously reported a significantly high binding energy of ∼ 1.5 eV between O atoms in octahedral position sites and vacancies, leading to a notable reduction in the formation energy (i.e., increased solubility) of O in the Fe matrix [65]. This finding indicates that a high concentration of vacancies induced by MA exhibits a strong affinity with O atoms, resulting in the formation of O-Vacancy (abbreviated as O-V) pairs [65,66]. The release of O charge confinement through electron delocalization into the newly created O-V pair has been identified as a significant contributing source in establishing the exceptionally strong binding between O and vacancies [65]. Furthermore, the calculations also demonstrated that the binding energy can be further enhanced by attracting neighboring atoms with a high affinity for O (e.g. , Ti and Y) to O-V pairs, resulting in the formation of large clusters composed of O-V-Ti (or Y). The binding energies in the energy-optimized configuration of these clusters were calculated to be 2.45 for O-V-Ti and 3.35 eV for O-V-Y [67]. Moreover, the coexistence of both Ti and Y results in a further increase in the binding energy of O-V-Ti-Y cluster, reaching a high value of 4.1 eV [67]. Consequently, the O-V-Ti-Y clusters, characterized by their highest binding energy, exhibit superior thermal stability compared to other potential clusters. Therefore, these clusters can serve as ideal nucleation sites for the precipitation of Y-Ti-O enriched nanoparticles during sintering or heat treatment at elevated temperatures of milled powders. The ODS alloys are typically prepared using mechanical alloying (MA) followed by hot consolidation, which is also the method employed for the investigated ODS HEAs in this study. The process of MA usually leads to a significant level of plastic deformation, thereby inducing the generation of numerous lattice defects, such as vacancies, in the milled alloy powders [27]. The first principle density-functional calculation study conducted by Fu et al. previously reported a significantly high binding energy of ∼ 1.5 eV between O atoms in octahedral position sites and vacancies, leading to a notable reduction in the formation energy (i.e., increased solubility) of O in the Fe matrix [65]. This finding indicates that a high concentration of vacancies induced by MA exhibits a strong affinity with O atoms, resulting in the formation of O-Vacancy (abbreviated as O-V) pairs [65,66]. The release of O charge confinement through electron delocalization into the newly created O-V pair has been identified as a significant contributing source in establishing the exceptionally strong binding between O and vacancies [65]. Furthermore, the calculations also demonstrated that the binding energy can be further enhanced by attracting neighboring atoms with a high affinity for O (e.g. , Ti and Y) to O-V pairs, resulting in the formation of large clusters composed of O-V-Ti (or Y). The binding energies in the energy-optimized configuration of these clusters were calculated to be 2.45 for O-V-Ti and 3.35 eV for O-V-Y [67]. Moreover, the coexistence of both Ti and Y results in a further increase in the binding energy of O-V-Ti-Y cluster, reaching a high value of 4.1 eV [67]. Consequently, the O-V-Ti-Y clusters, characterized by their highest binding energy, exhibit superior thermal stability compared to other potential clusters. Therefore, these clusters can serve as ideal nucleation sites for the precipitation of Y-Ti-O enriched nanoparticles during sintering or heat treatment at elevated temperatures of milled powders. The ODS alloys are typically prepared using mechanical alloying (MA) followed by hot consolidation, which is also the method employed for the investigated ODS HEAs in this study. The process of MA usually leads to a significant level of plastic deformation, thereby inducing the generation of numerous lattice defects, such as vacancies, in the milled alloy powders [27]. The first principle density-functional calculation study conducted by Fu et al. previously reported a significantly high binding energy of ∼ 1.5 eV between O atoms in octahedral position sites and vacancies, leading to a notable reduction in the formation energy (i.e., increased solubility) of O in the Fe matrix [65]. This finding indicates that a high concentration of vacancies induced by MA exhibits a strong affinity with O atoms, resulting in the formation of O-Vacancy (abbreviated as O-V) pairs [65,66]. The release of O charge confinement through electron delocalization into the newly created O-V pair has been identified as a significant contributing source in establishing the exceptionally strong binding between O and vacancies [65]. Furthermore, the calculations also demonstrated that the binding energy can be further enhanced by attracting neighboring atoms with a high affinity for O (e.g. , Ti and Y) to O-V pairs, resulting in the formation of large clusters composed of O-V-Ti (or Y). The binding energies in the energy-optimized configuration of these clusters were calculated to be 2.45 for O-V-Ti and 3.35 eV for O-V-Y [67]. Moreover, the coexistence of both Ti and Y results in a further increase in the binding energy of O-V-Ti-Y cluster, reaching a high value of 4.1 eV [67]. Consequently, the O-V-Ti-Y clusters, characterized by their highest binding energy, exhibit superior thermal stability compared to other potential clusters. Therefore, these clusters can serve as ideal nucleation sites for the precipitation of Y-Ti-O enriched nanoparticles during sintering or heat treatment at elevated temperatures of milled powders. The ODS alloys are typically prepared using mechanical alloying (MA) followed by hot consolidation, which is also the method employed for the investigated ODS HEAs in this study. The process of MA usually leads to a significant level of plastic deformation, thereby inducing the generation of numerous lattice defects, such as vacancies, in the milled alloy powders [27]. The first principle density-functional calculation study conducted by Fu et al. previously reported a significantly high binding energy of ∼ 1.5 eV between O atoms in octahedral position sites and vacancies, leading to a notable reduction in the formation energy (i.e., increased solubility) of O in the Fe matrix [65]. This finding indicates that a high concentration of vacancies induced by MA exhibits a strong affinity with O atoms, resulting in the formation of O-Vacancy (abbreviated as O-V) pairs [65,66]. The release of O charge confinement through electron delocalization into the newly created O-V pair has been identified as a significant contributing source in establishing the exceptionally strong binding between O and vacancies [65]. Furthermore, the calculations also demonstrated that the binding energy can be further enhanced by attracting neighboring atoms with a high affinity for O (e.g. , Ti and Y) to O-V pairs, resulting in the formation of large clusters composed of O-V-Ti (or Y). The binding energies in the energy-optimized configuration of these clusters were calculated to be 2.45 for O-V-Ti and 3.35 eV for O-V-Y [67]. Moreover, the coexistence of both Ti and Y results in a further increase in the binding energy of O-V-Ti-Y cluster, reaching a high value of 4.1 eV [67]. Consequently, the O-V-Ti-Y clusters, characterized by their highest binding energy, exhibit superior thermal stability compared to other potential clusters. Therefore, these clusters can serve as ideal nucleation sites for the precipitation of Y-Ti-O enriched nanoparticles during sintering or heat treatment at elevated temperatures of milled powders. The ODS alloys are typically prepared using mechanical alloying (MA) followed by hot consolidation, which is also the method employed for the investigated ODS HEAs in this study. The process of MA usually leads to a significant level of plastic deformation, thereby inducing the generation of numerous lattice defects, such as vacancies, in the milled alloy powders [27]. The first principle density-functional calculation study conducted by Fu et al. previously reported a significantly high binding energy of ∼ 1.5 eV between O atoms in octahedral position sites and vacancies, leading to a notable reduction in the formation energy (i.e., increased solubility) of O in the Fe matrix [65]. This finding indicates that a high concentration of vacancies induced by MA exhibits a strong affinity with O atoms, resulting in the formation of O-Vacancy (abbreviated as O-V) pairs [65,66]. The release of O charge confinement through electron delocalization into the newly created O-V pair has been identified as a significant contributing source in establishing the exceptionally strong binding between O and vacancies [65]. Furthermore, the calculations also demonstrated that the binding energy can be further enhanced by attracting neighboring atoms with a high affinity for O (e.g. , Ti and Y) to O-V pairs, resulting in the formation of large clusters composed of O-V-Ti (or Y). The binding energies in the energy-optimized configuration of these clusters were calculated to be 2.45 for O-V-Ti and 3.35 eV for O-V-Y [67]. Moreover, the coexistence of both Ti and Y results in a further increase in the binding energy of O-V-Ti-Y cluster, reaching a high value of 4.1 eV [67]. Consequently, the O-V-Ti-Y clusters, characterized by their highest binding energy, exhibit superior thermal stability compared to other potential clusters. Therefore, these clusters can serve as ideal nucleation sites for the precipitation of Y-Ti-O enriched nanoparticles during sintering or heat treatment at elevated temperatures of milled powders. The ODS alloys are typically prepared using mechanical alloying (MA) followed by hot consolidation, which is also the method employed for the investigated ODS HEAs in this study. The process of MA usually leads to a significant level of plastic deformation, thereby inducing the generation of numerous lattice defects, such as vacancies, in the milled alloy powders [27]. The first principle density-functional calculation study conducted by Fu et al. previously reported a significantly high binding energy of ∼ 1.5 eV between O atoms in octahedral position sites and vacancies, leading to a notable reduction in the formation energy (i.e., increased solubility) of O in the Fe matrix [65]. This finding indicates that a high concentration of vacancies induced by MA exhibits a strong affinity with O atoms, resulting in the formation of O-Vacancy (abbreviated as O-V) pairs [65,66]. The release of O charge confinement through electron delocalization into the newly created O-V pair has been identified as a significant contributing source in establishing the exceptionally strong binding between O and vacancies [65]. Furthermore, the calculations also demonstrated that the binding energy can be further enhanced by attracting neighboring atoms with a high affinity for O (e.g. , Ti and Y) to O-V pairs, resulting in the formation of large clusters composed of O-V-Ti (or Y). The binding energies in the energy-optimized configuration of these clusters were calculated to be 2.45 for O-V-Ti and 3.35 eV for O-V-Y [67]. Moreover, the coexistence of both Ti and Y results in a further increase in the binding energy of O-V-Ti-Y cluster, reaching a high value of 4.1 eV [67]. Consequently, the O-V-Ti-Y clusters, characterized by their highest binding energy, exhibit superior thermal stability compared to other potential clusters. Therefore, these clusters can serve as ideal nucleation sites for the precipitation of Y-Ti-O enriched nanoparticles during sintering or heat treatment at elevated temperatures of milled powders. The ODS alloys are typically prepared using mechanical alloying (MA) followed by hot consolidation, which is also the method employed for the investigated ODS HEAs in this study. The process of MA usually leads to a significant level of plastic deformation, thereby inducing the generation of numerous lattice defects, such as vacancies, in the milled alloy powders [27]. The first principle density-functional calculation study conducted by Fu et al. previously reported a significantly high binding energy of ∼ 1.5 eV between O atoms in octahedral position sites and vacancies, leading to a notable reduction in the formation energy (i.e., increased solubility) of O in the Fe matrix [65]. This finding indicates that a high concentration of vacancies induced by MA exhibits a strong affinity with O atoms, resulting in the formation of O-Vacancy (abbreviated as O-V) pairs [65,66]. The release of O charge confinement through electron delocalization into the newly created O-V pair has been identified as a significant contributing source in establishing the exceptionally strong binding between O and vacancies [65]. Furthermore, the calculations also demonstrated that the binding energy can be further enhanced by attracting neighboring atoms with a high affinity for O (e.g. , Ti and Y) to O-V pairs, resulting in the formation of large clusters composed of O-V-Ti (or Y). The binding energies in the energy-optimized configuration of these clusters were calculated to be 2.45 for O-V-Ti and 3.35 eV for O-V-Y [67]. Moreover, the coexistence of both Ti and Y results in a further increase in the binding energy of O-V-Ti-Y cluster, reaching a high value of 4.1 eV [67]. Consequently, the O-V-Ti-Y clusters, characterized by their highest binding energy, exhibit superior thermal stability compared to other potential clusters. Therefore, these clusters can serve as ideal nucleation sites for the precipitation of Y-Ti-O enriched nanoparticles during sintering or heat treatment at elevated temperatures of milled powders. The ODS alloys are typically prepared using mechanical alloying (MA) followed by hot consolidation, which is also the method employed for the investigated ODS HEAs in this study. The process of MA usually leads to a significant level of plastic deformation, thereby inducing the generation of numerous lattice defects, such as vacancies, in the milled alloy powders [27]. The first principle density-functional calculation study conducted by Fu et al. previously reported a significantly high binding energy of ∼ 1.5 eV between O atoms in octahedral position sites and vacancies, leading to a notable reduction in the formation energy (i.e., increased solubility) of O in the Fe matrix [65]. This finding indicates that a high concentration of vacancies induced by MA exhibits a strong affinity with O atoms, resulting in the formation of O-Vacancy (abbreviated as O-V) pairs [65,66]. The release of O charge confinement through electron delocalization into the newly created O-V pair has been identified as a significant contributing source in establishing the exceptionally strong binding between O and vacancies [65]. Furthermore, the calculations also demonstrated that the binding energy can be further enhanced by attracting neighboring atoms with a high affinity for O (e.g. , Ti and Y) to O-V pairs, resulting in the formation of large clusters composed of O-V-Ti (or Y). The binding energies in the energy-optimized configuration of these clusters were calculated to be 2.45 for O-V-Ti and 3.35 eV for O-V-Y [67]. Moreover, the coexistence of both Ti and Y results in a further increase in the binding energy of O-V-Ti-Y cluster, reaching a high value of 4.1 eV [67]. Consequently, the O-V-Ti-Y clusters, characterized by their highest binding energy, exhibit superior thermal stability compared to other potential clusters. Therefore, these clusters can serve as ideal nucleation sites for the precipitation of Y-Ti-O enriched nanoparticles during sintering or heat treatment at elevated temperatures of milled powders. The ODS alloys are typically prepared using mechanical alloying (MA) followed by hot consolidation, which is also the method employed for the investigated ODS HEAs in this study. The process of MA usually leads to a significant level of plastic deformation, thereby inducing the generation of numerous lattice defects, such as vacancies, in the milled alloy powders [27]. The first principle density-functional calculation study conducted by Fu et al. previously reported a significantly high binding energy of ∼ 1.5 eV between O atoms in octahedral position sites and vacancies, leading to a notable reduction in the formation energy (i.e., increased solubility) of O in the Fe matrix [65]. This finding indicates that a high concentration of vacancies induced by MA exhibits a strong affinity with O atoms, resulting in the formation of O-Vacancy (abbreviated as O-V) pairs [65,66]. The release of O charge confinement through electron delocalization into the newly created O-V pair has been identified as a significant contributing source in establishing the exceptionally strong binding between O and vacancies [65]. Furthermore, the calculations also demonstrated that the binding energy can be further enhanced by attracting neighboring atoms with a high affinity for O (e.g. , Ti and Y) to O-V pairs, resulting in the formation of large clusters composed of O-V-Ti (or Y). The binding energies in the energy-optimized configuration of these clusters were calculated to be 2.45 for O-V-Ti and 3.35 eV for O-V-Y [67]. Moreover, the coexistence of both Ti and Y results in a further increase in the binding energy of O-V-Ti-Y cluster, reaching a high value of 4.1 eV [67]. Consequently, the O-V-Ti-Y clusters, characterized by their highest binding energy, exhibit superior thermal stability compared to other potential clusters. Therefore, these clusters can serve as ideal nucleation sites for the precipitation of Y-Ti-O enriched nanoparticles during sintering or heat treatment at elevated temperatures of milled powders. The ODS alloys are typically prepared using mechanical alloying (MA) followed by hot consolidation, which is also the method employed for the investigated ODS HEAs in this study. The process of MA usually leads to a significant level of plastic deformation, thereby inducing the generation of numerous lattice defects, such as vacancies, in the milled alloy powders [27]. The first principle density-functional calculation study conducted by Fu et al. previously reported a significantly high binding energy of ∼ 1.5 eV between O atoms in octahedral position sites and vacancies, leading to a notable reduction in the formation energy (i.e., increased solubility) of O in the Fe matrix [65]. This finding indicates that a high concentration of vacancies induced by MA exhibits a strong affinity with O atoms, resulting in the formation of O-Vacancy (abbreviated as O-V) pairs [65,66]. The release of O charge confinement through electron delocalization into the newly created O-V pair has been identified as a significant contributing source in establishing the exceptionally strong binding between O and vacancies [65]. Furthermore, the calculations also demonstrated that the binding energy can be further enhanced by attracting neighboring atoms with a high affinity for O (e.g. , Ti and Y) to O-V pairs, resulting in the formation of large clusters composed of O-V-Ti (or Y). The binding energies in the energy-optimized configuration of these clusters were calculated to be 2.45 for O-V-Ti and 3.35 eV for O-V-Y [67]. Moreover, the coexistence of both Ti and Y results in a further increase in the binding energy of O-V-Ti-Y cluster, reaching a high value of 4.1 eV [67]. Consequently, the O-V-Ti-Y clusters, characterized by their highest binding energy, exhibit superior thermal stability compared to other potential clusters. Therefore, these clusters can serve as ideal nucleation sites for the precipitation of Y-Ti-O enriched nanoparticles during sintering or heat treatment at elevated temperatures of milled powders. The ODS alloys are typically prepared using mechanical alloying (MA) followed by hot consolidation, which is also the method employed for the investigated ODS HEAs in this study. The process of MA usually leads to a significant level of plastic deformation, thereby inducing the generation of numerous lattice defects, such as vacancies, in the milled alloy powders [27]. The first principle density-functional calculation study conducted by Fu et al. previously reported a significantly high binding energy of ∼ 1.5 eV between O atoms in octahedral position sites and vacancies, leading to a notable reduction in the formation energy (i.e., increased solubility) of O in the Fe matrix [65]. This finding indicates that a high concentration of vacancies induced by MA exhibits a strong affinity with O atoms, resulting in the formation of O-Vacancy (abbreviated as O-V) pairs [65,66]. The release of O charge confinement through electron delocalization into the newly created O-V pair has been identified as a significant contributing source in establishing the exceptionally strong binding between O and vacancies [65]. Furthermore, the calculations also demonstrated that the binding energy can be further enhanced by attracting neighboring atoms with a high affinity for O (e.g. , Ti and Y) to O-V pairs, resulting in the formation of large clusters composed of O-V-Ti (or Y). The binding energies in the energy-optimized configuration of these clusters were calculated to be 2.45 for O-V-Ti and 3.35 eV for O-V-Y [67]. Moreover, the coexistence of both Ti and Y results in a further increase in the binding energy of O-V-Ti-Y cluster, reaching a high value of 4.1 eV [67]. Consequently, the O-V-Ti-Y clusters, characterized by their highest binding energy, exhibit superior thermal stability compared to other potential clusters. Therefore, these clusters can serve as ideal nucleation sites for the precipitation of Y-Ti-O enriched nanoparticles during sintering or heat treatment at elevated temperatures of milled powders. The ODS alloys are typically prepared using mechanical alloying (MA) followed by hot consolidation, which is also the method employed for the investigated ODS HEAs in this study. The process of MA usually leads to a significant level of plastic deformation, thereby inducing the generation of numerous lattice defects, such as vacancies, in the milled alloy powders [27]. The first principle density-functional calculation study conducted by Fu et al. previously reported a significantly high binding energy of ∼ 1.5 eV between O atoms in octahedral position sites and vacancies, leading to a notable reduction in the formation energy (i.e., increased solubility) of O in the Fe matrix [65]. This finding indicates that a high concentration of vacancies induced by MA exhibits a strong affinity with O atoms, resulting in the formation of O-Vacancy (abbreviated as O-V) pairs [65,66]. The release of O charge confinement through electron delocalization into the newly created O-V pair has been identified as a significant contributing source in establishing the exceptionally strong binding between O and vacancies [65]. Furthermore, the calculations also demonstrated that the binding energy can be further enhanced by attracting neighboring atoms with a high affinity for O (e.g. , Ti and Y) to O-V pairs, resulting in the formation of large clusters composed of O-V-Ti (or Y). The binding energies in the energy-optimized configuration of these clusters were calculated to be 2.45 for O-V-Ti and 3.35 eV for O-V-Y [67]. Moreover, the coexistence of both Ti and Y results in a further increase in the binding energy of O-V-Ti-Y cluster, reaching a high value of 4.1 eV [67]. Consequently, the O-V-Ti-Y clusters, characterized by their highest binding energy, exhibit superior thermal stability compared to other potential clusters. Therefore, these clusters can serve as ideal nucleation sites for the precipitation of Y-Ti-O enriched nanoparticles during sintering or heat treatment at elevated temperatures of milled powders.
