The ODS alloys are typically prepared using mechanical alloying (MA) followed by hot consolidation, which is also the method employed for the investigated ODS HEAs in this study. The process of MA usually leads to a significant level of plastic deformation, thereby inducing the generation of numerous lattice defects, such as vacancies, in the milled alloy powders [27]. The first principle density-functional calculation study conducted by Fu et al. previously reported a significantly high binding energy of ∼ 1.5 eV between O atoms in octahedral position sites and vacancies, leading to a notable reduction in the formation energy (i.e., increased solubility) of O in the Fe matrix [65]. This finding indicates that a high concentration of vacancies induced by MA exhibits a strong affinity with O atoms, resulting in the formation of O-Vacancy (abbreviated as O-V) pairs [65,66]. The release of O charge confinement through electron delocalization into the newly created O-V pair has been identified as a significant contributing source in establishing the exceptionally strong binding between O and vacancies [65]. Furthermore, the calculations also demonstrated that the binding energy can be further enhanced by attracting neighboring atoms with a high affinity for O (e.g. , Ti and Y) to O-V pairs, resulting in the formation of large clusters composed of O-V-Ti (or Y). The binding energies in the energy-optimized configuration of these clusters were calculated to be 2.45 for O-V-Ti and 3.35 eV for O-V-Y [67]. Moreover, the coexistence of both Ti and Y results in a further increase in the binding energy of O-V-Ti-Y cluster, reaching a high value of 4.1 eV [67]. Consequently, the O-V-Ti-Y clusters, characterized by their highest binding energy, exhibit superior thermal stability compared to other potential clusters. Therefore, these clusters can serve as ideal nucleation sites for the precipitation of Y-Ti-O enriched nanoparticles during sintering or heat treatment at elevated temperatures of milled powders. The ODS alloys are typically prepared using mechanical alloying (MA) followed by hot consolidation, which is also the method employed for the investigated ODS HEAs in this study. The process of MA usually leads to a significant level of plastic deformation, thereby inducing the generation of numerous lattice defects, such as vacancies, in the milled alloy powders [27]. The first principle density-functional calculation study conducted by Fu et al. previously reported a significantly high binding energy of ∼ 1.5 eV between O atoms in octahedral position sites and vacancies, leading to a notable reduction in the formation energy (i.e., increased solubility) of O in the Fe matrix [65]. This finding indicates that a high concentration of vacancies induced by MA exhibits a strong affinity with O atoms, resulting in the formation of O-Vacancy (abbreviated as O-V) pairs [65,66]. The release of O charge confinement through electron delocalization into the newly created O-V pair has been identified as a significant contributing source in establishing the exceptionally strong binding between O and vacancies [65]. Furthermore, the calculations also demonstrated that the binding energy can be further enhanced by attracting neighboring atoms with a high affinity for O (e.g. , Ti and Y) to O-V pairs, resulting in the formation of large clusters composed of O-V-Ti (or Y). The binding energies in the energy-optimized configuration of these clusters were calculated to be 2.45 for O-V-Ti and 3.35 eV for O-V-Y [67]. Moreover, the coexistence of both Ti and Y results in a further increase in the binding energy of O-V-Ti-Y cluster, reaching a high value of 4.1 eV [67]. Consequently, the O-V-Ti-Y clusters, characterized by their highest binding energy, exhibit superior thermal stability compared to other potential clusters. Therefore, these clusters can serve as ideal nucleation sites for the precipitation of Y-Ti-O enriched nanoparticles during sintering or heat treatment at elevated temperatures of milled powders. The ODS alloys are typically prepared using mechanical alloying (MA) followed by hot consolidation, which is also the method employed for the investigated ODS HEAs in this study. The process of MA usually leads to a significant level of plastic deformation, thereby inducing the generation of numerous lattice defects, such as vacancies, in the milled alloy powders [27]. The first principle density-functional calculation study conducted by Fu et al. previously reported a significantly high binding energy of ∼ 1.5 eV between O atoms in octahedral position sites and vacancies, leading to a notable reduction in the formation energy (i.e., increased solubility) of O in the Fe matrix [65]. This finding indicates that a high concentration of vacancies induced by MA exhibits a strong affinity with O atoms, resulting in the formation of O-Vacancy (abbreviated as O-V) pairs [65,66]. The release of O charge confinement through electron delocalization into the newly created O-V pair has been identified as a significant contributing source in establishing the exceptionally strong binding between O and vacancies [65]. Furthermore, the calculations also demonstrated that the binding energy can be further enhanced by attracting neighboring atoms with a high affinity for O (e.g. , Ti and Y) to O-V pairs, resulting in the formation of large clusters composed of O-V-Ti (or Y). The binding energies in the energy-optimized configuration of these clusters were calculated to be 2.45 for O-V-Ti and 3.35 eV for O-V-Y [67]. Moreover, the coexistence of both Ti and Y results in a further increase in the binding energy of O-V-Ti-Y cluster, reaching a high value of 4.1 eV [67]. Consequently, the O-V-Ti-Y clusters, characterized by their highest binding energy, exhibit superior thermal stability compared to other potential clusters. Therefore, these clusters can serve as ideal nucleation sites for the precipitation of Y-Ti-O enriched nanoparticles during sintering or heat treatment at elevated temperatures of milled powders. The ODS alloys are typically prepared using mechanical alloying (MA) followed by hot consolidation, which is also the method employed for the investigated ODS HEAs in this study. The process of MA usually leads to a significant level of plastic deformation, thereby inducing the generation of numerous lattice defects, such as vacancies, in the milled alloy powders [27]. The first principle density-functional calculation study conducted by Fu et al. previously reported a significantly high binding energy of ∼ 1.5 eV between O atoms in octahedral position sites and vacancies, leading to a notable reduction in the formation energy (i.e., increased solubility) of O in the Fe matrix [65]. This finding indicates that a high concentration of vacancies induced by MA exhibits a strong affinity with O atoms, resulting in the formation of O-Vacancy (abbreviated as O-V) pairs [65,66]. The release of O charge confinement through electron delocalization into the newly created O-V pair has been identified as a significant contributing source in establishing the exceptionally strong binding between O and vacancies [65]. Furthermore, the calculations also demonstrated that the binding energy can be further enhanced by attracting neighboring atoms with a high affinity for O (e.g. , Ti and Y) to O-V pairs, resulting in the formation of large clusters composed of O-V-Ti (or Y). The binding energies in the energy-optimized configuration of these clusters were calculated to be 2.45 for O-V-Ti and 3.35 eV for O-V-Y [67]. Moreover, the coexistence of both Ti and Y results in a further increase in the binding energy of O-V-Ti-Y cluster, reaching a high value of 4.1 eV [67]. Consequently, the O-V-Ti-Y clusters, characterized by their highest binding energy, exhibit superior thermal stability compared to other potential clusters. Therefore, these clusters can serve as ideal nucleation sites for the precipitation of Y-Ti-O enriched nanoparticles during sintering or heat treatment at elevated temperatures of milled powders. The ODS alloys are typically prepared using mechanical alloying (MA) followed by hot consolidation, which is also the method employed for the investigated ODS HEAs in this study. The process of MA usually leads to a significant level of plastic deformation, thereby inducing the generation of numerous lattice defects, such as vacancies, in the milled alloy powders [27]. The first principle density-functional calculation study conducted by Fu et al. previously reported a significantly high binding energy of ∼ 1.5 eV between O atoms in octahedral position sites and vacancies, leading to a notable reduction in the formation energy (i.e., increased solubility) of O in the Fe matrix [65]. This finding indicates that a high concentration of vacancies induced by MA exhibits a strong affinity with O atoms, resulting in the formation of O-Vacancy (abbreviated as O-V) pairs [65,66]. The release of O charge confinement through electron delocalization into the newly created O-V pair has been identified as a significant contributing source in establishing the exceptionally strong binding between O and vacancies [65]. Furthermore, the calculations also demonstrated that the binding energy can be further enhanced by attracting neighboring atoms with a high affinity for O (e.g. , Ti and Y) to O-V pairs, resulting in the formation of large clusters composed of O-V-Ti (or Y). The binding energies in the energy-optimized configuration of these clusters were calculated to be 2.45 for O-V-Ti and 3.35 eV for O-V-Y [67]. Moreover, the coexistence of both Ti and Y results in a further increase in the binding energy of O-V-Ti-Y cluster, reaching a high value of 4.1 eV [67]. Consequently, the O-V-Ti-Y clusters, characterized by their highest binding energy, exhibit superior thermal stability compared to other potential clusters. Therefore, these clusters can serve as ideal nucleation sites for the precipitation of Y-Ti-O enriched nanoparticles during sintering or heat treatment at elevated temperatures of milled powders. The ODS alloys are typically prepared using mechanical alloying (MA) followed by hot consolidation, which is also the method employed for the investigated ODS HEAs in this study. The process of MA usually leads to a significant level of plastic deformation, thereby inducing the generation of numerous lattice defects, such as vacancies, in the milled alloy powders [27]. The first principle density-functional calculation study conducted by Fu et al. previously reported a significantly high binding energy of ∼ 1.5 eV between O atoms in octahedral position sites and vacancies, leading to a notable reduction in the formation energy (i.e., increased solubility) of O in the Fe matrix [65]. This finding indicates that a high concentration of vacancies induced by MA exhibits a strong affinity with O atoms, resulting in the formation of O-Vacancy (abbreviated as O-V) pairs [65,66]. The release of O charge confinement through electron delocalization into the newly created O-V pair has been identified as a significant contributing source in establishing the exceptionally strong binding between O and vacancies [65]. Furthermore, the calculations also demonstrated that the binding energy can be further enhanced by attracting neighboring atoms with a high affinity for O (e.g. , Ti and Y) to O-V pairs, resulting in the formation of large clusters composed of O-V-Ti (or Y). The binding energies in the energy-optimized configuration of these clusters were calculated to be 2.45 for O-V-Ti and 3.35 eV for O-V-Y [67]. Moreover, the coexistence of both Ti and Y results in a further increase in the binding energy of O-V-Ti-Y cluster, reaching a high value of 4.1 eV [67]. Consequently, the O-V-Ti-Y clusters, characterized by their highest binding energy, exhibit superior thermal stability compared to other potential clusters. Therefore, these clusters can serve as ideal nucleation sites for the precipitation of Y-Ti-O enriched nanoparticles during sintering or heat treatment at elevated temperatures of milled powders. The ODS alloys are typically prepared using mechanical alloying (MA) followed by hot consolidation, which is also the method employed for the investigated ODS HEAs in this study. The process of MA usually leads to a significant level of plastic deformation, thereby inducing the generation of numerous lattice defects, such as vacancies, in the milled alloy powders [27]. The first principle density-functional calculation study conducted by Fu et al. previously reported a significantly high binding energy of ∼ 1.5 eV between O atoms in octahedral position sites and vacancies, leading to a notable reduction in the formation energy (i.e., increased solubility) of O in the Fe matrix [65]. This finding indicates that a high concentration of vacancies induced by MA exhibits a strong affinity with O atoms, resulting in the formation of O-Vacancy (abbreviated as O-V) pairs [65,66]. The release of O charge confinement through electron delocalization into the newly created O-V pair has been identified as a significant contributing source in establishing the exceptionally strong binding between O and vacancies [65]. Furthermore, the calculations also demonstrated that the binding energy can be further enhanced by attracting neighboring atoms with a high affinity for O (e.g. , Ti and Y) to O-V pairs, resulting in the formation of large clusters composed of O-V-Ti (or Y). The binding energies in the energy-optimized configuration of these clusters were calculated to be 2.45 for O-V-Ti and 3.35 eV for O-V-Y [67]. Moreover, the coexistence of both Ti and Y results in a further increase in the binding energy of O-V-Ti-Y cluster, reaching a high value of 4.1 eV [67]. Consequently, the O-V-Ti-Y clusters, characterized by their highest binding energy, exhibit superior thermal stability compared to other potential clusters. Therefore, these clusters can serve as ideal nucleation sites for the precipitation of Y-Ti-O enriched nanoparticles during sintering or heat treatment at elevated temperatures of milled powders. The ODS alloys are typically prepared using mechanical alloying (MA) followed by hot consolidation, which is also the method employed for the investigated ODS HEAs in this study. The process of MA usually leads to a significant level of plastic deformation, thereby inducing the generation of numerous lattice defects, such as vacancies, in the milled alloy powders [27]. The first principle density-functional calculation study conducted by Fu et al. previously reported a significantly high binding energy of ∼ 1.5 eV between O atoms in octahedral position sites and vacancies, leading to a notable reduction in the formation energy (i.e., increased solubility) of O in the Fe matrix [65]. This finding indicates that a high concentration of vacancies induced by MA exhibits a strong affinity with O atoms, resulting in the formation of O-Vacancy (abbreviated as O-V) pairs [65,66]. The release of O charge confinement through electron delocalization into the newly created O-V pair has been identified as a significant contributing source in establishing the exceptionally strong binding between O and vacancies [65]. Furthermore, the calculations also demonstrated that the binding energy can be further enhanced by attracting neighboring atoms with a high affinity for O (e.g. , Ti and Y) to O-V pairs, resulting in the formation of large clusters composed of O-V-Ti (or Y). The binding energies in the energy-optimized configuration of these clusters were calculated to be 2.45 for O-V-Ti and 3.35 eV for O-V-Y [67]. Moreover, the coexistence of both Ti and Y results in a further increase in the binding energy of O-V-Ti-Y cluster, reaching a high value of 4.1 eV [67]. Consequently, the O-V-Ti-Y clusters, characterized by their highest binding energy, exhibit superior thermal stability compared to other potential clusters. Therefore, these clusters can serve as ideal nucleation sites for the precipitation of Y-Ti-O enriched nanoparticles during sintering or heat treatment at elevated temperatures of milled powders. The ODS alloys are typically prepared using mechanical alloying (MA) followed by hot consolidation, which is also the method employed for the investigated ODS HEAs in this study. The process of MA usually leads to a significant level of plastic deformation, thereby inducing the generation of numerous lattice defects, such as vacancies, in the milled alloy powders [27]. The first principle density-functional calculation study conducted by Fu et al. previously reported a significantly high binding energy of ∼ 1.5 eV between O atoms in octahedral position sites and vacancies, leading to a notable reduction in the formation energy (i.e., increased solubility) of O in the Fe matrix [65]. This finding indicates that a high concentration of vacancies induced by MA exhibits a strong affinity with O atoms, resulting in the formation of O-Vacancy (abbreviated as O-V) pairs [65,66]. The release of O charge confinement through electron delocalization into the newly created O-V pair has been identified as a significant contributing source in establishing the exceptionally strong binding between O and vacancies [65]. Furthermore, the calculations also demonstrated that the binding energy can be further enhanced by attracting neighboring atoms with a high affinity for O (e.g. , Ti and Y) to O-V pairs, resulting in the formation of large clusters composed of O-V-Ti (or Y). The binding energies in the energy-optimized configuration of these clusters were calculated to be 2.45 for O-V-Ti and 3.35 eV for O-V-Y [67]. Moreover, the coexistence of both Ti and Y results in a further increase in the binding energy of O-V-Ti-Y cluster, reaching a high value of 4.1 eV [67]. Consequently, the O-V-Ti-Y clusters, characterized by their highest binding energy, exhibit superior thermal stability compared to other potential clusters. Therefore, these clusters can serve as ideal nucleation sites for the precipitation of Y-Ti-O enriched nanoparticles during sintering or heat treatment at elevated temperatures of milled powders. The ODS alloys are typically prepared using mechanical alloying (MA) followed by hot consolidation, which is also the method employed for the investigated ODS HEAs in this study. The process of MA usually leads to a significant level of plastic deformation, thereby inducing the generation of numerous lattice defects, such as vacancies, in the milled alloy powders [27]. The first principle density-functional calculation study conducted by Fu et al. previously reported a significantly high binding energy of ∼ 1.5 eV between O atoms in octahedral position sites and vacancies, leading to a notable reduction in the formation energy (i.e., increased solubility) of O in the Fe matrix [65]. This finding indicates that a high concentration of vacancies induced by MA exhibits a strong affinity with O atoms, resulting in the formation of O-Vacancy (abbreviated as O-V) pairs [65,66]. The release of O charge confinement through electron delocalization into the newly created O-V pair has been identified as a significant contributing source in establishing the exceptionally strong binding between O and vacancies [65]. Furthermore, the calculations also demonstrated that the binding energy can be further enhanced by attracting neighboring atoms with a high affinity for O (e.g. , Ti and Y) to O-V pairs, resulting in the formation of large clusters composed of O-V-Ti (or Y). The binding energies in the energy-optimized configuration of these clusters were calculated to be 2.45 for O-V-Ti and 3.35 eV for O-V-Y [67]. Moreover, the coexistence of both Ti and Y results in a further increase in the binding energy of O-V-Ti-Y cluster, reaching a high value of 4.1 eV [67]. Consequently, the O-V-Ti-Y clusters, characterized by their highest binding energy, exhibit superior thermal stability compared to other potential clusters. Therefore, these clusters can serve as ideal nucleation sites for the precipitation of Y-Ti-O enriched nanoparticles during sintering or heat treatment at elevated temperatures of milled powders. The ODS alloys are typically prepared using mechanical alloying (MA) followed by hot consolidation, which is also the method employed for the investigated ODS HEAs in this study. The process of MA usually leads to a significant level of plastic deformation, thereby inducing the generation of numerous lattice defects, such as vacancies, in the milled alloy powders [27]. The first principle density-functional calculation study conducted by Fu et al. previously reported a significantly high binding energy of ∼ 1.5 eV between O atoms in octahedral position sites and vacancies, leading to a notable reduction in the formation energy (i.e., increased solubility) of O in the Fe matrix [65]. This finding indicates that a high concentration of vacancies induced by MA exhibits a strong affinity with O atoms, resulting in the formation of O-Vacancy (abbreviated as O-V) pairs [65,66]. The release of O charge confinement through electron delocalization into the newly created O-V pair has been identified as a significant contributing source in establishing the exceptionally strong binding between O and vacancies [65]. Furthermore, the calculations also demonstrated that the binding energy can be further enhanced by attracting neighboring atoms with a high affinity for O (e.g. , Ti and Y) to O-V pairs, resulting in the formation of large clusters composed of O-V-Ti (or Y). The binding energies in the energy-optimized configuration of these clusters were calculated to be 2.45 for O-V-Ti and 3.35 eV for O-V-Y [67]. Moreover, the coexistence of both Ti and Y results in a further increase in the binding energy of O-V-Ti-Y cluster, reaching a high value of 4.1 eV [67]. Consequently, the O-V-Ti-Y clusters, characterized by their highest binding energy, exhibit superior thermal stability compared to other potential clusters. Therefore, these clusters can serve as ideal nucleation sites for the precipitation of Y-Ti-O enriched nanoparticles during sintering or heat treatment at elevated temperatures of milled powders. The ODS alloys are typically prepared using mechanical alloying (MA) followed by hot consolidation, which is also the method employed for the investigated ODS HEAs in this study. The process of MA usually leads to a significant level of plastic deformation, thereby inducing the generation of numerous lattice defects, such as vacancies, in the milled alloy powders [27]. The first principle density-functional calculation study conducted by Fu et al. previously reported a significantly high binding energy of ∼ 1.5 eV between O atoms in octahedral position sites and vacancies, leading to a notable reduction in the formation energy (i.e., increased solubility) of O in the Fe matrix [65]. This finding indicates that a high concentration of vacancies induced by MA exhibits a strong affinity with O atoms, resulting in the formation of O-Vacancy (abbreviated as O-V) pairs [65,66]. The release of O charge confinement through electron delocalization into the newly created O-V pair has been identified as a significant contributing source in establishing the exceptionally strong binding between O and vacancies [65]. Furthermore, the calculations also demonstrated that the binding energy can be further enhanced by attracting neighboring atoms with a high affinity for O (e.g. , Ti and Y) to O-V pairs, resulting in the formation of large clusters composed of O-V-Ti (or Y). The binding energies in the energy-optimized configuration of these clusters were calculated to be 2.45 for O-V-Ti and 3.35 eV for O-V-Y [67]. Moreover, the coexistence of both Ti and Y results in a further increase in the binding energy of O-V-Ti-Y cluster, reaching a high value of 4.1 eV [67]. Consequently, the O-V-Ti-Y clusters, characterized by their highest binding energy, exhibit superior thermal stability compared to other potential clusters. Therefore, these clusters can serve as ideal nucleation sites for the precipitation of Y-Ti-O enriched nanoparticles during sintering or heat treatment at elevated temperatures of milled powders. The ODS alloys are typically prepared using mechanical alloying (MA) followed by hot consolidation, which is also the method employed for the investigated ODS HEAs in this study. The process of MA usually leads to a significant level of plastic deformation, thereby inducing the generation of numerous lattice defects, such as vacancies, in the milled alloy powders [27]. The first principle density-functional calculation study conducted by Fu et al. previously reported a significantly high binding energy of ∼ 1.5 eV between O atoms in octahedral position sites and vacancies, leading to a notable reduction in the formation energy (i.e., increased solubility) of O in the Fe matrix [65]. This finding indicates that a high concentration of vacancies induced by MA exhibits a strong affinity with O atoms, resulting in the formation of O-Vacancy (abbreviated as O-V) pairs [65,66]. The release of O charge confinement through electron delocalization into the newly created O-V pair has been identified as a significant contributing source in establishing the exceptionally strong binding between O and vacancies [65]. Furthermore, the calculations also demonstrated that the binding energy can be further enhanced by attracting neighboring atoms with a high affinity for O (e.g. , Ti and Y) to O-V pairs, resulting in the formation of large clusters composed of O-V-Ti (or Y). The binding energies in the energy-optimized configuration of these clusters were calculated to be 2.45 for O-V-Ti and 3.35 eV for O-V-Y [67]. Moreover, the coexistence of both Ti and Y results in a further increase in the binding energy of O-V-Ti-Y cluster, reaching a high value of 4.1 eV [67]. Consequently, the O-V-Ti-Y clusters, characterized by their highest binding energy, exhibit superior thermal stability compared to other potential clusters. Therefore, these clusters can serve as ideal nucleation sites for the precipitation of Y-Ti-O enriched nanoparticles during sintering or heat treatment at elevated temperatures of milled powders. The ODS alloys are typically prepared using mechanical alloying (MA) followed by hot consolidation, which is also the method employed for the investigated ODS HEAs in this study. The process of MA usually leads to a significant level of plastic deformation, thereby inducing the generation of numerous lattice defects, such as vacancies, in the milled alloy powders [27]. The first principle density-functional calculation study conducted by Fu et al. previously reported a significantly high binding energy of ∼ 1.5 eV between O atoms in octahedral position sites and vacancies, leading to a notable reduction in the formation energy (i.e., increased solubility) of O in the Fe matrix [65]. This finding indicates that a high concentration of vacancies induced by MA exhibits a strong affinity with O atoms, resulting in the formation of O-Vacancy (abbreviated as O-V) pairs [65,66]. The release of O charge confinement through electron delocalization into the newly created O-V pair has been identified as a significant contributing source in establishing the exceptionally strong binding between O and vacancies [65]. Furthermore, the calculations also demonstrated that the binding energy can be further enhanced by attracting neighboring atoms with a high affinity for O (e.g. , Ti and Y) to O-V pairs, resulting in the formation of large clusters composed of O-V-Ti (or Y). The binding energies in the energy-optimized configuration of these clusters were calculated to be 2.45 for O-V-Ti and 3.35 eV for O-V-Y [67]. Moreover, the coexistence of both Ti and Y results in a further increase in the binding energy of O-V-Ti-Y cluster, reaching a high value of 4.1 eV [67]. Consequently, the O-V-Ti-Y clusters, characterized by their highest binding energy, exhibit superior thermal stability compared to other potential clusters. Therefore, these clusters can serve as ideal nucleation sites for the precipitation of Y-Ti-O enriched nanoparticles during sintering or heat treatment at elevated temperatures of milled powders. The ODS alloys are typically prepared using mechanical alloying (MA) followed by hot consolidation, which is also the method employed for the investigated ODS HEAs in this study. The process of MA usually leads to a significant level of plastic deformation, thereby inducing the generation of numerous lattice defects, such as vacancies, in the milled alloy powders [27]. The first principle density-functional calculation study conducted by Fu et al. previously reported a significantly high binding energy of ∼ 1.5 eV between O atoms in octahedral position sites and vacancies, leading to a notable reduction in the formation energy (i.e., increased solubility) of O in the Fe matrix [65]. This finding indicates that a high concentration of vacancies induced by MA exhibits a strong affinity with O atoms, resulting in the formation of O-Vacancy (abbreviated as O-V) pairs [65,66]. The release of O charge confinement through electron delocalization into the newly created O-V pair has been identified as a significant contributing source in establishing the exceptionally strong binding between O and vacancies [65]. Furthermore, the calculations also demonstrated that the binding energy can be further enhanced by attracting neighboring atoms with a high affinity for O (e.g. , Ti and Y) to O-V pairs, resulting in the formation of large clusters composed of O-V-Ti (or Y). The binding energies in the energy-optimized configuration of these clusters were calculated to be 2.45 for O-V-Ti and 3.35 eV for O-V-Y [67]. Moreover, the coexistence of both Ti and Y results in a further increase in the binding energy of O-V-Ti-Y cluster, reaching a high value of 4.1 eV [67]. Consequently, the O-V-Ti-Y clusters, characterized by their highest binding energy, exhibit superior thermal stability compared to other potential clusters. Therefore, these clusters can serve as ideal nucleation sites for the precipitation of Y-Ti-O enriched nanoparticles during sintering or heat treatment at elevated temperatures of milled powders. The ODS alloys are typically prepared using mechanical alloying (MA) followed by hot consolidation, which is also the method employed for the investigated ODS HEAs in this study. The process of MA usually leads to a significant level of plastic deformation, thereby inducing the generation of numerous lattice defects, such as vacancies, in the milled alloy powders [27]. The first principle density-functional calculation study conducted by Fu et al. previously reported a significantly high binding energy of ∼ 1.5 eV between O atoms in octahedral position sites and vacancies, leading to a notable reduction in the formation energy (i.e., increased solubility) of O in the Fe matrix [65]. This finding indicates that a high concentration of vacancies induced by MA exhibits a strong affinity with O atoms, resulting in the formation of O-Vacancy (abbreviated as O-V) pairs [65,66]. The release of O charge confinement through electron delocalization into the newly created O-V pair has been identified as a significant contributing source in establishing the exceptionally strong binding between O and vacancies [65]. Furthermore, the calculations also demonstrated that the binding energy can be further enhanced by attracting neighboring atoms with a high affinity for O (e.g. , Ti and Y) to O-V pairs, resulting in the formation of large clusters composed of O-V-Ti (or Y). The binding energies in the energy-optimized configuration of these clusters were calculated to be 2.45 for O-V-Ti and 3.35 eV for O-V-Y [67]. Moreover, the coexistence of both Ti and Y results in a further increase in the binding energy of O-V-Ti-Y cluster, reaching a high value of 4.1 eV [67]. Consequently, the O-V-Ti-Y clusters, characterized by their highest binding energy, exhibit superior thermal stability compared to other potential clusters. Therefore, these clusters can serve as ideal nucleation sites for the precipitation of Y-Ti-O enriched nanoparticles during sintering or heat treatment at elevated temperatures of milled powders. The ODS alloys are typically prepared using mechanical alloying (MA) followed by hot consolidation, which is also the method employed for the investigated ODS HEAs in this study. The process of MA usually leads to a significant level of plastic deformation, thereby inducing the generation of numerous lattice defects, such as vacancies, in the milled alloy powders [27]. The first principle density-functional calculation study conducted by Fu et al. previously reported a significantly high binding energy of ∼ 1.5 eV between O atoms in octahedral position sites and vacancies, leading to a notable reduction in the formation energy (i.e., increased solubility) of O in the Fe matrix [65]. A rectangular ingot of a V 16(CoNi) 74Mo 10alloy with 100 × 35 × 8 mm 3dimensions was produced by vacuum induction melting (MC100V, Indutherm, Walzbachtal-Wössingen, Germany). The high-purity elements of 99.95% were stacked in a zirconia crucible as a sequence of Co, Mo, V, and Ni, and then cast in a graphite mold. Before the graphite mold was placed in a furnace, it was preheated to 100 °C for 6 h to remove water vapor. Prior to melting, the melting furnace chamber was evacuated to a pressure of 6 × 10 −2Pa and refilled with high-purity Ar gas until the pressure reached 0. This cleaning process was repeated five times to prevent the mixing of the impurity gas. The radiation pyrometer read the liquid temperature, and the elements were completely melted into liquid alloys by heating to 1520 °C with a maximum power of 5.2 kW for 2 min. After maintaining the convection for 2 min, the ingot was cast in a graphite mold. The alloy evacuated by quartz was annealed at 1200 °C for 24 h as a homogenization process, followed by water quenching. The homogenized ingot was cold-rolled along the longitudinal direction with a thickness reduction of 80% to 1.5 mm. The rolled sheet was then annealed at 1200 °C for 10 min in Ar atmosphere to fully obtain recrystallized microstructures referred to as ’AS’. The annealed sheet was subsequently aged at 600 °C for 4, 8, and 48 h in Ar atmosphere, followed by water quenching.

In this investigation, a wire-cutting apparatus was utilized to section the as-cast CoCrFeNi high-entropy alloy into 4 mm thick plates. Subsequently, solid solution treatment was performed at 1000 °C for 6 h to achieve a homogeneous microstructure. The solution-treated alloy specimens were subjected to cold-rolling at room temperature with compression rates of approximately 10 %, 20 %, 30 %, 40 %, 50 %, and 60 %. Following abrasion with #600 #800 #1000 #1500 #2000 #3000 sandpaper, the specimens underwent electrochemical polishing in a solution comprising perchloric acid, butanol, and methanol. All rolled deformed specimens were annealed at 800 °C for 60 minutes. The alloy with 60 % rolling reduction was subjected to annealing for 60 min at 700, 800, 900, and 1000 °C and annealed at 800 °C for 60, 90, 120, and 150 minutes.

5MEA with the following chemical composition (%, at.) was studied as a program material: 29. The obtained ingot was subjected to forging at temperatures of 950-1200 °C to attain a bar with a diameter of 42 mm and a length of 620 mm. The as-received bar was annealed at 1050 °C for 2 h with subsequent water-cooling to ambient temperature. Then, according to earlier works [ 37-39], the as-annealed bar underwent CRS with a feed speed of 180 mm/min, a strike speed of 1000 beats per min, and a workpiece rotation speed of 25 rpm. Strain sequences during CRS were as follows: from ∅42 mm → ∅38 mm ∅32 mm → ∅26 mm → ∅18 mm → ∅15.5 mm → ∅12 mm that was corresponded to ∼20 %, ∼40 %, ∼60 %, ∼80 %, ∼85 %, and ∼90 % area reduction, respectively. After CRS to a reduction of 90 %, the bar was subjected to post-deformation annealing at 500, 600, 700, 800, 900 °C for 10 min.

(FeCoCrNi) 94Al 2Ti 4alloy was prepared by vacuum arc melting a mixture of pure metals (purity higher than 99.9%) in a high-purity argon atmosphere. It was melted five times in order that Fe, Co, Cr and Ni were composed of equal atomic ratio before pure aluminum and pure titanium blocks were added according to the composition ratio, and subsequently manufactured directly as sheet with thickness of 3 mm using vertical type twin roll strip caster. It was annealed at 1100 °C for 1.5 h to improve its microstructure uniformity. The single-pass ASHR procedures were conducted on two-roll reversible rolling mill, followed by water-quenching and three velocity ratios were adopted, corresponding to 1, 2 and 4, as shown in Table 1. HEA-1, HEA-2, HEA-3 samples were cold rolled to 0.5 mm in thickness via four passes, and the final annealing temperature was 800 °C for 30 min, and then cooling in air.

In this study, Fe 60(CoNi) 30Cr 10(two ingots) and Fe 64(CoNi) 26Cr 10(one ingot) were fabricated in a vacuum induction melting furnace using pure metals (purity > 99. All cast ingots were homogenized at 1373 K for 6 h under an argon atmosphere, followed by cold rolling with a reduction ratio of 78.6% from 7 mm to 1.5 mm to break down the as-cast microstructure. After cold rolling, one of the Fe 60(CoNi) 30Cr 10FeMEA samples was kept in the rolled condition, and the other sample was subjected to a high-pressure torsion (HPT) process (pressure: 6 GPa, number of rotations: 5, and rotation frequency: 1 rpm) to fabricate a fine-grained microstructure. All the as-rolled and as-HPT samples were subsequently annealed at 1073 K for 10 min followed by water-quenching.

The CoCrFeNiMnX (X = 5, 20, and 35 at.%) alloys, reinforced with 5 at. The CoCrFeNiMnX (X = 5, 20, and 35 at.%) alloys, reinforced with 5 at. The CoCrFeNiMnX (X = 5, 20, 35 at.%) alloy (further denoted also as Mn5, Mn20, and Mn35) has been prepared by mixing the pure elements of Co (2 μm, 99. Furthermore, 5 at. % of SiC (≤74 μm, ≥97.5%) was added to each of these mixtures to create reinforced composite-like alloys. The mechanical alloying (MA) was performed using a Retsch PM 100 milling device operated at 400 rpm in 30 min alloying segments followed by 10 min cool-off pauses to obtain a total alloying time of 8 h. For this purpose, 10 g of the powder was closed in a graphite mould and compacted using a heating rate of 200 °C min −1until the compaction temperature of 1000 °C, previously optimized in the work [ 37], was reached. After this, the powder was compacted at a pressure of 48 MPa and remained compressed at the temperature for 10 min.

The mechanical alloying (MA) was performed using a Retsch PM 100 milling device operated at 400 rpm in 30 min alloying segments followed by 10 min cool-off pauses to obtain a total alloying time of 8 h. For this purpose, 10 g of the powder was closed in a graphite mould and compacted using a heating rate of 200 °C min −1until the compaction temperature of 1000 °C, previously optimized in the work [ 37], was reached. After this, the powder was compacted at a pressure of 48 MPa and remained compressed at the temperature for 10 min.
